## In the Dīgha Nikāya
## Sīlakkhandhavagga Abhinavaṭīkā
## (Second Part)
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## 2. Explanation of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta
## Explanation of the Talk on the King's Ministers

Now, to show that the sequence of the explanation of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta has been reached, the commentator said "Evaṃ... pe... suttaṃ" and so forth. In that passage "anupubbapadavaṇṇanā" means explaining the words in order, or explaining word by word in sequence. In fact, even the explanation that omits words already explained before or words with obvious meanings is also called "anupubbapadavaṇṇanā". For this reason, in this context, some also read it as "apubbapadavaṇṇanā", which means the explanation of words not previously explained.

Because it is endowed with special qualities such as being a region (janapada) difficult to travel to, and because it was primarily taken by kings, it is named "Rājagaha" for that reason, and not merely as a name; to show this, the commentator said "Tañhi" and so forth. Is it not that this person mentioned in the Mahāgovinda Sutta of the Mahāvagga is only a chaplain (purohita)? Since he is not a king, why is he taken as being expressed by the word "Rāja" (king)? Although it was taken by the chaplain Mahāgovinda, that city was indeed taken by the Magadhan king named Reṇu; because of this possibility of meaning, it is called "Rājagaha". Since that chaplain was not a king, he is not taken as one expressed by the word "Rāja". Indeed, mentioning that it was taken by the chaplain Mahāgovinda is a characteristic marking that it was taken by King Reṇu at that time. This is because that Mahāgovinda was the chaplain who performed all the affairs of King Reṇu. In the world, this kind of naming...
2:
...is common practice: "Even if done by one engaged in the king's business, it is said to be done by the king." The meaning is this: Because it was taken by King Mandhātu, and by King Reṇu after commanding the Bodhisatta chaplain Mahāgovinda, and by other kings, it is called "Rājagaha". However, some teachers say that "Mahāgovinda" was a powerful ancient king. "Because it was taken" means because it was taken as a royal capital. "Gaha" means that which is taken; because it is the house of kings or the house taken by kings, it is "Rājagaha". The neuter gender is used in consideration of the word "nagara" (city).

There are also other ways of explaining this name Rājagaha: Because the king who founded the city had all the houses built, it is "Rājagaha". Because it is surrounded by the five mountains such as Gijjhakūṭa, it is like a house surrounded by the kings of mountains, thus "Rājagaha". Because it has complete palatial dwellings, it is the house cherished by kings, thus "Rājagaha". Because it has well-arranged protection, it is like a place of capture (a prison) for enemy kings who come with harmful intent, thus "Rājagaha". Because it was well-established by kings upon seeing it, it is like the home of those kings, thus "Rājagaha". Because it shines with the beauty of parks and so forth, and because it is cherished and taken as "mine" by beings due to the happiness of living there, it is "Rājagaha"—thus it is explained in these various ways. The meaning is that it is just a name according to the method mentioned before. Because that place is a special location, it is the resort of noble beings; to show this, he said "Taṃ panetaṃ" and so forth. Therein, the phrase "In the time of the Buddhas and in the time of the Cakkavatti kings" is said with reference to what usually happens, because it can also happen at other times occasionally. The phrase "It becomes a city" is also just a marker for the absence of human habitation. Therefore, it is said "At other times it is empty" and so forth. "Tesaṃ" means of the yakkhas. "Vasanavanaṃ" means the great forest which is the place where yakkhas go, or thrive, or guard.

"Avisesena" means by way of living in general, without considering the distinction arising from the proximity of other words. The meaning is this: In such passages as "He dwells (viharati) restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint," "Having attained the first jhāna, he dwells," "He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness," and "Having attained the signless concentration of mind through non-attention to all signs, he dwells," the attainment of a specific way of living, such as dwelling in a physical posture, is shown by considering the distinction arising from the proximity of other words in sequence.
3:
This abiding (vihāra) does not indicate being endowed with a specific abiding such as abiding in a posture (iriyāpatha). Rather, this abiding, excluding the consideration of such specifics, merely indicates being endowed with one or another mode of abiding.

Although it indicates being endowed with one or another mode of abiding in the manner mentioned, the phrase beginning with "Idha pana" is stated to show that in this context, only the endowment with the specific abiding known as posture (iriyāpatha) is possible. Why is it that, even in the absence of a specific reference established by the proximity of another word, it is possible to show the endowment with a specific abiding here? It is precisely because of the absence of a specific word known as another term. For even when a specific word is absent, one who desires a specific meaning must employ that specific meaning. Furthermore, since the indication of being associated with a posture is established by the sense (attha), only such an indication is possible. Why is this sense established? Because it is common to the divine abidings (dibba-vihāra) and so on. For at no time can one exist without abiding in a posture, as the maintenance of the physical body (attabhāva) is impossible without that posture.

Movement (pavattana) is called 'iriyā' (bodily action). Because it is the means (upāya) for that movement, it is called 'patha' (path/cause). Therefore, 'iriyāpatha' (posture) refers to standing, sitting, and so on. Indeed, without states such as standing and sitting, it is impossible to carry out any bodily action; therefore, that posture is called the means for the occurrence of those bodily actions. One abides (viharati) or proceeds by this, or it is merely the act of abiding; thus it is called 'vihāra'. That posture itself is the abiding. In terms of meaning, however, this posture-abiding is merely the continuity of the fourfold produced matter (catu-santati-rūpa-pabandha) occurring in modes such as standing and sitting.

It is called 'dibba' (divine) because it occurs in the celestial realms. It means occurring in the celestial realms such as that of the Brahma-pārisajja because of its frequent occurrence there. Or, it is called 'dibba' because it conduces to the benefit of the power of the jhānas occurring in those celestial realms. Or, it is called 'dibba' because it has a great course of existence by way of the exercise of direct knowledge (abhiññā) and so on. That itself is an abiding; or, because it is an abiding that brings about a divine state, it is called 'dibba-vihāra' (divine abiding). These are the lofty (mahaggata) jhānas. In the Netti-pakarana, however, the four formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) are stated separately as 'āneñja-vihāra' (imperturbable abidings). That statement was made with reference to their being a specific form of meditation, just as the jhānas of loving-kindness and so on are called 'brahma-vihāra'. In the commentaries, however, those formless attainments are also called 'dibba-vihāra' because of their general nature of bringing about a divine state.

They are called 'brahma-vihāra' (sublime abidings) because they are the abidings of the Brahmas, or because they are noble abidings occurring by way of bringing about welfare and so on. These are the four immeasurables (appamaññā) occurring by way of the jhānas of loving-kindness and so on. They are called 'ariya-vihāra' (noble abidings) because they are noble (utttama), or because they are the abidings of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) as they are not shared with others (commoners). These are all four attainments of fruition (phala-samāpatti). In this context, however, the fourth jhana of the fine-material sphere, the immeasurables occurring by its power, and the attainment of the fruition of arahantship associated with the fourth jhana are the Buddha's divine, sublime, and noble abidings.
4:
The four immeasurables, the fourth jhana of the fine-material sphere, and the attainment of the fruition of arahantship associated with that fourth jhana are the Buddha's divine, sublime, and noble abidings. The phrase 'aññatara-vihāra-samangī-paridīpana' (showing endowment with a certain abiding) means showing the state of being endowed with one or two abidings, because those four abidings cannot occur simultaneously. This description is made either by eliding the word 'bhāva' or by emphasizing the essential meaning. For the Buddha, in a world overwhelmed by greed, hatred, and delusion, dwells by attaining various abidings for the purpose of disciplining beings (veneyya) through his own practice. Specifically, when beings practice wrongly regarding sensual pleasures, the Buddha dwells in the divine abiding (dibba-vihāra) to generate the root of wholesome non-greed in them, thinking, 'Perhaps by seeing this practice and developing a liking for it, they may become detached from sensual pleasures.' When beings practice wrongly toward one another for the sake of power, he dwells in the sublime abiding (brahma-vihāra) to generate the root of wholesome non-hatred in them, thinking, 'Perhaps by seeing this practice and developing a liking for it, they may appease hatred with non-hatred (loving-kindness).' When monks dispute over Dhamma matters, he dwells in the noble abiding (ariya-vihāra) to generate the root of wholesome non-delusion in them, thinking, 'Perhaps by seeing this practice and developing a liking for it, they may appease delusion with non-delusion (wisdom).'

By doing so, he brings about various kinds of welfare and happiness for beings through these divine, sublime, and noble abidings. And through the posture-abiding (iriyāpatha-vihāra), he maintains the physical body (attabhāva) so that it does not collapse, by cutting off the discomfort caused by one posture with another posture; thus it is said, 'showing endowment with a certain abiding'. The word 'tena' and so on shows the excellence of the aforementioned commentary, meaning 'therefore', or it is a confirmation of the aforementioned meaning. It should be connected as: 'He dwells with that posture-abiding.' In this context, the prefix 'vi' in the word 'viharati' indicates the sense of 'cutting off' (vicchedana), and 'harati' indicates the sense of 'carrying' or 'proceeding' (nayana), as shown by the phrase beginning with 'ṭhito pi' which describes the manner of cutting off and carrying. If this is so, the internal question—'What is cut off by what, and how is what carried?'—is addressed by the statement beginning with 'so hi'. This connection of words is also appropriate. Although the Buddha is able to proceed for a very long time in a single posture, the phrase 'the discomfort of one posture...' is stated to show the nature of the material body born of grasping (upādinnaka-sarīra). 'Apari-patantaṃ' means making it so that it does not fall or collapse. When the Buddha dwells anywhere, teaching the Dhamma to those to be guided, or spending time with various attainments, he brings about the happiness of beings and his own happiness; therefore, the meaning of this word 'viharati' should be understood as 'vividhaṃ harati' (he brings about various kinds of happiness). The word 'Rājagahe' is mentioned to show the village for alms-resort, and 'puna Ambavane' is mentioned again to show the dwelling suitable for Buddhas; to show this, the phrase beginning with 'idamassa' is stated.
5:
While dwelling in an unspecified place, when preaching the Dhamma to beings to be tamed, he abides passing the time with various attainments (samāpatti). He brings about various kinds of happiness for beings and for himself. Therefore, because he brings about various kinds of happiness, the meaning of the word "viharati" (abides/dwells) should be understood in this way in this context.

To show the resort village, he said "at Rājagaha" (Rājagahe), and to show the dwelling place suitable for Buddhas, he again said "in the Mango Grove" (Ambavane). The commentator, wishing to show this, said "Idamassa" etc. "Assa" refers to the Blessed One. "Tassa" refers to the resort village called Rājagaha. Because of dwelling near that village, the locative case (sattami vibhatti) "at Rājagaha" occurs. He shows that the Mango Grove is also to be spoken of as being near Rājagaha with the words "in the Mango Grove near Rājagaha" (Rājagahasamīpe Ambavane). "Samīpatthe" means in the sense of proximity to the Mango Grove. "Etaṃ" refers to the word "at Rājagaha". "Bhummavacana" is the locative word expressing the support (ādhāra). Things exist here, therefore that place of support is called "bhūmma". That "bhūmma" itself is the word. Or, the case ending occurring in the sense of support is "bhummavacana". A word joined with that locative case is "bhummavacana". It means a word joined with the seventh case (sattami vibhatti).

The following is the intended meaning: Certainly, the Blessed One abides in the Mango Grove itself. However, because of its proximity to it, to show the resort village, it is also said "at Rājagaha" by way of the locative case. For example, as in "cows graze by the Ganges" or "the Gagga clan lives by the well," the locative case is used in the sense of proximity. By these two words "at Rājagaha, in the Mango Grove," one might object: "If the Blessed One abides in Rājagaha, one should not say 'in the Mango Grove'; if in the Mango Grove, one should not say 'at Rājagaha'." It should be understood that this objection is rendered groundless, as the mention of two locations is appropriate here, unlike in phrases like "he lives in a palace in Pāṭaliputta" where there is no container-contained relationship (adhikaraṇādhikaraṇa).

Kumārabhata itself becomes "Komārabhacca" by a suffix in the same sense (sakattha) or by the method of linguistics (nirutti), just as "bhisagga" is the same as "bhesajja". With "Yathāha" etc., he establishes the meaning of that word "Komārabhacca" by way of the Cīvarakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga. To show the reason from the beginning why the Mango Grove is mentioned in connection with Jīvaka, he said "Ayaṃ pana" etc.

"Dosābhisannaṃ" means a patient with an excess of humors such as wind and bile. "Virecetvā" means having purged or cleansed from the aggravation of humors. "Siveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ" is a pair of costly cloths produced in the Sivi kingdom. "Divasassa dvattikkhattuṃ" means twice or thrice in a single day. Or, this genitive case (sāmivacana) is used in the sense of the locative, meaning twice or thrice within one day. "Tambapaṭṭavaṇṇena" means having the color of a copper plate. "Sacīvarabhattena" means with robes and food. By the words "Taṃ sandhāya", it is meant that the Blessed One does not abide merely in the Mango Grove, but rather in the monastery built in this way. However, because that monastery is located in that Mango Grove, it is not mentioned as a separate location.
6:
He shows the intended meaning. Indeed, when there is a general sense (sāmañña), the specific intended meaning must be extracted.

Thirteen with a half of the thirteenth is "aḍḍhateḷasa" (1250). It means with such hundreds of monks (12 and a half hundreds). Here, the word "aḍḍha" (half) refers only to half of a hundred. The word "aḍḍha" joined with "teḷasata" expresses half of that unit. That half is fifty. Therefore, to make known the meaning "thirteen hundred monks minus fifty" (1250), he said "aḍḍhateḷasena" etc. Likewise, "aḍḍhasata" is a hundred or half of a hundred.

"Rājati" means he shines or is beautiful through his own sovereign prosperity. "Rañjeti" means he pleases (beings) with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) such as giving (dāna), or with the four bases of sympathy such as "sassamedha" etc.; or it means he causes affection towards himself. Here, the word "ca" is used in the sense of an alternative (vikippanattha). The word "Magadha" denoting the country is said as "Magadhānaṃ" because it is followed by a plural case ending. Or, it is expressed in the plural "Magadhānaṃ" because the inhabitants are taken by the designation of the country. "Rañño" refers to the father, King Bimbisāra. He is called "sattu" (enemy) because he harms (hasati/hiṃsati). Because he was an enemy even before being born, he is called "Ajātasattu". According to the words "Nemittakehi niddiṭṭho", the state of being an enemy did not yet exist in the unborn prince. However, he shows that he is so called because the state of being an enemy was predicted by fortune-tellers. Some teachers also say that because the Queen's pregnancy craving (dohala) "to drink the King's blood" occurred while he was still unborn, he was the King's enemy even before birth.

With "Tasmiṃ" etc., he explains and completes the meaning of that (Ajātasattu). "Dohala" means desire (craving). "Bhāriya" means heavy or something that cannot be told to others. "Asakkontī" means being unable; "akathentī" means not wishing to tell. "Nibandhitvā" means having insistently questioned with words. "Suvaṇṇasatthakena" means with a small knife made of pure gold. Teachers say it is inappropriate to bring an iron knife to the King's body. Or, in the sense of an iron knife inlaid with gold, the meaning is the same. "Bāhuṃ phālāpetvā" means having the arm pierced by way of bloodletting. Because pure blood is difficult for a pregnant woman to digest, he mixed it with water and gave it to her to drink. "Haññissati" means he will be killed in the future. With the thought that the words of the fortune-tellers might be true or false, the King said, "It is not yet known whether it is a son or a daughter." With "Attano" etc., he showed another reason and prevented (the harm). The state of a king is "rajja" (kingship). That which exists near kingship is "oparajja" (viceroyalty), a position of rank.
7:
*Mahā* means great (*mahatī*). Just as in a compound (*samāsa*), the word *mahanta* is changed to *mahā* in a sentence (*vākya*) as well. *Dhurā* means the leader of a group, the burden-bearer, or the chief. *Dhuram nīharāmi* means "I will carry out the duties of the group" or "I will bring about the formation of the group." The phrase beginning with "*So na sakkā*" shows the manner of reflection once again. *Iddhipāṭihāriyena* means by the power of transformation (*vikuubbana-iddhi*), creating the appearance of a young prince with a snake belt. *Tena* means because of the state of having a short life. *Hi* is merely a particle. *Tena hi* is a particle used in the sense of urging. Therefore, it is said, "He urged the prince..." In the phrase *Buddho bhavissāmi*, the word *iti* has this meaning: according to the method mentioned in this *Khandhaka*. The words beginning with "*Pubbe kho*" are also from the *Cūḷavagga Khandhaka Pāḷi* (Cūḷavagga 339).

*Potthaniyaṃ* refers to a small dagger. That small dagger is also called *nakhara*. *Divā* means during the day. In the phrase *divā divase*, the locative case (*sattamī*) is used in the sense of the possessive (*sāmī*). This is because it is found as *divā divasassa* in other places. *Divassa divase* can also be used because the word *divasa* exists as an a-ending stem. Grammarians also accept the word *divā* as an indeclinable (*nipāta*). It means midday. That midday is called *divaso* because it is a special time of the day. "*Bhīto*" and so on are synonyms, or it means being afraid due to the body becoming stiff. *Ubbiggo* means being terrified due to the trembling of the heart. *Ussaṅkī* means being anxious due to the doubt, "Will they know or not?" *Utrasto* means being frightened due to the danger that would come to oneself if it were known. *Vuttappakāraṃ* means the manner spoken by Devadatta. *Vippakāraṃ* means offense, harm, or a perverted action. *Sabbe bhikkhū* refers to Devadatta's followers.

*Acchinditvā* means plundering by way of removal. *Rajjena* means by the conquered kingdom. The place where a king's authority extends is called *rajja*, or it means the state of being a king. The desire of the mind is called *manoratho*. It is formed by adding the letter 'ra' and eliding the letter 'ta'. Alternatively, because the mind wanders among various objects, it is like a chariot (*ratha*) of the mind, hence *manoratho*. Or, the mind itself is like a chariot; so say the etymologists (*neruttikā*). *Sukiccakārimhi* means "I am one who has performed his task well." *Avamānaṃ* means contempt or lack of respect. *Mūlaghaccaṃ* refers to the taking of life; it is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvana-napuṃsaka*). It is said that killing royalty with a weapon is not the custom of kings. Therefore, Ajātasattu said, "Is it not so, Bhante?" and so on. *Tāpanagehaṃ* means a heating house or a prison. Because that house is covered only with smoke, it is called *dhūmaghara* (smoke-house). It is for the purpose of inflicting torture. Because it is covered by something, the high limb...
8:
*Uccanga* means a high body part (lap or bosom) covered to carry something; this is the intended meaning here. Therefore, it is said, "Do not allow [him] to enter by making a lap." There is also a variant reading *ucchange katvā*; if so, it means having made something to be carried in the middle part of the body (the bosom). *Moḷiyaṃ* means the topknot (hair-knot), as in the phrase "having cut the topknot scented with excellent perfume," and so on. Therefore, it says, "having bound the topknot."

With *catumadhura*: Teachers say it is a special drink prepared with ghee, sugar, honey, and coconut oil. That statement does not agree with the *Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta Pāḷi*. In that Sutta, it is said, "Curd, honey, ghee, and molasses are mixed together." In that commentary, it is also said, "Pure curd and sweet honey... for one who drinks that medicine of four sweets..." King Bimbisāra, thinking "It is not proper to die by one's own effort," sustained himself by licking the body of the queen (receiving her care). Noble ones do not destroy themselves.

With the bliss of the Path and Fruit: it means he sustained himself by walking meditation (*caṅkama*) associated with the bliss of the Path and Fruit of Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). *Hāressāmi* means "I will remove." *Vītaccitehi* means with pure embers that are free from flames and free from blazes. *Kenasci saññatto* means well-informed or exhorted by someone. *Massukaraṇatthāya* means for the purpose of grooming the beard. *Manaṃ karotha* means "Do as the king desires."

*Pubbe* means in a previous life. *Cetiyangaṇe* means on the terrace of a stupa, which is a place of worship with incense, flowers, and so on. *Nisajjanatthāya* means for the purpose of the Sangha of monks to sit. *Paññattakaṭasārakaṃ* means an excellent mat that has been spread. Such a mat is called *kaṭasāraka*. *Tassa* means the result of the two aforementioned deeds. It should be understood that the king performed those deeds through mental corruption.

As it was said:
"Mind is the forerunner of all states, mind is their chief, they are mind-made. If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, suffering follows him even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the cart."

*Paricārako* means a companion. Although not distinct, it is common in the world to speak as if distinct, so it is said, "He was reborn as a yakkha." Even a single...
9:
In this context, although there is only one action of arising, there is a distinction in terminology (bhedavohāra). Alternatively, it should be applied respectively as 'having become' by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and 'he was reborn' by way of the course of existence (pavatti). Or else, the single action is expressed by two verbs, 'having become, he was reborn' (hutvā nibbatti), to indicate a superior arising that is merely the act of rebirth-linking. Such an expression is evident only in arising by way of the course of existence. It is like in the cases: 'The deva-son named Makkaṭaka, having become, was reborn,' 'Kaṇṭaka named... was reborn,' 'Maṇḍūka named... was reborn,' and so on. Alternatively, considering the state (bhāva) of the two words, the nominative case is used in the sense of possession (sāmi-attha) in words like 'Yakkha.' Because the preceding verb 'having become' (hutvā) is qualified by the succeeding verb 'was reborn' (nibbatti), it means 'he was reborn in the state of a deva who is an attendant.' Or, the suffix -tvā in the word hutvā is used in the sense of cause (hetu), meaning 'due to the cause of arising as the state of a deva.' It should be understood that King Bimbisāra, though possessing great merit, was reborn in that very realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) due to his long-standing familiarity and desire, having frequently been reborn there before.

'On that very day' (taṃ divasameva) means on the very day of his father's death. 'Having shaken' (khobhetvā) means that due to the strength of his love for his son and the overflowing momentum of joy (pīti) born with it, he agitated his entire body by pervading it with the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) produced by that momentum of joy. Therefore, it is said, 'It stood reaching even to the marrow of his bones' (aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi). 'Father's virtue' (pituguṇaṃ) refers to the father's quality of affection toward him. Thus, it is said, 'Even when I was born,' and so on. The repetition 'Release him! Release him!' (vissajjetha vissajjetha) was spoken due to haste and anxiety.

'Without discarding' (anuṭṭhubhitvā) means without abandoning.

In the phrase 'Having caused the Nāḷāgiri elephant to be released' (nāḷāgirihatthiṃ muñcāpetvā), the word iti has the sense of 'manner' (pakāra). By that word iti, it refers to the three manners previously mentioned, such as 'by sending assassins,' etc. In some versions, that word iti is not found. 'Five points' (pañca vatthūni) refers to the five points stated in the Vinaya, such as 'Venerable Sir, it would be good if the monks were forest-dwellers for as long as they live,' etc. In the word 'having requested' (yācitvā), it means 'acting as if requesting.' In truth, it is already stated in the Vinaya that Devadatta did not request because he wished to practice them. The connection is 'having thought, "I will make them understand," he created a schism in the Sangha' (saṅghabhedaṃ katvā). This is said to show his unyielding persistence; even before the schism was actually made, he was already persuading those people. 'Hot blood' (uṇhalohitaṃ) refers to blood that has become hot due to intense grief. 'In the great hell' (mahāniraye) means in the Avīci hell. 'The method of detailed exposition' (vitthārakathānayo) is merely the method of the story to be told in detail, such as the inspiring of faith in Ajātasattu. Why...
10:
In this context, that story is not told. Since there might be an objection that it should be told even though it appears in the Saṅgītikathā of the Cūḷavagga Khandhaka (343), the commentator said, "Because it has already appeared in the Khandhaka, the whole story is not told." The meaning is that there is no contradiction here because it has already appeared in the Khandhaka and only a small portion of the sequence of words is mentioned. The words beginning with "Thus" (evaṃ) are the conclusion by way of connection (anusandhi).

"The Kosalan King" (kosalarañño) refers to King Mahākosala, the father of King Pasenadi Kosala. The objection, "Is she not called Vedehī because she is the daughter of the King of Videha?" is refuted by the statement, "She is not the daughter of the King of Videha." If that is so, for what reason is she called Vedehī? It is said, "This is a designation for a wise person." It means a synonym for a wise person or the name of a wise person. As to what etymological definition (vacanattha) this word's meaning is derived from, it is stated starting with "tatrāyaṃ." "Vidanti" means they know. "Vedena" means knowing by way of knowledge (ñāṇa) which acts as the instrument. The meaning of the word "īhati" as "pavattati" (it proceeds/occurs) is also mentioned in the sub-commentary (ṭīကā). In this context, the word "Vedehī" belongs to the nadādi group of words, so it is stated as "vedehiyā."

That very day is called "tadahos." By the locative case, the word is established as "tadahū." "Ettha" means on that day. The word "vasa" qualified by the prefix "upa" occurs only in the sense of observing the Uposatha, not in the sense of mere living. To show that observing the Uposatha is indeed an undertaking (samādāna), the words beginning with "by virtue" (sīlena) are spoken. Here, "by virtue" (sīlena) is said in reference to the Ariya-uposatha (Noble Observance) in the Dispensation. "By fasting" (anasanena) refers to the external uposatha which consists merely of not eating. The word "or" (vā) here has an indefinite sense (aniyama-attha), and thus it also includes certain mental misconduct and immorality, etc. For this reason, the Gopālaka-uposatha is described by way of a mind accompanied by covetousness (abhijjhā), and the Nigaṇṭha-uposatha is described by way of false speech (musāvāda), etc. As it is said in the Visākhuposatha Sutta: "With that mind accompanied by covetousness, he passes the day," and "Thus, at the time when they should be established in truth, he establishes them in falsehood," and so on.

Having thus shown the etymological definition (vacanattha) consistent with the intended meaning, now, to show the intended meaning consistent with the etymological definition by way of extracting the meaning (atthuddhāra), the words beginning with "ayaṃ pana" are spoken. In this word "uposatha," extracting the various distinct meanings of words that sound the same is called "atthuddhāra." Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that "atthuddhāra" is the extraction of only the intended meaning among meanings expressed by the same word. Indeed, the showing of multiple meanings is only for the purpose of extracting the intended meaning. "Words are established based on the mere meaning," and so on...
11: In extracting the meaning, the objection (codanā) and the clarification (sodhanā) have already been mentioned below. Alternatively, since a specific word cannot express the full meaning, the word 'Uposatha' in contexts such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha is merely general in nature, is it not? If so, why is it used for specific matters like the recitation of the Pātimokkha? This is true; however, this meaning is stated not by taking such a general term, but by showing the possible meaning in each respective case. This should be understood in all instances of extracting meaning. It is called 'Uposatha' (the recitation of the Pātimokkha) because it is dwelt in (vasiyati) and not departed from (na uṭṭhīyati) by monks who are united and endowed with virtue and right view (purity of virtue). It is called 'Uposatha' (virtue) because it should be dwelt in (vasitabba) or resided in (āvasitabba) for the sake of noble living (ariyavāsa) and so on, through undertaking or determination. It is called 'Uposatha' (the observance of vows known as upavāsa) because it should be dwelt in (vasitabba) or observed repeatedly (anuvasitabba) by means of fasting and so on. In the case of the great noble elephant belonging to the ninth elephant clan, it is called 'Uposatha' by conventional usage (ruḷhī) without regard for any specific action, but merely because it is born of that clan; therefore, it should be understood as a designation (nāmapaññatti) for that elephant. It is called 'Uposatha' because it approaches and burns (destroys) the enemies (defilements); experts in grammar say that the word 'usa' also has the meaning of burning. The occurrence of the word 'Uposatha' regarding the day has already been mentioned in the Commentary. "For the pure, it is always the Phaggu day," etc. In this, 'for the pure' means for one who is completely pure due to the absence of the stains of defilements. 'Ve' is merely an expletive, or it means 'clearly.' 'Always' means at all times. 'Phaggu' means it is suitable as the Phagguṇī constellation; this word is established according to the method of linguistics (nirutti). A Brahmin named Sundarika Bhāradvāja held the view that if one performs a ritual bathing at a river landing on the day associated with the Uttaraphagguṇī constellation in the month of Phagguṇa, the sins committed throughout the year are washed away. To dispel that view, the Blessed One taught this in the Vatthu Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya: "For the pure, it is always the Uposatha." This means that for one who is pure due to the purity from the stains of defilements as mentioned, even if they do not formally undertake the factors of Uposatha or the vows, their life is a constant observance of Uposatha. In the passages such as "Not, O monks," it should be connected by extracting the meaning as "One should not go to a monastery where there are no monks." "Upavasitabbadivasa" means the day on which the observance of Uposatha is performed; or the suffix '-tabba' should be understood in the sense of the locative (adhikaraṇa). Only in this way will it agree with the etymology (vacanattha) mentioned in the Commentary. With the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇa) included within, and for the purpose of excluding other meanings, it is said, "for the purpose of excluding the remaining two." Based on the word "pannarasa," the aforementioned etymology by way of the day...
12: ...showing how it is done, the author of the Compendium says "Teneva vuttaṃ" and so on. Indeed, the day is called "pannarasa" (the fifteenth) by virtue of completing the fifteen lunar days (tithi). If only "These (water lilies) are here" were said, an objection might arise: "Are these lilies not present on other days as well?" To prevent that objection, the phrase "Tadā kira" and so on is stated. By this, it is shown that the scope of the derivative (taddhita) is applied here either frequently or pre-eminently. The words "cātumāsī" and "cātumāsinī" are synonyms used only in the feminine gender through specific suffixes. The phrase "pariyosānabhūtā" (being the conclusion) is also said with reference only to the state of completion, because the four months are completed only together with that (month of Kattika). "Idha" (here) refers to the Pali text. It is called "puṇṇā" (full) because it is filled in three ways, as shown by "māsapuṇṇatāya" and so on. Therein, it is "māsapuṇṇatā" (fullness of the month) because the month of Kattika is full at that time. Indeed, the period from the previous full moon day of Assayuja until the next full moon day of Kattika is conventionally called one month. It is "utupuṇṇatā" (fullness of the season) because the rainy season (vassāna) is full. It is "saṃvaccharapuṇṇatā" (fullness of the year) because the year marked by the month of Kattika is full. From the previous month of Kattika (Assayuja) until the next month of Kattika, it is one Kattika year; thus, it is meant by "due to the fullness of the year." According to the view of worldly scholars, the designation of "year" is marked by the months. Furthermore, there is a marking by way of the transition of Jupiter (garu-saṅkanti). It is said in the Jyotiṣa treatise: "The sun, rising with the constellation, reaches the mountain called Attha; the transition of that sun is spoken of in that month, and the year is spoken of only by the sequence of months." It is called "mā" (month/moon) because the day is measured by it. Indeed, by the movement of that moon, the days are measured as "the first day of the fortnight, the second, the third," and so on. Here, "puṇṇo" (full) means full because of the completion of all sixteen parts (kalā) of that night. Indeed, one-sixteenth part of the moon is called a "kalā," and at that time, the moon appears full by virtue of all sixteen parts. Here, the words "tadahuposathe pannarase" are spoken by way of the day, while "komudiyā" and so on are spoken by way of the night, which is a part of that day. To show a hint of the clarification for the objection, "Why does the King sit surrounded by ministers and not alone?", he says "evarūpāya" and so on, without merely stating the meaning of the Pali words. By these passages, this hint of clarification is shown: "Because it was occurring at such a pleasant night, the King sat thus surrounded by his ministers."
13:
## Explanation of the Talk about Kings and Ministers

In this phrase "dhoviyamānadisābhāgāya," the word "viya" (as if) should also be construed to obtain the meaning. "Rajatavimānanicchari tehi" means (moonbeams) that have emerged from a silver mansion or are diffused by the radiance of a silver mansion. This word "visada" is an adjective for pearl necklaces and so forth. Clouds, smoke, dust/mist, and Rāhu the Asura—these four are the obstructions (upakkilesa) according to the Pāḷi method. "Rājāmaccehi" means surrounded by ministers born of royal lineage, or alternatively, by princes and ministers worthy of a king. "Kañcanāsana" refers to the Sīhāsana (Lion Throne). It is stated in the dictionary: "The golden seat of kings is called Sīhāsana; there are also yak-tail fans and chowries." The question "Why is he sitting?" is a challenge directed at the mere act of sitting. "Etaṃ" means lamenting or awakening. "Iti" means for this reason. "Nakkhatta" refers to the Kattikā star festival (in the month of Tazaungmon). It is called "saṃghuṭṭha" (well-proclaimed) because it is said, "Now the festival should be well-proclaimed." The city, whose doors in every house are decorated with five-colored flowers, parched rice, and full water pots, is called the city "decorated at all doors with five-colored flowers, etc., and full water pots." Sīhala teachers say that a round banner is called "vaṭa" and a flat banner is called "paṭṭa." It is said that at that time, the festival was held primarily by lighting lamps. Therefore, in the Ummādantī Jātaka and others, it is stated in this very way regarding the month of Kattikā. For that reason, it is said, "All directions are decorated with rows of lit lamps." "Vīthi" refers to the main carriage road, and "racchā" refers to small alleys that are not thoroughfares. "Samabhikiṇṇa" (crowded all around) means that many people sitting in various places are enjoying the festival in their respective groups. Although it is said thus in the Mahā-Aṭṭhakathā, the meaning is that the conclusion was reached right there.

"Udāna" and "udāhāra" are the same in meaning. "Māna" refers to a measuring cup (the agent). "Avaseka" (pouring out) is due to the act of discarding the excess. "Ogha" (flood/current) is due to the power of the flowing liquid. "Pītivacana" refers to words (the object) arising from joy. "Hadaya" refers to the mind (the agent). "Gahetuṃ" means the inability to keep it within the heart without letting it out. Therefore, it is said, "having become excessive," and so forth. The intended meaning here is: "Udāna" refers only to those words that rush out of the mouth spontaneously by the power of great joy, without regard for a recipient.

It is called "dosinā" because it is free from faults (clouds, etc.). The letter "ta" is changed to "na." Just as it is said, "He is a Jina (Conqueror) because he has conquered (jita) the defilements," so too "dosāpagatā" means "free from faults." Even if it is taught in the Sutta Pāḷi: "Monks, there are these four obstructions of the moon and sun, by which obstructions the moon and sun are defiled, they do not burn, do not shine, do not glow..."
14:
"...they do not burn, do not shine, do not glow. Which four? Monks, clouds... mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu the Asura are the obstructions (upakkilesa) of the moon and sun" (as found in the Cūḷavagga Pāḷi). Nevertheless, in order to show the divisions of the third obstruction according to the Aṭṭhakathā method, it is said, "with five obstructions." This meaning is also known from the connection with words like "ramaṇīya" (delightful); thus it is said, "tasmā" (therefore), and so forth. The suffix "-aniya" also mostly denotes the agent (kattu), as shown in "niyyānikā dhammā" (leading out); therefore, it is explained by "ramayati" (causes delight). The beautiful appearance of the night due to the waxing moon is described as "free from the aforementioned faults," and so forth. Here, clouds and so forth are the "aforementioned faults" (dosa). This reason should also be connected to the phrase "fitting to show." The state of being pleasant to behold should be understood as being due to freedom from those faults and the perfection of the season. The days, months, seasons, and years associated with such a night are fitting to be the means of marking the characteristics of days, months, and so forth; therefore, because they are to be marked, they are called "lakkhaṇiya." That very "lakkhaṇiya" becomes "lakkhañña" by the substitution of the letter "ṇa" with "ña" when followed by the letter "ya." Just as it is said, "The lotus pond is well-created," so it is said, "of the days, months, and so forth."

Because of the statement, "When we attend upon [them], the mind would become clear," here, the ultimate (paramattha) Samana and the ultimate Brahmana are intended; not just a Samana by mere ordination, nor a Brahmana by mere birth. This is stated by "because of the state of having stilled evil," and so forth. According to the etymological (nirutti) method, one is called a "Brāhmaṇa" because he wards off or puts away evil. "Vacana-byattaya" (or vacana-vipallāsa) means using the singular when the plural should be used, or the plural when the singular should be used. In this context, however, while "payirupāsataṃ" (plural) should have been said, it was spoken as "payirupāsato" (singular); thus, the "vacana-byattaya" is shown by using the singular in place of the plural. The use of the plural for a single person is well-established for oneself or for a person in a position of respect. The expression "payirupāsato" is a case of metathesis (vaṇṇa-vipariyāya), just as in "payirudāhāsī." This metathesis is frequently seen in the word "pari-" when followed by the letter "ya." Therefore, grammarians say, "In words like 'pariya,' the letters 'raya' and so forth undergo metathesis with 'yara' and so forth." "Whom" refers to either the Samana or the Brahmana. "With all these words" refers to the words "How delightful," and so forth. "Obhāsanimittakamma" means making a sign or a hint (nimitta-karaṇa).
15:
Nimittakammaṃ means making a clear sign or mark. Mahāparādhatāya means because of the state of having great fault.

The words beginning with "Tena hi" are an explanation of the meaning of that term. In the phrase "Devadatto ca," the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of accumulation to bring out a specific meaning. By this word "ca," it conveys the meaning that just as King Ajātasattu committed a great offense by killing his father, who was a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) and an attendant of the Buddha, so too is there a great offense because of his reliance on Devadatta, who caused great harm to the Blessed One. The phrase "tassa piṭṭhichāyāya" (in the shadow of his back) is merely a figure of speech. It means that by relying on Jīvaka as a support, one attends to him, making Jīvaka the leader.

Vikkhepapacchedanatthaṃ means for the purpose of cutting off or preventing distraction that might arise in one's forthcoming speech. Therefore, it is said, "Tassaṃ hi," and so on. Asikkhitānaṃ refers to those who lack the training (sikkhā) in the restraint of body and speech. Kulūpake refers to teachers who visit families. Gahitāsāratāya means because of being devoid of the essence of virtue that should be taken. Nibbikkhepaṃ means being free from rejection by others. Bhaddaṃ means excellent because of being well-supported.

This meaning should also be understood through the implication of this Pali text. Alternatively, showing that this very meaning is included, it is stated in the Pali as "Tena ha," and so on. He is called "satthupaṭiññāto" because he claims to be a teacher (satthā) although he is not. This is said in reference to Pūraṇa Kassapa, who, though not a Buddha, claims to be a Buddha, saying, "I alone in the world am the one who teaches the meaning and the Dhamma." By the words "So kira," and so on, the method of the ancient commentaries is stated using the word "kira" to indicate hearsay. This method should also be understood later in the definition of the term "Makkhali." 

Ekūnadāsasataṃ pūrayamāno means completing a hundred slaves minus one by making himself the hundredth slave along with the others. Thus born, this Pūraṇa Kassapa became an auspicious slave (Maṅgala-dāsa). Jātarūpeneva means in the very form of birth from the mother's womb, or just as beings are born without clothes or coverings, in that natural state. Upasaṅkamanti means they approach and associate. Tadeva pabbajjaṃ aggahesi means he took that naked state as the "going forth," thinking, "This naked state alone is worthy of being called monkhood." Pabbajiṃsu means others followed that person who had gone forth and they also went forth.

By the phrase "pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto," it is shown that he is called "Saṅgha" merely by being a group of renunciants, and not because of being united by commonality of pure virtue and right view that leads out of Saṃsāra. To that Pūraṇa Kassapa who claims to be a Buddha...
16:
It is said "atthi" (exists) because he exists as a retinue for that self-proclaimed teacher. The two terms "Saṅghī" and "Gaṇī" are merely synonyms; it is said "Svevā," etc., to show they differ only in designation. "Svevā" also refers only to the group of renunciants. However, some teachers say, "He is called Saṅghī by virtue of a group of renunciants, and Gaṇī by virtue of a group of laypeople." That is merely the opinion of those teachers, because in the world, the word "Saṅgha" is well-known specifically for a sect or group. Conduct (ācāra) refers to self-conceived practices such as nakedness. He is well-known (paññāto) for being a leader of a Saṅgha, and so on. The two terms "appiccho" (of few wishes) and "santuṭṭho" (contented) are the same in meaning. Among them, to show the kind of fewness of wishes found there, it is said, "Because of fewness of wishes, he does not even wear clothes." In truth, the kind of fewness of wishes characterized by concealing one's existing virtues, as found in the Buddha's Dispensation, cannot be found in him. "Yasa" refers to fame or reputation. A doctrine is called "tittha" (a ford) because it is believed that by this view, one can cross the flood of Saṃsāra. The meaning that he is regarded as "good" (sādhu) by common people, but not by the virtuous, is stated with "Ayaṃ," etc. Indeed, he cannot be regarded as a good person by the truly virtuous. The word "sādhu" has two meanings: an excellent person and a virtuous person. Assutavato refers to one who has not heard the Noble Dhamma (an uninstructed worldling); here, the possessive case is used in the sense of the agent. He knows many nights (days), thinking, "I have well-practiced these undertakings of mine for this much time." Because his nights are of a long duration, it is said "ciraṃ pabbajitassa," etc. This compound is a Bahubbīhi compound where the part enters into the meaning of the other word, like "māsajāto."

If it is asked, "What is the difference between those two terms (rattaññū and cira-pabbajita)?" by the term "cira-pabbajita," his long-standing practice is shown, and by the term "rattaññū," his full awareness and understanding in that practice is shown; this is the difference between the two. To address the question of what meaning the minister intended, it is said "acira-pabbajitassa," etc. Okappanīyā means having the nature of being believable. Addhānaṃ means a long period of time. To the question "How long is that?" it is said, "Two or three royal successions," meaning the sequence of two or three kings ruling the country. Even after saying "addhagato" (gone a long way), the use of the word "vaya" (age) again is in consideration of the final stage of life; it is shown by the words "pacchimavayaṃ" because there can be a difference in the meaning of the two terms. Ubhayaṃ refers to both terms: "addhagato" and "vayoanuppatto."

Kājara is a specific type of tree, also called the "Paṇṇaka" tree (Kanyin or Kanpyin tree). The connection should be made as "unhappy as if seeing." Referring to having heard the Dhamma previously when visiting the Buddha with his father, it is said "jhānā...pe... kāmo." Tilakkhaṇabbāhataṃ means connected with the three characteristics. Dassanena means merely pointing out. For that King Ajātasattu, having seen him, the conversation with him...
17:
Having done so and heard the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda) from Pūraṇa Kassapa, King Ajātasattu became displeased. "Guṇakathāya" means by way of speech describing false virtues. Therefore, it was said, "He was exceedingly displeased." The objection as to why he remained silent despite being displeased is clarified by the words beginning with "Even though he was displeased."

"Gosāla" means he was born in a village of this name. Alternatively, in the sense that he was born in a rest house or a cow-shed (goshala) which was a place for cattle during the rainy season, the name of that slave became exceptionally appropriate based on that cow-shed, as it was a common and unique occurrence. However, since this meaning has not been heard from ancient teachers, it is treated as the view of some teachers. Based on the master's words, "Do not slip (mā khali)," it shows how the name "Makkhali" came to be, which is similar to the verbal form "mā khali." When intended as a name, even a verbal form can become a noun, as in the example "Aññāsikoṇḍañña." "Sesaṃ" refers to the words beginning with "So paṇṇena vā."

Like the name Sirivaḍḍhaka among slaves and others, "Ajita" is merely his name. The meaning that he is called "Kesakambala" because he has a blanket woven from human hair is also appropriate. "Paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ" means especially inferior or wretched. With the words beginning with "Yathāha," the Makkhali Sutta taught in the Tika Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya is cited. "Tantāvitāni" means woven on a loom. Through the six ways beginning with "It is cold when it is cold," the extreme wretchedness of that Kesakambala is shown.

The wanderer who is prone to anger and opposition towards those with right view is thus called "Pakudha." In the phrase "Even after voiding excrement," the word "pi" (even/also) includes the meaning of having eaten food or being smeared with some impurity [without washing]. "Having made a heap of sand" means that, based on the undertaking of a vow, after making a heap of sand, he again undertakes a vow in such a matter that does not lead to the Path, Fruition, or Nibbāna, and proceeds.

"Gaṇṭhanakilesa" is an explanation of the term "palibundhanakilesa." It means defilements such as lust (rāga) which have the function of binding one all around in Saṃsāra, having objects such as fields, property, children, and wives. By the words "because of having such a view," it shows that his name exists only by the power of his doctrine, but not in the true sense of the word. Indeed, as long as those defilements have not been uprooted by the Noble Path, they still exist. This is the derivation: he is called "Nigaṇṭha" because he holds the view, "I have no knots (defilements)." "Nāṭassa" means of the person with this name.
18:
## Commentary on the Story of Jīvaka Komārabhacca
Referring to the state of being silent in every way, it is said, "Like this noble elephant..." "Supaṇṇa" means a Garuda; according to Sanskrit, it is also called "Garuḍa." In that Sanskrit language, they say, "There is no distinction between the letters 'ḍa' and 'ḷa'." Because things did not happen as he desired, it is said, "Alas, it is a loss for me!" "Upasantassa" means to one who has attained peace through all forms of restraint. Jīvaka's silence is like crushing my desire; therefore, by asking about that very silence and making him speak, my desire should be fulfilled. To show the King's intention here, the words beginning with "Hatthimhi kho pana" were said. The word "kinti" is shown to be a particle used in asking for a reason by the words "kena kāraṇena" (by what reason). Or it shows the meaning, "For what reason are you silent? What is that reason?" To extract the possible reason for that silence and show the meaning, the words beginning with "Imesaṃ" were said. "Yathā etesaṃ" means, just as these ministers have a teacher who frequents their homes, he asks, "Are you silent because of one of these three reasons?"

"Kathāpeti" means he wishes to make [him] speak. "Pañcapatiṭṭhitena" here means standing before [the Buddha] with five limbs. It means having first paid homage by bowing down and standing before him, making the five limbs—namely the feet, knees, elbows, hands, and head—level [with the ground]. Citing the Vinaya Pali, "Upāli, when a junior monk pays homage to the feet of a senior monk, he should pay homage by establishing these five things within himself," some say that "five-point prostration" (pañcapatiṭṭhitavandanā) consists of placing the robe on one shoulder, raising the joined palms, massaging the feet, affection, and respect. That statement is not intended in this case of Jīvaka's homage, because when paying homage from a distance, the aforementioned five limbs cannot be fully accomplished. Here, paying homage is simply the act of bowing with joined palms. By the words "having paid homage with the five-point prostration," bodily homage (kāyapāṇama) is expressed. By the words beginning with "Mama satthuno," verbal homage (vacīpāṇama) is expressed. Through the sequence of those two, mental homage (manopāṇama) should be understood.

Although all the practices of the Blessed One are indeed wonderful and marvelous, being unique to him, the descent into the womb, birth, the great renunciation, the supreme enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the Twin Miracle, and the descent from the celestial realm are exceedingly well-known in the world including the devas. Since no one can prevent them, only those points are extracted and shown here.
19:
Reaching such a state or mode is called 'itthambhūta'. Proclaiming such a state is 'itthambhūtākhyāna'. That very meaning is 'itthambhūtākhyānattha'. Alternatively, because such a mode has arisen, it is called 'itthambhūta'. Proclaiming that such a mode has occurred is 'itthambhūtākhyāna', and it means that the accusative case (upayogavacana) is applied in that sense. In the word 'abbhuggata', the prefix 'abhi' is primarily a governing particle (kammapavacanīya) that highlights the sense of 'itthambhūtākhyāna' because it illustrates the manner of rising up by overpowering. Due to its association with that 'abhi', this accusative case in 'taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ', although it is in the possessive (sāmi) sense, is said to be in the 'itthambhūtākhyānattha' because it highlights that sense secondarily. Therefore, the teachers said, 'It means: of that Blessed One (tassa kho pana bhagavato)'.

One might ask: In the phrase 'taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ', the word 'abhi' is not directly used as it is in the example 'sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi'; why then is the accusative case used due to association with 'abhi'? It is because they are associated by way of meaning. Between meaning and verbal usage, association by meaning is primary. The point is this: just as in the example 'sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi', the accusative case is used in the sense of 'itthambhūtākhyāna' due to association with the word 'abhi', so too here, the accusative case is used in the sense of 'itthambhūtākhyāna' because it is associated by meaning with the word 'abhi' in the sense of 'taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ abhi evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo uggato'.

In the example 'sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi', instead of the locative case (bhumma) or genitive case (sāmi) which would mean 'Devadatta is very good in the role of a mother' or 'with respect to his mother', the accusative case is used because of the governing particle 'abhi' which highlights 'itthambhūtākhyāna'. Similarly, here, instead of the genitive case in the possessive sense, the accusative case is used due to association with 'abhi'. Just as in that example the meaning is understood as 'Devadatta is one who has reached the state of being good with respect to his mother', so too here, the meaning is understood as 'the sound of fame concerning the Blessed One has reached the state of rising up (spreading) by overpowering'. In that example, the concept of 'Devadatta' is like 'kittisadda' here, the usage 'mātaraṃ' is like 'bhagavantaṃ', and the word 'sādhu' should be understood as being like the word 'uggata'.

'Kalyāṇo' means good (bhaddaka). It means having a good state because it concerns the auspicious qualities of the Blessed One; thus it is said, 'kalyāṇaguṇasamannāgato' (endowed with auspicious qualities). It means being endowed with auspicious qualities, or being associated as the locus of those qualities. Here, 'endowment' (samannāgama) is simply the state of being the locus (visayatā). Because of being the locus of auspicious qualities (meaning it relies on those qualities). In the synonymous term 'seṭṭho' (excellent), the same method should be understood. The state of being the locus of excellent qualities is the very excellence of the word 'Bhagavā', and so on...
20:
The meaning is that [the fame] relies on that collection of auspicious qualities. In the synonymous word 'seṭṭho' (excellent), the same method should be understood. Only the state of being the locus of excellent qualities is the excellence of the sound of fame. This is like in the passages: 'The word Bhagavā is excellent; the word Bhagavā is supreme,' etc.

Because the qualities are heard through 'arahaṃ sammāsambuddho' etc., and because they are recited, the praised quality itself is called 'kittisadda' (the sound of fame); thus it is said, 'it is just kitti'. Only the praised quality is called 'kitti' because it is to be proclaimed, and it is called 'sadda' because it is to be recited. The word 'sadda' is a synonym for 'kitti', as in the passage: 'Sages of great fame (uḷāra-saddā), virtuous ascetics.'

The sound that occurs by way of praise is called 'kittisadda'; thus the distinction between the support (ādhāra) and the supported (ādheya) is shown by the words 'thutighosa' (the sound of praise). In this context, 'kittisadda' is a synonym for 'thuti'. Praise or intense praise is called 'kitti'. The sound that occurs by way of praise is 'thutighosa', meaning the utterance of intense praise. The prefix 'abhi' is in the sense of overpowering; here, overpowering means specifically overspreading, thus it is said 'ajjhottharitvā' (having overspread). Because it occurs with reference to qualities not shared by others, it means 'having pervaded'. Because of the inquiry as to what kind of sound of fame has spread, the words 'itipi so bhagavā' etc. are spoken. To show this connection (anusandhi), the word 'kinti' is used.

The connection of words is called 'padasambandha'. 'So bhagavā' (That Blessed One) refers to that Blessed One who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramīs) and having broken and destroyed all defilements (kilesas), has realized the peerless Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). He is the God beyond gods (atideva), the Sakka beyond Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond Brahmās, the Lord of the World. Because of reasons such as being the Fortunate One, His sound of fame has spread throughout the world including the devas as 'Bhagavā'; that is 'so bhagavā'.

The words 'yaṃ' and 'taṃ' are always mutually connected. The word 'Bhagavā' mentioned at this beginning is a term that proclaims the name of the Teacher. Therefore, the Venerable General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, said: 'This name Bhagavā was not made by His mother, nor by His father,' and so on. However, the word 'Bhagavā' mentioned later is a term that proclaims His qualities. Just as a person practicing meditation contemplates the Buddha's qualities by connecting the word 'itipi' to each of the nine qualities such as 'arahaṃ', so too here, to show that the hearer of the Buddha's praise should hear the qualities by connecting the word 'itipi' to each one, it is said: 'itipi arahaṃ ... itipi bhagavā'.

When the qualities are heard by connecting 'itipi' to each one in this way, those qualities of the Buddha which are exceedingly famous and well-known in the world including the devas through the nine terms such as 'arahaṃ' are clearly manifested in various ways. This is because the two words 'itipi' illustrate the various aspects of those qualities. 'For this reason also, that word is true'...
21: In passages such as "Iti pi etaṃ tacchaṃ," when describing the qualities of the Buddha, the word iti has the sense of direct perception in close proximity, and the word pi has the sense of aggregating the qualities. By this word pi, the various and diverse nature of the Buddha's qualities is shown. The reasons for noting these qualities are clearly manifest to the wise who are endowed with faith. Therefore, the wise person who praises those qualities should do so by making them present in the mind. To show this, it is said, "For this reason and for that reason." When one reflects and praises in this way, the listener develops great devotion to the Blessed One.  Ārakattā means being very far from defilements. Arīnaṃ means having destroyed the enemies, which are the defilements. Arānaṃ means having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra (hatattā). Paccayādīnaṃ means being worthy of the four requisites such as robes, as well as special offerings. Rahābhāvā means the absence of secret places, such as those hidden from the eye. The state of not doing evil in secret is called rahābhāva. Even when stated thus, the intended meaning is obtained. The details of these matters should be taken from the Visuddhimagga Commentary and from the Paramatthamañjūsā Ṭīkā, which is the explanation of that Visuddhimagga.  Because Jīvaka had heard the qualities of the Buddha many times in the presence of the Teacher, and because he had realized the Truths and was free from doubt in the Teacher's Dispensation, and because he had attained confidence in speaking of the Teacher's qualities, it is said "Jīvaka pana," etc., that he spoke thus in detail. With the words "Ettha ca," etc., the meaning obtained by way of power is stated. Thāma refers to the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa), while bala refers to the Ten Powers (dasabala-ñāṇa). The word vissatthaṃ is a neuter term indicating an action, meaning "being free from doubt."  Pañcavaṇṇāya refers to the fivefold joy, such as khuddikā pīti. Due to the influence of past meritorious deeds, that joy was constantly pervading his entire body. Due to the power of the obstructive kamma of killing his father, the king's "body of virtue" was destroyed. To answer the question of why King Ajātasattu ordered only Jīvaka to prepare the journey, it is said "Imāya," etc.  In saying uttama, it is shown that excellence is not the only reason, but quietness is also a reason; thus "assayāna rathayānāni," etc., is said. Among elephant vehicles, wishing to take only those elephants that were not in rut (or did not associate with the wicked), he had female elephants prepared. Padānupadaṃ means following the footprints of the elephant vehicle going in front, matching footprint to footprint. Here, the word pada is used in the sense of a footprint. Nibbutassa means...
22: To the one (the Buddha) who has calmed the heat of all defilements. Nibbutoheva means only by the calming of the disturbances of sound, due to the quietness.  The word kareṇu is a synonym for a female elephant (hatthinī). It is called kareṇu because it makes a sound (kaṇati). Or it is called kareṇu because it has only a hand-like trunk (kara) and no long tusks. There is also a reading kareṇukā. The formation of the word should be understood through the method of linguistics (nirutti). Preparing for riding (ārohanasajjana) means the fastening of blankets, harnesses, and so on. Opavayha means an elephant capable of carrying the king. Some also read it as opaguyha, meaning capable of protecting or concealing the king.  The phrase "Evaṃ kirassa," etc., is an explanation of his being wise. "Kathā vattati" refers to the occurrence of a Dhamma talk when the opportunity arises. The teacher Elder Dhammapāla said, "To dispel the king's suspicion, women were made to ride the female elephants as close attendants." In the Commentary, however, the reason is stated as: "Relying on women, men have no fear; I shall go happily surrounded by women." The teacher (Sub-commentator) likely meant that this could also be a reason. To show that the king is difficult for others to approach from afar, those women were made to take the appearance of men and carry weapons. In the term hatthinikāsatāni, the female elephants themselves are called hatthinikā. Although some manuscripts have "pañca hatthiniyā satāni," that reading is inappropriate because in such cases, as in "pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi," only the compounding of the latter word is seen. Kassacidēva means to any certain person among the gathered multitude. Intending that for others besides them, it will be a strong support (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits in the future, it is said, "That (Dhamma talk) will be of benefit to the multitude."  Paṭivedesi means he informed (reported). Upacāravacanaṃ is merely a conventional expression, because the intended meaning is not completed by that word alone. Therefore, it is said, "Do that matter according to your own wish." The meaning is completed only by this sentence. Maññasi means you know naturally. Tadeva refers only to going or not going. The meaning is: "If you wish to go, go; if you do not wish to go, do not go; your own wish is the standard here."  The Pali itself becomes paccekā by the power of sandhi. In the word mahañcaṃ, the first case (nominative) is used in the sense of the instrumental, so it is said to be mahata (great). The state of being great is called mahañcaṃ. There is not only a reading ending in niggahīta, but also a reading ending in the letter 'ā'.
23:
The teacher says there is also a variant reading "Mahaccā." Just as "Khatyā" is said where "Khattiyā" should be said, so too "Mahatyā" is said where "Mahatiyā" should be said. Furthermore, by applying the letter "ca," the word formation "Mahaccā" should be understood as being accomplished through euphonic combination (sandhi). When it should be expressed in the masculine gender, the deviation into the feminine gender is called gender reversal (liṅgavipariyāya). Indeed, an adjective usually takes the gender and so forth of the noun it qualifies.

"Tiyojanasatānaṃ" refers to the two great kingdoms, each having a circumference of three hundred yojanas. By the phrase "dvinnaṃ mahāraṭṭhānaṃ issariyasirī," the sovereignty over the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha is meant. The meaning is explained starting with the word "Tassā." "Paṭimukkaveṭhanāni" refers to those who have tied turbans. "Āsattakhaggāni" refers to those who have swords fastened by way of slinging them over the shoulder. "Maṇidaṇḍatomare" refers to those who hold goads with handles inlaid with gems.

By the words beginning with "Aparāpi," the attendants traveling on foot are mentioned. The female attendants of those women are shown by way of their appearance, such as the hunchbacked and the dwarfed, and by way of their birth, such as the Kirātas, Savaras, and Andhakas. The phrase "vissāsikapurisā" refers to men who are intimate with King Vessavaṇa. They are called "Mahāmattā" because they have a great measure (pamāṇa) by way of lineage, wealth, and authority; they are the great ministers of the king who possess great majesty.

"Vijjādharataruṇā viya" means like young Vijjādharas (knowledge-holders) endowed with supernormal powers consisting of science (vijjāmayiddhi) through the power of mantras. "Raṭṭhiyaputtā" means the sons of Bhojas (hunters' sons or village headmen's sons). Indeed, hunters are called "raṭṭhiya" because they wander in the countryside; the meaning is the sons who have become royal soldiers because of their familiarity with various weapons. Alternatively, the sons of the kings who enjoy the revenue within the country are called "raṭṭhiyaputtā"; the kings are the Bhoja-kings (bhojarājā) who enjoy the revenue. It should be noted that the word "Bhoja" mentioned in the Ṭīkā, as in the passage "Anuyuttā bhavantu te," etc., refers to a "Bhojaka" (village headman).

"Ussāpetvā" means having spread upwards. "Jayasaddaṃ" refers to the sound connected with victory, such as "May the great king be victorious!" "Dhanupantiparikkhepo" means being surrounded by rows of bows (surrounded by archers). This should be understood as being by way of holding those bows in all places. "Hatthighaṭā" means groups of elephants. "Paharamānā" means touching. "Aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanā" means being connected to one another by moving without interruption.

"Seṇiyo" refers to guilds of perfumers, guilds of cloth-merchants, and so forth. It is like in the passages, "Without informing the king, the Saṅgha, the group (gaṇa), the corporation (pūga), or the guild (seṇi)..." In some palm-leaf manuscripts, it is written as "eighteen akkhobhiṇī (divisions) of troops." That reading is not found in many manuscripts. Since more than one army has already been counted below, that reading is simply inappropriate. At that time, since only the arrow travels further than all other weapons, the king's retinue is arranged at a distance exceeding the range of an arrow's flight. To the question "For what purpose is it arranged?", it is answered with the words beginning with "Sace."

The agitation of the mind by the root "yasu," which has the meaning of being afraid, is called "bhaya" (fear) because it is afraid in such a manner. When an object that is truly fearful appears as a fearful danger, the knowledge is called "bhaya" because it investigates and reflects in a fearful manner, thinking, "This object is fearful." It is called "bhaya" because it investigates by way of danger. Therefore, it is said in the Visuddhimagga, "The knowledge of appearance as fearful (bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa) is fearful."
24:
It is called 'bhaya' (fear/danger) because it is the agitation of the mind (cittutrāsa) that fears in such a manner, due to the sense of being afraid oneself. When a fearful object appears as a danger, the knowledge that investigates it in a fearful manner, thinking 'this object is fearful,' is called 'bhaya' because it investigates through fear.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Visuddhimagga: 'Does the knowledge of appearance as fear (bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa) fear or not? It does not fear. That knowledge is merely the investigation that "past formations (saṅkhāras) have ceased, present formations are ceasing, and future formations will cease."' The sense object (ārammaṇa) is called 'bhaya' in the sense of being a place of fear, because one fears from that object. Moral dread (ottappa) is called 'bhaya' in the sense of being the cause of fear, because through that moral dread, one fears evil.

'Bhayānaka' refers to the mode of being fearful. 'Tepi' means even the long-lived devas. 'Dhamma-desana' refers to the Dhamma teaching adorned with the fifteen characteristics regarding the five aggregates. 'Yebhuyyena' means for the most part, referring to other devas while excluding the Arahant devas. Because they are Arahants, even the fear of mental agitation does not arise in those devas.

Although the fear of mental agitation is indeed mentioned as that meaning in the commentary on the Sīhopama Sutta, here, in accordance with the context of the text, only 'knowledge-fear' (ñāṇa-bhaya) is taken. 'Saṃvega' is knowledge accompanied by moral dread. 'Santāsa' is total agitation. Due to the sense of being fearful, 'bhaya' itself is called 'bherava' in the sense of being terrifying; therefore, 'bhaya-bherava' refers to a fearful object. Thus it is said, 'it comes'; it means that this terrifying danger is surely coming to that person.

'Bhīruṃ pasamsanti' means the wise praise one who is fearful because of fearing and being agitated by evil. They do not praise one who is brave, arrogant, and destructive in committing that evil. Therefore, it is said, 'The virtuous do not commit evil because of fear.' In this context, 'bhayā' means because of agitation from evil, due to the cause of moral dread.

'Chambhitassa' means of one who is stiffened (thambhitassa); the letter 'th' is changed to 'ch'. Its meaning is stated as 'shaking of the whole body,' meaning the trembling of the entire body due to fear. 'Uyyodhana' means battle (sampahāra).

'Eke' refers to the teachers residing in the Uttara-vihāra. The words beginning with 'Rājagahe' explain their intention. By making two small gates at each main gate, there are sixty-four small gates. With the words beginning with 'Tadā,' the reason for it being a non-cause is shown.

Now, to show his own view, the words beginning with 'Ayaṃ pana' are spoken. The words beginning with 'Jīvako kira' show the manner of having doubt. 'Assa' means of King Ajātasattu. 'Ukkaṇṭhito' means dissatisfaction. It is thought that he wishes to have the white parasol raised...
25:
In the connection, 'bhāyitvā' means because of fear. 'Tassa' refers to Jīvaka. The word 'samma' has the same meaning [as friend]; because of being equal in age, it is said to be 'vayassābhilāpo' (an address for one of equal age). One who is equal in age is called 'vayassa,' as in the verse 'Ekarājā harissavaṇṇo.' Experts in linguistics desire the substitution of 'sa' for the word 'samāna'; therefore, that address for an equal is 'ālapana' (a mode of address). This is a designation by usage (ruḷhī), like the address 'mārisa.'

Just as the address 'mārisa' is an address for one without suffering, yet it is also used in addressing hell-beings (nerayikas) who have suffering, in such passages as 'When, dear sir (mārisa), the stakes meet the stake in your heart,' similarly, any companion, even if not of equal age, is addressed as 'samma.' Therefore, it simply has the meaning of addressing a friend. 'Kacci na vañcesi' (Why would you not be deceiving?) is the connection with the Pali. Although it says 'na palambhesi,' here only the sense of conjecture is appropriate, so it is said 'na vippalambheyyāsi' (you should not deceive or lure). It means 'na palobheyyāsi' (you should not entice). Conversation is called 'sallāpa'; that very sound of conversation is 'nigghosa.'

'Vinasseyya' means one would perish through mental distress. With reference to the words beginning with 'Na taṃ devā,' it is said 'daḷhaṃ katvā' (having made firm). By the word 'taramānovā,' it is shown that this is a repetition (āmeḍita) in the sense of haste. Having said 'Abhikkama mahārāja' (Come forward, Great King), the words beginning with 'ete' are spoken to show the reason for that. Showing the meaning along with the connection, he said 'Mahārāja corabalaṃ nāma' etc.

## Sāmaññaphala-pucchā-vaṇṇanā

This area outside the gate-house is called the ground for elephants (nāga-bhūmi). Therefore, 'vihārassa' etc. is said. 'Bhagavato tejo' means the power and majesty of the Blessed One. It pervaded the King's body just as it pervaded the body of the Brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa when he was approaching the Blessed One and had entered the forest grove. 'Attano aparādhaṃ saritvā mahābhayaṃ uppajji' (Remembering his own fault, great fear arose) is the showing of the cause for sweating. In reality, sweating cannot occur because of the Buddha's majesty, because the Buddha's majesty is the cause for the tranquility (passaddhi) of body and mind.

'Eke' refers only to the teachers residing in the Uttara-vihāra. That their words are inappropriate is shown by 'iminā' etc. 'Abhimāra' refers to archers. 'Dhanapāla' refers to the elephant Nālāgiri. He was called 'Dhanapāla' because at that time he received heaps of wealth offered by the city-dwellers. Not only because of having seen him before, but also by nature, the Blessed One...
26:
The words beginning with "Bhagavā hi" are stated to show that the Blessed One should be known in this way. The term "Akiṇṇavaralakkhaṇo" is mentioned with reference to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. The term "Anubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍito" is mentioned with reference to the eighty minor marks (the details are found in the Vijātamangala-vaṇṇanā of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā). "Chabbaṇṇāhi rasmīhi" refers to the rays of light emanating at that time. "Issariyaliḷāya" means by way of the majestic grace of sovereignty. Since there might be an objection that asking with a majestic manner in the presence of the Blessed One would be disrespectful, the words beginning with "Pakati hesā" are stated. The meaning is that it is not disrespectful because the asking is according to the natural disposition of kings. Although the members of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha sitting around the Blessed One were positioned in front, in terms of meaning, he [the King] is said to be sitting in front of that Blessed One. Therefore, the words beginning with "Pariwāretwā" are stated.

The words "Yena" and "Tena" are also instrumental cases used in the sense of location (bhummatttha), as shown by the words "Yattha, Tattha". Since the manner of arrival is described as "Yena maṇḍalassa dvāraṃ, tenūpasaṅkami" (By whichever way was the door of the pavilion, by that way he approached), it is considered that only "approaching nearby" is appropriate here, thus "Upagato" is said. "Anucchawike ekasmiṃ padese" refers to the place where wise people stand. What is that suitable place? It is a place free from the six faults of sitting, such as being too far, or a place free from the eight faults of sitting, such as not sitting behind. The teachers of the Commentaries stated this as follows:

"Not behind, not in front, nor too near or far;
Not in the lee, not against the wind, nor in a low or high place;
Avoiding these faults, they stood in a suitable place."

At that time, to show that silence pervaded the Bhikkhu Saṅgha without exception, the repeated words "Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ" are stated. "Yato...pe...meva" means from whichever monk. Fidgeting with the hands or an unseemly movement of the hands is called "hand-fidgeting" (hatthakukkucce). It refers to lack of restraint and actions without clear comprehension. Likewise, the same applies to the term "foot-fidgeting" (pādakukkucce). The word "vā" is used in the sense of specifying what has not been mentioned. By that word "vā", it is made clear that there is no lack of restraint of other faculties like the eye, ear, etc., apart from the fidgeting of hands and feet. Among those restraints of the faculties, the lack of restraint of the eye is the foremost and difficult to prevent. Therefore, to show the absence of that lack of eye-restraint, the words beginning with "Sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ" are stated.

"Vippasannarahadamiva" means like a lake with clear water. "Yenetarahi...pe...iminā me...pe...hotu" should be connected. The order of meaning is one way, and the order of words is another...
27:
Regarding the order of words, the words beginning with "Yenā" are stated.
