In that statement, since mental tranquility is also obtained by inference through the obtained physical and vocal tranquility, it is said "and by mental tranquility." "Sīlūpasamena" means by the restraint of virtue. Wishing to accomplish the stated meaning through worldly nature, the words beginning with "Dullabhañhi" are stated. "Laddhā" means having obtained.

"Upasama" is the restraint characterized by perfection of conduct. By the words beginning with "Evaṃ", the reason for desiring in such a manner is shown. "So" refers to the grandfather King Bimbisāra or Prince Udayabhadda. The words beginning with "Kiñcāpi" are for the completion of that meaning. "Ghātessati" is said with regard to the future time of killing. Therefore, "Ghātesī" is said. This speech is made with regard to the present time. "Pañcaparivaṭṭo" means five successions of kings.

Why is this said? The intention is: "Indeed, the king says nothing referring to the Blessed One." "Vaci-bhede" refers to the utterance of the aforementioned inspired utterance (udāna). "Tuṇhī niravo" is a metaphorical expression. The words beginning with "Ayaṃ" show the manner of knowing the mind. It should be connected as "Knowing that 'This king... will not be able to...'". "Vacanānantaraṃ" means immediately after the inspired utterance. "Yena" means in whichever place or by whichever path of the ear. In the phrase "Yena pemaṃ" also, this method should be understood accordingly.

Intending that it is difficult to address face-to-face one against whom an offense has been committed, it is said "the face does not open" (cannot speak). Alternatively, it should be noted that this is said with reference to the sweet words of the Blessed One, which were expressed by the words "Indeed, O Great King, you have come according to your affection," and which were then proceeding in various wonderful ways to illuminate that meaning. Indeed, the Blessed One teaches even a single meaning in such a way that the wisdom of the listeners arises. With reference to that meaning, it is said in the Commentaries: "There is no such thing as a Pali term not explained by the Blessed One; He has also explained the meaning of all terms." "Pañcahākārehi" means by five reasons such as being equal towards the pleasant and the unpleasant. This matter is stated in the Mahāniddesa as follows:

'By five aspects one is Tādī (Steadfast): one is Tādī towards the pleasant and unpleasant; one is Tādī because of having crossed over (defilements); one is Tādī because of having crossed (the floods); one is Tādī because of being liberated (from defilements); one is Tādī because of the description of such qualities.'

How is an Arahant Tādī towards the pleasant and unpleasant? An Arahant is Tādī in gain and in loss, in fame and in obscurity, in praise and in blame, in pleasure and in pain. If one were to smear one arm with perfume, and [cut] the other arm...
28:
Some might anoint one arm with sandalwood perfume; some might scrape one arm with an adze. There is no lust (rāga) in that anointing with perfume; there is no resentment (paṭigha) in that scraping with an adze. Having abandoned affection and resentment, having transcended both praise and oppression, and having perfectly overcome attraction and repulsion, thus an Arahant is 'Such' (tādī) towards desirable and undesirable objects.

How is an Arahant called 'Such' because of having abandoned (cattāvīti)? For an Arahant... stubbornness, turbulence, conceit, overbearing pride, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations (wholesome volitional formations) have been abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and renounced. Thus, an Arahant is called 'Such' because of having abandoned.

How is an Arahant called 'Such' because of having crossed over (tiṇṇāvīti)? The Arahant has crossed the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. He has crossed, ascended, emerged from, transcended, perfectly transcended, and gone beyond the entire path of Saṃsāra. He has completed the holy life, practiced the conduct, and reached the end of birth and death; for him, there is no more rebirth in a new existence. Thus, an Arahant is called 'Such' because of having crossed over.

How is an Arahant called 'Such' because of being released (muttāvīti)? For an Arahant, the mind is released, specially released, and well-released from lust; from hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, hypocrisy, stubbornness, turbulence, conceit, overbearing pride, intoxication, and negligence. The mind is released, specially released, and well-released from all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all volitional formations. Thus, an Arahant is called 'Such' because of being released.

How is an Arahant called 'Such' because of being designated by those qualities (taṃniddesā)? An Arahant is called 'Such' because he is designated by virtue as 'one who has virtue' (sīlavā), by faith as 'one who has faith' (saddho), by energy as 'one who has energy' (vīriyavā), by mindfulness as 'one who has mindfulness' (satimā), by concentration as 'one who is concentrated' (samāhito), by wisdom as 'one who has wisdom' (paññavā), by true knowledge as 'one with triple knowledge' (tevijjo), and by direct knowledge as 'one with sixfold direct knowledge' (chaḷabhiñño). Thus, an Arahant is called 'Such' because of being designated by those qualities.

The Blessed One, however, is the supreme 'Such' among all those who are 'Such'. Therefore, it was said: 'well-established' (suppatiṭṭhito). This was also spoken by the Blessed One in the Kāḷakārāma Sutta: 'Thus, bhikkhus...'
29:
'Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is "Such" (tādī) among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. I say that there is no other "Such" who is superior or more excellent than that "Such"' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.24). Alternatively, it means he is well-established in the characteristic of "Suchness" through the five modes accomplished by the fivefold Ariyan psychic power. This was said by the Venerable Captain of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'What is Ariyan psychic power? Here, a bhikkhu, if he so desires, can dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive. If he so desires, he can dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive. If he so desires, he can dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive. If he so desires, he can dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive. If he so desires, he can dwell avoiding both the repulsive and the unrepulsive, and dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.17). 'Bahiddhā' means in doctrines outside of the Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Esā' refers to the manner of saluting the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. To prove this meaning with a worldly simile, the words 'rājānaṃ' etc. are spoken. 'Okāsa' means the place for asking questions.

The statement 'I have no burden in answering questions' shows that the Blessed One's knowledge moves unhindered in all things. This meaning is already implied by the words 'If you so desire'. The same principle applies to 'I will answer everything for you'. This meaning is established by the very words 'Ask whatever you desire'. This is connected to the 'Omniscient Invitation' (sabbaññupavāraṇā) which is unique to the Buddha. If others do not say 'Ask whatever you desire', how do they speak? They speak by saying 'having heard...', etc. It should be understood that they speak thus because they stand only in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa). The Buddhas, however, offer the Omniscient Invitation. 'Ask, friend, whatever you desire' and other such sutta passages occurred on account of certain persons; to show those persons, it is said: 'of yakkhas, kings, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers'. Therein, the words 'Ask, friend, whatever you desire' were addressed to Āḷavaka the Yakkha...
30:
It should be understood as the granting of permission: granting permission to the Yakkha; to the kings with "Ask, O Great King"; to Sakka, the lord of devas, with "Ask, Vāsava" and so on; to the monks with "If so" and so on; to the Brahmins with "And for Bāvarī" and so on; and to the wanderers with "Ask me, Sabhīya" and so on. "Vāsava" is an address for Sakka, the lord of devas. This is found in the Sakkapañha Sutta. "Manasicchasi" means desiring with the mind.

The construction is: "Since you have been granted permission by me, ask all your doubts just as you desire in your mind, for Bāvarī, for yourself Ajita, and for all the rest." Here, the meaning is: "Ask Bāvarī’s doubts with the mind; but for all of you, ask your doubts either with the mind or by other means as you desire." Indeed, Bāvarī commanded his disciples, "Ask your own doubts only with the mind." Regarding that command, it is said:
"If he is truly a Buddha, seeing without obstruction,
He will answer with words the questions asked with the mind." (Sn 1011).
This is in the Pārāyanavagga. Similarly, "Ask me, Sabhīya" and so on are the same.

"Buddhabhūmi" (the ground of a Buddha) refers to the station of a Buddha, the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), and the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). "Bodhisattabhūmi" (the ground of a Bodhisatta) refers to the station of a Bodhisatta, the knowledge of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīsambharaṇañāṇa). Alternatively, the word "bhūmi" denotes a stage or state; meaning the stage of a Buddha or the stage of a Bodhisatta. In the case of the aggregates proceeding by way of unity, the stage is simply the state depending on those various modes.

The connection is: "That very invitation of the Blessed One is wonderful, who, while standing in the stage of a Bodhisatta, in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), made an invitation like an omniscient one." How did he invite? He said, "Kondañña, the questions..." and so on. There, "Kondañña" is addressing the hermit Sarabhaṅga by his clan name. "Viyākarohi" means to explain or answer. "Sādhurūpā" means of a good nature. "Dhammo" refers to the ancient traditional Dhamma. The word "yaṃ" refers to the act of coming, or the connection is "answer because of the reason for which you have come." "Vuddha" refers to one who has reached growth through virtue, wisdom, and so on; it means venerable. "This burden" refers to the burden consisting of the cutting off of doubts; the meaning is "this burden that has come to you must certainly be borne by you."
31:
"Since I have granted permission, may the venerable ones ask. Why? Because I, having personally known this world and the next, will answer those various questions of yours." "Sayaṃ" means by oneself, without the instruction of others. Thus, the connection is: "During the time of Sarabhaṅga, he made an invitation like an omniscient one."

"Pañhānaṃ" refers to questions associated with the Dhamma. "Antakaraṃ" refers to one who brings things to an end (completion). "Suciratena" refers to a Brahmin of such name. "Puṭṭhuṃ" is for the purpose of asking. "Jātiyā" means by way of rebirth; some also say "vijātiyā." The construction should be: "Prince Sambhava, while playing in the dust, made the invitation while remaining seated."

"Taggha" is a particle in the sense of "certainly." "Yathāpi kusalo tathā" means "Just as the Buddha, who is skilled in all dhammas and knows all dhammas, knows and speaks, so shall I declare to you." Here, the word "jānāti" (knows) connects with the preceding sentence. As it is said: "Even if words are far apart, they should be connected if there is a relation between them." Here, "knowing" (jānanā) is indeed "speaking" (kathanā). This is the meaning stated by the Teacher: "By this, he knows (speaks) this Dhamma." "Rājā ca kho taṃ" means "Whether that King Koravya, who sent you here to ask, follows the meaning you asked, or the meaning I declared when asked by you, or does not follow it, I shall declare it to you according to the Dhamma."

In the Jātaka Commentary, however: "Rājā ca kho taṃ" means "I will explain that question as far as your king knows or is able to know. Beyond that, whether the king acts according to what he knows or does not act, the benefit or fault of acting or not acting will be his alone; there is no fault in me." This shows that the word "jānāti" is used as common to both sentences.

The craft itself is called "sippāyatana" (base of craft), because the word "āyatana" exists in the state of that craft. Alternatively, it is called "sippa" because it must be learned, and "āyatana" because it is the cause or support for the livelihood of beings; thus, it is "sippāyatana." "Seyyathidaṃ" is either a single particle or a group of particles. Of that "seyyathidaṃ"...
32:
Regarding the phrase 'What are they?', in this context, it means 'Who are those who possess those crafts?'. Taking the meaning individually as 'What are these crafts?' is also appropriate. This should be understood in the same way in all instances. Since this statement is made in anticipation of what is to be said later, it means 'Who are those who live by those crafts?'. After mentioning 'many crafts' in a general sense, the text specifies only those who live by various crafts through a person-centered discourse. Why? Because of the desire to avoid prolixity. In another way, after showing the intended crafts, one would have to show those who live by them again. In this context, the persons themselves are primarily intended. If presented that way, the discourse would become excessively long; therefore, to avoid such prolixity, the various crafts are included by way of those who live by them. To show this meaning, it is said, 'By elephant riders and so on, it shows those who live depending on various crafts.' Why is it shown? It is said starting with 'This person...'. Those who live depending on a craft are called sippūpajīvī.

They are called hatthāroha (elephant riders) because they ride elephants; these are elephant-mounted warriors. They are also called hatthāroha because they cause others to ride elephants; these are elephant trainers, elephant doctors, elephant keepers, and so on. All those who perform the effort by which a man becomes fit to ride an elephant should be included here. Therefore, it is said, 'all of them,' and so on. Among them, hatthācariya (elephant trainers) are those who train both the elephants and the elephant riders. Hatthivejja (elephant doctors) are those who treat elephants. Hatthimeṇḍa (elephant keepers) are those who guard the feet of the elephants. They are called hatthimaṇḍa because they adorn or protect the elephant; the same are called hatthimeṇḍa. Alternatively, they are called hatthimeṇḍa because they control the elephant well through discipline. By the word 'and so on,' those who give fodder to elephants, etc., are included. In the word assāroha (horse riders), the meaning should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. Those joined with chariots are called rathika (charioteers). Chariot guards are those who guard the linchpin of the chariot. They are called dhanuggaha (archers) because they hold the bow. They are also called dhanuggaha because they cause others to hold the bow; these are the archery teachers who teach the art of the bow.

They are called celaka (standard-bearers) because they go into battle with cloth banners. Therefore, it is said, 'those who in the battlefield,' and so on. Jayadhaja (victory banner) is a banner raised for the sake of victory or at the time of victory. 'In front' means in front of the army. They are called calaka because they move or shift the soldiers from place to place by the power of military maneuvering. Therefore, it is said, 'here, of the king,' and so on. Just as hawks and other birds snatch a piece of meat and fly away, they are called piṇḍadāyaka because they bravely cut through, leap upon, and depart from the mass of the enemy army. Therefore, it is said, 'those celakas,' and so on. Warriors who act with violence are called sāhasika. They are also called mahāyodha (great warriors). Regarding 'like a mass,' the teachers say it is like a cluster of palm fruits. The teacher Dhammapāla says it is like a piece of meat. In all places, when 'the teacher' is mentioned, it refers only to the Venerable Dhammapāla. In the second explanation, they are called piṇḍadāyaka because they move as if leaping within the narrow confines of a crowd. The word daya is in the sense of going. Or, it is formed by the arrival of the letter 'da' in the word daya.
33:
They are called *piṇḍadāyaka* because they leap over the mass of soldiers and depart. Therefore, the phrase starting with 'They, it is said' is spoken. They are called *sāhasika* because they act with violence; they are the same as the *mahāyodhā* (great warriors). 'Like a lump' (*piṇḍam-iva*) is said by some to be like a cluster of palm fruits; 'like a lump of meat' is said by the Teacher (Dhammapāla). In all places, when 'the Teacher' is mentioned, only the Venerable Dhammapāla should be understood. According to the second method, they are called *piṇḍadāyaka* because they move as if leaping in the narrow space of a crowd of people. The word *daya* is in the sense of going; or it is formed by the arrival of the letter 'd' in the word *aya*.

They are called *uggatuggata* because, having reached the battlefield, they are exceedingly distinguished by way of speed and effort. 'That very thing' (*tad-eva*) refers to that head or weapon mentioned by others. They are called *pakkhandanti* because they enter the enemy army without hesitation due to their heroic and brave nature. They are like great elephants (*mahānāga*) because they are endowed with power, speed, strength, and effort. Therefore, the phrase starting with 'even among elephants, etc.' is spoken. *Ekantathūra* refers to heroes who go about alone; since the word *anta* exists in that state, it means those who fight alone due to their brave nature. *Sajālika* refers to those who have armor. *Sannāha*, *kaṅkaṭa*, *vamma*, *kavaca*, *uracchada*, and *jālikā* are identical in meaning. *Sacammika* refers to those who have leather that protects the body like a net. *Cammakañcuka* is a tunic made of leather. 'Having entered' (*pavisitvā*) means being inside that tunic, i.e., having put it on. 'Leather for protecting against arrows' (*saraparittāṇa camma*) refers to a garment sewn with leather or a shield made of leather. *Balavasineha* means great affection for one's master. *Gharadāsayodhā* are warriors who belong to the group of slaves born in the house; there is also a variant reading *gharadāsikaputta*, meaning the sons of female household slaves.

A kitchen is called *āḷāra*; those appointed there are called *āḷārika* (cooks). *Pūvika* are pastry cooks who live by preparing and selling various kinds of cakes. They are called *kappaka* (barbers) because they arrange the ornamentation of people by way of fixing hair and nails. They are called *nhāpika* (bath attendants) because they bathe people to remove dirt and produce a beautiful complexion by using scented powders and ointments. The book of calculation, which proceeds by a method ending in nine, is called *acchiddaka* because there are no gaps in it; those who recite that book are called *acchiddakapāṭhaka*. Communicating one's intention or counting with the hand is called *hatthamuddā*. Indeed, the bending of fingers is called *muddā*, and by that, communication or counting occurs. Here, the word 'hand' (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to a part of it, the fingers, as in the Pali passage: 'If a person eating does not put everything with the hand...'
34:
Those who live by the art of finger-calculation (arithmetic), as mentioned in the passage beginning with "I will put the whole hand into the mouth" (Pācittiya Pāḷi 618), are called "muddikā." Therefore, it was said, "hatthamuddāya," and so on. The "ayakāra" is a blacksmith (kammārakāraka). The "dantakāra" is a turner or ivory-worker (bhamakāra). The "cittakāra" is a painter (lepacittakāra). By the word "ādi" (and so on), carpenters, scribes, basket-makers, masons, and wood-carvers are included.

"Diṭṭheve dhamme" (in this very life) refers only to this present existence. Showing it by way of the accomplishment of the cause, "sandiṭṭhikam eva" (certainly visible) means the meaning is one's own direct experience, to be seen by oneself and experienced by oneself, not being a benefit belonging to the future world.

"Upajīvanti" means they live depending on [those arts]. "Sukhitaṃ" means having reached happiness. Since the state of being endowed with strength and power is indeed "pīṇana" (refreshing/strengthening), it was said, "pīṇitaṃ thāmabalūpetaṃ" (refreshed and endowed with strength and power).

"Upari" (above) refers to the deva world. Likewise, "uddhaṃ" (upward) also refers to it. This is because the deva world is situated above the human world. "Aggaṃ viya" means like the foremost fruit. The Teacher (the author of the old sub-commentary) said, "Because the fruit is produced due to the performance of the action, that fruit is like the flame of the action's fire." Alternatively, "sagga" means the excellent fruit. "Sagga" means the well-excellent fruit, meaning it is worthy of accomplishing its own ten-fold fruit such as sights and sounds.

By the method of linguistics (nirutti), "su-aggikā" itself is called "sovaggikā." Because it refers to the word "dakkhiṇā," the feminine gender is used in all terms. "Sukho" means the cause of happiness, which is desired and pleasant. "Agge" means noble. The distinction between these is that "rūpa" is the external form to be enjoyed by oneself, and "vaṇṇa" is one's own beauty of complexion (vaṇṇapokkharatā). Because it increases through this volition, it is called "dakkhiṇā." Because it is merit accomplished through relinquishment, it is said, "dakkhiṇā dānaṃ."

The Path (magga) is called "sāmañña" because it is the state of a recluse (samaṇa) whose evils are calmed. Because it is the fruit of that Noble Path, the Noble Fruition is called the "fruit of recluseship" (sāmaññaphala).

By the passage beginning with "yathāha," the meaning is established according to the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi. King Ajātasattu did not know that meaning because he was unskilled in the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. However, this king thought, "For those who have gone forth from being slaves, farmers, and so on, the gaining of salutation and such in the world is called the visible fruit of recluseship (sandiṭṭhika sāmaññaphala)." Wishing to investigate, "Is there any recluse or brahmin who knows such a meaning?", he questioned Pūraṇa and others. Not finding satisfaction in their words, he also asked the Blessed One about this matter. Therefore, it is said, "He asks with reference to the simile of the slave and the farmer."
35:
"Rājāmacca" refers to ministers descended from royal families, as well as princes and ministers who follow and serve the king. "Kaṇhapakkha" (the dark side) refers to the side of defilement associated with wrong views found in the meaning of what was asked. "Sukkapakkha" (the bright side) refers to the side of purification (vodāna) mentioned later in the sutta, which is the opposite of that side of defilement. "Samaṇakolāhala" (the uproar of recluses) refers to the commotion among recluses, meaning the mutual contradiction of various doctrines of recluses. "Samaṇabhaṇḍana" (the quarreling of recluses) refers to the verbal abuse of those doctrines due to that very contradiction, such as saying, "This is the fault of those recluses and brahmins who hold such a view; this is the fault of those who hold that view."

The statement "The world follows the ruler" is the substantiation of that meaning by showing the natural law (dhammatā). It is the performance of the king's burden through the Buddha's own skill in teaching, and not for any other reason such as disparaging others.

Just like the particle "nu," the particle "no" is also used in the sense of a question; thus it was said, "Abhijānāsi nu" (Do you remember?). In the word "ayañca," the particle "ca" has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), connecting not only with the word "abhijānāsi" but also with the word "pucchitā." The question "How should it be connected?" is resolved by the passage beginning with "idañhi." "Pucchitā nu" means "Have you performed the act of questioning before?" "Naṃ puṭṭhabhāvaṃ" means "Do you remember the fact of having asked so?" "Na te sammuṭṭhaṃ" means "It is certainly not forgotten by you." "Aphāsukabhāva" means the state of discomfort caused by speaking in that way. "Paṇḍitapatirūpaka" refers to those who speak the language of the wise (to those who honor them, as if they themselves know), or those who pretend to be wise like raw fruit appearing ripe. "Pāḷipada-atthabyañjana" refers to the words known as Pāḷi, their meanings, and the syllables included therein; or the word "byañjana" is a synonym for a sentence (vākya), as in the passage "akkharaṃ padaṃ byañjanaṃ" (Netti 28). He is called "bhagavantatūpa" because his nature is like the nature of the Blessed One; it means he is absolutely wise like the Blessed One.

## Commentary on the Doctrine of Pūraṇa Kassapa

In the phrase "ekamidāhaṃ," the word "idaṃ" is merely a particle; the meaning is simply "at one time." "Sammodanīya" means that which causes rejoicing or friendliness. The suffix "aniya" often denotes the agent (kattu), as in the word "niyyānika." Alternatively, it is called "sammodanīya" by way of a derivative (taddhita) meaning that which generates rejoicing. "Sāraṇīya" means that which should be remembered, or that which is appropriate for remembrance. To show this meaning, it was said, "generating rejoicing and worthy of being remembered." "Saritabbayuttaka" means appropriate for remembrance.
36:
“Sahattha” means (doing) with one’s own hand. This term indicates the pure agent (suddha-kattā). The term “āṇattiyā” indicates the causative agent (hetu-kattā). In this context of killing (pāṇātipāta), instrumental means (nissaggiya-payoga), permanent means (thāvara-payoga), and so forth, are also included under the category of “with one’s own hand.” “Hands etc.” refers to hands, feet, ears, nose, and so forth. Referring to oppressing, burning, and harming, the teacher said, “to one who oppresses with a stick.”

In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī, a second meaning of this term “pacato” (to one who oppresses) is also stated as “to one who threatens.” In this Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, however, the sub-commentator states that threatening and reviling are included within (oppressing) with a stick, and thus it is only said, “to one who oppresses with a stick.” Nowadays, in palm-leaf manuscripts, the reading “tajjentassa vā” (or to one who threatens) is also frequently found.

“Soka” (grief) is the cause of sorrow. Since the effect is also attributed by fulfilling the cause, the meaning “sorrowing” is also appropriate. “By others” means by those who are the objects (kamma) who follow one’s words.

In this context of “phandato” (from trembling), the meaning of the pure agent cannot be obtained through the trembling of others; rather, it is obtained only through one’s own trembling. Thus it is said, “to one who himself trembles at the time another trembles.” It means one who himself trembles due to the effort of harming another performed by oneself. The term “atipātāpayato” (causing to kill) shows that it applies to both the pure agent and the causative agent by the words “to one who kills and to one who causes to kill.” “In all cases” means in terms such as “ādiyato” (taking). “By way of the cause of doing” means by way of doing it oneself or causing others to do it.

The junction between the inside and outside of a house wall is called “gharasandhi” (house-breach). Plundering without leaving anything behind is called “nillopa” (total plundering), and thus it is called “mahāvilopa” (great plundering). Plundering designated for only one house is called “ekāgārika.” Therefore, it says “only one house” and so forth. In the phrase “to one standing on the path,” the meaning that one stands only for the purpose of snatching is established by the context, as shown by “of those who come and go” and so forth. The teacher also stated the meaning: “Paripantha (ambush) means harming and killing from all sides on the path.”

By the words “with the perception ‘I will do’,” the state of being intentional is expressed. By this, it shows the meaning: “Even for one who does it intentionally, it is not called ‘done’ [in terms of producing a result], let alone for one who does it unintentionally.” “It is not called doing evil” means that since one is unable to produce what did not exist before, evil is called “not done.” Therefore, it says “There is no evil (akusala).”

If this is so, why do beings engage in evil? Pūraṇa Kassapa, wishing to remove the fault attributed to his doctrine by others, shows this meaning by saying “But beings...” and so forth. The phrase “they do evil” is merely a perception.
37:
In fact, it means that evil simply does not exist. Pūraṇa Kassapa has this view: The action (kiriya) such as harming these beings does not reach the self (atta) because of its permanence and its state of being unchanging. The body, however, is insentient, like a log or a piece of wood. Even if that body is destroyed, he considers that there is no evil.

The rim (nemi) is called “pariyanta” (limit) because it stands at the end. Therefore, the teacher (sub-commentator) said, “(a wheel) having an edge like a sharp razor.” In the second alternative (vikappa), only the end of the wheel is called pariyanta. Because it has an end like a razor, it is called “khurapariyanta.” Here, by the word “khura” (razor), the razor’s edge is taken, as it is included in that wheel. In the Pali, “cakkena” (with a wheel) means with a specific weapon made in the shape of a wheel. “Tatonidānaṃ” (from that cause) means having that cause, which is described as making a heap of flesh. In the Commentaries, it is said: “The suffix ‘-to’ is a substitute for the nominative case (paccatta-vacana), and there is no elision of that case in the compound.” The teacher Elder Sāriputta says: “The ablative case (nissakka-vacana) is also appropriate in the sense of the nominative.” Grammarians (akkharacintaka) say: “It is a group of particles in the sense of cause.”

The southern side of the Ganges is an unsuitable place, while the northern side is a suitable place; with this intention, it says “to the south” and so forth. This statement refers to the inhabitants of those regions by indicating the directions, saying “on the southern bank” and so forth. Indeed, the actions of killing and giving are connected to those southern and northern regions. “Mahāyāgaṃ” (great sacrifice) is a great sacrificial offering similar to the sacrifice of King Mahāvijita. The word “dama” (restraint) refers to the restraint of the sense faculties and the observance of the Uposatha precepts; thus it says “by restraint of the senses and by the Uposatha practice.” Some teachers say the word “uposathakammena” is an attribute of “restraint of the senses,” meaning “by restraint of the senses which is the Uposatha practice.” That is not appropriate, because the word “dama” expresses both meanings, and both meanings are distinct.

Nowadays, in some books, the particles “vā” (or) and “ca” (and) are also found. “Sīlasaṃyamena” (by restraint of virtue) means by the restraint of body and speech other than that. “Saccavacanena” (by truthful speech) means by speaking words that are unerring and true. The reason for mentioning truthful speech separately is that it is recognized in the world as a very great merit. Just as among evil things, false speech is the gravest fault, so among meritorious things, truthful speech is the greatest benefit. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Itivuttaka Pali:
38:
“For the person who has transgressed one law (of truthfulness), 
Who is prone to speaking falsehood, 
And who has abandoned the world beyond (the afterlife), 
There is no evil that they would not dare to do.” 
(Thus it was taught in the Itivuttaka Pali).

'Pavatti' refers to the arising [of results] as a causal state for the production of fruit within the continuum of the one who acts. In this way, the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda), which claims 'there is no action, there is no result of action,' reaches completeness. If there were indeed results of action, how could the state of non-action (akiriya) of deeds be possible? 'Sabbathāpi' means in all the ways mentioned, starting with the phrase 'for one who acts.'

'Labuja' refers to the monkey-fruit (Artocarpus lacucha). [Pūraṇa Kassapa] rejects only the performance (kiriya) of good and evil; he does not answer the question asked by the King regarding the visible fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) obtainable in the present life. This restriction of the meaning [using 'only the performance'] is to prevent the rejection of the result (vipāka). For whoever rejects action, by implication, also rejects the result. Therefore, it will be said later, 'even by one who obstructs action,' and so forth.

'Vijita' is so called because it is specifically conquered such that it cannot be overcome by rival kings; it is the territory where the authority of a single king prevails. Expelling someone with the words 'Do not live within my realm' is indeed a form of harassment known as banishing one who has gone forth; hence it is said 'to be harassed' (viheṭhetabba). The King's rejection of the meaning spoken by him [Pūraṇa Kassapa], through wise reflection, mindfulness, and learning, is called 'not taking it as essence.' Retaining that meaning in the mind for the sake of long-term stability is called 'nikkujjana'; the rejection of this is shown by the phrase 'not establishing it... by way of essence.' 'By way of essence' means as the most excellent; or, because it is unerring and true, the stable meaning that cannot be moved by others is called 'essence' (sāra) due to its lack of fluff; 'by way of that essence' is the meaning. 'Nissaraṇa' means the escape from the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). 'Paramattha' means the unerring meaning, or the meaning that is the object of supreme knowledge. As for the phrasing (byañjana), the King both learned and retained it, and spoke it exactly as such in the presence of the Blessed One.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla

'By both' (ubhayena) refers to the statement rejecting both cause (hetu) and condition (paccaya). By the phrase 'only what exists' (vijjamānam-eva), it is shown that his ignorance (aññāṇa) is the only cause for rejecting what clearly exists by nature. 'Cause of defilement' (saṃkilesapaccaya) means the cause of becoming defiled or stained.
39:
...is the cause. 'Cause of purification' (visuddhipaccaya) means the cause of purification (vodāna) from defilement. In the term 'attakāre', the formation of the word ending in 'e' by way of the nominative case (paccattavacana) is like the example 'vanappagumbe yathā phusitagge.' Alternatively, it is the use of the locative case (bhummavacana) in the sense of the nominative, as in the example 'idampissa hoti sīlasmiṃ.' This very meaning is shown by the term 'attakāro.' That 'attakāra' is the work to be done by each being themselves, or the effort and application to be accomplished by oneself. Therefore, it says 'by which,' etc. 'Sabbaññutaṃ' means the Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). 'Taṃ' means the action performed by oneself.

It is shown by the second term, 'there is no effort by others' (natthi parakāre). What is called 'parakāra' is the effort and application that succeeds through the leadership or assistance of others. Therefore, it says 'which effort by others,' etc. 'Ovādānusāsanī' means instruction that is advice. Or, the initial advice is 'ovāda', and the subsequent instruction is 'anusāsanī'. This is an explanation of the meaning of the term 'parakāra' by way of its characteristics. Since there is no reliance on the effort of others in the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma), it says 'except for the Great Being (Mahāsatta).' Such reliance on others does exist in mundane states (lokiya-dhamma). For example, our Bodhisatta attained the five mundane super-knowledges and attainments by relying on Āḷāra and Uddaka. That statement is made with reference to the Great Being in his final existence (pacchimabhavika). The Paccekabodhisatta-to-be should also be included here, because they too lack such reliance on others.

'Manussasobhagyataṃ' means the state of being fortunate or splendid among humans. 'Thus' (evaṃ) means by the rejection of the doctrines of action (kammavāda) and performance (kiriyavāda) in the manner described. 'In the Conqueror's Wheel' (jinacakke) means in the Buddha's Dispensation (Buddhasāsana), which clearly demonstrates the existence of actions and their results through methods such as 'Monks, there is dark action with dark results.' Speaking in opposition is like delivering a blow; hence it is said 'he delivers a blow.'

Intending that because of the absence of the aforementioned personal effort and effort by others, there is no such thing as individual manly effort (purisakāra) for beings, the rejection of that by Makkhali Gosāla is shown by the phrase 'there is no manly effort' (natthi purisakāre), starting with 'by which,' etc. These are the varieties mentioned as 'even the state of a deity' and 'human splendor,' etc. After saying 'they stand in power' (bale patiṭṭhitā), it says 'having made an effort' to show that here, energy (vīriya) is indeed power (bala). Makkhali Gosāla rejects the power of energy that brings about the welfare of the present life, the future life, and the bliss of Nibbāna for beings. This is merely an illustration of rejecting the power that leads to purification, for he also rejects the power that leads to defilement. If energy and so on are synonyms for manly effort, why are they taken separately? To answer this, it says 'this is by our energy,' etc. 'This is by our energy' means this result has proceeded because of our energy. By way of rejecting the statement of occurrence, [he rejects] the conventional usage of others regarding occurrence...
40:
It means by way of making a rejection. By way of rejecting the doctrine of those who usually speak of the results arising from connection with energy, strength, and effort, it is understood that he (Makkhali Gosāla) takes all these terms like the word "there is no strength." That statement is spoken in terms of the object to be expressed (vacanīyattha); however, in terms of the derivation of the word (vacanattha), it is called 'bala' (strength) because of its abundance in various actions. It is called 'vīriya' (energy) because it brings about a state of courage. That same energy is called 'purisathāma' (manly strength) because of its firmness and because it must be exercised by one who carries the burden of a man. It should be known as 'purisaparakkama' (manly exertion) because it proceeds by way of stepping onto successive stages.

They are called 'satta' (beings) because of their attachment to forms and so on. They are called 'pāṇa' (living beings) because they exist by way of breathing; although these two terms are identical in meaning, he (Makkhali Gosāla) speaks by distinguishing beings according to their having a single faculty and so on, making a distinction from 'satta', thus he says "ekindriya" and so on. They are called 'bhūta' (beings) because they have come to be; although there are synonymous terms like 'satta' and 'pāṇa', they are distinct from those beings because of the sense of appearing within eggshells and so on, therefore he shows they are mentioned by the words "egg... pe... speaks." 'Vatthikosa' means the womb (gabbhāsaya). They are called 'jīva' (souls/vitality) because they grow as if maintaining life through living. Therefore, he says "sāliyava" and so on. By the word 'ādi' (and so on), grass and trees which have the nature of growth are included. They are called 'avasa' (powerless) because they have no power or ability over their own defilement or purification. Likewise, they are 'abala' (without strength) and 'avīriya' (without energy). Therefore, he says "tesaṃ" and so on. 'Niyata' means fixedness (niyamanā); it means the fixity (niyāma) by way of destiny (gati), birth (jāti), bondage (bandha), and liberation (apavagga), because of proceeding in a fixed manner like an unbreakable gem threaded on an uncuttable string. It means in those various lives. The movement connected with the six classes of birth (abhijāti) is called 'samāgama' (convergence) by way of coming together in unison. The word 'bhāva', even without depending on a relative term, expresses the meaning of inherent nature as if it were accompanied by a relative term; therefore, he says it is just 'sabhāva' (nature). Just as the sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of wood-apple fruits and so on, and the diverse forms of animals and birds exist, so too, the transformation of the entire world into various forms in such and such ways, excluding causes and conditions (hetu-paccaya), is just the uncreated inherent nature (sabhāva). Therefore, it is said "yena" and so on. 'Pariṇamana' means reaching various different states. 'Yena' means by way of being a 'satta', 'pāṇa', and so on. It is connected as: "it happens exactly as it must be."

I shall elaborate on the six classes of birth (abhijāti) later. In saying "they experience pleasure and pain," it is said that Makkhali does not know the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (adukkhamasukhabhūmi) at all, thus it is said: "he shows that there is no other plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure." This "sukhañca dukkhañca..."
41:
...paṭisaṃvedenti" is the opinion of the Teacher (the Commentator) stated by taking the word as an instrument (karaṇa). However, in the manuscripts, only this reading is seen: "he shows that there is no other plane of pleasure and pain," and the reading "adukkhamasukhabhūmi" is not found. If this is the case, it should be understood that by taking the phrase "only in the six classes of birth" as the locus (adhikaraṇa), he shows that the experience of pleasure and pain occurs only in the six classes of birth and not elsewhere, and that those six planes alone are the grounds for pleasure and pain, and none other than those. This [interpretation] is more appropriate because the meaning to be rejected is stated by way of the plane (bhūmi).

If the rejection of the meaning were shown by the statement "they experience pleasure and pain," then he should only show "there is no other neither-pain-nor-pleasure (feeling)." He should not show "adukkhamasukhabhūmi" (the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure), because the word which is the reason for showing it lacks the meaning of 'plane' (bhūmi). And this [statement] shows only the non-existence of the plane for those feelings; therefore, it is understood that this reading and this meaning are more appropriate.

"Pamukhayonīnaṃ" refers to the principal origins, such as the Khattiya and Brāhmaṇa among humans, and the lion and tiger among animals. Here, 'principal' (padhānatā) means 'noble' (uttamata). Therefore, he says "uttamayonīnaṃ" (of noble origins). "Saṭṭhi satāni" means six thousand (6,000). The meaning of the phrase "pañca ca kammuno satāni" is "pañca kammasatāni ca" (and five hundred karmas). By the phrase "eseva nayo," he refers only to this meaning: "he explains a useless wrong view by mere reasoning." Here, the Teacher, in saying "takkamattakena" (by mere reasoning), clarifies this intention: because those who rely on reasoning exclude the 'goad-method' (aṅkusa-naya) of grasping the truth which is the basis, and because of their lack of a goad, they regard whatever they have imagined by their own speculation as the essence, and being firmly attached to it, they hold a dogmatic view; therefore, the wise should not investigate their objects of view with wisdom.

"Keci" (some teachers) refers to the teachers residing in the Uttaravihāra. "Pañcindriyavasena" means by way of the five faculties such as the eye-faculty. They say: "The heretics designate these five faculties known as eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body as 'five karmas', and they designate bodily, vocal, and mental actions as 'three karmas'." "Kammanti laddhi" means that both of these (the five faculties and three karmas) are the doctrine of 'complete karma' because they are gross. Mental karma is the doctrine of 'half-karma' because it is not gross—this is the construction of the meaning. While it should be said "dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā" (sixty-two practices), he says "dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā" because he does not know the natural linguistics (sabhāvanirutti). Therefore, the Teacher says "dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā." Grammarians, however, say that in the word "dvāsaṭṭhi," the letter 'sa' is dropped and 'ā' becomes 'a'. That is inappropriate because it does not accord with natural linguistics.
42:
(The elision of the letter 'sa' occurs) because it is not established. If that word were established by being associated with the letter 'sa', it would thus be a natural language (sabhāvanirutti); and if that were the case, it is said that it would contradict the opinion of the teachers. Except for the examples already seen, such as "Cullāsīti sahassāni," other observed examples are indeed natural language. This is seen in texts such as the Visuddhimagga:

"For eighty-four thousand aeons, those deities remain;
Yet even they do not remain, being associated with two thought-moments."

"Ekasmim kappe" (in one aeon) refers to one of the four incalculable aeons (asaṅkheyya-kappa). Among those four, "dwaṭṭhantarakappa" is said with reference only to the one known as the aeon of evolution-duration (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī). The meaning is that Makkhali Gosāla, not having heard the Dhamma of the Dispensation, does not know the other aeons; he says this without knowing because it is not the domain of those outside the Buddha's Dispensation.

Those who kill sheep, or those who make a living by killing them, are called sheep-butchers (orabbhika). This method also applies to bird-hunters (sākuṇika) and others. "Ludda" (hunters) refers to those who make a living by killing any remaining four-footed animals. In the term "māgavika," only species of deer such as the hog-deer are taken. Those who employ others in prison are called jailers (bandhanāgārika). "Kurūrakammanta" means those with cruel occupations. This entire group of people is called "kaṇhābhijāti" (of black birth) because they are devoted to dark, unwholesome deeds, meaning they have the arising of dark states of mind. "Bhikkhū" refers to monks in the Buddha's Dispensation. "Kaṇṭaka" (thorns) refers to desire and lust (chandarāga). Their inclusion is by way of association. Indeed, with the intention that they eat while associated with desire and lust which are like thorns, it is said, "having thrown in thorns."

Why is this? Because Makkhali Gosāla holds the false view that "those monks enjoy very refined requisites." Therefore, he says that even though they consume requisites obtained rightfully, because it is contrary to the Ājīvika doctrine, they are said to eat by throwing thorns of desire and lust into their requisites. "Kaṇṭakavuttika" means making a living together with the aforementioned thorns of desire and lust.

"Ayañhissa pāḷiyeva" means this statement is the very text (Pali) composed by himself to explain the doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla, thus completing the aforementioned meaning. There are other external ascetics called "kaṇṭakavuttika"; the meaning is that he calls them "nīlābhijāti" (of blue birth). They especially practice the devotion to self-mortification. Because they live as if they are on thorns, they are called "kaṇṭakavuttika." One is called "nīlābhijāti" because of the arising of blue (dark) unwholesome states. This method should also be understood for the other classes of birth.
43:
External ascetics who hold the view that "we have no bonds (saṃyojana)" are called Nigaṇṭhas (Jains). Those who habitually wear only a single cloth are called Ekasāṭakas. One who is purer than the black is called Nīla (blue/dark), and beyond that is Lohita (red), and so on; in order to show his doctrine of purity, the phrase beginning with "Ime kira" (these, it is said) is stated. "Paṇḍaratara" (whiter/purer) refers to those who are especially pure due to being associated with practices such as rejecting eating and bathing. This is because, compared to the black and blue, the red is also spoken of as being pure. "Odātavasana" refers to those who wear white clothes. "Acelakasāvaka" refers to those who are disciples of the Ājīvikas. It is said that they are even whiter (purer) than the Nigaṇṭhas because of the purity of mind in the Ājīvika doctrine. This is because, compared to those mentioned before, those with the color of turmeric also attain a state of purity. By the word "Evaṃ" (thus) and so on, he shows Makkhali Gosāla's following of his own desires. Ascetics who are disciples of Nanda and others are Ājīvikas. Likewise, there are female Ājīvikas. It is said that Nanda and others remained having brought such Ājīvika practice to its excellence. Therefore, because they are purer than the Nigaṇṭhas and the ordained Ājīvika disciples, they are called "paramasukkābhijāti" (the highest white birth). This is his doctrine.

"Purisabhūmi" (stages of man) is the primary designation. Makkhali Gosāla desires these stages for women as well. "For seven days" is a term expressing continuous association; it should be understood that for this long, they are dull and deluded. "From the narrow place" is said with reference to the mother's womb. Remembering that, they cry and wail. Including both exhaustion and play under the word "khiddā," it is called "khiddābhūmi" (the stage of play). Placing the foot is "padanikkhipana." The meaning is that when one is able to place the foot in such a way, it is then called "padavīmaṃsabhūmi" (the stage of testing the steps). This is at the time of knowing what is a practice and what is not. The passage beginning with "Bhikkhu ca pannako" is also the very text (Pali) of those external heretics. Therein, "pannaka" means one who wanders for alms, or one who has undertaken their practice. "Jina" means one who is old and of weak faculty due to decay, or one who remains having conquered the opposite states through his own practice. It is said that such a monk does not preach the Dhamma to anyone. Therefore, he said, "he says nothing." Teachers also say that even when improper behaviors such as calling him a camel's face are done, he says nothing by way of patience. "Alābhī" (one who receives nothing) refers to one who receives no gains due to being associated with the causes of non-gain mentioned in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, such as not accepting alms from the mouth of a pot. Because of that very reason, being overwhelmed by the weakness of hunger and being prone to lying down, he calls such a monk "pannabhūmi."

"Ājīvavuttisatāni" refers to the hundred varieties of livelihoods of beings. Although it is said "paribbājakasatāni" (hundreds of wanderers), this Makkhali Gosāla, not knowing the natural gender...
44:
It says "paribbājakasate" (hundreds of wanderers). This applies to other terms as well. Therefore, it is said "paribbājakapabbajjāsatāni" (hundreds of wanderer-ordinations). The abode of the Nagas is called "Nāgamaṇḍala" (Naga-circle), similar to "Mahisakamandala". Dust such as atomic dust is called "rajo". By the term "pasu" (beasts), the species of goats is taken. By the term "miga" (wild animals), species such as ruru-deer and gayals are taken. "Gaṇṭhi" (knot) refers to the knots or joints of a tree. Deities are numerous due to the power of the Cātumahārājikā and others, the Brahmakāyikā and others, and through their internal distinctions. Among those deities, some internal distinctions of the Cātumahārājikā deities should be understood through the Mahāsamaya Sutta.

With the words "so panā" etc., it is shown that Makkhali Gosāla, without knowing, says there are only "seven" types of deities even though they are many, thus demonstrating the limitlessness of his [wrong] view. Humans are also infinite due to divisions of islands, regions, clans, livelihoods, and so on. "Pisāca" (goblins) are called "Pesāca". These ghosts and demons are very numerous and large due to the power of other types of ghosts. In external doctrines, however, the teacher says, "The Chaddanta and Mandākinī lakes are referred to by the names Kuvāḷiya and Mucalinda."

"Gaṇṭhikā" refers to trees with knots. The word "pavuṭṭha" occurs in the sense of a knot. "Mahāpapātā" refers to great precipices. By the method of remainder (pārisesanaya), there are hundreds of small precipices. This should be understood in the same way regarding dreams. The word "mahākappino" should be understood by its meaning as "mahākappānaṃ" (of great aeons). Linguistically, however, this Makkhali says this without knowing, so it is not worthy of investigation. Similarly, the phrase "cullāsīti satasahassāni" is the same. That Makkhali, being unable to say "caturāsīti satasahassāni" (eighty-four hundred thousand), says it this way. Grammarians, however, say that in the word "caturāsīti", the syllable "tu" is dropped, "ca" is changed to "cu", "ra" is changed to "la", and the "la" is doubled to become "cullāsīti".

"These many great lakes" refers to the seven great lakes of this magnitude. The word "kira" is a particle used when his doctrine is heard through tradition. Whether one is a wise man... one cannot transcend [the cycle]. Why? Because the period of wandering in saṃsāra for beings is fixed.

"Whether by the practice of nakedness or by any other practice" is indicated by the term "tādiseneva". "Tapokammena" means by performing ascetic practices. Here too, the term "tādiseneva" follows. In the sentence "whoever... is purified", it should be connected and understood as "that person causes unripened kamma to ripen". "Antarā" means within the eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons. "Phussa phussā" means having reached again and again. "Vuttaparimāṇaṃ kālaṃ" refers to the duration of time measuring eighty-four hundred thousand great aeons. The meaning is this: unripened kamma, which is the cause for wandering in saṃsāra, is quickly [ripened] by virtue and so on...
45:
...is said to be ripened for the sake of attaining purity. By repeatedly touching the ripened kamma and bringing it to the state of being ripened by time, it is said to be exhausted or removed.

"Doṇena" means as if measuring with a "doṇa" (a measuring vessel). Because the meaning is obtained through a metaphorical comparison, the teacher said "as if measured". The fact that there is no decrease or increase [in the cycle] by the power of the wise or the fool is shown by the words "na saṃsāro" etc. "Vaḍḍhanaṃ" means increase (excellence), and "hāpanaṃ" means decrease (deficiency).

"Kaṭasuttaguḷe" means in a prepared ball of thread. "Paleti" means "pareti" (runs/goes), as in the term "abhisamparāyo", but it is said as "paleti" by changing the letter "r" to "l". Since that word "paleti" occurs in the sense of going according to the Curādi group [of verbs], it means "goes". By this analogy, this Makkhali clarifies the meaning that the saṃsāra of beings only exhausts itself sequentially and does not increase because it has a finite nature. Therefore, he says "sutte khīṇe" etc. "Tattheva" means only at the place of exhaustion.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambala

By the word "dinnaṃ" (given), only the intention of giving (dāna-cetanā) is stated, taking the gift-object as the primary head. That the fruit is also intended through that intention is shown by the words "the non-existence of the fruit of what is given". In the primary sense, "dinna" refers to objects such as food; how could this Ajita deny those objects such as food? This same method applies to the terms "yiṭṭhaṃ" (sacrifice) and "hutaṃ" (offering). A great gift common to all is called "mahāyāga". The honor to be performed for those who have arrived as guests is called "pāhunakasakkāra". "Phalaṃ" refers to both the benefit (āniśaṃsa) and the result (nissanda). "Vipāko" means the fruit similar to the kamma. For instance, in a gift endowed with four factors, attaining a high position etc. is the benefit (āniśaṃsa). In the gift of the Brahmin Saṅkha, obtaining protection while shipwrecked in the ocean is the result (nissanda). The fruit similar to the kamma, known as rebirth-linking, is the resultant (vipāka). "This world" and "the next world" refer to the worlds to be obtained through kamma, because they are denied with the intention of the non-existence of fruit. Indeed, by what reason could that Ajita deny the world that is directly perceived? By the words "all are annihilated in those very places", he states the reason: in whatever birth-origins etc. these beings are situated, they are annihilated in those very places; the meaning is that they perish through the power of destruction without re-arising. "Tesu" refers to mothers and fathers. He speaks only in terms of the non-existence of fruit, not that mothers and fathers do not exist, nor because of the non-existence of honor or dishonor currently performed towards those mothers and fathers. This is because those mothers and fathers are directly evident in the world. The arising of these beings is merely an arising, like that of a bubble; there is no such thing as coming [to this life] after having passed away [from a previous one]...
46:
To show the meaning of the statement "Natthi sattā opapātikā" (There are no beings who are reborn spontaneously), it is said, "There is no such thing as a being who, having passed away, is reborn." A recluse (samaṇa) who knows things as they truly are should remain restrained without telling anyone; otherwise, it would be a mere boastful display of a man (ahopurisikā). How can one person do anything for another? Likewise, there can be no reliance on anyone for the fulfillment of one's own goals, because existence is cut off right there in those various lives. With this meaning in mind, it is said, "Those who... proclaim thus." This is the remaining meaning from the Commentary.

Because it is connected with the four great elements, it is called "cātumahābhūtika." To show the meaning, it is said "made of the four great elements." Just as a pot made of clay is called a clay pot (mattikāmaya), so too this being is called "made of the four great elements" (catumahābhūtamaya) because it arises from the four great elements. The internal earth element (ajjhattika-paṭhavīdhātu) refers to the earth element within the continuity of beings. The external earth element (bāhira-paṭhavīdhātu) refers to the great earth outside; by this, it shows that the earth element itself is the body (kāya). "Anugacchati" means it follows. "Ubhayenāpi" means by both terms. "Upeti upagacchati" means the earth element, which is a part of the external earth mass, comes and reaches the internal continuity, existing as a being; and just as the earth element in a pot etc. returns to the great earth, now too it returns to that same external earth mass which is the aggregate. In every way, it means it reaches a state of no distinction, a state of oneness with that external earth mass. "The same method applies to the water element etc." In this context, just as water taken from the great ocean by the rain-god returns to the great ocean as rainwater; just as the heat element called Indra's fire (indaggi) taken from the sun's rays returns to the sun's rays; just as the wind that comes out from a great mass of wind returns to the great mass of wind—this is the intention of the one with wrong view, expressed through mere imagination.

"Manas-chaṭṭhāni indriyāni" means the sense faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, of which the mind (manas) is the sixth. They say these faculties fly into the sky because the sky is the object of those faculties. By taking the possessor of the object (visayī), the objects (visaya) are also taken. To the question "How are the things with the couch as the fifth (mañcapañcamā) counted?", it is said "The couch... meaning." The two terms "āḷāhana" and "susāna" (cemetery) are the same in meaning. "Guṇāguṇapadāni" refers to the groups of merits and faults. Or, "padāni" refers to the body (sarīra) itself because it is reached through various actions. "Pārāvatapakkhi-vaṇṇāni" means having a color like that of a pigeon. There is also a reading "pārāvatapakkhavaṇṇāni," meaning having a color like the wings of a pigeon.
47:
"Bhasmanta" means ending in ashes. Therefore, it is said, "only ending in ashes." In this doctrine, by the word "āhuti," all types of giving described as "given, offered, sacrificed" are included, as shown by the phrase "giving such as hospitality and honor." Alternatively, this description "āhutiyo" is a virūpa-ekasesa-niddesa. "Ākāsaṃ" (space) is the meaning by intention, because that meaning cannot be reached through the word itself. In such cases, the wise should understand. Fools who are deluded are called "dattū." Regarding those fools, to the question "What is meant by 'Fools give' etc.?", it is said "Bālā denti" etc. In the Pali, those who hold the view "the world exists" are called "atthika." The word "atthi" is an indeclinable (nipāta). Their doctrine is called "atthikavāda." That atthikavāda is being explained.

Among those three aforementioned holders of wrong views: [One] denies action (kamma) because of being a proponent of non-action (akiriyavāda). [One] denies the result (vipāka) because of rejecting rebirth in a future life entirely. "Vipāka" refers to the three types of results: blessing-result (āniśaṃsa-phala), consequence-result (nissanda-phala), and similar-result (sadisa-phala). [One] denies both because by denying the cause (hetu) in every way, the result (phala) is also denied. "Both" refers to action and result. That Ajita, by saying "Beings are defiled and purified without cause or condition," shows that there is no cause for defilement or purification of the result, just as there is none for action; thus he is said to deny both. If there is no action, there can be no result; thus the result is denied. If there is no result, action becomes futile; thus action is denied. The word "iti" indicates the aforementioned meaning. "Atthato" means in essence; although they appear separately in the Pali as representing various wrong views, the meaning is that they all deny both [cause and effect].

Because they deny both, they are each holders of the three types of views. The description "deniers of both" is a causal statement because it contains the reason (hetu). "Ahetukavādā ceva" etc. is a statement of admission because it is determined as the result of that. Therefore, the connection of cause and effect should be understood as follows: by denying the result, it is "natthikavāda" (nihilism); by denying action, it is "akiriyavāda" (non-action); by denying both, it is "ahetukavāda" (non-causality). One who is a proponent of annihilation (ucchedavāda) with the view of nihilism by denying the result, is also in essence a proponent of non-action by denying action, and a proponent of non-causality by denying both. The same method applies to the other two doctrines.

With the words "Ye vā pana" etc., the decision on the fixed entry into wrongness of the followers of those wrong views is stated. In that sentence, "tesaṃ" refers to [the views of] Pūraṇa Kassapa and others. "Sajjhāyanti" means they learn and recite the texts composed by Pūraṇa Kassapa and others that explain those views.
48:
They learn and recite the treatises on wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) composed by Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, and Ajita exactly as they were made. "Vīmaṃsanti" means they investigate and reflect on the meaning of those treatises. The words beginning with "tesaṃ" show the manner of investigation. The connection of the meaning should be made as: "to those who investigate in this way, 'For one who acts... it is abolished'."

"In that object" means in the object of the view known as wrong vision (micchā-dassana), which proceeds by way of "For one who acts, no evil is done," etc., based on the imagined absence of the results of kamma. Craving (taṇhā) accompanied by the view known as wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) is established there. Indeed, when the meaning received through oral tradition by way of "For one who acts, no evil is done," etc., appears in the mind in its own form as if it were a physical body through reflections on that manner, it reaches a state capable of being contemplated as "This is so" due to long-term familiarity. For one who, through such capability of contemplation, repeatedly resorts to and cultivates the view taken in such a manner, it is well-led by wrong thought (micchā-vitakka) and supported by wrong effort (micchā-vāyāma). Thus, craving accompanied by wrong view, which takes even that which is not the true nature as "the true nature," is called "wrong mindfulness" because it occurs by way of remembering what is false and distorted. This meaning is also stated in the Caturaṅguttara-ṭīkā. In the commentary on the Sallekha Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it is stated that there is no separate dhamma called wrong mindfulness like wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa), etc.; it is merely a designation for the four unwholesome aggregates taken with craving as the head.

"The mind is one-pointed" means that by obtaining the appropriate conditions such as vitakka, etc., the mind becomes one-pointed as if reaching absorption (appanā), having abandoned non-one-pointedness due to its stability in that object. Here, by way of the mind, only wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi) is intended. It should be understood that this wrong concentration, having gained the power of development (bhāvana) through specific conditions, performs the function of a counterfeit concentration in such a state of wrong view, similar to the concentration used in hair-splitting (vālavedhī) and so on. "Javanas run" means that after the preceding javana-processes have occurred many times in that manner, seven javanas run in the final javana-process which constitutes the decision. The statement, "In the first javana, it is remediable; likewise in the second, etc.," is merely a demonstration of the nature of dhammas (dhamma-sabhāva). It does not mean that anyone is able to cure them at that moment, because once established in those javanas, it is impossible to turn back the seventh javana which will inevitably arise, and because in such a rapidly changing mental process, curing through advice and instruction is impossible. Therefore, [the teachers] said, "Even the Buddhas cannot cure them."
49:
"Those who do not turn back" (anivattino) refers to those who are like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇḍaka. It means that like them, they are incurable and cannot be restrained, having been born into the destiny of those with wrong views.

Among those three types of wrong views, "someone enters one view" means that if a person has obsession and repeated practice in only one wrong view, that person enters only one view. "Someone enters two, someone enters three" means that if a person has obsession and repeated practice in two or three views, that person enters two or three. By this statement, the state of having all views—which was previously shown by way of the obstruction of both [kamma and its result] through the words "Thus all these, in meaning, are obstructors of both," etc., and which is established in meaning—is the preceding stage. However, the state of having all views that constitutes the entry into the fixedness of wrongness (micchatta-niyāma) is shown to be unmixed with one another, just as there is no simultaneous attainment of distinct realizations like the jhānas, paths, and fruits which have different objects, because it is established through the fulfillment of its own respective conditions.

By the words "Even if one enters one," etc., the equal potency and equal result of all three views are made clear. These views have equal potency and equal result by way of obstructing heaven, etc. Therefore, even if these three views arise in a single person, they remain unmixed and distinct. It should be understood that when one view gives its result, the other two wrong views provide support to that result-giving view. Having stated "He reaches the obstruction of the path to heaven," etc., the meaning is made clear by the word "incapable" (abhabbo). "Obstruction of the path to liberation" means the blocking of the Noble Path which is the way to Nibbāna. "Pageva" (let alone) is a particle in the sense of rejection; the meaning is: what need is there to speak of going to Nibbāna, which is called liberation? Alternatively, dividing "pageva" as "pā eva," it means he is incapable of going to liberation in the first place; he is very far from reaching liberation. This should be understood accordingly in other places as well.

The statement "This being is called a stump of the round (vaṭṭakhāṇu)" is a statement of provisional meaning (neyyattha), not of definitive meaning (nītattha). Thus, it is said in the Majjhima Nikāya commentary named Papañcasūdanī: "Is this person fixed only in one existence (attabhāva), or in another as well? He is fixed only in one existence; however, due to the power of repeated practice, he certainly delights in those views in other lives as well." Unwholesome states are weak and feeble; they are not powerful and great in strength like wholesome states. Therefore, it is said in that commentary that "he is fixed only in one existence." Otherwise, the fixedness of wrongness (micchatta-niyāma) would be eternal like the fixedness of rightness (sammatta-niyāma), but it is not eternal. If it is not eternal, how can the illustration as a "stump of the round" be appropriate? Because of such a potential objection...
50:
The statement "This person is called a stump of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭakhāṇu)" is a statement of interpretable meaning (neyyattha), whose meaning must be drawn out. It is not a statement of definitive meaning (nītattha). For this very reason, in the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī, the question was asked: "Is this person of wrong view fixed only in one individual existence, or is he fixed in other existences as well?" and the answer given was: "He is fixed only in one individual existence; however, through the power of repetition (āsevana), he continues to delight in that same wrong view in other lives as well."

In truth, that unwholesome state is not as powerful as the wholesome; it is quite weak. Therefore, he is fixed only in one individual existence. Otherwise, if it were an absolutely fixed wrongness (micchattaniyāma) like the Noble Path, how would the illustration of being a "stump of the round of rebirths" be appropriate? Therefore, it was said in the commentary, "by way of repetition" (āsevana-vasena), and so on. Just as it is stated in the Sattakanipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, "A fool, even if he sinks once, remains sunk," so too is the illustration of the "stump of the round of rebirths" mentioned here. The reason is that it cannot be said that this person, having entered into various wrong views based on certain causes, will never have the opportunity to raise his head from the round of rebirths by depending on causes that are contrary to those wrong views at some later time. Therefore, both in that Majjhima Nikāya commentary and in this Sīlakkhandhavagga commentary, the term "mostly" (yebuyyena) is used in the phrase, "For such a person, there is mostly no emergence from the round."

Thus, because he delights in various wrong views in other lives through the power of repetition, it means that for him, there is mostly no emergence from the round. Therefore, this person is called a "stump of the round of rebirths." He is not called a "stump" because of an absolute certainty of fixed wrongness (micchattaniyāma). In this way, it should be understood that this statement is only of interpretable meaning (neyyattha) and not of definitive meaning (nītattha), as its meaning must be drawn out. With this meaning in mind, it was also stated in the Khandha Yamaka of the Abhidhamma: "The Arahants and those worldlings who will not attain the Path do not fully understand the aggregate of form, nor will they fully understand the aggregate of feeling," and so on. "Earth-protector" (pathavigopaka) refers to one who guards the earth for the reasons mentioned above. To confirm this meaning, the phrase "mostly" (yebuyyena) and so on was stated.

Thus, following the explanation of the extreme fault of wrong view, the phrase beginning with "Therefore" (tasmā) was said to arouse mindfulness in the listeners. Therein, "therefore" (tasmā) should be connected as: "Since the cause of his being a stump of the round is like a sproutless [stump] in this manner, therefore one should avoid [him]." "Unvirtuous person" (akalyāṇajana) means a person devoid of good qualities, a wicked person. "Venomous snake" (āsīvisa) means a snake with deadly poison that acts quickly. "Desiring welfare" (bhūtikāma) means one who desires the growth of one's own virtues by way of benefits in the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal. "Discerning" (vicakkhaṇa) means a wise person (dhīra) who sees various meanings with the eye of wisdom.

## Commentary on Pakudha Kaccāyana’s Doctrine
In the word "akaṭā," the letter 'ta' is substituted with 'ṭa', thus it means "uncreated" (akata). It means they are not made or fashioned by any cause, whether even or uneven. The same applies to the word "akaṭavidhā." They are called "akaṭavidhā" because there is no process of creation or fashioning for them. Through both terms, he shows that they do not arise in the world through any cause or condition. Therefore, he said "Do it thus," and so on. They are not created even by the psychic power of any person who has attained mastery over the mind, nor by a deity, a creator god (Issara), or others. "Animmāpitā" means they are not caused to be created by anyone.
51: It is not created by anyone. Although it is appropriate in terms of grammar and similar in meaning to the previous word, the fact that it does not appear in the Pāḷi and the Commentary is the reason it should not be accepted, as shown by the words "Taṃ neva pāḷiyaṃ" and so on. It is exactly as explained in the Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. Here, I will provide only the connection (yojanā): "Vañjhā" means it is fruitless and does not produce anything, like a barren animal or a barren palm tree. By this word "vañjhā", the ability of the earth-body (pathavīkāya) and others to produce form (rūpa) and so on is rejected. It is the view of that Pakudha that form, sound, and so on are independent and not connected to the earth-body and others. They are called "kūṭaṭṭhā" because they stand like a mountain peak. Just as a mountain peak is not created by anyone and does not produce any effect, so too are these seven bodies—this is the meaning. When it is said, "A sprout arises from a seed," that sprout emerges only because it already exists in that seed; it does not emerge if it does not exist. Otherwise, one thing could be found arising from another. Since these seven bodies are also like that, they stand firm like a gate-pillar (esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhitā). "Ṭhitattā" means standing well without change. "Na calanti" means they do not undergo alteration. Because there is no alteration, these seven bodies stand firm like a gate-pillar, are unshakable, and always remain in their original nature. Therefore, it is said, "Na vipariṇamanti—they do not change or transform." "Pakati" refers to nature. Because they have no nature of changing, they do not harm one another. Only if there were a condition that could cause change could there be a harmer; likewise, only if there were a condition that could provide benefit could there be a benefactor. To show that there is no such harmer or benefactor, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "Nālaṃ" and so on. The earth itself is called "pathavīkāya" because it is a portion of the body, just as one says, "The ocean is seen." Alternatively, because the word "kāya" denotes a group, a collection of earth is called "pathavīkāya," just as one says, "an elephant-body (a herd of elephants)." Because the seven bodies, with the soul (jīva) as the seventh, are permanent and changeless, they cannot be harmed or killed. Therefore, to show that there is no killer or one who causes to kill, it is stated in the Pāḷi as "Sattannaṃ tveva kāyānaṃ" and so on. If there is no killer, how can there be a blow with a weapon? To answer this objection, it is stated as "Yathā" and so on. There, "sattannaṃ tveva" means only seven. The word "iti" here is a mere particle. "Pahataṃ" means a blow; a sharp-edged weapon and so on merely passes through the space between the bodies, not into the bodies themselves. This means that there is only the perception in those people that "I am depriving this person of life." In the ultimate sense, because the bodies are indestructible, there is no such thing as harming or killing.
52:
## Explanation of the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta

Four parts are called catuyāma; that catuyāma itself is called cātuyāma. Here, the word yāma has the meaning of "part", as in "the first watch (yāma) of the night". Because that part is marked by restraint in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, it is said, "one who is restrained by the restraint consisting of four parts". Alternatively, the word yāma has the meaning of restraint; making restraint yāma, even without a prefix, it expresses the meaning of restraint just like a word with a prefix, as in "yatatto" and so on. Since that restraint is performed in four ways, it is said, "by the restraint consisting of four parts". The words ākāra (way/aspect) and koṭṭhāsa (part) are identical in meaning.

For whichever Nātaputta the use of all cold water is forbidden, he is called "one for whom all water is forbidden", like the word "ajyāhito". Therefore, it is said, "one who has all water forbidden". Here, by the word vāri (water), the use of water is meant, as in "rattūparato" (abstaining at night). He for whom all cold water and its use are rejected is so named. The word "taṃ" refers to cold water.

By the word "sabbavāriyutto", only the characteristic of restraint is mentioned. By the word "sabbavāridhuto", the characteristic of being free from the affliction of evil is mentioned. By the word "sabbavārifuṭṭho", the characteristic of the exhaustion of karma is mentioned. To show this meaning, it is said "sabbေna" and so on. "Endowed with the prevention of all evil" means being possessed of the prevention of evil which has the characteristic of restraint in every way. "Dhutapāpo" means one whose evil is shaken off by the prevention of evil which has the characteristic of nijjara (wearing away). "Phuṭṭho" means one who is pervaded by the prevention of all evil which has the characteristic of the exhaustion of karma, due to reaching liberation (mokkha) by exhausting the eight types of karma; the meaning is that he stands having reached that state.

Just as in "There are only two destinations, no other" and so on, the root gamu has the meaning of "reaching the end", so it is said, "one whose mind has reached the end". The meaning is one whose mind has reached the highest limit by the attainment of liberation.
