Because there is no longer anything to be restrained in the senses such as the body, he is called "one with a restrained mind". Here, the suffix "ta" is in the past tense. Because there is no remaining thing to be restrained, he is called "one with a well-established mind".

"It is somewhat in accordance with the Teaching" is said with reference to the prevention of evil. "Because of having an impure view" means because of having a defiled view such as "The soul exists; that soul is sometimes permanent, sometimes impermanent," and so on. "Sabbā" refers to all views that are capable of being contemplated, such as those concerning the analysis of the nature of karma. "Diṭṭhiyeva" means they are only wrong views.
53:
## Commentary on the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta

179-181. The phrase "in the same manner as stated in the Amarāvikkhepa [doctrine]" means in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Amarāvikkhepavāda (Endless Equivocation) in the Brahmajāla Sutta (DN-A. 1.61). Why? Because it is an explanation of a wavering or equivocal answer, and because the Vikkhepavāda (Doctrine of Equivocation) appears there in the same way.

## Commentary on the First Visible Fruit of Recluseship

"Pīḷetvā" means squeezing with an oil mill; by this, the mental application (ābhoga) of King Ajātasattu is expressed. Indeed, the determination of meaning in all instances is made through the power of the speaker's mental application. The teachers of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathācariya) also knew that king's mental application, and they do not contradict the meaning handed down through the lineage of teachers. Therefore, in all instances, the meaning is not stated merely because there is an opportunity to say so, but rather it should be understood that it is stated according to what those teachers intended to say. Having done so, the discernment of meaning is performed through the power of extracting the sense in various places.

"Yathā te rucceyya" means "in whatever way the meaning I am now asking about may please your mind," or "it should be pleasing to your mind." This verb "rucceyya" is used in the passive sense (kamma). Alternatively, it can mean "may the meaning I am now asking about be pleasing to you, who are the recipient (sampadāna)." A slave born from the womb of a female slave in the house is called "antojāta." A slave bought with wealth is called "dhanakkīta." A slave captured and brought from the battlefield is called "karamarānīta." One who has entered into slavery by oneself for some reason is called "sāmaṃdāsabyopagata." "Sāmaṃ" means by oneself. "Dāsabyaṃ" means the state of a slave. Even if someone is a slave, if they are lazy and do not perform work, they are not called a "kammakāra" (worker); but because this slave is not like that, the qualification "analasa" (not lazy) etc., is used. "Dūrato" refers to the master coming from a far distance. "Paṭhamameva" means even before [the master] approaches one's own immediate vicinity. "Uṭṭhahati" means standing up out of respect, or it means going out to meet (paccuṭṭhāti). "Pacchā" means lying down to sleep after the master has slept. "Sayanato avuṭṭhite" means before [the master] has risen from bed at the time of dawn. "Paccūsakālato" means starting from the dawn of the past night. "Yāva sāmino rattiṃ niddokkamananaṃ" means until the time of falling asleep in the early part of the coming night. It means that having performed all duties between the dawn of the past night and the early night of the coming night, he sleeps afterwards.
54:
This is the intended meaning. "Kiṃ kārameva" means asking "What task should I perform?" and because it is done after asking, it means "service (veyyāvacca) performed after inquiring." Because the state of moving about nearby is expressed through attentive listening, it is said, "he moves about listening." By the words "joyful and delighted," it is also shown that he is not one who is unable to look at an angry face.

"Like a god (deva)" means like a chief deity endowed with sovereignty, retinue, and so on. By this, it is made known that the word "maññe" here has the sense of a simile (upama), as in the Pali: "I think (maññe) it stood like the axle-stroke, beautifying the inner palace of King Mahāsudassana" (DN. 2.245). In the phrase "so vatassāhaṃ," the word analysis is "so vata assaṃ ahaṃ," meaning "May I also be like that king." If it be asked, "By what means?", the meaning is "If I were to perform meritorious deeds, then [I would be like him]," hence it is said "so vat vata ahaṃ" etc. The word "vata" is used in the sense of a simile. Therefore, it says "of such a nature." "Meritorious deeds (puññāni)" refers to particularly noble merit, because it intends the noble renunciation (pabbajjā) which is more excellent than merit performed at other times.

In the reading "so vatassāyaṃ," it also means "May this 'I' also be like that king." How? Because the meaning "If I were to perform meritorious deeds" is possible, it is said "this is the very meaning." Although the word "ahaṃ" is not directly used with the first-person verb "assaṃ," it is as if it were used because it is referred to by the word "ayaṃ." Some teachers desire the meaning of the first reading to be: "If I were to perform meritorious deeds, oh, may I be of such a nature [as that king]." If this were so, in the second reading, it should not be said "this is the very meaning," because in that second reading, the word "ahaṃ" is referred to by the word "ayaṃ," and because there is the possibility of another [the king] being referred to by the word "so."

"Yaṃ" refers to the gift (dāna). "Even a hundredth part" means having divided the gift given by the king into a hundred parts, even one single part among them. "I shall not be able to give as long as I live" means that even if one strives to give for the duration of one's life, one would not be able to give even a hundredth part; therefore, having made an effort towards renunciation, the meaning is "I shall renounce." The particle "yaṃnūna" is in the sense of reflection, hence it is said "the state of thinking thus."

"Guarded by the body (kāyena pihito)" means closed by way of restraint of unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) that tend to occur through the body-door and which should be restrained by the body. Because the meaning, by way of expressing diligent effort, must be connected with the word "vihareyya," it is said "having closed the door of entry for unwholesome states." The word "having become (hutvā)" is the remaining part of the Pali. "The door of entry for unwholesome states" refers to the door known as bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), which is the place of entry for unwholesome deeds consisting of bodily actions.
55:
"In the remaining two phrases" means in the two phrases "he should be restrained in speech, he should be restrained in mind." "Because of being limited by food and clothing" means being limited by the power of austerity in seeking food and clothing; or, being established in the highest state, for this monk, food and clothing alone are the ultimate limit and measure; he does not seek or long for any other material gain beyond that. Therefore, he is called one who is limited by food and clothing. His state is "the state of being limited by food and clothing"—this is also a method outside the commentary. It is called "ghāsa" (food/nutriment) because it is eaten. It is called "acchādana" (clothing/robe) because one is covered or enveloped by this cloth. Alternatively, eating is called "ghāsa," and enveloping is called "acchādana"—this is also appropriate. "For this purpose also" means for the purpose of food and clothing. "Improper seeking" refers to the twenty-one types of improper seeking.

"Those whose bodies are established in seclusion" means those whose bodies are established in a place secluded from the crowd; it is the connection of "kāyaviveka" (physical seclusion) for those monks who are thus connected. "Delighting in renunciation" means those monks who delight in jhāna. "Reached supreme purity" means those monks who have reached the supreme, especially pure, purity of mind through that very delight in jhāna. "Without substrates" means those monks who are absolutely free from the substrates of defilements (kilesūpadhi) and the substrates of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhārūpadhi). Nibbāna is called "visaṅkhāra" (the unconditioned); those who are "visaṅkhāragata" (gone to the unconditioned) are the Arahants who have attained that Nibbāna. By the words "When this was said," it shows the occurrence in the Mahāniddesa Pāḷi.

In this context, the first seclusion (physical seclusion) should be mentioned together with the remaining two seclusions, because when the remaining seclusions are accomplished, that physical seclusion is also accomplished. However, apart from that physical seclusion, even if physical seclusion is accomplished, the remaining seclusions cannot be accomplished. Likewise, the second seclusion (mental seclusion) is the same. The third seclusion (seclusion from substrates), however, should only be mentioned together with the remaining seclusions. It should be understood that the third seclusion can only be accomplished when the remaining seclusions are accomplished. The words beginning with "abandoning the gathering of the crowd" are a clear explanation of the meaning of those seclusions. In that context, gathering among the people is called "gaṇasaṅgaṇikā"; it means abandoning that gathering. He dwells and wanders alone bodily because of being without a companion by way of person. The gathering of defilements in the mind is called "cittakilesasaṅgaṇikā"; it means abandoning that gathering. He dwells alone because of being without a companion by way of defilements.

Because the path (magga) lasts for only a single mind-moment, and because states such as change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) are merely the act of taking an object, the experience of the supreme bliss of peace cannot be achieved through the power of that path or change-of-lineage. Since the experience of the supreme bliss of peace can only be achieved through the power of fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), it is said, "either fruition attainment or the attainment of cessation." Indeed, the attainment of cessation culminates in fruition. "Having entered" means having made it internal by way of attainment. In the phrase "having reached Nibbāna," this is a word expressing effort, because reaching peace is desired through taking the object and through the cessation of mind and mental factors.
56:
Because reaching peace is desired, and in the sense of making an effort to make it known (this is said).

'Abhiharitvā' means bringing forward in a face-to-face manner. 'Naṃ' refers to one who dwells in the monkhood in such a manner. 'Abhihāra' means bringing forward by way of invitation. It should be construed and read with the remaining words: "I will fulfill the need with robes and so forth." Likewise, it should also be construed with the words: "Whatever you have need of, please say so." 'Cīvarādivēkalla' refers to the state of deficiency due to the coarseness of robes and so forth. 'Tadubhayaṃ' refers to both of those types of abhihāra. 'Sappāya' (suitable) refers to that which is beneficial by removing all illnesses. Guarding by preventing future harm is called 'rakkhāgutti'. Guarding by prohibiting present harm is called 'āvaraṇagutti'. Because it was asked what the purpose of the qualifier "dhāmmika" (righteous) is, the words beginning with "Sā panēsā" are stated. 'Vihārasīmāya' means in the precinct boundary or in the boundary of gains.

The entire phrase 'yadi evaṃ' (if so) refers back to the meaning previously stated, thus the words beginning with "If he is your slave" are stated. 'Evaṃ sante' means if it is obtainable in this way. The state of being the first occurs in relation to the second; therefore, one who says "first" also indicates the existence of another. Based on that very reason, the king also spoke thus; to show this, the words beginning with "saying first" are stated. 'Tēneva' means only by indicating the existence of another through that word "first" (the Description of the Second Visible Fruit of Recluseship is finished).

## Description of the Second Visible Fruit of Recluseship

'Kasati' means he scratches (with a plow), he performs farming. In the term 'gahapatika', the suffix '-ka' expresses the sense of "small/minor," thus it is said: "one who is the head of only a single house." This is what is meant: the master of a house is a 'gahapati'; a small householder is called 'gahapatika' because he is the head of only a single house. Since his state of being small is only by way of the house, it is said: "in only a single house." By that word, being the head of many families is excluded. The terms 'gaha' and 'geha' are identical in meaning. The word 'kara' occurs in the sense of tax/tribute, thus it is said: "that which is called tax." 'Karoti' means he accomplishes or completes. 'Vaḍḍhēti' means he makes a great accumulation by producing more and more.

As to why both (small and large wealth) are mentioned, it is stated with the words beginning with "Yathā hi." It is to show that it is difficult to renounce even a small amount of wealth to become a monk, and to make it known that it is needless to say how much more difficult it is to renounce a large amount of wealth (both are mentioned).
57:
It is the nature of the commentators to make known another meaning in a certain way. The difficulty of renouncing even a small amount of wealth to become a monk is shown in the Laṭukikopama Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka in the Majjhima Nikāya. In that Sutta, it is preached in detail: "Udāyī, there is a poor man, who has no property of his own, who is not wealthy. He has a small, dilapidated hut, frequented by crows, which is not of excellent appearance, and a single dilapidated bamboo couch, which is not of excellent appearance."

If renouncing even a small amount of wealth to become a monk is difficult, one might ask why wealth (bhoga) is not included in the section on the slave (dāsavāra). Therefore, the commentator said, "Dāsavāre pana," and so on. "Not even master of himself" means he himself has no self-mastery. Just as the slave's possessions are not truly his own because they belong to another (his master), so it is with his relatives. Therefore, it should be understood that the circle of relatives (ñātiparivaṭṭa) is also not included in the section on the slave. It is called "parivaṭṭa" because it revolves all around in succession; it refers to relatives. Therefore, it is said, "The relative himself is the circle of relatives (ñātiparivaṭṭa)."

## Commentary on the More Excellent Fruits of Recluseship

"Taṃ" refers to the meaning intended when investigating: "Just as 'even so' (evam-eva) was said in the section on the slave, why is that word not said here in the section on the farmer?" If "evam-eva" were said, it would mean: "Just as the first and second fruits of recluseship were designated, can they be designated in the same way?" "Of such a nature" refers to similes similar to the previously mentioned similes of the slave and the farmer. Because of the state of having infinite and brilliant wisdom, and because of the nature of the teaching having diverse methods, he is able to show the fruits of recluseship.

In showing it thus, there is no such thing as a limit because it is a teaching preached with infinite methods. Alternatively, because it creates a desire to hear again and again due to not being satiated by hearing, it means there is no limit to the desire to hear. "Even so" means "Even though the teaching has the quality of being diverse with various methods that are increasingly superior," as said by the Teacher. The meaning "even though there is such an infinite state" is also appropriate. Thinking with the knowledge of inference, "distinction above" means setting aside that (sāmañña) and asking only about the fruit of recluseship that is more distinguished than that. Why? He said "savane," and so on. By this, he shows this meaning: "Even though words have many meanings, they indicate those respective meanings only according to the sequence of the intended desire to speak."

"Sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" are the same in meaning. This is because the word "sādhu" itself is spoken by increasing it with the letter "ka." Therefore, the Teacher, when stating the meaning of the word "sādhukaṃ," used the word "sādhu"...
58:
...is brought forth by way of extracting the meaning. By such extraction, the objection that "only the meaning of the word sādhukaṃ should be stated, not the specific meaning of the word sādhu" is prohibited. "Āyācana" means requesting in person, meaning an aspiration. "Sampaṭicchana" means accepting. "Sampahaṃsana" means gladdening or pleasing by way of existing virtues, meaning making one's manner uplifted.

The verse "Sādhu dhammaruci" is found in the Ummādantī Jātaka. In that verse, the sequence of the commentary's decision is as follows: He is called "dhammaruci" because he delights in the Dhamma of good conduct, meaning one who delights in the Dhamma. Such a person, even if he were to give up his life, would not do what should not be done. "Paññāṇavā" means one who is wise, endowed with knowledge. "Mittānamaddubbho" means not betraying friends. "One who does not wrong, one who does not harm," said the Teacher. There is also a reading as "adrubbho," by changing the letter "da" to "dra."

"Daḷhīkamma" occurs in the sense of doing constantly. "Āṇatti" occurs in the sense of commanding. "Here also" means in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta as well. "To him" means of the word sādhukaṃ. In the sentence "Suṇohi sādhukaṃ manasi karohi," the word sādhukaṃ illuminates both the constant performance of listening and paying attention, and the command to so listen and pay attention. Because the general nature of urging is included in requesting, commanding (āṇatti) is not separately mentioned in the extraction of meanings. There is this distinction: commanding (āṇatti) is for one who is worthy of a command, and requesting (āyācana) is for one who is not worthy of a command. "In the beautiful also" means it also occurs in the sense of beautiful. Now, to show the distinction revealed by the three meanings of the word sādhukaṃ as mentioned, or to clarify the suitability of those three meanings here, he said "Daḷhīkammatthena hi," and so on. "Suggahitaṃ gaṇhanto" means taking by making a good grasp. The word "sundaraṃ" is an abstract neuter term (bhāvana-napuṃsaka) that illustrates the action. "Bhaddakaṃ" has the meaning of being praised and should be connected with the word "dhammaṃ." Alternatively, the two words "sundaraṃ" and "bhaddakaṃ" are synonymous terms used in listening and grasping.

In the phrase "manasi karohi," it is not the attention (manasikāra) characterized by presenting the object, but rather the attention characterized by establishing in the mind preceded by the attention that prepares the cognitive process (vīthipaṭipādana) and the attention that prepares the impulsion (javanapaṭipādana); to show this, he said "āvazza samannāhara" (advert and bring together). "Avikkhittacitto" means having an undistracted (steady) mind by way of establishing on a single object through the sequence of consciousness preceded by the two aforementioned types of attention. "Nisāmehi" means listen, or it also means to store up the difficult-to-obtain Dhamma-treasure in one's mind as if storing a priceless jewel in a golden casket. Therefore, it is said to be characterized by establishing in the mind.
59:
Regarding the meaning—therefore it is said, 'Keep it in mind.' Having thus shown the meaning by way of the individual application of these two words, he now says 'Apica' (moreover) etc., to show it by way of contrast. In that statement, it is the restraining of the distraction of the ear faculty (sotindriya) by way of engaging in listening, because it prohibits other activities; therefore, it shows the meaning of 'lending an ear.' It is the restraining of the distraction of the mind faculty (manindriya) by way of engaging in firm attention (manasikāra), because it prohibits thinking of other objects. Because it is specifically stated as 'sādhukaṃ' (well/thoroughly), it is the restraining of the distortion of phrasing (byañjanavippallāsa). In the restraining of the distortion of meaning (atthavippallāsa) as well, this same method applies.

In the phrase 'dhāraṇūpaparikkha-ādīsu,' the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes comparison, investigation, and so forth, as well as the thorough penetration by wisdom. It is called 'byañjana' (expression/syllable) because it manifests the intended meaning, or because it manifests itself through this word. It is the natural linguistics (sabhāva-nirutti). It is called 'sabyañjana' because it is together with expression. It means having accomplished phrasing. Co-occurrence (sahappavatti) has many varieties such as accomplishment, consistency, and existence. Here, however, only accomplishment (sampannatā) is appropriate, as other meanings are not possible. Therefore, even though the grammatical derivation is made as 'together with expression,' it should be understood that the Teacher stated the meaning as 'accomplished in phrasing.' For example, it is like saying, 'Those which are not wholesome are unwholesome; they are the opposites of the wholesome.' It is called 'attha' (meaning/benefit) because it is to be reached or approached. This refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) and so forth. It is called 'sāttha' because it is together with meaning (benefit). By the method already mentioned, it means having accomplished meaning. The single word 'sādhukaṃ' should be applied to both (listening and paying attention) by way of the method of repetition (āvuṭṭi-naya) and so forth. If one asks how, he says 'yasmā' (because) etc. 'Dhamma' refers to the Pali text (tanti). 'Desanā' refers to the exposition of that Pali text as determined by the mind. 'Attha' refers to the meaning of the Pali text. 'Paṭivedha' refers to the penetration and realization of the Pali text and its meaning as they truly are. Because (yasmā) these—Dhamma, Desanā, Attha, and Paṭivedha—are difficult for those of dull wisdom to dive into, just as the great ocean is for creatures like hares, and because no footing can be found, they are therefore 'gambhīra' (profound). Therefore it is said, 'yasmā...pe... manasi karohi.' Here, because realization (paṭivedha) is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of diving into the Dhamma and Attha should be understood. Because the knowledge of exposition (desanā-ñāṇa) is difficult to achieve, the difficulty of diving into the exposition (desanā) should be understood, both because of the inability to produce it and because of the difficulty for knowledge to arise regarding that exposition. What should be said here has already been stated in the Nidāna-vaṇṇanā.

The Teacher, in saying 'Listen well' and 'Pay attention well,' shows that this connection is made not only according to the sequence of meaning but also because it is connected to both by the sequence of words. In this context of 'Sakkā mahārāja' (It is possible, O Great King), also another...
60:
Because this statement, 'the fruit of recluseship visible in this very life... and even more excellent,' follows, he says, 'the teaching on the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala-desanā) thus promised.' He confirms the meaning of 'speaking in detail' by saying, 'to say "I shall teach" is a brief indication,' and so forth. Here, the word 'hi' is implied. This is what is meant: Desanā means a brief indication (uddisana). Bhāsana means a detailed exposition (niddisana) and clear explanation. Therefore, this meaning is possible; and to establish the aforementioned meaning through the verse in the Vangīsa Sutta of the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta, he says 'Tena āha' (Therefore he said) etc.

'Like the sound of a salika bird' means just like the sound of a salika bird. It means that just as the speech of a salika bird is sweet, pleasant to the ear, and lovely, so it is here. 'Paṭibhāna' (inspiration/ready wit) is a modifier (vissessana) of the mind. Even though there is a difference in gender, it is seen as a modifier, like the example 'guṇo pamāṇam' (virtue is the measure). The sound is also called 'paṭibhāna' because it appears or manifests in various forms. 'Udīrayi' means he uttered or it was spoken; this verb is one that contains the object within it (kammagabbha). By this, he shows: the Venerable Vangīsa Thera, who possessed the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and wished to praise the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati), and wishing to show the distinction between desanā and bhāsana, used the modifiers 'in brief' and 'in detail.' Therefore, this meaning should be understood.

'When this was said' means when it was said, 'I shall speak.' It means that upon hearing that word, 'The Blessed One will not teach only in brief, but will also speak in detail,' enthusiasm arose, one became enthusiastic, joyful, and glad. This is the intention of the Teacher. Moreover, the entire manner of urging and promising, 'Therefore, O Great King, listen well, pay attention, I shall speak,' is the cause for generating enthusiasm. Since enthusiasm can arise from all the words, 'when this was said' should be understood as enthusiasm arising because of all three phrases. 'Paccassosi' means he respectfully assented. He assented immediately at the end of the Blessed One's words, or he assented by saying 'Very well, Bhante' after first asking 'Is it possible, Bhante?' and so forth. Since that assent is, in meaning, an acceptance, he says 'he accepted, he received.' For that very reason, instead of saying 'this is the meaning,' he said 'this is what is meant.'
61:
Having shown only the connection of the sentence, "Then the Blessed One said this to that King Ajātasattu," he said "Idāni" and so forth, wishing to explain the meaning by analyzing the phrase "Etam avoca." By this word "Idha," he shows the meaning that the context (adhikaraṇa) to be mentioned refers only to the world which is the place of the Tathāgata's arising, through the phrase "Desopadese nipāto" (a particle indicating a location). The pointing out of a place is called "desopadesa"; it is used in that sense of pointing out a place. If it were used for pointing out all places, there would be an objection that this meaning should not be stated because it could be understood even if not stated; therefore, he said "Svāyaṃ" and so forth. Taking the word "idha" in its general (sāmañña) sense, it is said as "svāyaṃ," but not in a specifically qualified manner. For this reason, it will be said later (in the commentary), "In some places, it is merely a filler of the verse (padapūraṇa)." It is spoken in reference to the world because it shares the same locus (samānādhikaraṇa) with the word "loka." In the phrase "idha loke," it refers to the world as the field of birth (jātikhetta), and within that field of birth, this universe (cakkavāḷa) is intended. It is spoken in reference to the Dispensation (Sāsana) because of its proximity to the specific word "samaṇa." This is from the Catukkanipāta of the Aṅguttara Pāḷi. In that Pāḷi, the 'first recluse' (pathama samaṇa) is the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The 'second recluse' (dutiya samaṇa) is the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī). For it is said in that very Pāḷi:

"Monks, what is the first recluse? Here, monks, a monk, with the destruction of the three fetters, becomes a Stream-enterer," and "Monks, what is the second recluse? Here, monks, a monk, with the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, becomes a Once-returner," and so forth.

It is spoken in reference to a certain place (okāsa) because of its proximity to the specific word "tiṭṭhamānassa." "Idheva tiṭṭhamānassa" means staying right here in this Indasāla Cave. "Devabhūtassa me sato" means of me who has become a deva, or of me being a deva. The word "me" is in the possessive case (sāmivacana) used in the sense of disregard (anādara). Again, the word "me" is in the sense of the agent (kattu). This passage is cited from the Sakkapañha Sutta. Since pointing out a place is impossible and does not convey a specific meaning, it is merely a filler of the verse. The word "loka" is spoken referring only to the place of the Tathāgata's arising mentioned previously. That which occurred previously in the context of urging and making a promise (paṭiññā)...
62:
Furthermore, it means addressing him as "Great King" (Mahārāja). The construction is that the words such as "Arahaṃ" have been elaborated. Since elaboration in terms of meaning occurs primarily through the medium of words, the term 'word' (sadda) is used in both instances. However, because the word "Tathāgata" has been elaborated by the Teacher in other ways in the Udāna Commentary and elsewhere, such as in the passage "The Blessed One is the Tathāgata for eight other reasons," and the words such as "Arahaṃ" have been elaborated in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, their meanings should also be understood according to the methods stated in those texts. Because the Tathāgata is included within the world of beings (sattanikāya), he said, "In this context, the world of beings (sattaloka) is intended," and to show that world of beings and the location (okāsa) where this Tathāgata arises within that world of beings, he said the words beginning with "Even though arising in the world of beings." The statement regarding "Not in the deva world, not in the brahma world" will come later.

"Tassāparena" means outside of that town, or beyond it. "Tato" means from the great Sal tree. "Orato majjhe" means the interior, the region of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). "Evaṃ paricchinne" means in a region defined by the five mentioned landmarks, like a boundary (sīmā) fixed by five signs. "Aḍḍhateyyayojanasate" means in a region of three hundred leagues minus fifty (i.e., two hundred and fifty leagues). This Middle Country is shaped like a drum (mudinga); it is neither perfectly circular nor perfectly square. In a straight line, it is eighty leagues in some places and a hundred leagues in others. Nevertheless, when this Middle Country is measured by its winding boundaries, it is nine hundred leagues in perimeter. Therefore, it is said, "nine hundred leagues." The phrase "eighty great elders" (asītimahātherā) is spoken generally, because the Elder Puṇṇa of Sunāparanta is also included among the great disciples. The Sunāparanta region is a border country (paccantajanapada). Indeed, it is stated in the commentaries on the Majjhima Nikāya and Saṃyutta Nikāya: "On the day the Blessed One accepted the sandalwood pavilion, he did not let the dawn rise at that monastery." "Sārappattā" refers to those who have reached the essence by way of lineage, wealth, and power, as well as by way of the essence of virtue and so forth. "Brāhmaṇagahapatikā" refers to brahmins such as Brahmāyu and Pokkharasāti, and householders such as Anāthapiṇḍika.

"Tattha" means in the Middle Country, or it refers specifically to the word "uppajjati." "Sujātāya" refers to the mother of the Elder Yasa, who was the first woman to go for refuge. Furthermore, among these four alternatives, the first alternative is for the sake of becoming a Buddha...
63:
The first interpretation is stated by way of showing the practice that is very close to attaining Buddhahood. Indeed, even one standing in the practice that is very close is said to be 'arising' because the arising is certain; how much more so for one who has reached the summit of practice (the Path of Arahatship)? The second interpretation is stated by way of showing the close practice starting from the renunciation that leads to Buddhahood. The third interpretation is stated by way of showing the practice for attaining Buddhahood starting from the fulfillment of the thirty varieties of the ten perfections (pāramī). In truth, for the Great Beings (Bodhisattas), there is no such thing as accumulating the requisites of enlightenment (bodhi-sambhāra) starting from the time they reach their final birth, because they remain in that state of Buddhahood while merely awaiting the time to become a Buddha. The fourth interpretation is stated by showing the certainty of Enlightenment (bodhi) starting from the initial undertaking of the perfections that bring about Buddhahood. From the moment the certainty of Enlightenment is reached, the wise are able to say, 'A Buddha arises,' because the arising is certain.

Just as the present tense is used in the phrase 'rivers flow' based on the uninterrupted action of flowing, so too in all four interpretations, 'arising' is said based on the uninterrupted action of practicing to attain Buddhahood; this is the usage of the 'pavattāparata-vattamāna' (the present tense of what has begun but not yet ended). The four characteristics of the present tense are declared in the grammar treatises thus:
'Constant occurrence (niccapavatti), proximity (samīpa),
likewise, having occurred and ceased (pavattūparata),
and having occurred but not yet ceased (pavattāparata)—
thus the present tense is of four kinds.'

Since the psychic powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa) and so forth do not arise for the Buddhas in succession as they do for the disciples, but rather the entire mass of qualities such as Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) arrives simultaneously with the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga), it is stated in the Ekanguttara Commentary that because all their tasks are completed, they are called 'arisen' (uppanna) at the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). If all tasks were not completed, one would not deserve to be called 'arisen' by that much. Among the four interpretations, the very first statement, 'The Tathāgata... is born (uppajjati) of Sujātā,' refers to the state of existence known as the arising of the Tathāgata. It is with reference to that state of existence that 'arising' is said, because it is intended only for one who stands in the practice very close to attaining Buddhahood. Only this meaning should be primarily called 'arising.' Therefore, it is said, 'The Tathāgata... is the meaning.'

In this context, if 'arisen' (uppanna) is said, someone might take the meaning in the sense of past time; to prevent that, it is said, 'is arisen' (uppanno hoti). As in the phrases 'arisen phenomena' (uppannā dhammā) and so forth, the word 'uppanna' here indicates the present time. Is it not that only the arisen Tathāgata, endowed with the Fruition of Arahatship, accomplishes the proclaimed teachings and so forth? However...
64:
Why is the Tathāgata intended as 'arising' only at the conclusion of the Path of Arahatship as stated? Does he not accomplish the proclaimed teachings and so forth? Is it because from the time of consuming the sweet milk-rice until the Path of Arahatship, he cannot perform those tasks such as teaching the Dhamma? It should not be viewed thus. By taking the 'arising' one who stands in the practice very close to Buddhahood, the 'arisen' one who is endowed with the Fruition of Arahatship is also taken. For by taking the cause (the Path), the effect (the Fruition) is also taken, as they are inseparable. Thus, because the Tathāgata endowed with the Fruition of Arahatship—who accomplishes the teachings and so forth—is to be taken, this word 'uppajjati' (arises) should be understood as a term whose meaning is to be inferred (neyyattha). This is true; in the Anguttara Commentary, when analyzing the meaning through the three times—'about to arise' (uppajjamāno), 'arising' (uppajjati), and 'arisen' (uppanna)—it is said: 'From receiving the prophecy at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the Fruition of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), he is called 'about to arise'; at the moment of the Path of Arahatship, he is called 'arising'; and at the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship, he is called 'arisen'.' This is the opinion of the teacher, Elder Dhammapāla, in this matter. However, since in the Ekanguttara Commentary, in the explanation of the sutta passage, 'Monks, a single person arising in the world arises,' it is stated: 'In this sutta, 'uppajjati' is spoken with reference only to the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship; the meaning here is 'is arisen' (uppanno hoti),' therefore, it is shown by the phrase 'with reference to the state of having first arisen' that in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta as well, 'uppajjati' is said with reference only to the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship. Therefore, he said, 'The meaning here is 'is arisen'.' And 'the state of having first arisen' means the state of having arisen by way of the Fruition of Arahatship earlier than all those who are to be disciplined (veneyya). And by this phrase 'is arisen,' he shows the past time by way of the moment of the Fruition of Arahatship. This very method is also intended by the teacher, Elder Sāriputta, the author of the Anguttara-ṭīkā.

'So Bhagavā' (That Blessed One) refers to that Tathāgata whose qualities are extolled starting with 'Arahaṃ.' Now, he points out the world to be mentioned with the word 'ima' (this), because it refers to the meaning about to be stated. This is what is meant: in saying 'this world' (imaṃ lokaṃ), it is not said with reference merely to the presence of the great assembly of people; rather, it is said with reference to the world to be mentioned as 'including the devas' (sadevaka) and so forth, which is taken inclusively without remainder. The word-definition (viggaha) is stated according to the sentence as 'sadevaka' because he is together with the devas; but according to the word itself, it should be stated as 'sadevako' and so forth. These compounds are 'tagguṇa-saṃvijñāṇa-bāhirattha-bahubbīhi' compounds. In this case, although the word-definition is made by way of a part, the whole is the meaning of the compound.
65:
This is because the collective world is appropriately obtained through the analysis (vigga-ha) made by a part of the world. Indeed, when associated with the word 'saha' (with) expressing the sense of inherence (samavāya), this compound is understood only as such (tagguṇasaṃvijñānabāhiratthabahubbīhi). In the phrase 'together with devas' (sadevaka), it refers to the devas residing in the five sense-sphere deva realms, or to the formless-sphere devas. In the phrase 'together with Brahma' (sabrahmaka), it refers to both form-sphere and formless-sphere Brahmas, or only to form-sphere Brahmas. Their formation is established like words such as 'bahukattuka'. The term 'pajā' (progeny/beings) is so called because they are produced in various ways by their respective kamma and defilements (kilesa).

Having thus shown the meaning through the word-definition (vacanattha), the text says 'therein' (tattha), etc., to show the meaning to be expressed (vacaniyattha). The inclusion of the five sense-sphere deva realms is by the method of remainder (pārisesa-naya), because the others (devas and Brahmas) are taken separately by other terms such as 'samārakaṃ sabrahmakaṃ'. The inclusion of the sixth sense-sphere deva realm (Paranimmita-vasavatti) is by the method of proximity (paccāsatti-naya). Indeed, Māra was born there and is a resident there. Since this Māra is well-known for living in that deva realm like a riotous prince, he is specifically mentioned as 'samārakaṃ' (together with Māra) even though other deva kings like Vasavatti exist. This method is also explained in the Commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya. By the inclusion of Māra here, the devas associated with him are also included, because the world of beings (sattaloka) is taken together with the world of locations (okāsaloka). Only in this way is the world of beings in the Vasavatti realm included without remainder. The inclusion of Brahmas such as the Brahmakāyika is also by the method of proximity. In the phrase 'inclusion of recluses and brahmins who are enemies', 'paccāmitta' means those who are indeed enemies; they are the recluses and brahmins, and their inclusion is such. By this, the inclusion of recluses and brahmins outside the Dispensation (bāhiraka) is meant. This is merely an illustration, because even those recluses and brahmins who are not enemies are included by this term 'samaṇabrāhmaṇa'. However, by the term 'inclusion of recluses and brahmins who have calmed evil and removed evil', the inclusion of recluses and brahmins within the Dispensation (sāsanika) should be understood.

Certainly, by the power of qualifiers such as 'together with devas' (sadevaka), the word 'loka' (world) having beings as its scope is understood, because they have a similar application by the power of the sense of inherence. However, in phrases like 'together with hair' (salomaka) or 'together with wings' (sapakkhaka), this compound is also found where there is a dissimilar application by the power of the sense of existence; thus, a deviation is seen. Therefore, the term 'pajā' is mentioned as a non-deviating indicator of the meaning. Thus it is said, 'By the word pajā, the world of beings (sattaloka) is included.' This is not said because the world of beings is not included by the word 'loka'. Therefore, it is said, 'By the three terms, the world of beings is included together with the world of locations.' Since the devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva) are included by the word 'sadevaka' etc., and the devas by purity (visuddhi-deva) are included by the word 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī', it is said 'the inclusion of devas, humans... etc.' Therein, kings are...
66:
...called conventional devas (sammuti-deva). The 'inclusion of the remaining humans' means the inclusion of humans remaining after the conventional devas and the recluses and brahmins. 'Herein' refers to these terms. 'By the three terms' refers to the terms sadevaka, samāraka, and sabrahmaka. 'By the two terms' refers to the terms sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī and sadevamanussā. Since the world of beings (sattaloka) is also included in the meanings of the compound terms by the method already stated, it is said 'the world of beings together with the world of locations (okāsaloka)'.

By the phrase 'another method' (aparo nayo) etc., another expressible meaning is stated. Even formless beings, while dwelling in their imperturbable abiding (āneñja-vihāra), deserve to receive the definition 'devas because they shine (dibbanti)'; thus it is said, 'By the inclusion of sadevaka, the formless-sphere world is included.' Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Brahmajāla Sutta etc., 'the companionship of devas who have reached the sphere of infinite space,' etc., which means the world of locations and the world of beings belonging to the formless sphere are included. Likewise, in the six sense-sphere deva worlds and the form-sphere Brahma world (the world of locations and the world of beings are included). Because the world of the six sense-sphere deva realms specifically proceeds under the influence of Māra, it is said, 'By the inclusion of samāraka, the world of the six sense-sphere deva realms is included.' For he has the authority to exercise his will in that deva world like a riotous bandit king. The form-sphere Brahma world is included by the method of remainder (pārisesa-naya) because the formless-sphere Brahma world has been taken separately. 'By the power of the four assemblies' means that among the eight assemblies—namely, nobles (khattiya), brahmins (brāhmaṇa), householders (gahapati), recluses (samaṇa), devas of the Four Great Kings, devas of the Thirty-three, Māra, and Brahma—only the four assemblies starting with nobles are taken; this is because the assemblies other than those nobles etc. are taken by terms like sadevaka. How is the human world included here by the power of the four assemblies? By the term 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇီ', the assembly of recluses and the assembly of brahmins are included; by the term 'sadevamanussā', the assembly of nobles and the assembly of householders are included. By the term 'pajā', however, these very four assemblies are meant. For here, the meaning of 'pajā' is the beings known as the four assemblies.

Another way of taking the meaning is stated as 'the human world together with conventional devas'. How is it taken? By the term 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī', recluses and brahmins are included; by the term 'sadevamanussā', the nobles known as conventional devas and the remaining humans known as householders and workers (sudda) are included. Since there are no other human beings apart from these, by the term 'pajā', only these human beings existing in four ways are meant. For here, the meaning of 'pajā' is the beings (pajā) divided into the four castes. Thus, in both alternatives, since only humans are included by the term 'pajā' through the power of the four assemblies etc., now, in order to show the inclusion of beings other than humans as well, the phrase 'the rest of all...' [is mentioned].
67:
(Since humans have already been included), now, to show the inclusion of the remaining beings as well, it is said: "Or the entire remaining world of beings." In this context, the entire remaining world of beings is taken together with the human world taken by way of the four assemblies; or it should be connected as the entire remaining world of beings together with the conventional gods (sammutideva). The entire remaining world of beings is also taken by way of Nāgas, Garuḍas, and so forth. The meaning is: the world of beings such as the remaining lowly beings, Nāgas, Garuḍas, denizens of hell, and so forth, together with the four assemblies is taken; or the world of beings such as the remaining Nāgas, Garuḍas, denizens of hell, and so forth, together with humans of the four classes is taken.

Having shown the connection by taking the world in parts with this much text, now, to show the connection by taking the world as a whole without dividing into parts through various distinctions, "Apice'ttha" etc. is said. In that statement, "ukkaṭṭhapariicchedato" means by way of the highest limit of destinations, through the knowledge of that highest destination. Indeed, according to the first method, among the five destinations, only those beings included in the deva destination are noble because of distinctions such as being endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure and long life. According to the second method, however, the formless (arūpa) Brahmās are extremely noble because of distinctions such as having discarded the suffering of defilements far away, being endowed with the peaceful and sublime imperturbable dwelling (āneñjavihāra), and having an extremely long life. The teachers, however, said this with reference only to the second method.

Even though the entire world has been realized by the primary method through the first word alone, to show that the remaining words were spoken because of this specific reason mentioned, "Tato yesaṃ" etc. is shown. "Tato" means it should be connected with the word "āha" after the first word. If it were said only "the ruler of the six sense-sphere heavens," there might be doubt that Mara's lordship also extends over Sakka and others; to dispel that doubt, "Vasavatti" is said. By that word, it is shown that his lordship is only the wielding of power by forceful oppression to make others follow his will. Indeed, that Mara is not the ruler of even the sixth heaven, because only the King of the Vasavatti devas is the ruler there. Therefore, the Blessed One said in detail in the Dānānisaṃsa Sutta of the Book of Eights in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: "Monks, therein the young deva Vasavatti, having performed the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving to excess... surpasses the Paranimmitavasavatti devas in ten respects." In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary also, it is said: "Indeed, in that Paranimmitavasavatti heaven, the King Vasavatti exercises kingship. Mara, however, lives in one place exercising authority over his own retinue, like a rebel prince (dāmarika) on the border of a kingdom." "Brahmā...
68:
The words "Mahānubhāvo" etc. are spoken with reference to the Great Brahma in the ten-thousandfold world system. The phrase "Ukkaṭṭhapariicchedato" has already been explained below. The words "Ekanguliyā" etc. show the greatness of power by way of a single part. "Anuttaraṃ" means the noble nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). "Puthū" means many or distinct. "Ukkaṭṭhaṭṭhānānaṃ" means of those who have reached the highest destinations.

"Bhāvānukkamo" means the sequence of words such as "sadevakaṃ" according to the dispositions and inclinations of others. Or, "bhāvānukkamo" means the sequence of connection (anusandhi) by way of state or disposition. It means the order of connection of both meanings and words. This reading "bhāvānukkamo" alone is the correct one as it is found in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary and was explained by the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta. Although the reading "vibhāvanānukkamo" is also found, it is not a good reading as it is not found in those commentaries.

Now, to show the method of explanation of the ancient commentators, "Porāṇā panāhu" etc. is said. In that statement, because the world of beings is taken without remainder by the word "anya" (other), it speaks of the inclusion of the world without remainder in all words. Because of such inclusion, it is said: "beings who have reached the three worlds" (tibhavūpage satte). It means beings who have reached the three worlds known as the three elements (tedhātuka). "Tīhākārehi" means by the three modes known as being together with devas, Maras, and Brahmas. "Tīsu padesu" means in the three words such as "sadevakaṃ". "Pakkhipitvā" means including by way of meaning. To make it known that those very beings who have reached the three worlds are included in the two words "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ sadevamanussaṃ", the word "puna" (again) is said. By saying so, the teachers who say "tibhavūpage satte" by way of various distinctions such as being with devas, etc., and being with recluses and brahmins, etc., and then say "tedhātukameva" (only the triple element), show that the world of beings is taken together with the world of locations (okāsaloka). The ancient teachers say that only the triple world-element consisting of the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial realms is completely included.

"Sāmaṃ" means by oneself. The rejection of that meaning by excluding other meanings or by the word "eva" having the sense of inclusion (avadhāraṇa) is stated as "aparaneyyo hutvā". It means having known by oneself without needing to be made known by others. The designation "abhiññā" is the word "abhiññāya" indicating the elision of the letter "ya", just as it is said "paṭisaṅkhā yoniso". By the word "abhi", not only the distinction is highlighted, but also the instrument (karaṇa) by way of distinction is shown, as indicated by the words "adhikena ñāṇena" (with superior knowledge). In this statement "anumānādipatikkhepo"...
69:
By the word 'ādi' (beginning), it includes making known through mere indications such as comparison (upamāna), implication (atthāpatti), context (saddantara-sannidhāna), association (sampayoga), dissociation (vippayoga), and accompaniment (sahacaraṇa), because they have the same scope of meaning. Since the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have knowledge that is unimpeded in all things, they have personally realized all phenomena. The word 'bodheti' (awakens) means 'to make known' (viññāpeti) according to the literal word, while 'pakāseti' (illustrates) means 'to illustrate' according to the intended meaning. In this way, distinctions should be noted in all places.

'Anuttaraṃ vivekasukhaṃ' refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). The use of the word 'pi' (even/also) in 'hitvā pi' is because the Buddha's teaching sometimes occurs even while he is pausing within the attainment of fruition. While the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma, at the moment when the audience says 'Sādhu' or when they are reflecting on the Dhamma they have heard, he enters the attainment of fruition for a duration determined by his prior resolution. Having emerged from that attainment according to the determined time, he continues to teach the Dhamma from the point where he previously stopped; this is the meaning stated in the Commentaries.

'Appam vā bahum vā desento' (teaching little or much) means teaching a little for a person of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), or teaching much for a person who understands through expansion (vipañcitaññū) and for one who needs guidance (neyya). If one asks how he teaches, it is said 'ādi mhi pi' and so on. The goodness of the Dhamma is due to its being leading out of suffering (niyyānika), and its being leading out of suffering is only due to its state of being entirely blameless; thus it is said 'anavajjam eva katvā' (having made it only blameless).

'Desanā' refers to the Dhamma of scriptural learning (pariyatti-dhamma). Because it is the special arrangement and making known through methods such as authority (āṇā) related to the Buddha who is the teacher, the scriptural Dhamma is called 'desanā'. Although in the ultimate sense there is no such thing as a 'whole' separate from its parts, when the parts are considered as a whole, designations such as 'verse' (gāthā) arise. Treating that part as if it were distinct from the whole and applying conventional usage, it is said, 'There is a beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (desanā).'

'Sāsana' refers to the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-dhamma). Because it is the instruction (anusāsana) according to the faults that have arisen in the person to be disciplined, and the disciplining (vinayana) by means of discipline by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vinaya) and so on, the Dhamma of practice is called 'sāsana'. The connection is: 'There is a beginning, middle, and end of the instruction (sāsana).'

In the word 'catuppadikāya pi' (even of a four-lined stanza), the word 'pi' is used in the sense of commendation. By that word 'pi', it commends: if there is goodness in the beginning, middle, and end of even such a small teaching, how much more so in a much larger teaching? Here, a fourth part of a verse is called a 'pada' (line), which is also called a 'pāda'. By this term 'catuppadikā', the division is shown as applicable to verses with three lines or six lines as well. Having thus shown the three types of goodness in a portion of a Sutta, to show it in the entire Sutta, the words 'ekānusandhikassa' and so on are said. In that statement, with a sequence (anusandhi) that is suitable and not excessively divided...
70:
Referring to a Sutta with a single sequence, it is said 'of a Sutta with a single sequence' (ekānusandhikassa). In other Suttas with multiple sequences, however, since the beginning, middle, and end are obtained through that very division of the Dhamma, it is said 'of a Sutta with multiple sequences' (anekānusandhikassa) and so on. The 'Nidāna' (introduction) is the introductory text characterized by the indication of time, place, teacher, audience, etc., as established by the Elder Ānanda. The concluding words 'Thus he spoke' (idamavoca) are merely a marker. This is because the conclusion 'Thus, that which was spoken, was spoken in dependence on this reason' is also to be taken. The introductions and conclusions established by the Elders who performed the Rehearsal (saṅgītikāraka) should be understood as being included within the Teacher's teaching itself, as they were composed in accordance with it. The 'sequence at the end' (ante anusandhi) is the very last sequence of the entire meaning.

By the words 'virtue, concentration, insight' (sīla, samādhi, vipassanā), the state of the Dhamma of practice (paṭipatti-dhamma) in this Sāsana is made clear. However, in the Vinaya Commentary, because it is called 'sāsana-dhamma'—

'Not doing any evil,
Fulfillment of what is wholesome,
Purifying one's own mind,
This is the instruction (sāsana) of the Buddhas.'

Only the Dhamma of scriptural learning (pariyatti-dhamma), which illustrates the instruction of the Teacher thus spoken, is mentioned in the clarification of the three types of goodness by way of the meanings of virtue and so on. But in this context, only the practice (paṭipatti) is the Sāsana. Therefore, it will be said later: 'In this context, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (desanā) are intended.' Virtue, concentration, and insight are called the 'beginning' because they are the root of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) which constitute the fulfillment of the Sāsana. 'Of wholesome states' means of blameless states. 'Diṭṭhi' (view) here refers to insight (vipassanā); however, concentration (samādhi) is also included here because it is inseparable from it. This Sutta passage is the Bāhiya Sutta passage found in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta. Although the state of being the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā) of the Noble Path is mentioned in the Sutta because of its departure from the two extremes, yet because of the commonality of being in the middle, the Noble Path is called the 'middle' as it can also accomplish the state of being in the middle between the undertaking and the completion of the right practice. Thus it is said: 'Bhikkhus, there is a Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata.' The meaning is that the Noble Path is called the 'middle' because it occurs in the middle between the undertakings known as virtue, concentration, and insight, and the completions known as fruition and Nibbāna. Fruition is called the 'end' by way of the Nibbāna element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Nibbāna, however, is the 'end' by way of the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). For the Nibbāna element is the end of the Sāsana. Alternatively, it is so stated because the completion of the Path occurs by way of fruition and by the realization of Nibbāna, and after that, there is nothing further to be done. Now, to prove the state of both of these being the end of the Sāsana by means of scripture, he said 'etad-atthaṃ idaṃ' and so on.
71:
Because it has this very fruition of Arhatship as its purpose, it is called 'etadattha'. 'Brāhmaṇa' refers to the Blessed One addressing the Brahmin Piṅgalakoccha. This is a term found in the Cūḷasāropama Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya. Because it has this fruition of Arhatship as its essence (sāra), it is called 'etansāraṃ' with the addition of the niggahīta. Similarly, it is 'etaṃpariyosānaṃ'. 'Nibbānogadhaṃ' means plunging into Nibbāna (entering within Nibbāna). 'Friend Visākha' (Āvuso Visākha) is the address used by the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā to the householder Visākha. This occurs in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, and because it is stated as 'with meaning and with phrasing' etc., it is intended here to mean the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (desanā).

Having thus shown the division of the threefold goodness of the teaching by way of the sequence of words, he says 'Bhagavā hi' etc., to show it by way of the meaning as well. He confirms the Blessed One's intention even by way of meaning with the word 'hi'. Through such confirmation and by way of meaning, he shows the division of the threefold goodness. In showing it by way of meaning, the 'teaching' (desanā) here refers to the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) established by way of verses (gāthā) and discourses (sutta), which is the sequence of words arranged for those respective meanings. Since the meaning of that scriptural Dhamma is specifically virtue (sīla) and so on, he says 'virtue at the beginning' etc. This is a specific description. Generally, by taking 'virtue', virtue along with its requisites is taken; similarly, by taking 'the path', the path along with its requisites is taken. In this way, by way of the three meanings, it encompasses the meaning of the scriptural Dhamma without remainder. Otherwise, the division of the threefold goodness would not be universal. Here, because the Dispensation (sāsana) is rooted in virtue, the goodness in the beginning (ādikalyāṇa) is said to be through virtue. Because it is the middle state in the fulfillment of the Dispensation, the goodness in the middle (majjhekalyāṇa) is said to be through the path. Because there is nothing further to be done after attaining Nibbāna, the goodness in the end (pariyosānakalyāṇa) is said to be through Nibbāna. By showing virtue and so on, the goodness in the beginning etc., is stated in this teaching by way of meaning. The words 'Therefore' etc., show the instruction to the listeners in accordance with what has been said.

'This' refers to the preaching in the manner already described. 'Kathikasaṇṭhiti' refers to the posture of the Dhamma preacher (the proper establishment by way of preaching).

'Vaṇṇanā' means the explanation of the meaning or praise. That person does not preach so as to fulfill the meaning, because that teaching is devoid of the liberating meaning (niyyānattha) that leads out of the round of suffering. 'Therefore' is said because he preaches the liberating meaning such as the four foundations of mindfulness. 'Endowed with a single consonant' etc., refers to being associated with a consonant of only one variety or two varieties among the ten types of consonants such as sithila (lax) and dhanita (tense). For example, like the Tamil language...
72:
...among the ten consonants, it is like the Tamil language, which is associated with consonants of only one or two varieties. 'Sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjanā' (all non-labial consonants) is like the Kirāta (Karen) language, which has consonants entirely free from labial contact, to be pronounced by opening the mouth without letting the lips touch. 'Sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjanā' (all released consonants) is like the Savara (Chin) language, which has consonants that are entirely released because all syllables are associated with the vissajjanīya. 'Sabbaniggahītabyañjanā' (all nasalized consonants) is like the Milakkha (Taungthu) languages such as Persian, which have consonants entirely accompanied by the bindu (dot) because all syllables are nasalized. Thus, the phrase 'like the languages of the Damiḷa, Kirāta, Savara, and Milakkha' should be applied to each. Milakkha refers to peoples such as the Persians. Since all these languages proceed only by way of a portion of the consonants, they have incomplete phrasing; therefore, it is said, 'They are called non-phrasing (abyañjanā) because of the absence of full phrasing (byañjanapāripūri).'

A letter to be pronounced by relaxing the points of articulation and the effort is called 'sithila' (lax); these are the first and third letters in the five consonant groups (vaggas). A letter to be pronounced by making those same points of articulation and effort firm is called 'dhanita' (tense); these are the second and fourth letters in those same groups. A letter lasting for two measures of time (mattā) is 'dīgha' (long). One lasting for one measure of time is 'rassa' (short).

The duration of one measure is said to be the time of a blink of an eye or a flash of lightning.
They also say it is the duration of a snap of the fingers.

A letter followed by a conjunct (saṃyoga) and a long letter are called 'garu' (heavy). A letter not followed by a conjunct and a short letter are called 'lahu' (light). A letter to be pronounced with the mouth not open, pressing the points of articulation and the effort, is 'niggahīta'. A letter to be pronounced in connection with the following word is 'sambandha'. Similarly, one to be pronounced without connection is 'vavatthita'. A letter to be pronounced with the mouth open, releasing the points of articulation and the effort, is 'vimutta'. In the words 'tenfold' (dasadhā) etc., the meaning is that the differentiation of consonants is into ten types by way of the ten kinds of mind that produce the letters, known as 'consonant-consciousness' (byañjanabuddhi), through sithila and so on. For all letters originate from the mind; and because they manifest the intended meaning, they are called 'consonants' (byañjanā). Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that the differentiation of consonants into ten types is by means of the 'consonant-consciousness' which acts as the instrument.

'Amakkhetvā' means without smearing, without destroying, without diminishing. He states that meaning with the words 'paripuṇṇabyañjanameဝ katvā' (making the phrasing complete). It means that whatever meaning the Blessed One teaches, even in a single verse or a single sentence, He teaches that meaning only through a discourse that has perfectly complete words and phrasing. Therefore...
73:
Because of the teaching of the Dhamma with complete phrasing in every respect, the word 'kevala' (entire) here expresses the whole meaning without remainder. It does not mean 'unmixed' or 'pure' alone; therefore, it is said to be 'a term for the whole'.

'Paripuṇṇa' (perfectly full) means full in every aspect. Since this fullness, in terms of meaning, excludes both deficiency and excess, it is called 'speech without deficiency or excess'. In that speech without deficiency or excess, it is known as 'not deficient' because it accomplishes the purpose for which the Dhamma was taught. It is known as 'not excessive' because it does not accomplish what is contrary to that purpose. Alternatively, it is known as 'not deficient' because there is no pure meaning that should have been included but was left untaught; it is known as 'not excessive' because there is no defiled meaning that should have been removed but was taught. 

'Sakala' (entire) means having all parts. 'Paripuṇṇa' means full in every aspect. Therefore, it is said, 'There is nothing that is not full, even by a single part.' A teaching becomes impure when it is defiled by craving (taṇhā). Requisites such as robes are called 'worldly baits' (loka-āmisa) because they are grasped by worldlings through craving. One who has no attachment to those requisites is one who is 'indifferent to worldly baits'. By pervading with welfare (by bringing welfare), one becomes 'soft-hearted' due to the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā). 'Ullumpana-sabhāva-saṇṭhitena' is said in the sense of compassion (karuṇā) established in the manner of wishing to uplift beings from all defilements and from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

Giving (dāna) is called a 'vow' (vata) in the sense that it is well-undertaken, as in 'From now on I shall give, and I shall give in this way.' Dāna itself is called 'brahmacariya' (noble practice) because it is noble (brahma) in the sense of being prescribed by the wise, or because it is the practice of noble persons. Dāna itself is called 'suciṇṇa' (well-practiced) because it is practiced by suppressing stinginess, greed, and so on. 'Iddhi' means divine power. 'Juti' means radiance or majesty. 'Balavīriyūpapatti' means the attainment of great strength and energy. 'Nāgā' is the address used by the wise Vidhura toward the Nāga King Varuṇa.

'Dānapati' means the lords of giving (donors). 'Opānabhūta' means being like a watering place (a well). 'Dhīrā' (O wise one) is the address used by the Nāga King Varuṇa toward the wise Vidhura. 'Madhussava' means the flowing of sweet taste. 'Puñña' (merit) refers to the result of merit, using the cause to denote the effect. 'Brahmacariya' means service (veyyāvacca) because it is a noble practice or the practice of noble persons. This method should be understood for the remaining uses of the word 'brahmacariya' as well.

'Tittiriya' refers to the words spoken by the King of Partridges named Tittira. 'Aññatra tāhi' means excluding those who are the wives of others. 'Amhaṃ' means of us.
74:
Because of performing the fourfold difficult practice—being an ascetic (tapassī), being austere (lūkha), loathing evil (jegucchī), and being secluded (pavivitta)—he is endowed with the four factors. The word 'su' is a mere particle (nipāta). In the Mūlapaṇṇāsa of the Majjhima Nikāya, the Lomahaṃsana Sutta is also called the 'Mahāsīhanāda Sutta'.

'Iddha' means prosperous; 'phīta' means flourishing; 'vitthārika' means widespread; 'bāhujañña' means known by many people as the way to liberation; 'puthubhūta' means become extensive. In the phrase 'yāva devamanussēhi', the commentary on the Pāsādika Sutta states that it means 'well-proclaimed from the deva world to the human world'; the meaning is 'unto both devas and humans'. Because the entire Dispensation (Sāsana), which is comprised of the Threefold Training (sikkhattaya), is intended here by the word 'brahmacariya', it is so stated. The commentator, wishing to show the meaning by connecting all terms that are in apposition with 'brahmacariya', says 'He teaches the Dhamma', and so on. By saying 'Even though he teaches in this way', he shows that the words 'brahmacariya' and 'dhamma' have the same meaning. He also clarifies that even after saying 'He teaches the Dhamma', the statement 'He proclaims the brahmacariya' is said for the purpose of explaining the meaning in its specific form.

'Vuttappakārasampada' means being endowed with the qualities of the aforementioned divisions, such as being 'good in the beginning'. Right practice in the Dispensation is possible only for one whose conceit (māna) has been discarded far away, not for one of a conceited nature; thus it is said, 'because of having suppressed conceit'. 'Ussannattā' means because of being abundant. Intoxication (mada) based on objects of sensual pleasure such as wealth and beauty can be easily abandoned because their cause (nimitta) is unstable; however, intoxication based on lineage (kula) and knowledge (vijjā) is not like that, as their cause is stable. Therefore, even those of the Khattiya and Brahmin castes who have gone forth find it difficult to abandon the talk of conceit based on their birth and knowledge; thus it is said, 'For the most part... they indulge in conceit.' 'Vijātitāya' means because of having a distorted birth, meaning a low birth. It is said that, for the most part, those endowed with the strong supporting conditions (for the paths and fruits) are only those of good birth, not those of bad birth. 'They are unable to stand' means they are not able to stand in virtue (sīla), or they are not able to protect their virtue to the point of extreme purity. Virtue is indeed the foundation (patiṭṭhā) in the Dispensation. Alternatively, 'to stand' means to stand in the supramundane foundation through the penetration of the Truths. That supramundane foundation is, in the primary sense, the foundation in the Dispensation.

Having thus stated the meaning by way of exclusion (vyatireka), he also states it by way of inclusion (anvaya) with the words 'But the sons of householders', and so on. 'With sweat releasing from armpits'—here the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūta-lakkhaṇa). Likewise, 'with salt forming on the back'—the instrumental case is used there as well. Sweat...
75:
It means they are marked by such signs as sweat pouring from the armpits and salt crystals forming on the back. "Bhūmiṃ kasitvā" means by plowing the earth or by making a living through farming. "Tādisassa" refers to one who relies on birth (caste) and the Vedas. Weak conceit is called māna, while strong pride is called mada (dappa). "Kamma" refers to the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). With the words beginning with "itarehi," the causal term "ussannattā" is explained. After stating the word "iti," the meaning referred to by that word "iti" is shown by the words beginning with "nihatamānattā." Alternatively, since the word "iti" is used in the sense of illustration, it means "in this aforementioned manner." In such cases, it should be understood in this way.

In the word "paccājāto," since the letter "ā" is merely a prefix (upasagga), it is said as "patijāto." "Parisuddha" (perfectly pure) means being pure in every way, because it indicates the absolute abandonment of lust (rāga) and so forth, and because of the absence of defilements (kilesa). He is called "Dhammassāmī" (Lord of the Dhamma) because he gives rise to that Dhamma which is free from defilements, or because he rules the world together with the devas by means of the Dhamma. "Saddhaṃ" refers to the belief through the faith (saddhā) that arises in worldlings (puthujjana). For those of a wise nature, the accomplishment of faith through first hearing the excellence of the Dhamma occurs because they are of the type known as dhamma-ppamāṇa (one who measures by the Dhamma) among the four types of individuals. One gains faith by reflecting, "The Blessed One has well-expounded the Dhamma in this way; truly, that Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)." This can be attained even from a distance of a hundred leagues (yojana).

"Jāyampatikā" refers to a husband and wife. Although the term "jāyampatikā" itself implies the two—the master and mistress of the house—the word "dve" (two) is used to show that even living with just one wife is initially very confining (sambādha), let alone for a man who has many wives. Anxiety (kiñcana) arises because of lust (rāga) and so forth, and hindrance (palibodha) arises because of fields, property, and so forth. Because it is accompanied by both, household life is called "sakiñcana-palibodha." Lust itself is called "dust" (raja); likewise, hatred and delusion, which begin with lust, are also dust. The Blessed One taught: "Lust is dust, but actual dust is not called dust," and so forth. Since they refer to the place of origin, both explanations (saṃvaṇṇanā) have the same meaning, differing only in phrasing. "Alagganathena" is due to the sense of not being attached or due to the nature of not being bound. The word "viya" (as if) is used to show the similarity to the open air (abbhokāsa) through the power of metaphors (rūpaka) and so forth. Thus, after showing the confinement of household life and the openness of monkhood as the place and non-place for the occurrence of the unwholesome and the wholesome, the words beginning with "api ca" are now stated to show them as the place and non-place for the occurrence of the wholesome alone. It should be connected as "like a place where dust accumulates."

Explaining the meaning in summary without extracting each word individually is called a brief explanation (saṅkhepakathā). "Ekampi divasaṃ" means even for a single day. "Akhaṇḍaṃ katvā" means making it unbroken and unperforated, without committing even a minor offense (dukkaṭa). "Saṅkhalikhitaṃ" means made as pure as a conch shell, free from impurities, without being defiled by impurities such as craving (taṇhā) at the final moment of death-consciousness (cuti-citta). However, to show just the meaning, the explanation (saṃvaṇṇanā) "likhita-saṅkha-sadisaṃ" is given. The word "saṅkha-sappaṭibhāgaṃ" is also an explanation with that same meaning. Alternatively, like a pure conch shell...
76:
It means making [virtue] flawless and untorn by not committing even a minor offense (dukkaṭa). Carimakacitta refers to the final consciousness, the death-consciousness (cuticitta). Kilesamala refers to the stain caused by impurities such as the defilement of craving (taṇhā). Amallīna means being unstained. It is called saṅkhalikhita (polished conch-shell) because it is pure like a conch-shell that has been polished and washed to be completely white and free from impurities. To show only the literal meaning, it is stated as 'similar to a polished conch-shell.' The phrase 'similar to a washed conch-shell' is also an explanation of that same meaning. Alternatively, just as in the word 'ajjhāhita' where the adjective follows, a polished conch-shell is called saṅkhalikhita; because this virtue is similar to such a polished conch-shell, it is also presented as saṅkhalikhita. This term is a bhāvanapuṃsaka (neuter of state).

In the word 'ajjhāvasata,' because it is associated with the prefix 'adhi,' the word 'agāraṃ' is a term with an accusative ending used in the sense of the locative (place); thus, it is explained as 'in the midst of the house.' The connection should be made as: 'If I were to go forth, it would indeed be good.' The fact that clothes dyed with astringent juice are called 'kāsāya' is shown by the phrase 'because they are dyed with astringent juice.' As to why those clothes are worn, it is said, 'because they are suitable for those practicing the supreme holy life.' 'Acchādetvā' is merely a conventional expression; it means 'having dressed.' This occurs through the acts of wearing the lower robe and donning the upper robe. In the term 'agāravāsa' (living in a house), the latter word 'vāsa' is elided, and it is called 'agāra.' The state of a monk, where there are no activities such as farming or trading that promote the welfare of those living in a house, is called 'anagāriya' (homelessness).

'Sahassato' means starting from a thousand pieces of money (kahāpaṇa). 'Bhogakkhandha' is a mass of wealth. Because of the sense of binding by making a distinction through affection such as 'son, grandson, great-grandson,' it is shown that the word 'parivaṭṭa' has the meaning of binding by distinction. Alternatively, it is also appropriate to say 'parivaṭṭa' in the sense of revolving according to the lineage of grandfather, father, son, and so on. They are called 'ñāti' (kinsmen) because they are known as 'these are our relatives.'

A monk whose bodily and vocal doors are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha is said to be 'endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha' because he is possessed of that restraint. The detailed explanation of conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara) should be taken from the Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā and other commentaries. The phrase 'endowed with conduct and resort' and so on is a demonstration of the cause for that very state of being restrained by the Pātimokkha. Because it is like an atom, a very small thing is called 'aṇu'; thus, it means 'in the slightest faults.' It is called a slight fault because of the minor offenses (anukhuddaka-āpatti) committed unintentionally, and because of the unwholesome thoughts that arise suddenly. 'Bhayadassī' means one who has the nature of seeing [faults] as danger. 'Sammā' means without distortion, or excellently. Such lack of distortion or excellence arises through the practice of not transgressing respectfully throughout one's life. When it is stated 'in the training rules' (sikkhāpadesu)...
77:
In the phrase 'in the training rules' (sikkhāpadesu), the Buddha did not explicitly state the object because the meaning 'having undertaken the training rule, he trains,' which is a part of that training rule, can be understood. Therefore, in saying 'taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ,' it refers to each group of training, or the means of attaining the threefold training, or the support for that training.

'Ettha' refers to this statement beginning with 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha.' 'Ācāragocara-ggahaṇeneva' means by the very inclusion of conduct and resort. Therefore, it is said, 'even though wholesome bodily and verbal actions are taken.' It is not possible to take wholesome bodily and verbal actions by the mere words 'conduct and resort' alone. By stating this again, a hint of a possible objection is shown. 'Tassa' refers to the purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla). 'Uppattidvāra-dassanatthaṃ' means for the purpose of showing the doors of origin, known as bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) and vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), by way of action. By this, the resolution of the aforementioned objection is shown.
