This is what is meant: even when the meaning is already established, a further effort is made either to make the meaning firm or to make a special meaning known. In this case, it is stated to show the doors of origin because of the desire to make a special meaning known. 'Kusalena' means being blameless due to the total abandonment of improper search (anesanā). To the possible question of how the doors of origin are shown by that word, the passage beginning with 'yasmā pana' is stated. It means that because one is endowed with blameless bodily and verbal actions arising in the bodily and vocal doors, it is pure livelihood. Being endowed with both those blameless bodily and verbal actions is called the purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla) which has livelihood as its cause.

Now, to compare it with another sutta, it is said, 'or it is stated thus by way of the Muṇḍikaputta Suttanta.' The word 'vā' (or) here has the sense of providing an alternative explanation, which is the comparison with another sutta. The Muṇḍikaputta Sutta is a sutta taught in the Majjhima-paṇṇāsaka of the noble Majjhima Nikāya. That sutta is also called the 'Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta Sutta.' In that sutta, the Blessed One addresses a carpenter named Pañcakanga as 'thapati.' The word 'thapati' is a synonym for a carpenter. This is what is meant: 'Thapati, what are wholesome virtues? They are wholesome bodily actions and wholesome verbal actions.' Having thus shown the nature of virtue as wholesome bodily and verbal actions, He said, 'Thapati, I also speak of the purity of livelihood within virtue.' This teaching of the Muṇḍikaputta Sutta and this teaching of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, which states, 'being endowed with blameless bodily and verbal actions, he has pure livelihood,' have the same inclusion. They truly merge and agree just as the water of the Yamuna merges with the water of the Ganges. Therefore, such magnificence of the Blessed One's teaching exists.
78:
The term 'Atthevā' means: In the phrase 'Sīlasmiṃ vadāmi', I say 'virtue'. Alternatively, it refers to being included or contained within virtue as a support (ādhāra). Or, I say 'one virtue' among the collection of virtues from which it is selected.

'Tividhena' means: Threefold, by way of the Small Section on Virtue (Cūḷasīla), the Middle Section on Virtue (Majjhimasīla), and the Great Section on Virtue (Mahāsīla). By the phrase 'manacchaṭṭhesu' (with the mind as the sixth), he prohibits taking only the five [senses] starting with the body. Regarding the seven instances to be mentioned later in the description (niddesa), 'tividhena' means being threefold in each of the four requisites according to what is obtained, according to strength, and according to suitability.

## Explanation of the Small, Middle, and Great Sections on Virtue

194-211. 'Evaṃ' (Thus) is to be understood in the manner of 'That monk, having thus gone forth, dwells possessed of the restraint of the Pātimokkha,' and so on. The word 'Sīlasmiṃ' is in the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). Because one virtue is selected from that collection of virtues, he says 'one virtue'. Alternatively, by this word, he shows the locative case in the sense of support (ādhāra), because it is the basis for the parts of the whole, just as one says 'a branch on a tree'. With the word 'idaṃ', it is in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) by way of the sense of the agent (kattā). Since the locative case occurs in the sense of the agent, it is like saying 'in a forest with blossoming tips'. This meaning is shown by the phrase 'or this locative is in the sense of the nominative (paccatta)'. 'Ayamevattho' means it is only the sense of the nominative. 'Brahmajāle' means it is in the manner already stated in the explanation of the Brahmajāla Sutta or in the words of the Brahmajāla Sutta. In the phrase 'Idamassa hoti sīlasmiṃ', since there is no virtue being selected by the end of the Great Section on Virtue, only the sense of the nominative is appropriate. Therefore, he says, 'The meaning is: This is his virtue.' For that very reason, it should be understood that the word 'api' is not included in the Pali text.

212. The fear of self-reproach (attānuvāda), the fear of reproach by others (parānuvāda), the fear of punishment (daṇḍa), and so on, are fears rooted in non-restraint (asaṃvara). The Teacher said: 'Sīlassāsaṃvarato means because of the non-restraint of virtue, meaning the absence of the restraint of virtue.' However, because the phrase 'yadidaṃ sīlasaṃvarato' is interpreted as 'whatever fear might arise because of the restraint of virtue,' and because it fits the meaning 'he does not see fear due to the restraint of virtue,' the meaning of 'sīlasaṃvarato' as 'due to the restraint of virtue' is indeed appropriate. Indeed, the reading 'whatever fear might arise because of the restraint of virtue' is also seen. Having stated the cause as 'saṃvarato' (due to restraint), he also states the cause by way of the meaning obtained through that restraint as 'due to the absence of fear rooted in non-restraint'.
79:
He states the cause. 'Yathāvidhānavihitena' means accomplished according to the prescribed ritual. 'Khattiyābhisekena' means by the consecration that brings about the status of a Khattiya. 'Muddhani avasitto' means anointed specifically on the crown of the head.

Here also, by the phrase 'yathāvidhānavihitena', he shows one factor, which is being endowed with the ritual practiced by ancient kings. By 'khattiyābhisekena', he shows one factor, which is bringing about the status of a Khattiya. By 'muddhani avasitto', he shows one factor, which is the state of being anointed specifically on the crown of the head. Thus, the royal consecration (khattiyābhiseka) endowed with three factors is spoken of. By that consecration, the royal majesty of the anointed kings is perfected.

By what means is this meaning known? It is known by the method found in ancient scriptures. For it is said in the Aggañña Sutta Commentary, in the explanation of the consecration of King Mahāsammata: 'Those [people of the beginning of the aeon] also performed the consecration for that Bodhisatta, the lord of the fields, with three conch shells.' In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, in the explanation of the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, it is said: 'Muddhāvasittena means anointed on the crown of the head with the royal consecration by means of three conch shells.' In the Sīhaḷa Commentary, in the explanation of the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, it is said: 'For kings receiving consecration for the first time, it is proper to obtain three conch shells, such as those made of gold, as well as water from the Ganges and a royal maiden,' and so on.

This is the decision regarding the ritual of consecration according to the method found in that Sīhaḷa Commentary: For the purpose of the auspicious consecration, inside a decorated pavilion, in the middle of a small pavilion made of fig-wood (udumbara) branches, on a noble throne made of fig-wood that is well-placed, a king of noble birth worthy of consecration is seated. First, a royal maiden of pure birth, adorned with auspicious ornaments, takes with both hands a golden right-spiraled conch shell filled with Ganges water, raises it above the king's head, and with that conch shell, pours the consecration water on the crown of the king's head. She speaks thus: 'Your Majesty, all the hosts of Khattiyas make you the consecrated Great King for the sake of protecting themselves. May you, established in the ten royal virtues, rule the kingdom with righteousness and impartiality. May you have a heart possessed of love and compassion like that for a son toward these hosts of Khattiyas, and a heart of metta equal to their welfare. May you be the protector of them through protection, defense, and guardianship.'

Then again, the Chaplain (Purohita), adorned with ornaments suitable for the office of chaplain, takes with both hands a silver conch shell filled with Ganges water, raises it above the king's head, and with that conch shell, pours the consecration water on the crown of the king's head. He speaks thus: 'Your Majesty, all the...'
80:
The groups of Brahmins, for the sake of protecting themselves, make you a consecrated Great King through this consecration. Established in the royal virtues (Rājadhamma), rule the kingdom righteously and fairly. Towards these groups of Brahmins, be one who has a mind endowed with love and compassion as for a son, and a mind of loving-kindness equal in seeking their welfare and happiness. Be their protector through the guarding that is called protection and defense.

Then again, the merchant (Setthi), adorned with ornaments suitable for the position of a merchant, respectfully takes with both hands a conch shell made of the seven gems and filled with water from the Ganges River. Holding it above the king's head, he pours the water of consecration upon the crown of the king's head. He also says: 'Your Majesty, all the groups of householders and merchants, for the sake of protecting themselves, make you a consecrated Great King through this consecration. Established in the royal virtues, rule the kingdom righteously and fairly. Towards these groups of householders and merchants, be one who has a mind endowed with love and compassion as for a son, and a mind of loving-kindness equal in seeking their welfare and happiness. Protecting them with protection and defense, be their guardian.'

It should be understood that when they speak to the king in this way, it is as if they are cursing the king, saying: 'If you rule the kingdom in accordance with our words, this is good (blameless). If you do not, may your head split into seven pieces.' This meaning should be illustrated by the Vaḍḍhakīsūkara Jātaka and others. The requisites for consecration should also be taken from texts such as the Samantapāsādikā.

The connection is that because the enemies have been destroyed, he does not see them. Because it is wholesome, it is blameless. Therefore, it is said: 'Having wholesome virtue as the proximate cause...' and so on. This is the meaning: From wholesome virtue as the proximate cause, the states of non-remorse, gladness, joy, and tranquility arise. One experiences mental happiness born of causes such as non-remorse (avippaṭisāra). For one whose body is touched by the refined material phenomena produced by mental happiness, one also experiences the physical happiness that arises.

## Explanation of the Talk on Restraint of the Faculties

Because the general sense depends on the specific, the specific meaning intended here is not abandoned by that general term 'eye' (cakkhu). Therefore, it is said: 'The word "eye" in some places refers to the Buddha-eye,' and so on. Indeed, a specific word clarifies another specific meaning by excluding other specifics through its established denotation, but not something non-existent. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Because it is the eye (vision) of the Buddhas, which is not shared with others, it is called the Buddha-eye. It consists of the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa).
81:
Vision refers to the Buddha-eye, the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies, and the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings. The All-around Eye (samanta-cakkhu) is the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), in the sense of seeing everything in every way. 'Tathūpamaṃ' means having a simile like a mountain peak, and it should be connected with 'dhammamayaṃ pāsādaṃ' (a palace made of Dhamma). The meaning is: 'O Wise One, O All-seeing One, look upon the multitude of beings.' The wisdom of the three noble paths refers to the wisdom of the three lower noble paths. Although it is said in the Saḷāyatana-vagga Commentary that 'the Dhamma-eye refers to the three lower paths and the three fruits,' here it is shown by including the fruits within the paths. It is called the Dhamma-eye because it sees the Dhamma known as the Four Noble Truths. It is called the Wisdom-eye (paññā-cakkhu) because it sees through wisdom alone; it consists of the knowledge of recollection of past lives and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. The Divine-eye (dibba-cakkhu) occurs in the second knowledge (vijjā). In this text, 'having seen a form with the eye,' the word 'eye' refers primarily to the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). Figuratively, according to the usage of dependence (nissaya-vohāra), it also refers to the eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) which depends on the eye-sensitivity. This is like saying, 'The beds are shouting.' Since the discussion of the constituent parts (sasambhāra-kathā) remains here, the word 'pi' should be taken in the remaining terms as well; this same method should be noted in terms such as 'na nimittaggāhī' (not grasping at signs).

Various types of exhaustion (vyāseka) are indeed the defilements. Being free from those defilements of disturbance, being unmixed, and being pure due to the absence of association, it is said: 'unmixed and pure' (asammissaṃ parisuddhaṃ). The meaning is that it is unmixed with the suffering of defilements and is therefore very pure. When there is such very pure restraint of the faculties, because the evil states which are the primary hindrances (nīvaraṇa) have disappeared, the practice of the higher mind (adhicitta/concentration) is as if it has reached one's hand. Therefore, it is shown by the term 'happiness of the higher mind' (adhicitta-sukha) that the happiness of the higher mind itself is called 'happiness free from disturbance' (avyāseka-sukha).

## Explanation of the Talk on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension

One is called 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāna) because one knows in various ways from all around, or knows excellently and specifically. The state of such a person is 'clear comprehension' (sampajañña), which is the knowledge functioning in that way. The analysis of that is the 'Sampajañña-bhājanīya' (Classification of Clear Comprehension). By the word 'gamanaṃ' (going), it refers to going forward (abhikkamana). Likewise, 'nivattanaṃ' (turning back) refers to going backward (paṭikkamana). Here, 'going' means going whether having turned back or not, while 'turning back' is just the act of turning back; both are merely actions taken in relation to each other. How is this obtained? It is said: 'in going' (gamane), and so on. 'Abhiharanto' means bringing the body forward by way of going.
82:
*Paṭinivattento* means turning back from there again. *Apanāmento* means directing by way of moving away. *Āsanassa* refers to a seat such as a bench, etc. *Purimaṅgābhimukho* means facing the front parts such as the frame [of the seat], etc. *Saṃsaranto* means moving. *Pacchimaṅgapadesaṃ* refers to the region of the hind parts such as the frame, etc. *Paccāsaṃsaranto* means moving back again. By the words "in this very way," he shows the forward movement and the backward movement of one who is lying down. Indeed, in standing, sitting, and lying down, the forward movement of the body that is distinct from walking is called *abhikkama* (going forward), and the backward movement is called *paṭikkama* (going back); thus the characteristic should be understood.

Knowing clearly and in various ways is called *sampajāna*. Because one habitually performs one's duties with that *sampajāna*, it is said, "one who performs all duties with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*)." Alternatively, by the words "one who performs only clear comprehension," he shows that one is a *sampajānakārī* (doer of clear comprehension) by habitually practicing *sampajāna*. The words beginning with "*So hi*" serve to establish the second alternative. Furthermore, by the word "*sampajañña*," it is meant that the word *sampajāna* is a synonym for *sampajañña*. Regarding this, the teacher Elder Ānanda said: "Knowing in various ways—completely, rightly, or evenly—is called *sampajāna*; that very knowing is *sampajañña*." This is another method from the Commentary: In whatever way one produces non-delusion in going forward, etc., the performance of *sampajāna* in that way is called *sampajānakāra*; one who possesses that *sampajānakāra* is called *sampajānakārī*.

Going forward, etc., are called *sātthaka* (purposeful) because they are accompanied by the benefit called growth through wholesome states such as meditation subjects. Knowing clearly and completely that going forward, etc., are accompanied by the benefit of the growth of wholesome states is called *sātthakasampajañña* (clear comprehension of purpose). Knowing clearly what is suitable for oneself is called *sappāyasampajañña* (clear comprehension of suitability). When going forward, etc., to a village for alms or elsewhere, knowing clearly the object called the meditation subject which is not to be abandoned is called *gocarasampajañña* (clear comprehension of the resort). Indeed, the word *gocara* applies to both meanings, whether by way of general description (*sāmaññaniddesa*) or by the method of ellipsis (*ekasesa*). Since non-delusion in going forward, etc., is itself clear comprehension, it is called *asammohasampajañña* (clear comprehension of non-delusion).

*Cittavaseneva* means only by the power of the mind, or only by following the will of the mind. *Pariggahetvā* means having weighed with knowledge, having investigated with knowledge, or having reflected with wisdom. Going for the purpose of the *Uposatha* or *Pavāraṇā* ceremonies, etc., is included simply by the mention of seeing the Saṅgha. By the word "*ādi*" (etc.), the preliminary work for *kasiṇa* meditation, etc., are included. To explain that very meaning which was stated in brief, he said "or a shrine (*cetiya*)," etc. The statement "attains Arahantship" is an exalted description. Indeed, the arising of tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) is also growth for a monk. *Tattha* refers to *asubhārammaṇe* (in the object of foulness). *Keci* refers to the monks residing at the Abhayagiri Monastery.
83:
*Āmisato* means because of material requisites such as robes, etc. To the question "Why?", he said "depending on that [requisite]," etc.

"In that benefit" means in the benefit grasped by the power of clear comprehension of purpose (*sātthakasampajañña*). Since only growth through the Dhamma is called "benefit," someone might have a general doubt that every journey intended as "purposeful" would also be "suitable" (*sappāya*). To dispel that doubt, he began by saying "firstly, seeing a shrine," etc. *Mahāpūjāyāti* means at a great offering ceremony, on the day of a public offering ceremony. *Cittakammarūpakānī viya* means like artistic paintings, or like statues with various intricate movements through mechanical devices. In those assemblies, *asammapekkhanam* for that monk means grasping the object unwisely (*ayoniso*) by the power of equanimity devoid of knowledge that is based on sensual pleasures. With reference to that meaning, it is said: "Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the foolish, deluded worldling," etc. There may be the occurrence of an offense of bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*) due to contact with a woman, danger to life due to being trampled by elephants, etc., or danger to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) by looking at disagreeable (*visabhāga*) forms, etc. It is just as described in the passage beginning with "Assemblies within ten or twelve leagues gather," etc. *Mahāparisaparivārānaṃ* refers to an entourage of mixed men and women for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, etc., on occasion.

*Tadatthadīpanatthaṃ* is for the purpose of showing the benefit of contemplating foulness (*asubha*), which is called the state of being purposeful (*sātthakabhāva*). From the day of ordination, it is customary to follow the monks by giving a reply in conversation. Therefore, the speech that does not follow by not giving a reply is called his second speech. Thus it is said, "He has never spoken two kinds of speech." The two kinds of speech are complying and not complying with words. Of those two, he had only spoken complying words, but never the second kind. Therefore, it means that he, being easy to admonish, gave a reply.

By the word *evaṃ*, all the aforementioned details beginning with "If at a great offering ceremony for a shrine," etc., are considered. It does not consider only "the foulness of a woman for a man," etc. One who has grasped what is purposeful (*sātthaka*) and suitable (*sappāya*) is called *pariggahitasātthakasappāya*. By that term, the method of grasping clear comprehension in due order is shown. Because it is the place of occurrence for the work of meditation to be described, the object of meditation is called *kammaṭṭhāna*. That very *kammaṭṭhāna*...
84:
It is called 'gocara' (resort) because it is the object of meditation. It means 'the resort known as the meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Uggahetvā' means having performed the learning by fulfilling the proficiency in learning (uggahakosalalla) just as the learning sign (uggahenimitta) arises. 'Bhikkhācāragocare' refers to the resort known as the village for alms-round. By this term, it is shown that the word 'gocara' is used both for the meditation subject and for the place of alms-round.

'Idha' means in this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Harati' means carrying by way of maintaining the meditation subject, meaning one practices until returning from the alms-round. 'Na paccāharati' means not bringing back (not abandoning) the meditation subject after consuming food until reaching the place for the day's stay. Among those four types of monks, 'āvaraṇီyehi' refers to the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). 'Pageva' means very early (early in the morning). 'Sarīraparikammaṃ' refers to the care of the body, such as washing the face and so on. 'Dve tayo pallaṅke' means sitting for two or three sessions. Here, sitting with legs crossed is called 'pallaṅka'. 'Usumံ' is said with reference to warming oneself two or three times. 'Kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitvā' means having practiced the primary meditation subject on that day. 'Kammaṭṭhānasīseneva' means with the meditation subject as the priority, meaning without abandoning the meditation subject. Therefore, it shows the practice of not abandoning either the meditation subject that will be described as 'the bowl is also inanimate (acetana),' etc., or the meditation subject being maintained.

'Gantvā' means having arrived. If it is the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), that meditation itself fulfills the act of showing respect. To show that if it is another meditation subject, it is as if one does not show respect, the words 'sace' (if), etc., are stated. Since it is not the domain of a meditation subject other than that Buddhānussati, setting that aside, the words 'mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ ce,' etc., are said to show that for a monk meditating, there is no delay in reflecting on the original meditation subject. Other monks, however, should pay homage in that way or in another way. 'Tatheva' means only three times. Considering that a bodily relic shrine (sārīrika-cetiya) is more worthy of respect than a shrine of use-relics (paribhogacetiya), it is stated with the preceding verb 'cetiyံ vanditvā' (having paid homage to the shrine). As stated in the Commentary, 'A Bodhi branch that obstructs the shrine should be cut,' this is the teacher's view. However, according to the words 'even when reaching the Bodhi courtyard,' if there is a Bodhi courtyard on the path to the alms-round from the shrine courtyard, that Bodhi tree should also be worshipped. Therefore, the phrase 'cetiyံ vanditvā' is stated according to the sequence of the path, not according to the sequence of importance. In this case, a monk who reaches the Bodhi courtyard first should pay homage to the Bodhi tree and then to the shrine. If he reaches only one of them, he should pay homage only to the one he reached.
85:
The meaning that a monk who has not yet reached both the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard should not pay homage is well understood. This is to show the intermediate duty (antarāvatta) to be performed at the place reached on the path of the alms-round, not the constant duty (dhuvavatta). This monk has already performed his duties earlier. Therefore, it is said, "Having first performed the duties of the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard," and so on. By the words "showing respect as if in the presence of the Blessed Buddha," it is shown that showing respect (humility) even at the Bodhi tree and other use-relic shrines is appropriate only through the power of recollecting the Buddha's qualities. 'Paṭisāmitaṭṭhāna' (place of storage) is mentioned generally as being the base of the stairs; it means having reached a place outside the shrine courtyard and Bodhi tree courtyard, which are the objects of joy (pīti) having the Buddha as the object.

'Near the village' means in the village precinct (gāmūpacāra). The connection should be made as: first they ask questions, or they wish to hear the Dhamma. 'For the sake of favoring the people' means for the benefit of supporting the multitude of people by way of the Dhamma, thinking, "If I do not preach, who will preach to them?" To strengthen the words of the teachers of the Commentaries, it is said, "There is no such thing as a Dhamma talk that is separate from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)." 'Therefore' means because the teachers of the Commentaries say, "Dhamma talk should indeed be given," or because there is no Dhamma talk separate from the meditation subject; therefore, the connection is 'having preached the Dhamma talk.' However, Elder Ānanda connects this word 'therefore' with 'they say it should indeed be preached.' 'With the meditation subject as the priority' means by way of not abandoning the meditation subject one is maintaining, having preached a Dhamma talk that is consistent with that meditation subject; this same method applies to the second phrase as well. In the phrase 'having performed the anumodana (thanksgiving),' the phrase 'with the meditation subject as the priority' also applies. 'In that place' means only at the place of departure from the village.

By showing the practice of the ancient monks with the words "the ancient monks," etc., the aforementioned meaning is solidified. 'Only by the limit of arrival' means without making a distinction such as "familiar or unfamiliar," but only by the point of arrival; it means simply by meeting. 'By the power' means by the power of favor. 'In danger' means in dangers such as enemy armies. 'In famine' means at a time when food is scarce.

It is in the manner stated as "having passed the time even in the last watch (pacchimayāma) by sitting and walking," and so on. 'To the one who performs' means even while performing; here the genitive case is in the sense of disregard (anādara). 'Kamma-born heat' (kammajatejo) is said with reference to the digestive fire (gahaṇī). 'It burns' means it produces heat. Because it produces such heat, it takes up the clung-to matter (kamma-born matter); sweat is released. To the path of meditation...
86:
One who has a body exhausted by the fatigue of hunger cannot ascend to the path of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) due to the lack of concentration. Matter such as rice is called 'unacquired matter' (anupādinnarūpa). The abdominal lining is called 'acquired matter' (upādinnarūpa). When there is no matter like rice in the stomach, the kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo) arises and seizes the abdominal lining, causing one to say, 'I am hungry, give me food.' When food is eaten, it releases the abdominal lining and takes the matter such as rice; at that time, the being attains concentration of mind. Therefore, it is said in the Commentaries, 'The kamma-born heat is like a shadow-guarding ogre (chāyā-rakkhasa).' In this phrase 'so pageva', the word 'tasmā' is the remainder. 'Go-rūpānaṃ' means only at the time when cattle or herds of cattle depart from the pen for their grazing ground. By the reverse of the method already mentioned, it releases the acquired matter and takes the unacquired matter. 'Antarābhatte' means in the interval of the meal, for as long as one has not yet eaten the meal. Therefore, it is said, 'Having the meditation subject as the foremost and also consuming food.' 'Ava-sesa-ṭṭhāne' refers to the place where the gruel is not taken. 'Tato' means from eating. 'Poṅkhānu-poṅkhaṃ' is a demonstration of the non-interruption of the repeated appearance of the meditation subject, meaning 'successively.' Just as there is no interruption in a sequence of arrows discharged successively, so too, it means, there is no interruption in the appearance of this meditation subject. By the words 'edisā ca' and so forth, he shows the fruitfulness of attending to the meditation subject in such a manner. 'Āsanaṃ' means the sitting-place.

'Nikkhitta-dhuro' refers to one who has laid down the burden in the practice of meditation (one who does not strive), one who has unexerted energy. By not fulfilling the duties of practice, he destroys all duties and becomes one whose mind is associated with the five types of mental barrenness (cetokhīla) and mental bondages (vinibandha). In the Cetokhīla Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it is said thus: 'Monks, which five mental barrennesses are not abandoned? Here, monks, a monk doubts the Teacher, doubts the Dhamma, doubts the Saṅgha, doubts the training, and is angry with his fellow practitioners.' And also: 'Which five mental bondages are not cut off? Here, monks, a monk is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, is not free from lust for the body, is not free from lust for forms, and having eaten as much as his stomach can hold, he lives devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of sleep, and he practices the sublime life aspiring to some company of devas.'
87:
I shall speak further in detail. The teacher (the sub-commentator of the Dīgha Nikāya) has shown the state of the mind associated with the five types of mental bondages by highlighting only a portion of the term. Indeed, the state of the mind being like rubbish or a stump is called 'mental barrenness' (cetokhīla). The nature of binding the mind and seizing it as if in a fist is called 'mental bondage' (cetovinibandha). Between these two, the first, cetokhīla, is spoken of by way of the faults of doubt (vicikicchā) and anger (dosa); the second, cetovinibandha, is spoken of by way of greed (lobha). This is the distinction between them. 'Caritvā' means having wandered. It is 'empty' because of being devoid of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna).

The duty of a monk who goes for alms and returns only with the meditation (bhāvanā) is called the 'Gatapaccāgatika-vatta' (the duty of going and returning). That very duty is the Gatapaccāgatika-vatta. One should practice by the power of that duty. 'Attakāmā' means those who desire their own welfare and happiness, those who desire the path, fruit, and Nibbāna. The reason is that welfare and happiness, and the bliss that has that welfare as its cause, are called Dhamma. Alternatively, for the wise, because the Dhamma is not different from the self (atta) and because it is included within one's own being (attabhāva), the Dhamma is called 'atta'; because they desire that Dhamma, they are called 'attakāmā.' Nowadays, however, the reading 'atthakāmā' is seen with the word 'attha' meaning benefit; it means those who desire the benefit associated with the Dhamma, or those who desire the Dhamma which is the benefit. 'Iṇaṭṭā' means those oppressed by debt. The same applies to the other two terms (bhaya and jīvikāpakata). 'Ettha' means in this Dispensation (Sāsana).

Twenty rods (yaṭṭhi) are called one usabha; eighty usabhas are called one gāvuta. With such a perception of a stone as a marker, they go knowing, 'I have reached this much of a place,' while attending to the meditation subject. 'Naṃ' refers to the defilements (kilesa). He stands because he does not wish to lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject; the monk coming behind also stands because he does not wish to pass the standing monk in front. That monk is the one in whom defilement has arisen. 'Ayaṃ' refers to the monk coming behind. 'Etaṃ' refers to the knowledge of the other. 'Tattheva' means only at the place where he stood. The method mentioned regarding standing, such as 'ayaṃ bhikkhu' and so forth, is the same for sitting. Because of the fear that the monks coming behind might miss their meal, he also increases wise attention (yoniso manasikāra); this point should also be understood by the wise as being included in the knowledge of the other. 'Purima-pāde-yeva' means only in the footprint of the foot previously lifted with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject. 'Etī' means he goes. This was spoken of in an inappropriate place (a-ṭṭhāne), just like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, a resident of Ālindaka. It removes the doubt, 'Where has this monk practiced like this before?'

'Maddantā' refers to those who are threshing ears of hill-paddy and so forth at the threshing floor. The word 'assa' refers to the Elder and is a word that looks both ways (to what precedes and what follows). On the day the Elder reached Arahantship, he stood at the edge of the walkway. Thus, it is a word that regards both the preceding and following terms. Because of having fulfilled his desire in attaining the extraordinary Dhamma, he spoke according to the truth only after making known the distraction and the oppression.
88:
In the phrase 'caṅkamanakoṭiyanti ca' (and at the end of the walk), with the desire to attain the fruition of Arahantship, having dispelled mental distraction, and having persevered firmly in meditation and acknowledged it, he then announced the attainment of the special Dhamma.

The phrase 'paṭhamaṃ tāva' is a figurative expression used to beautify the sentence. 'Mahāpadhānaṃ' refers to the Buddha's practice of austerities (dukkara-cariyā). It means, 'I shall honor, according to my strength, the practice of austerities performed for six years by the Lord of the World for our benefit.' Worship through practice (paṭipatti-pūjā) is indeed the most praised form of worship of the Teacher; worship with material offerings (āmisa-pūjā) is not like that. 'Ṭhānacaṅkamameva' is said by way of the postures to be undertaken; it is not said by way of prohibiting the sitting that must necessarily be done at meal times and so on. By the word 'eva,' only sitting and lying down other than walking meditation are prohibited. 'Vippayuttena uddhaṭe paṭinivattento' refers to placing a footstep, which was lifted with a mind dissociated from meditation, back into that same footprint with a mind associated with meditation. Having said 'gāmasamīpaṃ gantvā' (having gone near the village), he explains the meaning with 'gāvī nu' (is it a cow?), and so on. 'Kacchakantarato' means from the armpit; it means from the kamaṇḍalu water-pot carried under the armpit. 'Udakagaṇḍūsaṃ' means a mouthful of water. 'Katimī' means the completion of how many lunar days (tithi); it means asking the day, such as 'Is it the fifth or the eighth of the fortnight?'. Since not announcing the date is not to be done, he announces it. For it was said, 'Bhikkhus, I allow all of you to learn the calculation of the fortnight,' and so on.

'Udakaṃ gilitvā āroceti' (having swallowed the water, he announces) is according to the method already mentioned. 'Tattha' means at that village gate. 'Niṭṭhubhanaṃ' means the place for spitting out water. 'Tesu' means among those people. Because he is endowed with the eye of wisdom, he is called 'cakkhumā' (one with eyes). 'Īdiso' refers to such things as a well-swept monastery courtyard. 'Visuddhipavāraṇā' is the pavāraṇā performed by the state of being an Arahant.

Descending to the road, one should first observe the streets without looking here and there; thus it is said, 'vīthiyo sallakkhetvā' (having observed the streets). This refers to the manner of going mentioned as 'with graceful advancing and receding,' and so on. To show that manner of going, he says 'tattha ca,' and so on. By the statement 'There is no such thing as going quickly in the dhutaṅga of a monk going for alms,' he shows the impropriety of going quickly, which is like the conduct of the flighty. 'Udakasakaṭaṃ' means a cart loaded with water. Such a cart should be made to remain steady even when it reaches uneven ground. 'Tadanurūpaṃ' means in accordance with the offering of alms. What should be said regarding 'having established the perception of repulsiveness in food,' and so on, will come later. It refers to food that has three similes: the greasing of a chariot axle with oil, the application of medicine to a wound, and the eating of a son's flesh. 'Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ' means...
89:
...having made it endowed with the eight factors mentioned in such passages as "only for the endurance and maintenance of this body," etc. However, "not for fun," etc., is merely to show what is to be rejected. "Bhattakilamatha" means the fatigue arising on account of the meal. "Purebhatta" (before the meal), etc., is said by way of the day; "purimayāma" (the first watch), etc., is said by way of the night.

Wishing to show the meaning that carrying the meditation subject during the going for alms and the returning is a duty (vatta), he said "haraṇapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ" (known as carrying and bringing back). This phrase "if he is endowed with the sufficing condition (upanissaya)" should be connected to all sentences such as "having become a deva," etc. Therein, the perfection of the sufficing condition for Paccekabodhi is the fulfillment of the accumulations of merit and wisdom (puñña-ñāṇa-sambhāra) appropriate for that Paccekabodhi for two asankheyyas and a hundred thousand aeons. In the case of Sāvakabodhi, for the Chief Disciples, it is one asankheyya and a hundred thousand aeons; for the Great Disciples, it is exactly a hundred thousand aeons. For other ordinary disciples, however, it is the wholesome state leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-kusala) produced without a fixed time limit by way of the sufficing condition for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in past lives. By the words "seyyathāpi," etc., he provides the testimony of the elders who were placed in the foremost positions (etadagga) in various capacities. Among those elders, the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya was known as "Bāhiya" because he was born and raised in the Bāhiya country, and as "Dāruc|īriya" because he wore bark (dārucīra). That venerable one—

"Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the sensed, only the sensed; in the cognized, only the cognized.' Thus, Bāhiya, you should train yourself. When, Bāhiya, for you in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard; in the sensed, only the sensed; in the cognized, only the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be 'by that.' When, Bāhiya, you are not 'by that,' then, Bāhiya, you will not be 'in that.' When, Bāhiya, you are not 'in that,' then, Bāhiya, you will be neither here nor beyond nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering."

Through this much teaching alone, he realized the fruit of Arahantship. In this way, the sutta passages illustrating the great wisdom and so on of the Elder Sāriputta and others should also be stated in detail. Specifically, the Etadagga sutta passages in the Aṅguttara Nikāya (should be stated). "Sikhāpatta" means reaching the crest, reaching the conclusion, because of being complete in every way.
90:
That [clear comprehension of non-delusion] is non-confusion. 'In this way' should be understood by the manner now to be described. It shows the confusion of the blind worldling in going forward through three types of misconceptions: by way of clinging to view as 'The self goes forward,' by way of clinging to conceit as 'I go forward,' and by way of clinging to craving, since those two [view and conceit] cannot occur without craving.

Having said, 'Thus, being non-confused,' and wishing to show the breaking down of compactness by which that non-confusion occurs, he said 'I go forward,' and so on.

'Air element originated by consciousness' (cittasamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu) means the air element originated by that very consciousness that desires to go forward, or the air element that has that consciousness as its cause. 'Intimation' (viññatti) refers to bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). It arises, producing bodily intimation due to the altered state of that air element. 'Iti' means because of such arising. [It should be understood] by the power of bodily intimation, which is called the manner of movement of the air element originated by the functional consciousness that completes the action of going. 'Tassa' refers to the skeleton. 'Abhikkamato' refers to the person going forward. 'Omattā' means having a deficient or inferior measure. By the power of the air element and fire element, the other two elements are inferior.

This is the meaning: Among these four elements, the fire element followed by the air element is the cause for lifting the foot. Indeed, the fire element has the nature of lifting; because it has the nature of lifting, the air element follows in that lifting by the fire element. Therefore, among these four elements, these two—fire and air—are predominant in terms of capability, and because they lack such predominance, the other two elements are inferior. Furthermore, the air element followed by the fire element is the cause for stretching forward and moving across. Indeed, the air element, which has the nature of action, has excessive exertion in stretching forward and moving across; therefore, the fire element follows the air element in those movements. Thus, among these four elements, these two—air and fire—are predominant in terms of capability, and because the other two elements lack such predominance, they are inferior; this is shown by the words 'Thus also in stretching forward and moving across.'

In this context, although there is a distinction between the following element and the element to be followed, the word 'tathā' (thus/likewise) is used merely with reference to the state of being the fire element and air element. In the first method, the fire element is the follower and the air element is the one to be followed. In the second method, however, the air element is the follower and the fire element is the one to be followed. Among those [lifting, etc.], the lifting of the foot from the place where it was trodden is called 'uddharaṇa' (lifting). Carrying it forward beyond the place where it stood is called 'atiharaṇa' (stretching forward). Carrying it sideways to avoid a stump or the like, or to avoid striking the standing foot, is called 'vītiharaṇa' (moving across).
91:
The extent to which the standing foot remains, carrying it that far is called 'atiharaṇa.' Carrying it beyond that standing place to another spot is called 'vītiharaṇa.' Alternatively, this is the distinction between lifting, stretching forward, and moving across.

Because the water element followed by the earth element is the cause for dropping the foot (vossajjana). Since the water element has a very heavy nature, the earth element follows the water element in that dropping. Therefore, among these four elements, the earth and water elements are predominant in terms of capability, and the remaining fire and air elements are inferior as they lack that capability; to show this, he said 'In dropping... are powerful.' Furthermore, because the earth element followed by the water element is the cause for placing the foot down (sannikkhepana). Just as in the state of standing, the earth element has a predominant function in the act of placing down, so the water element follows that earth element. Likewise, because the act of pressing the foot down (sannirujjhana) is accomplished by the power of the earth element which performs the action of striking [the ground], the water element follows the earth element in that pressing down as well. Therefore, it was said, 'Thus also in placing down and pressing down.'

Even though there is a distinction between the following element and the element to be followed, the word 'tathā' is used merely with reference to the state of being the earth element and water element. In the first method, the earth element is the follower and the water element is the one to be followed. In the second method, however, the water element is the follower and the earth element is the one to be followed. In this context, 'vossajjana' is called dropping by way of inclining the foot. After that, establishing the foot on the ground etc. is called 'sannikkhepana.' After establishing the foot, the cessation of movement (or momentary stopping) by way of treading is called 'sannirujjhana.'

'Tattha' means in that going forward, or in those six groups mentioned as lifting, stretching forward, moving across, dropping, placing down, and pressing down. 'Uddharaṇe' means at the moment of lifting the foot. 'Rūpārūpadhammā' refers to the material phenomena occurring in the manner of lifting the foot and the immaterial phenomena that originate them. Because they last only for a moment, they do not reach the stage of stretching forward (atiharaṇa). This method applies everywhere. 'Tattha tattheva' means they cease right in those respective places where lifting etc. occurred. Indeed, there is no migration of phenomena to another location because they change and perish so rapidly. 'Pabbaṃ pabbaṃ' means part by part; 'sandhi sandhi' means joint by joint; 'odhi odhi' means section by section. All these terms should be understood as being spoken with reference to the groups of lifting etc. by way of a similar succession (sabhāgasantati). For indeed, the moment of occurrence of material phenomena is even swifter than the meeting of razor edges on the heads and feet of deities running in opposite directions, based on the consciousness associated with movement. For example, like sesame seeds being broken [when parched]...
92:
Just as when roasting sesame seeds, their destruction is known by the sound 'paṭapaṭā', the word 'paṭapaṭāyantā' (making the sound paṭapaṭā) is used so that the destruction of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) can be perceived through their arising (uppāda). It means that although they do not actually make the sound 'paṭapaṭā' by the power of arising, it is as if they do. Just as the 'paṭapaṭā' sound is the sign of the destruction of sesame seeds, arising is the sign of the destruction of conditioned phenomena, because things that have arisen are certainly destroyed.

'Tattha' (therein) refers to 'stepping forward' (abhikkamana). Who is the one person who steps forward? Indeed, no one steps forward. Or, for which one person could there be a stepping forward? Indeed, there could not be. Why? Because in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is only the existence of elements (dhātu). This statement refers to the stepping forward and turning back of the self, which is a delusion of blind worldlings (andhabāla-puthujjana). Alternatively, the objection 'Who is the one... stepping forward?' is clarified by the explanation starting with 'In the ultimate sense...'.

'Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ koṭṭhāse' (in each of those parts) is said because in the aforementioned six groups, there is no involvement of going and so forth. It should be connected with the verse: 'It arises and ceases together with matter (rūpa)'. Therein, in connection with the first phrase, 'with matter' means with any matter that arises together with it. However, in connection with the second phrase, 'with matter' refers to the matter that has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments, which arises at the arising moment of the seventeenth mind-moment prior to the mind that is about to cease, and which ceases along with the cessation of that ceasing mind. Otherwise, material and mental phenomena would have the same lifespan. If they had the same lifespan, it would contradict the Commentarial statements such as 'Matter is heavy in transformation and slow to cease,' and the Sutta passages such as 'Monks, I do not see any other single thing that changes as quickly as this mind.'

Mind and mental factors (cetasika), having the nature of taking an object (sārammaṇa), cease immediately after manifesting the object that serves as their condition. Material phenomena, however, do not take an object (anārammaṇa), and it takes sixteen mind-moments for them to reach the state of being manifested. Therefore, it is intended that material phenomena have a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments, including one past mind-moment. The distinction of consciousness changing quickly is because it arises from the mere meeting of conditions; thus, the three aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—and consciousness change quickly. Matter, however, is slow to change because it has the heavy great elements (mahābhūta) as its cause. The knowledge of various elements as they really are belongs only to the Tathāgata. That Tathāgata spoke only of material phenomena that assist through the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya) and the post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya). Therefore, it is not fitting for material and mental phenomena to have the same momentary duration. Thus, the Teacher (Ācariya Dhammapāla) states that the meaning here should be understood only in the manner described. However, this was said to make it easy to understand that intimation-matter (viññatti-rūpa), which arises following the mind, has a cessation similar to the mind. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: the mind ceases along with the matter that arose at the arising moment of the first of the seventeen mind-moments, and another mind arises. In this way, it should be understood that one mind ceases and another mind arises.
93:
The phrase 'together with matter' (saddhiṃ rūpena) is stated because the state of intimation (viññatti), which follows the mind, having a common cessation with the mind is easily understood. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: another mind ceases together with the matter that arose at the arising sub-moment (uppādakkhaṇa) of the seventeenth mind prior to that matter which is accompanied by intimation. It should be construed and understood that 'another mind ceases, another mind arises.' This is because the order of words and the order of meaning are different.

That mind which arose first and is about to cease, ceases only after assisting the other mind that will arise later through the power of the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth. In the same way, the other mind that has obtained the proximity condition and so forth also arises. In this context, arising and ceasing occur in a particular way according to the specific moment. To dispel the objection, 'If that is so, would there not be a gap between those two—the arising mind and the ceasing mind?', it is said, 'avīci manusambandho' (uninterrupted connection). Just as wise men consider 'this mind is that very mind' because no gap or hole is found, so too the mental continuum and the material continuum proceed like a current of water flowing in a river. The word 'avīci' is a term in the neuter gender expressing the state (bhāva) of being without interval.

Since looking straight ahead is called 'ālokita', it is stated as 'looking directly in front.' It means looking ahead towards the direction in which one is going, standing, sitting, or lying down. Because such 'ālokita' (looking ahead) exists, looking towards the corners (sides) following that direction is called 'vilokita', and thus it is stated as 'looking according to the directions.' It means looking in various ways towards the left and right sides in accordance with the direction faced. Looking downwards, looking upwards, and looking behind are to be understood as 'olokita', 'ullokita', and 'apalokita' respectively.

'Sāruppavasena' means looking in a manner suitable for recluses. By this very statement, it is established that other unsuitable ways of looking are not to be performed. Looking downwards (olokita) may occur when sweeping or plastering the ground; looking upwards (ullokita) when taking an object from above; and looking behind (apalokita) when avoiding a danger coming from the rear. Thus, by saying 'or by this' (iminā vā) etc., it is shown that these types of looking are merely illustrative examples (upalakkhaṇa).

'Kāyasakkhi' means a witness who has personally realized with the body, one who brings about the result. When that Venerable Nanda was developing insight (vipassanā), the effort arose in him: 'Depending on the lack of guarding the doors of the sense faculties, I have reached states of abnormality such as dissatisfaction in the Dispensation; I shall well restrain that very unguarding of the doors.' Thus, he became one possessed of strong moral shame and dread (hiri-ottappa). Because of his previous practice in that insight, he reached the pinnacle of perfection in the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara). For that reason, the Teacher placed him in the foremost rank (etadagga), saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who guard the doors of the sense faculties, Nanda is the foremost.' The word 'Nandassa' is a genitive case used in the sense of the agent (kattu). 'Iti' means 'by this looking'.
94:
The connection should be made by supplying the missing words: 'Purposefulness (sātthakatā) and suitability (sappāyatā) should be understood regarding looking ahead (ālokita) and looking aside (vilokita).' Therefore, this is said because for a monk who does not abandon his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), looking ahead and looking aside constitute the clear comprehension of the domain (gocarasampajañña). The meaning is that one should look ahead or aside only by the power of one's own meditation subject, such as the aggregates (khandha), and no other means should be sought. It is meant primarily in terms of the meditation subject.

Since what is called 'ālokita' and so forth is only a specific occurrence of mere phenomena (dhamma), the statement 'abbtantare' (internally) etc. is made to show that knowing it as it really is constitutes the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña). 'Āloketa' means one who looks ahead. Likewise, 'viloketa' means one who looks aside. 'Viññatti' refers to bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). 'Iti' means 'because of arising in that way.' It means arising by the power of bodily intimation, which is the mode of movement of the air element (vāyodhātu) originated by functional consciousness (kiriyacitta). 'Akkhidala' means the eyelid. It goes down as if sinking. It goes up as if leaping. 'By a machine' (yantakena) means like movement by a mechanical device that turns by holding strings attached to the eyelids. The knowledge of the root cause of the impulsion (javana) occurring in the mind-door, which arises due to such sinking and rising of the eyelids, is called 'root full-understanding' (mūlapariññā). It means arising by the power of those [minds] which are adventitious (āgantuka) and temporary (tāvakālika), existing only for that moment.

Among the seven types of consciousness shown in that verse, it means 'becoming the body (sarīra) while accomplishing the primary function of the limb (aṅgakicca).' For the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), being similar to rebirth-linking, is the primary limb; and what is primary is called the 'body' (sarīra). Or else, it means 'accomplishing the function of the cause' by being the reason for the uninterrupted occurrence. 'Having adverted to that life-continuum' is stated by way of the life-continuum in general. However, by way of the specific mode of occurrence, there are three types: past life-continuum (atītabhavaṅga), vibrating life-continuum (bhavaṅgacalana), and arrested life-continuum (bhavaṅguppaccheda). Among these, 'adverting' (āvaṭṭana) refers only to the arrested life-continuum. 'Because of the cessation of that [adverting]' is a statement of cause by way of the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya).

'In the first impulsion... in the seventh impulsion'—this is said with reference to the absence of lust, hatred, and delusion in the sense of 'this is a woman, this is a man' in the five-door process. For in that five-door process, because of the occurrence in an improper way by the power of unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) occurring prior to adverting (āvajjana) and determining (vuoṭṭhabbana), there arises an impulsion merely accompanied by greed towards a desirable female form etc., and an impulsion merely accompanied by hatred towards an undesirable object. However, absolute lust, hatred, and so forth do not occur.
95:
Attachment, aversion, and so forth occur exclusively at the mind-door. However, the javana occurring at the five-door is the root cause for that attachment, aversion, and so forth occurring at the mind-door. Alternatively, all the aforementioned states such as the bhavanga are the root causes. Thus, the 'full understanding of the root' (mūlapariññā) is stated by way of the root cause of the javana occurring at the mind-door. The adventitious nature (āgantukatā) and the temporary nature (tāvakālikatā) are stated only for the javana of the five-door, by way of its unprecedented nature and its brief duration. 'Yuddhamandale' means in the place of battle or on the battlefield. 'Heṭṭhupariyavasena' means by way of revolving below and above, or by way of the successive occurrence of the bhavanga. Indeed, it is by way of the occurrence of the bhavanga that their falling away occurs. By this phrase 'heṭṭhupariyavasena', the arising of the mind-door javana—which is dissimilar to the five-door javana—is shown by way of the successive occurrence of the lower and upper bhavanga. This is because attachment and so forth proceed only by the power of that mind-door javana. Therefore, it is said: "Looking and looking around occur by way of attachment and so forth."

'Āpāthaṃ' means coming into the range of the object. 'Sakakiccanipphādanavasena' means by way of performing one's own function, such as the function of adverting (āvajjana) and so forth. 'Taṃ' refers to the javana. Because the adverting and so forth occur due to the visible form coming into the range of the eye-door, it is said to be "like a house" only by way of being the cause of occurrence, not by way of being a physical support (nissaya). 'Āgantukapuriso viya' means like a visiting man who has arrived. Indeed, there are two kinds of visitors: the 'atithi' (a familiar guest) and the 'abbhāgata' (an unacquainted visitor). Among them, one who is familiar is called an 'atithi', and one who is not familiar is called an 'abbhāgata'; here, only the 'abbhāgata' is intended. Therefore, it is said: "As in another's house," and so forth. 'Tassa' is connected to the meaning that attachment, aversion, and delusion of the javana are improper. 'Āsinesu' means among those who are sitting. 'Āṇākaraṇaṃ' means making others follow one's own will.

Together with the associated states (sampayuttadhamma) such as contact (phassa) and so forth, they perish right there in the respective places where they perform their functions. 'Iti' means 'therefore', because the consciousnesses starting from adverting and ending with determining (vottabbana) perish. 'Ittarāni' means states that do not last long. In that context, the meaning is that this is a metaphor. Those states have a duration that is limited by arising and passing away; therefore, they are called 'tāvakālikāni' (temporary states), occurring by way of that nature.

'Etaṃ' refers to the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammohasampajañña). 'Ettha' means in that aforementioned collection of states. 'Dassana' is eye-consciousness; because looking and looking around are evident only by the power of that eye-consciousness, adverting and so forth are not taken. 

'Samavāye' means in the combination (of conditions). 'Tattha' means when looking and looking around are evident by way of the five aggregates. This word 'tattha' is in the locative case in the sense of a sign (nimitta). Who is there, liberated from those aggregates...
96:
A certain person looks, but [in reality] does not look. Who is the one person who looks here and there? [In reality] he does not look here and there—this is the meaning.

The passage beginning with 'Tathā' shows the process by way of the sense bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). The eye and visible forms are, as appropriate, the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) and object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for seeing (eye-consciousness). Similarly, adverting is the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) and so forth. Light is the decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Thus, the conditionality of seeing is stated figuratively according to the Suttanta method. The conascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya) also belongs only to seeing. This statement is merely an indication, as other conditions such as mutuality (aññamañña), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) are also obtained. At present, the reading 'sahajātādipaccayā' is also seen. The passage beginning with 'Evaṃ' is the conclusion.

Now, wishing to clarify clear comprehension (sampajañña) in bending and stretching according to the Pali text, he said 'Samiñjite pasārite' and so forth. In that context, 'pabbānaṃ' means of the joints (of the hands and feet). Indeed, it is only through the bending and stretching of those joints that the bending and stretching of all the hands and feet occur. Alternatively, those hands and feet have joints, therefore they are called 'pabbā'. Just like the word 'saddho', it means 'those having joints'. 'Cittavasena' means only by the will of the mind or by the power of the mind. Whatever mind arises to bend or to stretch, whether for benefit or for harm, it means that one should not bend or stretch merely by following those respective minds (but should do so with clear comprehension). In those instances of bending and stretching, it should be understood that the connection is 'the comprehension of benefit and non-benefit is to be known'. 'Khaṇe khaṇe' is a statement intended to pervade every moment that exists in such a manner. 'Vedanā' refers to the pain caused by stiffness and so forth. By the passage 'Vedanā uppajjati' and so forth, he shows the successive benefits. Likewise with 'Tā vedanā nuppajjanti' and so forth. For the preceding statement is the cause for the succeeding statement. 'Kāle' means at the appropriate time for bending or stretching. 'Phātiṃ' means increase or growth. 'Jhānādi' refers to the distinguished states such as jhāna, path, fruition, and nibbāna.

'Tatrāyaṃ nayo' refers to the method described as showing an example in the case of not comprehending with wisdom what is suitable and unsuitable. By showing the disadvantage in not comprehending, the advantage in comprehending is also clarified. Therefore, the examples of comprehending or not comprehending what is suitable (sappāya) and unsuitable (asappāya) should be understood here. 'Mahācetiyaṅgaṇe' means on the terrace of the Great Stupa named Hemamālī, built by King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī. For it is said:

"The Elder who brought faith to the island,
To the King, my grandfather,
Thus, it is said, spoke: 'Your grandson,
King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, the ruler of the earth,
Will build the Great Stupa named Hemamālī,
Which is delightful to the heart,
And one hundred and twenty cubits high.'"
97:
## 
“The great meritorious King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī will, in the future, build the magnificent Mahāthūpa, the Suvaṇṇamāli, one hundred and twenty cubits high, which is delightful to the heart.”

In this context, the ground area is called 'aṅgaṇa' (precinct/courtyard). It is similar to the usage in the Jātaka Pāḷi such as “udaṅgaṇe tattha pappaṃ avindu.” Therefore, it means a well-prepared ground area in the vicinity of the stupa. For that very reason, “becoming a layman” means returning to the low state of a householder, being weary and exhausted due to the cause of entering into physical contact with a woman. “Jhāyī” means reaching a state of burning (worry/anxiety).

It is said “cīvarakuṭidaṇḍake” referring to the practice of making a robe-hut on the precinct of the Mahāthūpa and reciting/studying there. It means the sticks or poles made for the purpose of covering the robe-hut. Ācariya Ānanda and Ācariya Dhammapāla stated that “Maṇisappa” is a species of snake existing in the island of Sri Lanka. The use of the word “they say” (vadanti) without saying “some” or “others” is to indicate that it should be taken as the essence, as there is no other way to interpret it. Therefore, in this context, Maṇisappa should not be understood as a green snake (nīlasappa) and so forth.

“Mahātheravatthunā” means by the story of the Elder of that name. “Antevāsikehi” means questioning by one among the many disciples sitting there. Therefore, it is said, “The disciples questioned that Elder.” “Kammaṭṭhānaṃ” refers to the meditation on the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhāna) in the manner that will be described later, such as “internally, there is no so-called self...” The meaning can also be understood from the context (pakarana). The use of the plural “you” (tumhehi) again is for the purpose of including all those present who were questioning.

One who has such a nature is called “evarūpo.” By way of eliding the niggahita (niggahitalopa), it means one whose nature is the practice of meditation. In the phrase “evam-etthāpi,” the word “api” refers back to the section on looking ahead and looking aside (ālokita-vilokita) mentioned below. This method applies to the sections above as well.

“Suttākaḍḍhanavasena” means by way of pulling the strings attached to a machine. “Dāruyantassa” means a mechanical figure (puppet) made of wood. It is called “yanta” because it reaches various actions or because it moves while performing various gestures with hands, feet, etc. A puppet such as a dancer’s puppet with five limbs (pañcālikā) is indeed a mechanical figure made of wood. This is merely an illustration. Such a figure is called “potthalikā” because it is decorated with cloth and ornaments, and “pañcālikā” because it has five limbs like a living being. “Hatthapādalalanaṃ” means the shaking of hands and feet, or performing graceful movements with hands and feet.
98:
## 
In the phrase “saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe,” the double robe and the bowl are mentioned together to avoid the heaviness of the text, as they share the same act of carrying. The meaning should be understood appropriately: the inner robe (antaravāsaka) by way of wearing (nivāsana), and the remaining robes by way of draping (pārupana). “Tattha” refers to the carrying of the double robe and the bowl. “Vuttappakāro” refers to the various types mentioned in the Pāḷi text regarding the method of reflection (paccavekkhaṇā).

“One of a hot nature” (uṇhapakatika) refers to a monk whose body is predominantly hot and prone to feverish heat. “One of a cold nature” (sītālukassa) refers to a monk whose body is predominantly cold. “Thick” (ghana) means layered. The word “double-layered” (dupaṭṭa) is merely an example. For it is said: “For robes that have exceeded their season, a four-fold double robe, a double-layered upper robe, and a double-layered inner robe are suitable; in the case of refuse-rag robes (paṃsukūla), one may make as many layers as desired.”

“Opposite” (viparīta) means a robe that is the opposite of those two, which is unsuitable for all three types of persons. Why? It is said, “by giving a patch (aggaḷa), etc.” A piece of cloth added after removing an old part is called an “aggaḷa.” The word “ādi” (etc.) includes needlework and so forth. The word “tathā” has the sense of drawing in the meaning of “unsuitable” (asappāya).

Cloth produced by silkworms in the region of Paṭṭuṇṇa is called “paṭṭuṇṇa” (silk). White cloth made from a special fiber is called “dukūla” (fine linen). The word “ādi” includes silk-thread, woolen blankets, and other allowable robes with fringe. Why? It is said, “For such a robe...” etc. By the statement that it causes danger to the life of a monk living alone in the forest, it refers to a part of the danger to the holy life (brahmacariya). It is also said so because it is common to thieves and others. The connection is that such a robe is absolutely unsuitable. Thus, the aforementioned unsuitability is not absolute, because such a requisite may sometimes be suitable for someone under certain conditions. However, these two (robes obtained through wrong livelihood and robes that increase unwholesome states) are shown to be absolutely unsuitable, as they are never suitable for anyone at any time.

“Wrong livelihood” (micchā-ājīva) is so called because one lives wrongly through improper effort; it is the act of seeking requisites through improper search (anesana). Wrong livelihood proceeding through signs (nimittakamma) and so forth is the same. By this, the twenty-one types of improper search are meant. Indeed, it is stated in the Commentaries to the Suttanipāta and Khuddakapāṭha, in the explanation of the Metta Sutta:

“A monk who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, does not apply himself properly, whose virtue is broken, and who makes his living depending on the twenty-one types of improper search. What are they? Giving bamboo, giving leaves, giving flowers, giving fruits, giving tooth-sticks, giving face-water, giving bathing powder, giving scented powder, giving clay, flattery (cāṭukamyatā), 'bean-soup' talk (muggasūpyatā—speaking half-truths), acting like a nurse (pāribhaṭatā), running errands (jaṅghapesanika), medical practice (vejjakamma), messenger work (dūtakamma), going on errands (pahiṇagamana), exchanging alms for alms (piṇḍapaṭipiṇḍa), giving gifts in return (dānānuppadāna), the art of site-divination (vatthuvijjā), the art of astrology (nakkhattavijjā), and the art of reading body marks (aṅgavijjā).”
99:
Moreover, the teacher Elder Ānanda, who composed the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā, said this: "The twenty-one kinds of improper search (anesanā) are: practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, performing errands, lancing boils, applying ointment to wounds, administering emetics, administering purgatives, preparing nasal oil, preparing wound oil, giving bamboo, giving leaves, flowers, fruits, bath powder, soap, tooth-sticks, face water, scented powder, and clay, performing flattery (cāṭukamma), speaking 'bean-soup' talk (muggasūpiya), and nursing or carrying children (pāribhaṭu). The twenty-second, acting as a foot-messenger (jaṅghapesanika), is similar to messenger work, and thus they are counted as twenty-one." This is stated in the Mūla-ṭīkā.

In this matter of wrong livelihood (micchājīva), the words of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) are spoken according to the Suttanta method, such as in the Brahmajāla Sutta. However, the words of the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) are spoken according to the Abhidhamma method, such as in the Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga. Because of this discrepancy, it is said that there are differing views among some teachers in this regard. The wise should investigate and then accept. Alternatively, by the phrase "nimittakamma etc.," the terms nimitta (hinting), obhāsa (signaling), and parikathā (roundabout talk) are indicated. "Wrong livelihood" (micchājīva) refers to the aforementioned efforts. Therefore, a gain that arises through the power of nimittakamma and micchājīva is unsuitable (asappāya) because it destroys virtue and brings about harm. Even in a collective compound (samāhāra-dvanda), the masculine usage is sometimes seen, as in the example "cittuppādo."

Lust and other unwholesome states arise toward a very pleasing object, while hatred and other unwholesome states arise toward a very displeasing object; therefore, it is said, "unwholesome states increase." "That (taṃ)" refers to both the increase of the unwholesome and the decrease of the wholesome. "By the power of not abandoning the meditation subject" means by the power of not letting go of the meditation subject that will be described.

Having shown the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) in brief with the words "Inside, there is no such thing as a self," etc., he then explains that meaning by demonstrating the emptiness of self (atta-suññatā) of the body, saying "the body also is insentient," just as "there, the robe also is insentient." It should be understood that he clarifies the reason for the aforementioned contentment with whatever is available (itarītara-santosa) with the words "Therefore, even if one obtains a fine robe," etc. The connection should be stated thus: wishing to show the clear comprehension of non-delusion, he spoke the words beginning with "Abbhantare." To explain that meaning by demonstrating the emptiness of self, he spoke the words beginning with "Tattha cīvaraṃ." Now, wishing to manifest the acquired quality known as contentment with whatever is available, which is the benefit of demonstrating the emptiness of self, he spoke the words beginning with "Tasmā neva sundaraṃ."
100:
In that context, wishing to show the clear comprehension of non-delusion, he spoke the words beginning with "Abbhantare." In those words, "Abbhantare" means within one's own continuity (santāna). "Tattha" means in that act of wearing the robe, or in the body of the monk who wears it and the robe that is worn. "Kāyopi" means the body, which is a mere designation of a self, is also (insentient). The word "tasmā" (therefore) should be added, meaning "because it is insentient." "Ahaṃ" (I) refers to the body produced by kamma. "Dhātuyo" refers to the external elements known as robes. "Dhātusamūhaṃ" refers to the internal collection of elements known as the body. The connection is: just as elements cover a collection of elements in the covering of a modeled figure (potthaka-rūpa).

"Pottha" means the pouring of resin or filling. Because it is made by the act of painting or carving/sculpting, it is called "potthaka." That potthaka itself is the modeled figure (rūpa). Here, a figure made of wood, clay, etc., produced by the act of carving is intended. "Tasmā" means because it is insentient, or because it is empty of self.

An anthill which is the dwelling of snakes is called "nāgavammika." A tree that is a place of veneration is called "cetiyarukkha." These are mentioned here because they are suitable as similes for the body, which is respected by some and not respected by others. "Tehi" means by flowers, scents, excrement, urine, etc. The meaning is that just as one should not feel joy or displeasure toward an anthill or a shrine-tree because they are empty of self, so too one should not feel joy or displeasure toward the self known as the body.

One should accept only after first reflecting, "Will I receive it or not?" and seeing the benefit, "I will receive it." Intending that only such acceptance constitutes the clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), he said, "without taking it suddenly," etc.

"Garupatto" means a bowl that is excessively heavy. "Catupañcagaṇṭhikā" refers to bowls that have four or five patches (knots). As in the examples "dwa-tti-pattā" and "cha-ppañca-vācā," the meaning of the word "vā" (or) within the compound is primary here. A bowl patched with four knots or five knots is called "dubbisodhanīya" because it is difficult to clean; this meaning is taken by way of deliberation (vikkappana). A bowl that has four or five patches is called "catupañcagaṇṭhikāhata," similar to the example "ajyāhita." Or it can be said it is struck (patched) with four or five knots. This word is a qualitative description containing the reason for its being difficult to clean. 

Although it is indeed taught in the Ūnapañcabandhana training rule that a bowl patched with five knots may be used, it should be understood as "unsuitable" (asappāya) here in the section on suitability because it causes an impediment (palibodha) merely by being difficult to clean. "Dudhotapatto" refers to a bowl that is naturally difficult to clean even if it has no patches. The words beginning with "Taṃ dhovantasseva" (are intended to show the reason for the unsuitability of both types of bowls).
101:
This is also the reason for the unsuitability of both types of bowls. By the statement, "A bowl with the color of a gem is desirable," it is shown that although such a bowl is allowable according to the method of the Vinaya, it is unsuitable according to the method of the Suttanta because it causes an obstacle (to meditation). For in the Vinaya commentaries, only the act of baking is forbidden, as stated: "It is not allowable to place a bowl on a wheel, polish it, and bake it with the intention, 'I will make it the color of a gem.'" Therefore, they say: "If one receives a gem-colored bowl made by another, it is allowable to use it." According to the method stated regarding robes, such as "Such a bowl causes an obstacle to the living of one dwelling alone in the forest," and the method stated by us, such as "A bowl obtained through hinting (nimittakamma) and so forth is absolutely unallowable because it brings about harm through the destruction of virtue," these should be applied accordingly. The phrase "for one who associates with" is a word included within the cause (hetu) of the increase (of unwholesome states) and the decrease (of wholesome states).

The word "Inside" and so forth is a summary. The word "Therein" and so forth is an elaboration by clarifying the state of being empty of self. "With tongs" refers to a specific type of iron-gripper used by blacksmiths. "In taking hold of a bowl that has the color of fire" means taking hold of a bowl that has become the color of fire because it has been burnt by fire. This analogy is appropriate for a bowl that causes the burning of lust and so forth; thus it is so stated.

By the phrase "Furthermore" and so forth, he shows the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) collectively regarding the wearing of the outer robe, the inner robe, and the carrying of the bowl. "Helpless people with severed hands and feet" is the connection. Blue flies (nīlamakkhikā) are wild flies that lay eggs. The eggs laid by blue flies in the wounds of cattle and so forth, which cause harm and destruction, are called "āsāṭikā" (maggots). "In a hospice" means in a dwelling place for helpless people. "Compassionate people" means those with much compassion (karuṇā). "Pieces of cloth just the size of the wound" means small pieces of cloth cut for the purpose of covering according to the size of the wound. "To some people" means to some helpless people among many. "Thick" means coarse or thick cloths. "In such a case" refers to when that occurs; this locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic state (bhāvalakkhaṇa) or a sign (nimitta). Because it is asked why (joy or displeasure does not arise), it is stated "merely for covering the wound" and so forth. In the words "with a piece of cloth" and "with a potsherd," when connected with the meaning, the third case (instrumental) is used in the sense of the object (kamma) or the instrument (karaṇa). "Merely for covering the wound" and "merely for medical treatment" are modifiers (visesana); it should be understood that they are not intended for the purpose of decoration or enjoyment.
