Since this analogy of a sick person is perfect for the bowl and robes which are the requisites of the body that is constantly pained by the suffering of formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā) and so forth, the statement should be seen in that way. Because one habitually practices supreme clear comprehension by noting the state of subtlety, and because one is superior to those who practiced clear comprehension previously, one is called "uttamasampajānākārī" (one who acts with supreme clear comprehension).
102:
Because of the connection with the specific object of the action such as eating, the specific action together with its specific object is understood only through words such as "asita" (eaten). Thus it is stated, "Asita means in the eating of alms-food" and so forth. The "eight meanings" (attha) refer to the eight kinds of specific benefits.

Therein, among the eating of alms-food and so forth, the word "purpose" (attha) shows the eightfold purpose taught in the Sutta text beginning with "for the maintenance of this body" (kāyassa ṭhitiyā) according to the view of the Elder Mahāsīva. For the Elder Mahāsīva says: "The lower four factors are factors to be rejected (paṭikkhepa), whereas the upper eight factors should be combined by way of purpose (payojana)."

Among those eight factors, "for the maintenance of this body" (yāvad-eva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā) is one factor, "for keeping it going" (yāpanāya) is one, "for ending discomfort" (vihiṃsūparatiyā) is one, "for supporting the holy life" (brahmacariyānuggahāya) is one, "thus I shall destroy old feelings" (iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi) is one, "and I shall not arouse new feelings" (navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi) is one, "and there will be sustenance for me" (yātrā ca me bhavissati) is one, and "blamelessness" (anavajjatā ca) is one. Living at ease (phāsuvihāra), however, is merely the advantage of eating. In this way, the eight factors should be combined by way of purpose.

By another method, "not for fun" (neva davāya) is one factor, "not for intoxication" (na madāya) is one, "not for beautification" (na maṇḍanāya) is one, "not for adornment" (na vibhūsanāya) is one, "merely for the maintenance and keeping going of this body" (yāvad-eva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya) is one, "for ending discomfort and supporting the holy life" (vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāya) is one, "thus I shall destroy old feelings and I shall not arouse new feelings" (iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi) is one, and "there will be sustenance for me" (yātrā ca me bhavissati) is one. The factors stated as "blamelessness and living at ease" (anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro ca) are merely the benefits of eating and are not intended here. Why are they not intended? Because of the absence of those purposes, and because only those eight purposes are mentioned here by the word "attha" (purpose).

It might be asked: "Is it not understood that only the second method is intended here by the limiting statement (mariyādavacana) that it is stated by the method beginning with 'not for fun' (neva davāya)?" It is not so understood. This is because the Paccavekkhaṇa Pāḷi (text of reflection) was taught by first showing the factors to be rejected, such as "not for fun" and so forth, and because it is shown as a limit only according to the order of the Pāḷi as it was taught. For it is stated "by the method beginning with 'not for fun'" only according to the order of the text (pāṭhakkama), not according to the order of the meaning (atthakkama). According to the order of the meaning, it should be stated "by the method beginning with 'for the maintenance of this body'" (imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā).
103:
When the donor gives in three ways and the recipient receives in two ways, it is called 'paṭiggahaṇa' (acceptance), referring to that receiving. The process of eating, such as lowering the hand to receive food and making a morsel for the purpose of eating, is clearly shown to occur only through the power of the wind element (vāyodhātu). In the phrase 'only through the diffusion of the wind element,' the word 'eva' (only) indicates the exclusion of any [other agent], such as 'there is no one [who eats],' etc. Kuñcikā refers to a key that opens a door, which is also called 'tāḷa'. Yantaka refers to a machine. It is called yantaka because one strives with this machine in opening, closing, raising, lowering, etc.

Crushing into powder is the function of the pestle (musala). Placing inside and keeping it there is the function of the mortar (udukkhala). Turning it over by means of stirring forward and backward is the function of the hand. 'Iti' means 'thus.' 'Tattha' is a word with a locative case ending, used in the sense of accomplishing the hand's function, or in the sense of a characteristic state (bhāvalakkhaṇa) or a sign (nimitta). Tanukakheḷa is clear saliva. Bahalakheḷa is thick, turbid saliva. Turning the food here and there by means of stirring forward and backward with the 'hand' known as the tongue is called jivhāhatthaparivattaka (turning with the tongue-hand).

The terms kaṭacchu and dabbī are synonyms in some places. It is said in the dictionary, 'kaṭacchu is masculine, dabbī is feminine.' However, in this context, the object with which one takes food into oneself is called kaṭacchu (spoon/ladle). The object with which one performs the extraction of that food is called dabbī (ladle/scoop). Palālasanthāra refers to a bed of straw that serves as a support. This is merely an illustration. Dhārento means receiving as a support. Just as water that carries the earth is supported by wind, the food that is eaten stays in the stomach (āmāsaya) only by the wind element; this is shown by the words 'it stays only by the power of the wind element.' Indeed, the wind element creates a dense path below and across for the consumed food, and keeps it established in the stomach by controlling it well until it is digested.

Uddhana is the place where pots etc. are placed for cooking; it is also called 'cullī' (stove/fireplace). A short stick is called daṇḍaka. A goad is called yaṭṭhi. The word 'iti' refers to the manner already described. It is the manifestation of the described manner through the power of the elements. Among those words, 'atiharati' means bringing forward as far as the mouth. 'Vītiharati' means bringing it from the mouth into the stomach while mixing it thoroughly; thus says the teacher Dhammapāla Thera. The teacher Ānanda Thera, however, says, 'It brings it from the mouth as far as the stomach.' Both views are the same in meaning, as both intend only the bringing [of food] in connection with the stomach.

Alternatively, 'atiharati' means bringing while passing the door of the mouth. 'Vītiharati' means bringing the food that has reached the stomach nearby. 'Dhāreti' means making it stay in the stomach...
104:
Parivatteti means performing the turning from one place to another. Sañcuṇṇeti means crushing into fine powder as if with a pestle. Visoseti means drying without making it excessively dry. Nīharati means expelling from the stomach to the outside. In the functions of the earth element (pathavīdhātu), the meaning should be understood exactly as described.

The wind element (vāyodhātu) associated with the earth element is able to perform those functions of carrying, turning, crushing, and drying the food; the wind element alone cannot do so. Therefore, those are also described as functions of the earth element. Sineheti means moistening. Allattañca anupāleti means preserving the moist state without making it too wet, so that excessive drying does not occur due to the wind element and others. Añjasa (pathway) refers to the path for the entry, turning, and exit of food.

Viññāṇadhātu (consciousness element) refers to the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu), because the cognition of seeking, swallowing, etc., is intended. Tattha tattha means in those various functions of seeking, swallowing, etc. The effort (exertion) that is the cause of those various cognitions and that accomplishes those tasks is called sammāpayoga (right application). The effort by which seeking etc. are accomplished is said to also accomplish the cognition of those objects, because it is inseparable from them. Tamanvāya means 'depending on that effort.'

Ābhujati means reflecting on or knowing those acts of seeking, swallowing, digestion, indigestion, etc., by way of seeking and by way of experiencing the swallowing, digestion, indigestion, etc. Since cognition is preceded by reflection (āvajjana), it should be understood that cognition is also included here. Alternatively, sammāpayoga means right practice. Depending on that right practice, one reflects, attends to, or knows: 'There is no such thing as a self (attā) who is the eater inside,' and so on. Since all activities of consciousness are preceded by attention (ābhoga), it is simply said 'ābhujati.'

Gamanato (by way of going) is because of going towards the village for alms by way of alms-round. Returning is also included in this term because it has the nature of going. Pariyesanato (by way of seeking) is because of wandering in the village for alms. Since it has the nature of seeking, approaching the refectory (paṭikkamanasālā) etc. is also included in this term.

Paribhogato (by way of consumption) is because of consuming the food which, at the very moment it is crushed by the 'pestles' of teeth and turned by the tongue, loses its specific characteristics of color, smell, and preparation, becoming extremely loathsome like dog's vomit in a dog's trough. Āsayato (by way of repository) means because the consumed food reaches the state of being a repository for bile, phlegm, pus, and blood, thus becoming a cause for extreme loathsomeness; and also because it is the repository of the four things such as bile that are situated above the stomach. Together...
105:
Even though it exists as a single whole, it is defined by the power of kamma; because it stands and proceeds without mixing with one another by way of boundaries, it is called 'āsaya' (receptacle). These are the fourfold receptacles such as bile, etc., situated above the stomach (āmāsaya). Here, the letter 'ā' carries the meaning of boundary (mariyāda). 'Nidhānato' means from the stomach. Because the consumed food remains accumulated in this stomach, the stomach is called 'nidhāna' (repository). 'Aparippakkato' refers to the state of not yet being digested by the karmically-born fire element (kammaja-tejo) known as the digestive faculty (gahaṇī), which digests the consumed food. 'Paripakkato' means being digested by that same karmically-born fire element. 'Phalato' means from the result. Or it means the result in the sense of the sequential production of diseases such as the rotting of hair, etc., and skin diseases like ringworm, from food that is either well-digested or poorly digested. It is said, "This is its fruit." 'Nissandanato' means because of trickling and flowing out here and there from many doors such as the eyes, ears, etc. For it is said:

"Expensive snacks, meals,
Rice and drinks,
Having entered through a single door,
Flow out through nine doors."

'Sammakkhanato' means because of being smeared everywhere as appropriate during the time of consumption and after consumption on the nine doors and limbs such as the hands and lips. It should be understood in connection with the remaining text that "the repulsiveness of food should be contemplated in all circumstances." This sequence starting with 'gamanato' (from going) is established according to the order of the completion of those various actions. Although smearing (sammakkhana) is found during consumption, etc., it is placed last because it is especially repulsive by way of trickling (nissanda). 'Pattakāle' means at the proper time, or at the time when it reaches the state of feces and urine due to being digested by the aforementioned fire element. Due to the distress arising from suppressing the urge for feces and urine, sweat is released from the entire body. Because of that, the eyes roll, and the mind is not concentrated. Other diseases such as colic and fistula arise. 'Sabbaṃ taṃ' refers to all those things such as the release of sweat. 'Aṭṭhāne' means in an improper place such as fields or shrines possessed by humans or non-humans. For humans or non-humans who are angry at one doing so in such a place may even bring about the end of life. 'Āpatti' refers to the occurrence of offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) or expiation (pācittiya) as appropriate for monks and nuns. 'Patirūpe ṭhāne' means in a suitable place, which is the opposite of the aforementioned place. 'Sabbaṃ taṃ' refers to all things such as the falling into an offense.
106:
When reaching the state of feces and urine, due to the distress arising from suppressing the urge, sweat is released from the entire body. Because of that, the eyes roll, and the mind is not concentrated. Other diseases such as colic and fistula also occur. Such sweating, etc., happens in improper places. Humans or non-humans who possess fields, shrines, etc., which are improper places, may become angry and bring about the end of life for a monk who excretes there. Specifically, offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for monks and expiation (pācittiya) for nuns occur as appropriate. In a suitable place, which is the opposite of the aforementioned place, those offenses, etc., do not exist.

To prevent the foolish misconception that "there is a self (attā) that causes the excretion, and the excretion happens because of that self's desire," it is said "without desire" (akāmatāya). It means that it exits only through the diffusion of the air element (vāyo-dhātu) without one's own desire and without effort. 'Sannicitā' refers to (feces and urine) that stand as an accumulation. 'Vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā' means being pressed from all sides by the force of the air element; this is a statement of the cause for the exit. After saying "sannicitā uccārapassāvā" (accumulated feces and urine), saying "so panāyaṃ uccārapassāvo" (now this feces and urine) again is to show that the masculine usage is possible even in a collective compound (samāhāra-dvanda). For the fixed characteristic of that collective compound is the singular number. Because it is discharged without any regard for oneself, it does not exist for one's own benefit or as one's own property. It means it has no benefit for others either, because it is not given to anyone as a gift and because it is loathsome. 'Sarīranissando' means it is merely a trickling out from the body. Some say, "It is merely a benefit of the body," saying that it exists when the body exists and does not exist when the body does not. That statement is improper because it does not agree with the illustrated example. In that commentary, it is said "merely a cleaning," which means merely a process of purification. A water vessel made of a bamboo tube, etc., is called 'udakatumba'. 'Taṃ' refers to the discarded water.

'Gate' refers to (the posture) in walking. Since the carrying forward and backward of the body during walking was already mentioned by the terms 'abhikkama' (advancing) and 'paṭikkama' (retreating), the teacher Ānanda says that here only 'walking' (gamana) is taken. The teacher Dhammapāla designates that statement as 'keci-vāda' (the view of some teachers). Why? Because the carrying forward and backward of the body that occurs in walking is inseparable from that walking, and because it is included in the act of walking defined by the stepping of feet, and because it contradicts the Vibhaṅga Commentary, etc. Indeed, in that commentary, the inclusion of walking in both (advancing and retreating) and its distinction are stated: "Here, one posture comes in two places. Below, in the context of 'abhikkante paṭikkante,' it is spoken of as walking a journey (addhāna-gamana) by one going to and returning from the village for alms. Here, in 'gate ṭhite nisinne,' it should be understood as spoken of as the posture of subtle lifting of the feet (cuṇṇika-pāduddhāra) within the monastery." To show that in the words 'gate', etc., there is only a difference in action due to the difference in state, but no difference in meaning, 'gacchanto vā' (or one walking), etc., is said. Therefore, it is said:
107: ## The passage beginning with "Tasmā". In that Sutta (in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta recited in the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya), "addhāna-iriyāpathā" refers to postures that occur for a long time, for a long duration. This is because the word "addhāna" denotes a long time, as in "addhāniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ" etc. Alternatively, they are postures involving traveling a long distance, having a long path. This is because the word "addhāna" is a synonym for a long path, as in "addhānagamanasamayo" etc. "Majjhimā" refers to postures occurring by way of alms-round etc., which are not of a very long duration or not of a very long path. "Cuṇṇiya-iriyāpathā" refers to postures occurring in the monastery or elsewhere by way of turning here and there, etc., which are minute and subtle because of their slight nature. In the world, even a slight thing is called "powdered" (cuṇṇavicuṇṇa). There is also a variant reading "khuddakacuṇṇika-iriyāpathā," meaning small and subtle postures as explained. "Tasmā" (Therefore) is said because of stating only the distinction of postures by way of such states. "Tesupi" (In those also) refers to "gate ṭhite" (in going, in standing) etc. "Vuttanayena" (In the manner stated) refers to the manner stated in "abhikkante" (in moving forward) etc. "Aparabhāge" (In the subsequent part) means after the posture of going. "Ṭhito" (Standing) means one endowed with the posture of standing. "Ettheva" (Right here) means only in the walking path (caṅkama). Thus it should be understood appropriately in all places. The sequential mention of sitting and lying down, like going, standing, and sitting, is not appropriate because usually they do not occur in that order; therefore, it is said simply as "uṭṭhāya" (having arisen). In this context, because of the proximity to the word "wakefulness" (jāgarita), "lying down" (sayana) refers only to falling asleep by way of entering the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and does not mean merely stretching the back; this is shown by "kiriyāmayapavattānaṃ" etc. It should be noted that stretching the back is also included here because it has the same characteristic as the posture of lying down, as in the training rule on daytime sleep. Action is called "kiriya" (activity), which is the function of the body etc.; because they accomplish that function of the body etc., they are called "kiriyāmaya" (made of activity). This is because taddhita (derivative) words have multiple meanings. Alternatively, the function of the two advertings (āvajjana) is called "kiriya"; because they are performed or accomplished by that activity, they are called "kiriyāmaya." When the life-continuum is interrupted by the power of adverting, the process-consciousnesses (vīthicitta) arise. They are called "pavatta" (occurring/proceeding) because they occur and revolve in various ways through repeated arising. In some versions, there is the reading "cittānaṃ" (of consciousnesses), but it should be known that this is not the ancient reading because it contradicts the Abhidhamma commentaries etc. and their sub-commentaries. Those things that occur being "kiriyāmaya" are indeed the same, whether the impulsion (javana) or the entire process-consciousness of the six doors. Therefore, it is said in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā:
108: The teacher said in the Jhānavibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā: "Because they are made of the activity of the body etc., and because they are originated by the activity of adverting, the impulsion (javana), or indeed the entire occurrence in the six doors, is called 'kiriyāmayapavatta' (occurrence made of activity)." "Appavattaṃ" (non-occurrence) means the non-arising of process-consciousness at the time of falling asleep; this should be understood as the meaning of "sleeping" (suttaṃ). This is a statement with a meaning to be inferred (neyyattha). Otherwise, if taken as a direct meaning (nītattha), the occurrence of all door-freed consciousnesses (dvāravimuttacitta) that arise by way of preceding or following the six-door consciousnesses would also be called "sleeping." If so, it should be understood that the occurrence of door-freed consciousnesses arising at times other than the time of falling asleep would also be included in "wakefulness" (jāgarita). Regarding the arising of sound in its respective place depending on the lips etc., which are the causes of the mind's effort, it is said: "depending also on the lips" etc. The intention is: although sound arises according to its place, it arises only through effort such as moving the lips, and not without that effort. Some teachers say that the passage "depending also on the lips" etc. is a demonstration of the place of origin of sound, but that is inappropriate because it is not stated so in the commentary. For it is not possible to express the "place" (ṭhāna) using an accusative case (kamma) along with the conjunction "ca" (also) in "oṭṭhe ca paṭiccā" etc. "Tadanurūpaṃ" means in accordance with that sound. Because speaking is contrary to reflection, in the section on silence, it is not said "the one who speaks in the subsequent part reflects thus." By this, it should be understood that "one reflects only while remaining silent." If there is a difference in nature between speaking and silence, this distinction would be appropriate; if not, it would not be. To address this inquiry, it is said: "upādārūpapavattiyāñhi" etc. The occurrence of the sound-base (saddāyatana), which is derived matter (upādārūpa), is called "speaking" (bhāsana), and its non-occurrence is called "silence" (tuṇhī). In the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsiva, clear comprehension of action (sampajānākāritā) is taken as seeing the cessation of material and immaterial phenomena occurring in each successive posture right then and there. Therefore, that doctrine should be understood by way of the section on insight (vipassanā-vāra) in the clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) mentioned in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, and not by way of the fourfold division of clear comprehension. Hence, showing that it is intended only in that Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and not here (in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta), he said "tayidaṃ" etc. A statement that has non-delusion as its chief or head is called "asammohadhura." This statement contains the reason why that meaning is intended only in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. However, in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, all four types of clear comprehension are obtainable to the extent that...
109:
Since this teaching primarily aims at showing the special fruits of the monkhood, the phrase "In this [sutta] however" (imasmim pana), etc., is stated to show that these four types of clear comprehension (sampajañña) are intended in this Sāmaññaphala Sutta. The phrase "in the same manner as stated" (vuttanayeneva) means in the same manner as already described regarding going forward and so forth.

Is this not the exposition (niddesa) of the summary (uddesa) "endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension"? If so, why is the detailed explanation given only by way of clear comprehension? To resolve this objection, the phrase "acting with clear comprehension" (sampajānākārī), etc., was stated. The meaning is that the detailed explanation is given in this way because the meaning is to be understood through the power of clear comprehension which is indeed associated with mindfulness. By the phrase "only that which is associated with mindfulness" (satisampayuttasseva), it is shown that just as clear comprehension is taken as predominant in its function of knowing, so too is mindfulness taken as predominant in its function of remembering. This phrase does not merely show the state of mindfulness and clear comprehension existing together. For there is never an occurrence of knowledge (ñāṇa) that is devoid of mindfulness.

Is this detailed explanation not only by way of clear comprehension? If so, why should the meaning be understood through the power of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness? This objection is also resolved by the statement: "This is the detailed explanation of the phrase 'endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension'." The meaning is this: because it is the expansion of the meaning briefly stated together as "endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension," both mindfulness and clear comprehension are to be taken as having equal predominance in the exposition (niddesa) just as in the summary (uddesa). By this sentence, the equal predominance of mindfulness with clear comprehension is clearly manifested. This is because the meaning of their equal predominance is established by showing that it is an expansion of the meaning briefly stated together. Now, to establish that meaning of equal predominance of mindfulness and clear comprehension also by way of the Vibhaṅga method, the phrase "In the Book of Analysis however" (Vibhaṅgapakaraṇe pana), etc., is stated. By this Vibhaṅga method as well, the predominance of mindfulness is shown just like that of clear comprehension. In that Vibhaṅga, "these words" (etāni padāni) refers to the summary terms such as "he acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning." "Only as analyzed" (vibhattāneva) means they are analyzed separately in all instances without conjoining mindfulness with clear comprehension.

Furthermore, the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhima-bhāṇakas) and the Abhidhammikas say: One monk walks while thinking of something else and reflecting on something else; another monk walks without letting go of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Likewise, one monk stands while thinking of something else and reflecting on something else; another stands without letting go of the meditation subject. One monk sits while thinking of something else and reflecting on something else; another sits without letting go of the meditation subject. One monk lies down while thinking of something else and reflecting on something else; another lies down without letting go of the meditation subject. Considering that clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) is not yet evident by this much alone, they demonstrate it by way of the walking meditation. For a monk who has descended to the walkway and stands at the end of the walkway, comprehending: "The mental and physical phenomena occurring at the eastern end of the walkway..."
110:
"Mental and physical phenomena (rūpa-arūpa dhammā) do not reach the western end of the walkway and cease right here [at the eastern end]; those arising at the western end do not reach the eastern end and cease right here; those arising in the middle of the walkway do not reach either end and cease right here; mental and physical phenomena arising during walking do not reach the standing posture and cease right here; those arising during standing do not reach the sitting posture; those arising during sitting do not reach the lying posture and cease right here." While repeatedly comprehending and reflecting in this way, he lets the mind enter the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). When rising from sleep, he rises only after grasping the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). This monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in going, etc.

In this way, however, the meditation subject is often not clear during sleep. The meditation subject should not be allowed to be unclear. Therefore, a monk, after walking, standing, and sitting as much as he can, when lying down, comprehends thus: "The body is insentient (acetana), the bed is insentient; the body does not know 'I am lying on the bed,' and the bed does not know 'The body is lying on me.' An insentient body is lying on an insentient bed." While repeatedly comprehending in this way, he lets the mind enter the life-continuum. When waking up, he wakes up only after grasping the meditation subject. This monk is called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in sleep.

"Because of accomplishing the actions of the body, etc., and thus being identified with those actions, and because of arising from the action of adverting (āvajjana), the impulsion (javana) is called 'consisting of action' (kiriyāmaya-pavatta). Or, all process-consciousness occurring at the six doors is called 'consisting of action.' When such consciousness exists, it is called 'waking' (jāgarita)." A monk who comprehends thus is called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in waking. Alternatively, a monk who divides the day and night into six parts and remains awake for five parts is also called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in waking.

A monk who preaches the Dhamma by making the bases of liberation (vimuttāyatana) the priority, or a monk who, having abandoned the thirty-two kinds of low talk (tiracchāna-kathā), speaks suitable talk based on the ten subjects of talk (katha-vatthu), is called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in speaking.

A monk who applies attention (manasikāra) to whichever of the thirty-eight meditation subjects he prefers, or a monk who enters the second jhāna, is called "one who acts with clear comprehension" in silence. For the second jhāna, being devoid of the verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra) of initial and sustained application, is specifically called "silence" (tuṇhībhāva). This method, being a specialized method compared to the previous one, should also be brought in and stated here. Thus, in the Abhidhamma commentaries (Abhidhamma-aṭṭhakathā), etc., it is said: "This, however, is another method in this context."
111:
In this matter of clear comprehension (sampajañña) as well, the method beginning with "But here is another way" has already been shown.

The phrase "Thus, O King" and so forth is the conclusion of the meaning as previously indicated. Therefore, wishing to show the meaning in accordance with the detailed explanation (niddesa) in that conclusion, he said "Thus" and so forth. Indeed, the phrase "clear comprehension associated with mindfulness" (sati-sampayutta-sampajañña) is the statement of meaning in accordance with the detailed explanation. The decision on that term has already been stated. The word "Thus" (evaṃ) means in the seven instances such as going forward and returning, each in four ways as previously described.

## Explanation of the Talk on Contentment (Santosa-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

Because the meaning of the term can be understood by showing its sense, without regarding the word itself, it is said "He is endowed with contentment with whatever requisites" (itaritara-paccaya-santosa) to show merely the meaning that a monk is called "contented" (santuṭṭha) because of the existence of contentment (santosa) in himself. Indeed, the word-definition (nibbaccana) of the term is: "He is satisfied, he is not greedy." Alternatively, when the meaning is stated by way of the word-definition, the specific contentment due to whose existence in himself he is called "contented" might not be clear; so, to make it clear, he stated merely the meaning as "endowed with contentment with whatever requisites." This means he is possessed of contentment with any allowable requisite, such as robes, etc.

Indeed, the word "itara" expresses an indefinite (aniyama) meaning. When said twice (itaritara), it has the same meaning as the word "yaṃ kiñci" (whatever). Therefore, it is said "with whatever allowable requisite" (yattha katthaci kappiya-paccaye). Alternatively, "itara" is said of the low because it is other than the excellent; likewise, the excellent is called "itara" because it is other than the low. Indeed, this "otherness" (itaratā) is established by mutual reference. Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is: "He is possessed of contentment with allowable requisites such as robes, whether they be low or excellent."

It is called "contentment" (santosa) because one is satisfied with that, or because it is merely the act of being satisfied. It refers to non-greed (alobha) occurring in such a manner. Or, it refers to the four mental aggregates in which non-greed is predominant. Obtaining is "gain" (lābha). Contentment in accordance with one's gain is "contentment with what is obtained" (yathālābha-santosa). "Strength" (bala) means physical strength. Contentment in accordance with one's strength is "contentment in accordance with strength" (yathābala-santosa). "Suitability" (sāruppa) means what is appropriate and fit for a monk. Contentment in accordance with what is suitable for oneself is "contentment in accordance with suitability" (yathāsāruppa-santosa).

Another way: It is called "gain" (lābha) because it is obtained. Whatever gain is obtained is "as obtained" (yathālābha), which is "whatever requisite" (itaritara-paccaya). Contentment with whatever gain is obtained is "contentment with what is obtained." It is called "as strength" (yathābala) because it occurs in accordance with strength; it is a requisite suitable for one's own strength. In this term "yathābala," the word "yathā"...
112:
...expresses an appropriate action (anurūpa-kiriya) along with its means (sādhana), just as in the term "higher mind" (adhicitta), the word "adhi" expresses a locative action (adhikaraṇa-kiriya) along with its means. Contentment with a requisite according to one's strength is "contentment in accordance with strength." Suitability (sāruppa) means being appropriate, or it is called "sāruppa" because it brings about beauty. Whatever is suitable is "as suitable" (yathāsāruppa); it is a suitable requisite (sappāya-paccaya) for a monk. Contentment with such a suitable requisite is "contentment in accordance with suitability." The commentary that follows the aforementioned divisions is called the "explanation of divisions" (pabheda-vaṇṇanā).

"Here" (idha) means in this Dispensation (sāsana). By the phrase "he does not long for another [requisite]," the state of not longing for what is not yet obtained (appatta-patthanā-bhāva) is stated. By the phrase "even when receiving, he does not take [more]," the state of not longing for what is already obtained (patta-patthanā-bhāva) is stated. If only the state of not longing for what is not yet obtained were mentioned by the first phrase, the non-longing for something other than what was received might be a mode of behavior belonging to "fewness of wishes" (appicchatā), and thus there might be a confusion with fewness of wishes. Therefore, to show the true nature of contentment as distinct from that fewness of wishes, it should be understood that the state of not longing for what is already obtained is stated by the second phrase. This applies to the following points as well.

"Naturally weak" (pakati-dubbala) refers to one who is weak by nature even in the absence of illness. One is "similar" (sabhāga) because of having a similar portion of virtue (sīla), etc., or one is "similar" because of existing together with qualities such as virtue; this refers to a conscientious and amiable monk. By the phrase "having exchanged that robe," it is meant that for those who are naturally weak, a heavy robe does not bring comfort and brings bodily fatigue; thus, the exchange is mentioned for the sake of utility, not because of great greed (atricchatā), etc. Indeed, exchanging and using a light robe out of great greed, etc., would be contrary to contentment. However, since that [greed] is absent in him, using a light robe after exchanging it for the sake of the aforementioned utility is not contrary to contentment; thus it is said: "Even when subsisting on a light robe, he is truly contented." If even using a light robe after exchanging it for the sake of utility is not yet contrary to contentment, how much more so when using it without such an exchange? To show this commendable meaning, the word "even" (api) is used here.

In the detailed explanation of robes (cīvara-niddesa), the statement "one or another of the alms-bowl, robes, etc." is intended to show that contentment with the remaining requisites, as taken literally, is included within contentment with robes. In passages such as "This Venerable Mallaka is an Elder (thera)," the term "Elder" is used even as a mere designation (paññatti). To make it known that here it applies only to those who have been ordained for a long time, starting from ten years [of seniority], it is said "for Elders who have been long ordained." Or, by "for Elders" (therānaṃ), he refers to the Elder of the Saṅgha (saṅghathera), and by "those long ordained" (cira-pabbajitānaṃ), he refers to the other senior monks remaining. "From a dust heap" (saṅkārakūṭa) means from a pile of rubbish, etc. "Rags" (anantakāni) refers to scraps of cloth (pilotika) without borders.
113:
## 
In the Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā, it is stated that in the word 'anantakāni', the letter 'a' is merely a particle. Similarly, teachers say 'nandaka, kappaṭa, jiṇṇavasana, paṭaccara'. Old rags that have no borders or limits are called 'nandaka', and if the 'na' sound is changed to 'an', it is appropriate to use 'anantakāni'. However, since teachers skilled in conventional designations did not say so, it should be accepted only after careful investigation. There is also a reading 'sanantakāni', meaning 'paṃsukūla' robes sewn together with old rags. 'Saṅghāṭi' refers to one of the three robes. All three robes are called 'saṅghāṭi' because they are joined together. Obtaining a costly robe or many robes, then giving them away and accepting another is not contrary to contentment because it does not fall under the category of great desire, but rather under the method of 'yathāsāruppa' (suitability). Therefore, it is said, 'Even while wearing those robes... he is one who is contented.'

If even giving away what was obtained according to suitability and accepting another suitable robe is not contrary to contentment, how much more so is using what was obtained according to suitability without seeking another? To show this praiseworthy meaning, the word 'api' is used here. Similarly, the meaning of the use of the word 'api' in the descriptions of 'yathābala' and 'yathāsāruppa' regarding the remaining requisites should be understood. 'Pakativiruddha' means naturally unsuitable. To indicate the special meaning that seeking and using suitable requisites is more appropriate when prioritizing the practice of monkhood, the phrase 'samaṇadhammaṃ karontopi' (even while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse) is used instead of 'yāpentopi' (even while subsisting). 'Missakāhāra' refers to food made by mixing various grains and pulses such as rice and green gram.

To show another type of 'yathāsāruppa-santosa' regarding lodgings, the passage beginning with 'yo hi' is stated. In the first method, 'yathāsāruppa-santosa' is described by giving away what was obtained, while in the second method, it is described by not accepting what has arrived. This is the distinction between these methods. Here, the word 'hi' indicates another alternative (pakkhantarajotaka). In the Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, however, the word 'pi' is found. Stating that 'an excellent lodging is a cause for negligence,' and to show that state of negligence, the passage beginning with 'tattha nisinnassa' (to one sitting there) is stated. 'Niddābhibhūta' means overcome by sleep, which is the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) due to the sickness of the mind and mental factors through the onset of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha); it means one who is sleeping. 'Paṭibujjhato' refers to one who is waking up due to some such object.
114:
## 
It means that sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) manifest due to the cause of waking from sleep. In some versions, the reading 'paṭibujjanato' is also found. This statement is also made based on the first method.

'Tesaṃ ābatena' should be connected by adding 'brought by those elders' or 'with something belonging to those elders.' 'Muttaharītaka' refers to a yellow myrobalan (gallnut) soaked in cow's urine or discarded because of rot. Although the reading 'gomuttaharītaka' is found in books today, it is not the ancient reading because it contradicts the commentary's explanation. 'Catumadhura' refers to the group of four sweets—curd, honey, ghee, and molasses—as taught in the Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya. It means placing the four sweets in a single bowl and saying, 'Venerable sir, please take whichever of these medicines you desire.' With the words beginning with 'sacassā', the ability of both those medicines to cure illness is shown. 'Buddhādīhi vaṇṇitaṃ' means praised by the Fully Enlightened Buddhas and others with such words as 'the going forth is dependent on the medicine of fermented urine.' One who is contented with supreme, excellent contentment because of being devoted to contentment distinguished by fewness of wishes is called 'paramasantuṭṭha' (supremely contented).

In truth, the divisions of contentment (santosa) are more numerous than what has been mentioned. There are 20 types of contentment regarding robes, 15 regarding alms-food, 15 regarding lodgings, and 20 regarding medicinal requisites; however, here only 12 types of contentment are taught in brief. The more detailed divisions should be taken from the commentary to the Mahā-ariyavaṃsa Sutta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya. Therefore, the words beginning with 'iminā panā' are stated. Thus, having shown the divisions of contentment with the word 'santuṭṭha' (contented) specified through the person-centered method (puggalādhiṭṭhāna) in the phrase 'Here, O Great King, a monk is contented,' he now speaks thus to clarify the appropriate types of requisites for a monk endowed with that contentment and their nature of being 'carried by the body and the belly' in accordance with the teaching 'with robes to protect the body, with alms-food to protect the belly.' This is how the connection should be understood.

Although in the Pali text, contentment with robes and alms-food as protecting the body and belly respectively is taught in sequence, wandering without the other four requisites is not proper. Therefore, it should be noted that the decision is given in the commentary that the nature of protecting the body and belly should be applied to all requisites. 'Dantakaṭṭhacchedanavāsī' (an adze for cutting tooth-sticks) is merely a symbolic mark. Since other tasks can also be accomplished with that adze, it will be said later: 'also at the time of preparing the legs of couches and chairs, robe-rails, and hut-posts.' It is said that this statement does not appear anywhere in the Pali text but only in the ancient commentaries.
115:
## Explanation of the Talk on Contentment

Bandhana means the waist-band. It means a water-filter together with [another] water-filter, or together with that water-filter. One who is possessed of the effort known as the development of meditation subjects, or in whom effort is joined, is called yuttayoga (one joined with effort).

Those robes carry the body; they nourish it. Or, because the purpose of these is merely the nourishment of the body, they are called kāyaparihāriya. Here, the letter 'ka' is changed to 'ya' to use the term kāyaparihāriya. In this context, nourishment means growth or sustenance (maintenance). Similarly, kucchiparihāriya (belly-nourishing) should also be understood. Because it is beneficial only to the exterior of the body, it is called kāyaparihāriya (body-carrying); because it is beneficial for the maintenance of the body through swallowing, it is called kucchiparihāriya (belly-carrying). This is the distinction between the two. Therefore, it is said "Ti-cīvaraṃ tāva" and so on. The meaning of the word "pariharati" is "nourishes." The word "iti" is a particle used in illustration. Or it is a particle used to show the cause, indicating that "nourishing the body occurs in the manner mentioned above." Therefore, it means it is kāyaparihāriya because of nourishment. The same applies to the following parts. Cīvarakaṇṇena means with the hem of the robe.

Kuṭipari-bhaṇḍakaraṇakāle means at the time of plastering and finishing around the hut.

An aṅga is a specific main structural part placed above the legs of a couch or chair. On that part, they place planks, backrests, and so on. It is also called aṭanī.

Madhuka is the flower of the Madhuka tree. Or it is a honeycomb made by small bees. Parikkhāramatta means the measure or amount of requisites. The phrase "seyyaṃ pavisantassa" is said with reference to the use of bedspreads and keys at the time of entering sleep. Therefore, it is said "tatratthakaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ." A bedspread that remains in that very place, having been determined as one's own bedspread, is called tatratthaka. Because the word "vā" (or) expressing an alternative is used, any one of those requisites becomes the ninth. It is only the ninth in the order mentioned; those requisites are not permanently fixed as such. Why? Because they are not always carried in that way. The same should be understood for the tenth and so on. A bamboo tube etc. used for storing and carrying oil is called telanāḷi (oil-tube). In the inquiry "When showing a contented person, should not only a contented person with eight requisites be shown?", [the author] said "etesu ca" etc., wishing to show the appropriate contentment of those [monks]. Because those monks have a heavy burden known as requisites, they are called mahābhārā. This is the current reading. However, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla, having seen the reading mahāgajā, says mahāgajā because they are like great elephants in being difficult to maintain. In truth, those monks should not be called greedy, discontented, difficult to maintain, or having many belongings just because of these requisites. This is the meaning. If other monks who carry nine, ten, eleven, or twelve requisites also possess qualities such as fewness of wishes and contentment, it should be understood that the Buddha intends to include those monks in this teaching by virtue of their contentment.
116:
In the Dīgha Nikāya Sub-commentary (Volume 1, 215), it is stated: "Because they are difficult to support, they are like great elephants; therefore, they are called mahāgajā (great elephants)." The meaning is that these monks, with only these few requisites, should not be called "those of great desires, the discontented, those difficult to support, or those of many possessions." To resolve the question of whether this teaching is intended for other monks (who carry nine or ten requisites, etc.) if they also possess contentment and fewness of desires, the phrase beginning with "Bhagavā pana" is spoken. The question of how it is known that this teaching is intended for a monk with eight requisites is dismissed with the phrase beginning with "So hi." It means that because only a monk carrying those eight requisites departs in such a manner, and because it fits the Pāḷi text beginning with "with a robe just enough to protect the body," it can be known that the teaching is intended for such a monk. By showing the reason for the meaning taught, the reason for the teacher is also shown. Therefore, the statement beginning with "Iti imassa," which describes the attained quality, is also appropriate.

One who has a light livelihood (jīvikā) is called sallahu-kavutti. The state of such a person is called sallahu-kavuttitā. The term "kāyapārihāriyena" is shown by the phrase "by merely carrying the body" to be either an exposition emphasizing the state (bhāva-ppadhāna-niddesa) or an exposition omitting the state (bhāva-lopa-niddesa). It means "by the measure of supporting the body." The same applies to the term "kucchipārihāriyena." It should be understood that there are two types of word-definitions (vacanattha) according to the method mentioned. Since the word-definition of the first term was already mentioned below in the Sub-commentary, only the word-definition of the second term is stated here. There is no attachment (āsaṅga) through the craving of "mine-making" (mamāyana-taṇhā). There is no bond (bandha) through the craving of possession (pariggaha-taṇhā). "Jiyāmutto" means like an arrow released from a bowstring. "Yūthā" means from a herd of elephants. "Pabhinnamado" means a great elephant in rut. "Vanapabbāraṃ" means a cave or a sloping place in the forest.

Because he dwells happily in the four directions, the four directions are places of happy dwelling; or, by the method beginning with "pervading one direction," the four directions are the places where the development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā) pervades. These four directions belong to this monk; therefore, he is called catuddisa. That very catuddisa is called cātuddisa. Or, because he possesses the four directions in the manner mentioned, he is called cātuddisa, similar to the word "saddho." In those directions, he does not strike (oppress) any place, beings, or formations out of fear, nor is he struck by them; therefore, he is called appaṭigha (unobstructed). "Santussamāno" refers to a monk who is equally content with his own property or with whatever property is available. "Itarītarena" means with any kind of requisite, whether superior or inferior. They are called parissaya (dangers/obstacles) because they arise depending on the body and mind, or because they overwhelm and oppress the body and mind. These include external dangers such as lions, leopards, and tigers, as well as internal dangers to the body and mind such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda).
117:
The genitive case "parissayānaṃ" is used in the sense of the accusative (upayogattha). "Sahitā" means being able to endure or remove as appropriate through the qualities of patience (adhivāsana-khanti) and energy (vīriya), etc. He is called asambhī (unwavering) because he is free from the danger that causes trembling or stiffness. "Eko care" means he is able to practice or live alone without a companion. Indeed, the suffix "eyya" is used in the sense of ability, as in "Who can untangle this tangle?" By the term "khaggavisāṇakappo," it is shown that he is one who dwells alone, being like the horn of a rhinoceros. An animal that has a single horn on its head, which in shape is like a sword, is called "khagga." Since the word "khagga" refers to that sword-like horn, it means a special animal the size of a buffalo called a rhinoceros. In the world, that animal is also called "palāsāda" or "gaṇṭhaka." It means being similar to the single horn of that rhinoceros. Alternatively, it is also stated thus to show that he is like a rhinoceros horn because of his solitary dwelling. The detailed meaning of this should be understood according to the method stated in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta Commentary and the Cūḷaniddesa.

"Evaṃ vaṇṇitaṃ" means it was revealed or praised by the Blessed One through such a teaching in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta. It is just like the horn of the animal named khagga. Here, the word "kappa" is used in the sense of similarity, as in "Friends, let us consult with a disciple who is like the Teacher," etc. The state of being like that rhinoceros horn is called "khaggavisāṇakappatā." The connection is that the monk attains that state.

Although a bird might have broken wings or unfledged wings due to wind strikes, etc., here a winged bird capable of flight is intended. To show this distinction, it is stated in the Pali as "pakkhi sakuṇo," and not merely as a synonym as in "He walks in the sky, in the air," etc. Thus it is said, "a bird endowed with wings." "Uppatati" means flying upwards or going up; it means soaring. "Vidhunantā" means breaking and destroying, or shaking. "Ajjatanāya" means for the sake of today. The same applies to the word "svātanāya." One whose only burden is his own bowl is called "sapattabhāro." He is free from attachment (nissaṅga) because of the absence of the craving of "mine" (mamāyana-taṇhā). He is free from longing (nirapekkha) because of the absence of the craving of possession (pariggaha-taṇhā). "Yena kāmaṃ" means in whatever place he desires. Alternatively, this term is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvana-pumsaka). In whatever manner the desire arises, that is "yenakāmaṃ," meaning "according to desire" (yathākāmaṃ).
118:
## Explanation of the Talk on Abandoning the Hindrances

With the intention of asking what the benefit is of restating the four previously mentioned meanings together, the author raises an objection and clarifies it with the words beginning with "So... pe... kiṃ dasseti."

"Fulfillment of the requisites" (paccayasampatti) refers to the completion of the equipment (sambhāra) for attaining the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. "These four" refers to the four requisites of a forest-dwelling monk previously taught: restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara), restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara), clear comprehension (sampajañña), and contentment (santosa). "Does not succeed" (na ijjhati) means it is not fulfilled and is fruitless. The author shows with the words beginning with "tiracchānagatehi vā" that it is not merely a lack of fulfillment, but indeed, this fault also occurs.

"Becomes subject to being spoken of" (vattabbataṃ āpajjati) means reaching a state of being criticized, such as: "For this monk, dwelling in the forest is merely like the dwelling of animals or forest-dwelling hunters; there is no proper practice suitable for forest-dwelling at all." Because it contradicts the presentation of this meaning, the word "saddhiṃ" should be understood as not being an ancient term. Alternatively, it means reaching a state of dwelling together with forest animals or with incompatible forest-dwellers by way of improper practice. The word "vatthabba" is a synonym for "vasitabba" (should dwell), as in passages such as: "Monks, one should not dwell in the forest having made a resolution [without requisites]; should one dwell there, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." For this reason, it is said in the Vibhaṅga Commentary: "The forest-dwelling of such a monk is like the forest-dwelling of black monkeys, bears, leopards, tigers, and deer."

"Adhivatthā" refers to those who dwell or those who preside. First, they make terrifying sounds. If the monk does not flee by that much, they strike his head with their hands to make him flee; thus it was said by the teacher, the Elder Sāriputta. Having thus shown the fulfillment of requisites by way of exclusion (vyatireka), the author now states "yassa panete" etc., to show it by way of presence (anvaya).

To the question "How is it fulfilled?", he said "so hi" etc. "Kāḷaka" and "tilaka" are metaphorical terms used elsewhere for diseases that cause skin discoloration. It is said in the Abhidhāna:

"Dunnāmaka and arisa refer to hemorrhoids,
Chaddika and vamathu refer to vomiting,
Davathu and paritāpa refer to feverish heat,
Tilaka and tilakāḷaka refer to moles/spots."

It is called "tilaka" because it arises in the shape of a sesame seed; it is called "kāḷaka" because it arises as a black spot. In this context, however, a gross fault (thullavajja) consisting of a transgression of a regulation is called "kāḷaka" because it is like a black spot; a subtle fault (aṇumattavajja) consisting of a minor transgression is called "tilaka" because it is like a sesame spot.
119:
"Tilaka" is this distinction. In this context, a gross fault (thullavajja) consisting of a transgression of a regulation is called "kāḷaka" because it is like a black spot, and a subtle fault (aṇumattavajja) consisting of a minor transgression is called "tilaka" because it is like a sesame spot. The rapture (pīti) thus produced is contemplated by way of its disappearance, through the method of rise and fall (khaya-vaya). Indeed, it is called "khaya" (exhaustion) because it disappears in the sense of being exhausted, or it is called "vaya" (decay) because it goes away after having undergone change.

"Noble plane" (ariyabhūmi) refers to the supramundane plane. It is said that the monk's fame spreads either because of entering the Noble plane or because of the deities speaking of his virtues, having heard the words of the deities in various places. In this way, the "spread of ill-fame" (ayasapattharaṇa) mentioned below should also be understood as being by way of the deities' announcement.

The word "vivitta" (secluded) is said to be "suñña" (empty/void) because it refers to seclusion from a crowd of people. That emptiness should be understood by the absence of the sound and noise of people. To show that sound is a thorn to jhāna, it is said: "the meaning is little sound, little noise." By the mention of "janaka" (people), the noise made by people (janya) is also included here. Thus it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "That which is without noise is that which is secluded from the wind of people (vijanavāta)." The term "appasadda" (little sound) refers to the absence of natural sounds. The term "appanighosa" (little noise) refers to the absence of sounds such as city noises. In such places, it is said in the commentaries that while the phrasing (syllables) may seem to have a remainder, the meaning is without remainder (complete).

In the sub-commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, however, the teacher Elder Dhammapāla said: "Considering the meaning of 'appasadda' as 'pariṭṭa' (small/little), it was said that 'the phrasing might have a remainder.' Therefore, he said 'na hi tassa' etc. But here, the word 'appasadda' can also be understood in the sense of 'absence' (abhāva), as in 'appābādhatañca sañjānāmi' (I perceive the absence of illness)." Correlating that meaning with the Vibhaṅga Pali, he said "etadeva" etc. "Etadeva" means it is only the silence (nissaddatā) that I am describing. "Santikepi" means that if there is such seclusion even near a village, it is called "vivitta"; how much more so in a distant place. "Anākiṇṇa" means not interspersed with people, not cramped. If a monastery is surrounded by a league (gāvuta) or half a yojana of mountain thickets, forest thickets, or river thickets, such that no one can approach at an improper time, this is called "anākiṇṇa" (uninterspersed) even if it is nearby. "Seti" means sleeping, and "āsati" means sitting. By the word "ettha," he shows the locative sense (adhikaraṇa) of the words "sena" and "āsana," and by the word "ca," he shows the dvanda compound (catthasamāsa) of those two terms. With "tenāha" etc., he cites the Vibhaṅga Pali itself.

Now, to clarify the meaning of that same passage by showing the different types of lodgings (senāsana), he said "apica" etc. This is the classification of the lodgings that were shown in their own form as examples in the Vibhaṅga Pali. There, "vihāra" refers to what is enclosed by a wall...
120:
An entire monastery compound demarcated by a wall is called a vihāra. A long mansion is called an aḍḍhayoga; it is also called a "mansion shaped like a garuda's wing." A mansion with a square base is called a pāsāda. A mansion with a flat roof (shaven-roofed) is called a hammiya. A special dwelling structure with four or five stories, suitable for warding off opposing enemy kings, is called an aṭṭa. A special dwelling structure with a single pinnacle and many corners is called a māḷa.

Another method: A mansion with a long front is called a vihāra. A dwelling with a roof on only one side is called an aḍḍhayoga. In that dwelling, the wall on one side is higher and the other side is lower; therefore, that dwelling has a single-sloped roof. A rectangular mansion is called a pāsāda. A flat-roofed mansion joined with a moon-deck (balcony) is called a hammiya. Any mountain cave is called a guhā. A mountain slope/cleft fitted with a door is called a leṇa. The remaining meanings are as previously mentioned. "A maṇḍapa is a leaf-pavilion," say the teacher Ācariya Dhammapāla and the author of the Aṅguttara Ṭīkā, Ācariya Sāriputta.

In the Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā, however: A vihāra is a dwelling with a walkway all around, with night-quarters and day-quarters made only inside. An aḍḍhayoga is a dwelling with a curved roof like a garuda's wing. A pāsāda is a long mansion made by taking two pinnacles. An aṭṭa is a special dwelling structure with thick walls made of bricks, having four or five stories, for the purpose of warding off enemy kings and others. A māḷa is a circular pavilion similar to a refectory. In the Vinaya Aṭṭhakathā, it is called "a square mansion gathered under a single pinnacle." A leṇa is a dwelling made either by excavating a mountain or by raising a wall in an insufficient space of a mountain slope. A guhā is said to be an underground cave, a mountain cave, or an earth cave where it is necessary to keep a lamp lit day and night.

That dwelling which serves as a residence is called vihārasenāsana in the sense of being "dwellable" and in the sense of being a "place of dwelling." A couch of four kinds, such as masāraka, is called a mañca. A chair (pīṭha) is the same. A bolster of five kinds, such as uṇṇabhisi, is called a bhisi. A pillow of the size of the head is called a bimbohana. Here, "size of the head" means one span and four finger-breadths in width, and the width of the couch in length. Because masāraka and others are types of beds and chairs, and because bolsters and pillows are connected to beds and chairs, they are called mañcapīṭhasenāsana. A dwelling consisting of beds and chairs, and the utensils connected to beds and chairs, are called "mañcapīṭhasenāsana" by way of general designation (sāmaññaniddesa) or by way of the elision of similar terms (ekasesa). Ācariya Sāriputta also speaks in this way. Ācariya Dhammapāla, however, says: "Mañcapīṭhasenāsana refers to the bed and chair themselves, and the dwelling utensils connected to the bed and chair."
121:
A *cimilikā* is a floor covering made by stitching together pieces of cloth and the like to protect the color of a floor that has been well-finished with plaster. A *cammakhaṇḍa* (piece of skin) refers to any skin, such as that of a lion, tiger, leopard, or hyena. In the commentaries, no skin is found to be forbidden by the Buddha for use as a dwelling requisite. A *tiṇasanthāra* is a covering made of any kind of grass. The same method applies to a leaf-covering (*paṇṇasanthāra*). Because *cimilikā* and others are to be spread on the ground, they are called *santhatasenāsana* (spread-out lodging).

In the phrase "wherever the monks retire to," it is stated in the commentary that, setting aside beds and the like, all places where monks assemble are called *senāsana* (lodging). Other places such as the roots of trees where monks retire, because they lack preparation and serve merely as spaces for sleeping and sitting, are called *okāsasenāsana* (space-lodging). In the phrase "a secluded lodging," the term *senāsana* is used to denote or refer to a secluded dwelling. This is because a general (universal) designation applies to a specific instance, and one who desires a specific thing must employ the specific term.

If this is so, one might ask why terms like "forest" (*arañña*) are mentioned again. To address this inquiry, the phrase "Here, for that monk..." and so on is stated. The intention is that although lodgings have been mentioned in this way, the Buddha spoke again to show only the lodging that is suitable for that monk. The phrase "coming by way of the bhikkhunīs" refers only to the forest as mentioned in the Vinaya, not as mentioned in the Abhidhamma. In the Vinaya, in the *gaṇamhāohīyana* training rule, because the forest-dwelling practice (*āraññaka-dhutaṅga*) is forbidden for bhikkhunīs, this place is also called "forest" for those bhikkhunīs. However, it is not only the remote forest five hundred bow-lengths away that is considered a lodging; this [closer] forest also causes an offense for those bhikkhunīs if they remain behind from the group. It does not mean only the forest five hundred bow-lengths away. It is said there:

"Whether alone or remaining behind from the group, for a bhikkhunī in a forest that is not a village, if she leaves the sight or hearing range of her companion bhikkhunī, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; once she has left it, there is a *saṅghādisesa* offense."

In the Vinaya commentaries, the meaning is stated in that very way. In the Abhidhamma, however, it is stated: "Forest means everything outside the threshold (*indakhīla*) after one has exited." Both the Vinaya and the Suttanta are known as *pariyāyadesanā* (indirect or conventional teaching), while the Abhidhamma is *nippariyāyadesanā* (direct or literal teaching). Therefore, to show literally that any place not included within the village boundary is the forest, it was stated in that way. "Everything outside the threshold after one has exited is the forest" is the meaning here. Another statement, "The forest-dwelling practice is the near and the far," is said in the Suttanta method with reference to a monk living in the forest in the *araññaka* training rule. Since this is suitable for this monk, the characteristics of that forest are appropriately stated in the *Dhutaṅganiddesa* of the *Visuddhimagga*. Therefore, the intention is to take it according to the method stated in that *Visuddhimagga*. "Having cool shade" means possessing a cool shade. Therefore, the phrase "in such and such a place" and so on is said. "At the root of a tree" means near a tree. As much space as is called "tree-root"...
122:
The meaning here is that everything that exists outside the threshold is called 'forest' (arañña). The statement 'āraññakaṃ nāma... pacchimaṃ' was spoken according to the Suttanta method in the Araññaka training rule (āraññaka-sikkhāpada) with reference to a monk living in the forest. This is suitable for this monk. Therefore, whatever characteristic of the forest is mentioned in the Dhutaṅganiddesa of the Visuddhimagga, that characteristic is indeed appropriate. Thus, the meaning is that it should be understood according to the method stated in that Visuddhimagga.

'Sandacchāya' means having cool shade. Therefore, it is said, 'Tattha hi,' and so on. 'Rukkhamūla' means the vicinity of a tree. It is also stated: 'As far as the shade spreads around at midday, and where leaves fall when the wind is still, that much space is called rukkhamūla (the foot of a tree).'

'Pabbata' (mountain) refers to all three types: pure rock, pure earth, or a mixture of both; it does not mean only a rocky mountain. Since the word 'sela' is a synonym for 'pabbata' without distinction, it is stated thus. By the words 'Tattha hi,' etc., the suitability of both types is shown.

'Disāsu khāyamānāsu' means being clearly visible in the ten directions. It is stated that for such a reason, one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā) can occur. Some teachers, however, say this is stated to show the benefit of being fanned by the wind coming from all directions.

Water is called 'kaṃ' because it dispels thirst. 'That place which is called nadītumba or nadīkuñja is called kandara (a glen/cleft). Even in a non-mountainous region, a difficult-to-access river bend is shown as a kandara,' said the teacher Ānanda Thera. From this, it is understood that the words 'nadītumba' and 'nadīkuñja' are terms denoting a river bend (or a place where river water turns back). A river bend (nadīnivattanapadesa) is a difficult-to-access place where water coming from a river turns back again. The teacher who says 'even in a non-mountainous region' shows that although the mountain region was mentioned first as an example in the Commentary, the aforementioned river region is also indeed a kandara.

By the words 'Tattha hi,' etc., the suitability for that monk is stated merely as an example. 'Ussāpetvā' means having made a heap. Teachers say, 'Between two mountains situated very close together, there is an opening (vivara) similar to a room, etc.; but in a single mountain, it is like a tunnel.' Since it is covered from above, an inner cave like a tunnel can only exist in a single mountain; it cannot exist between two mountains because they are not so covered. Therefore, the term 'umaṅgasadisaṃ' (like a tunnel) should be connected with the term 'ekasmiṃ yeva' (only in one). The term 'mahāvivaraṃ' (great opening), however, should be connected with both. 'Umaṅgasadisaṃ' is also described by the teacher as 'suduṅgāsadisaṃ' (like a very difficult-to-access underground cavern). 'Suduṅgā' means...
123:
The name 'suduṅgā' is a name for an underground house (bhūmighara), as in the passage: 'Having seized that child, the ogress threw him into a very difficult-to-access underground house while he was crying.'

'A place not in the vicinity of humans' (anupacāraṭṭhāna) means a place where humans do not normally travel. This is because the intended meaning here is the prohibition of normal travel for activities such as plowing and sowing. Therefore, it is said: 'Where they do not plow, where they do not sow.'

By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the remainder of the Vibhaṅga Pali is included: 'Vanapattha is the name for monasteries in the forest; it is the name for those that are fearsome, those that cause hair-raising, those that are on the outskirts, and those that are not in the vicinity of humans.'

'Pattha' is level ground similar to a mountain, also called 'sānu' (a plateau/ridge). Because it is similar to that plateau, a forest where humans do not travel is meant as 'a forest like a plateau'; thus, 'vanapattha' should be understood as a compound with the qualifier placed at the end.

An open space facing all directions (without cover or shelter) is called 'abbhokāsa' (the open air). It means a place not covered by any roof, not even by a tree branch. A hut made by covering sticks with a robe is called a 'cīvarakuṭi' (robe-hut).

'Nikkaḍဎိတွာ' means having taken out. Here, only a straw heap (palālarāsi) that is like a mountain-cleft cave inside is intended. Otherwise, it might be thought to include spreads of grass and leaves; therefore, it is said, 'in a place like a mountain-cleft cave,' meaning like a cleft (pabbhāra) or like a cave (leṇa).

In the phrase 'gacchagumbādīnampi,' the word 'pi' includes the previous method. Seeking alms-food is called 'piṇဍပါတ' (piṇḍapāta) by dropping the latter word 'pariyesana' (seeking). Returning from that alms-round is called 'piṇḍapātapāṭikkanta.'

In the word 'pallaṅka,' the prefix 'pari' denotes the meaning 'all around.' Therefore, sitting with legs bound all around is called 'pallaṅka.' It is formed by changing 'r' to 'l' and doubling, as in 'palibuddha.' 'All around' means placing the left thigh and the right thigh equally and connecting the two feet with each other. Therefore, it is said, 'sitting with thighs bound all around.' Here, 'pallaṅka' refers only to sitting with thighs bound; it does not refer to a throne made with animal figures.

'Ābhujitvā' means bending and binding the two feet just as one sits in a cross-legged position; thus, it is said, 'bandhitvā' (having bound).

In the phrase 'ujuṃ kāyaṃ' (straight body), the word 'kāya' (body) refers only to the upper body. This is because the fact that the lower body is not kept straight can be understood from the word 'nisajjā' (sitting) itself. Therefore, it is said, 'keeping the upper body straight.' This means keeping it so that the eighteen vertebrae are touching end to end. Now, wishing to show the benefit of keeping the body thus, the words beginning with 'evaṃ' are spoken. In that context, 'evaṃ' means 'because of keeping the body in that way.'
124:
Keeping the upper body straight is shown by the words beginning with 'eighteen' (aṭṭhārasa). It means placing the eighteen vertebrae of the backbone end to end. 

Now, to show the benefit of such a posture, he says the words beginning with 'for thus' (evaṃ hi). In that context, 'thus' (evaṃ) means when it is so placed, or because of such placement. 'They do not bend' (na paṇamanti) means they do not stoop. The words beginning with 'then his' (athassa) show the successive benefits. 'Then' (atha) means when there is no such stooping. 'Pain' (vedanā) refers to pains such as backache. 'It does not fall away' (na paripatati) means it does not deviate from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), it does not overstep the path of the meditation subject. Because it does not overstep the path of the meditation subject, the meditation subject reaches growth, increase, and abundance through the distinction between the preceding and the following.

Here, the word 'pari' is a synonym for 'abhi', meaning 'towards'. Therefore, it is said 'facing the meditation subject' (kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ). It means having the meditation subject as the priority, having restrained the mind from the many objects external to the meditation subject. The meaning of 'pari' as 'near' is shown by the words 'or having made it near the mouth' (mukhasamīpe vā katvā). It means making it by way of establishing it firmly in the mind as if it were near the mouth. To prove the meaning of 'pari' as 'near' by the Vibhaṅga Pali, the words beginning with 'by that very' (teneva) are said. 'At the tip of the nose' (nāsikagge) means at the tip of the nostrils. The 'sign of the mouth' (mukhanimitta) is the central region of the upper lip, where the air from the nose strikes.

In this context, just as a dwelling suitable for meditation is shown by the words beginning with 'he resorts to a secluded dwelling' (vivittaṃ senāsanaṃ bhajati), so too, by the word 'he sits' (nisīdati), a peaceful posture that is neither sluggish nor agitated is shown. By the words 'having folded his legs crosswise' (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā), the firmness of the sitting is shown. By the words 'having set up mindfulness in front' (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā), the means of grasping the object is shown. The word 'pari' has the sense of 'grasping' (pariggaha), as in words like 'leader' (pariṇāyikā). The word 'mukha' has the sense of 'emergence' (niyyāna), as in words like 'the door to the signless liberation' (suññatavimokkhamukha). Indeed, emergence from the opposite states is 'emergence' (niyyāna). The state of non-confusion has the sense of 'establishment' (upaṭṭhāna).

'Therein' (tatra) refers to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga. 'Grasped emergence' (pariggahitaniyyānaṃ) means having made mindfulness that is grasped by way of non-forgetfulness of the object in every way, and which is an emergence because it is the opposite of abandoning forgetfulness; it means having established supreme mindfulness and wisdom. This is the view of the Elder Dhammapāla and the Elder Sāriputta.

Alternatively, it is 'grasped' because of its good occurrence in the body, etc., and for that very reason, it is endowed with the nature of emergence; or it is 'grasped' because of being associated with the knowledge that grasps the body, etc., and for that very reason...
125:
"...having made the establishment that has become an emergence—this is the view of the Elder Ānanda.

One covets, is greedy for, or desires by means of this, thus it is 'covetousness' (abhijjhā), which is the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa). The sense of 'disintegrating' (luccana) means the sense of breaking, the sense of breaking moment by moment—this was stated by the Elder Dhammapāla and the Elder Sāriputta, the author of the Aṅguttara Commentary. In the Suttas, it is also seen: 'Monk, it is called "the world" (loko) because it disintegrates (luccati). And what disintegrates? Monk, the eye disintegrates, forms disintegrate, eye-consciousness disintegrates,' and so on. In the Abhidhamma Commentary and in this commentary, it is currently written in books as 'by the sense of disintegrating and crumbling' (luccanapaluccanaṭṭhena). There, 'disintegrating' (luccana) itself is stated with the synonym 'crumbling' (paluccana) for emphasis. Indeed, the word 'luca' also occurs in the sense of looking, etc., as in 'he looks at' (oloketi), but here it means the sense of breaking and disintegrating. In the Vaṃsatthappakāsinī, however, it is said: 'It is called "the world" because of its nature of disintegrating by way of momentary dissolution, and its nature of crumbling by way of the dissolution of death.' Some teachers, however, say the meaning is 'by the sense of breaking and arising.' This is improper because it contradicts the meaning of the words spoken directly in the texts, and because the word 'luca' does not express 'arising.' Furthermore, the teachers might have cited the reading 'by the sense of disintegrating and crumbling' and explained the meaning accordingly, but later, through the lineage of transmission, it should be understood that it is not seen in various places due to scribal negligence. If one takes the meaning as 'it does not disintegrate, it does not crumble,' it is not so; that very meaning is 'the world.' Or else, the world is to be taken as that which disintegrates, breaks, and perishes through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); for the supramundane states (lokuttara) which are devoid of such grasping, there is no state of being 'the world.' Or, the truth of suffering is called 'the world,' as it is said: 'The five aggregates of clinging are the world.' Thus, according to the statements in various texts, the meaning given by some teachers is also improper.

Therefore, it is because only the five aggregates of clinging are the world. In the phrase 'by way of suppression' (vikkhambhanavasena), 'suppression' here means non-arising or non-occurrence only by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna), but it does not mean the thorough abandonment of the opposing states by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna). For the word 'because of being abandoned' (pahīnattā) is said only with reference to being similar to such abandonment. Why is this said? Because jhāna has not yet been attained. Thus, only because of such abandonment through preliminary meditation (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) is this mind called 'devoid of covetousness.' To show that it is not devoid of covetousness by nature like eye-consciousness, the words 'similar to eye-consciousness' (cakkhuviññāṇasadisena) are said. In the phrase 'as that' (yathā taṃ), the word 'that' (taṃ) is merely a particle. Alternatively, for that mind to effect the liberation from defilements at the present time and the non-grasping again in the future is called 'purification' (parisodhana). Because it has been purified by the preliminary meditation of this jhāna-mind, its state of being devoid of covetousness is known. How? In the same way, its state of being without ill will is also known."
126:
To show that [being free from covetousness] is not because of being naturally free from covetousness like eye-consciousness, it is said, "not like eye-consciousness" (na cakkhuviññāṇasadisena). In the phrase "yathā taṃ," the word "taṃ" is merely a particle, or it refers to that consciousness of meditation. Purification (pari-sodhana) means effecting release [from defilements] in the present and ensuring they are not taken up again in the future.

Just as it should be understood that this mind is free from covetousness because it has been purified by the preceding stage of meditation, it should also be understood that it is free from ill-will, free from sloth and torpor, free from restlessness (anuddhatatā), and free from doubt (nibbicikicchatā). To indicate this, it is said, "The same method applies to the phrases 'having abandoned ill-will and malice' (byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya), and so on." "Pūtikummāsādayo" refers to fermented barley bread and the like. "Purima-pakati" refers to the pure and white original nature; by this term, it shows the meaning of reaching a state of alteration.
