"Vikārāpattiyā" means by reaching an alteration characterized by the abandonment of the original nature. By the word "ubhayaṃ" (both) and so on, the state of a compound with equal meaning is stated.

Because it is stated in the Abhidhamma, "That which is the indisposition of the mind at that time," and so on, for sloth (thīna), and "That which is the indisposition of the body at that time," and so on, for torpor (middha), it is said, "Sloth is the sickness of the mind, and torpor is the sickness of the mental factors." Even though sloth and torpor are always conjoined with each other, just as with the lightness of mind and body, the specific indisposition that arises due to various specific causes for the mind and mental factors respectively should be understood as their nature.

"Diṭṭhāloka" refers to the light of the moon, lamps, meteors, etc., seen at night, and the light of the sun, etc., seen by day. The perception capable of perceiving that light whether by night or by day is called "perception of light" (āloka-saññā). The presence of that perception of light, which is pure and free from hindrances, is intended in this context of meditation. To show that the suffix "ī" in the word "āloka-saññī" indicates an extraordinary sense of "possession," it is said, "even at night" (rattimpi), and so on. This is stated because it is the cause for being free from sloth and torpor; this meaning is clear in the Suttas.

One is "mindful" (sato) because one remembers; one is "clearly comprehending" (sampajāno) because one knows in various ways. That this is a designation of a person is shown by the phrase "endowed with mindfulness and wisdom." Why are only these two mentioned when other qualities like energy and concentration exist? Or why are these two mentioned only here and not in the sections on being free from covetousness, etc.? To remove such inquiries, it is said, "these two" (idaṃ ubhayaṃ), and so on. This means these two, known as mindfulness and clear comprehension, are described through the method of personal designation (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). By the meaning "having transcended and remained," the past tense meaning of the suffix "ta" is stated. The abandonment [of defilements] through the preceding stage of meditation is itself called "transcending."
127:
Because it occurs as "How is this? How is this?" (Kathaṃ idaṃ? Kathaṃ idaṃ?), it is called "kathaṃkathā" (doubt/vicikicchā). One who has such doubt, thinking "Is it thus or is it so?" is called "kathaṃkathī." One who does not have such doubt is "a-kathaṃkathī" (one without doubt). This is the word-definition. To show the mere meaning, it is said, "One is 'a-kathaṃkathī' because [the thought] 'How is this? How is this?' does not occur in this way." The phrase "in wholesome states" (kusalesu dhammesu) should be connected with the word "a-kathaṃkathī." Therefore, the meaning is stated as "does not doubt, does not hesitate." In the phrase "vacanatthalaakkhaṇādibhedato," by the word "ādi" (and so on), the inclusion of the abandonment of causes and the wholesome states that abandon [defilements] should be understood. Those states are also spoken of in detail.

Wealth taken with interest is called "debt" (iṇa). Therefore, it is said, "having taken wealth with interest." One whose end (limit) is gone is "byantī." Therefore, it is said, "vigatanta." The meaning of this term should be understood as "one should make an end to the debt that must be repaid." "Tesaṃ" refers to the debts of wealth taken with interest. The remaining debt to be paid beyond the wealth taken is called "pariyanta." Because that person has no debt, he is "aṇana" (debtless). The state of being debtless is "āṇaṇya." Because that freedom from debt is the cause, it is called "āṇaṇya-nidāna." It means "due to the cause of being debtless." Alternatively, "āṇaṇya-nidāna" means that freedom from debt alone is the cause for him. This term is connected with the words "joy" (pāmojja) and "happiness" (somanassa). He gains strong joy, thinking, "I am free from the obstacle (palibodha) of debt." He attains happiness, thinking, "I still have remaining wealth for my livelihood."

Dissimilar feeling (visabhāga-vedanā) means painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Indeed, that painful feeling is dissimilar to pleasant feeling because it is contrary to the continuity of wholesome results. By being the cause of the arising of that [dissimilar feeling], the phrase "kaceneva" means "as if [cutting] with a saw." "Catu-iriyāpathaṃ" refers to the four postures. Just as a sick person is unable to stand or walk, he is likewise unable to sit, etc. "Ābādheti" means it oppresses. The altered and uneven state of the winds, etc., is called "sickness" (ābādha). Therefore, it is said, "he reaches suffering through the pain caused by that sickness." It means he reaches suffering and is endowed with suffering through the pain known as painful feeling caused by the sickness. Alternatively, by the power of oppression of painful feeling, the word-definition is made as "it oppresses at the beginning, thus it is ābādha"; then, one is "ābādhika" (afflicted) by the primary sickness called ābādha, and one is "dukkhita" (suffering) by the subsequent sickness called the recurring pain. In this way, the fact that the word "dukkhita," spoken in terms of painful feeling, is distinguished by the word "ābādhika" becomes clear.
128:
This which has been stated is the method explained by the Teacher Dhammapāla Thera regarding this [the term 'dukkhito ābādhiko']. A measure that exceeds the normal limit is called 'adhimatta' (excessive); it also implies intensity. One whose body is exhausted due to the depletion of the elements and is severely ill is called 'adhimattagilāno'. Being afflicted by an extremely severe disease is called 'adhimattabyādhiparetatā'. 'Na rucceyya' means it would not be pleasing; this term has a passive sense, as the agent 'assa' is seen in the phrase 'bhattañcassa'. 'Balamattā' means 'balam-eva' (mere strength), thus the word 'mattā' has no [additional] meaning; or it refers to a slight amount of strength. 'Both of them' refers to gladness (pāmojja) and joy (somanassa). One would obtain gladness thinking, 'I am free from disease.' One would attain joy thinking, 'I still have physical strength'—this is the meaning of the Pali.

What is called 'kākaṇikamatta' is said by teachers to be 'the measure of one guñja seed.' In the Vinaya Commentary, it is said to be 'about one and a half grains of paddy.' Alternatively, the word 'kaṇa' has the meaning of broken rice (kuṇḍaka).

'The pure, huskless, bran-less,
Fragrant rice, the fruit of the grain,
Having cooked it in a pot,
They then eat that food.'

Thus it is said, and also 'Kaṇa should be broken rice.' A small amount of broken rice is called 'kākaṇa', similar to 'kālavaṇṇa' (a slight blackness). Therefore, because that [debt] has the measure of a kākaṇa, it is called 'kākaṇika'. Kākaṇika itself is kākaṇikamatta. It should be understood to mean only the measure of a small grain of broken rice. In this way, it is not inconsistent with the words of the Umangga Jātaka, which states: 'The royal gift (rājadāyo) is not even worth a kākaṇika; he gives meat worth half a māsa.' Vaya means exhaustion or breaking up. For one who reflects, 'I am free from bonds,' both of these (gladness and joy) occur. Therefore, it is said, 'He would obtain gladness, he would attain joy.' Regarding the remaining words, it is said, 'The rest is in the same manner as previously stated,' and so on. 'Vuttanayena-eva' means in the same manner as stated for the first and second terms. 'Sabbapadesu' refers to the three groups starting from the third. Each individual group of similes is called a 'pada'.

## 221-222.
Adhīno means dependent on another, not possessing independence. Therefore, it is said, 'He does not get to do anything according to his own wish.' The same should be understood for the other term [parādhīno]. To show the connection with the remaining text—that he does not go where he wishes to go as he pleases—it is said 'yena' and so on. This word 'kāmaṃ' is an adverbial neuter. Alternatively, going according to one's desire (kāmena) is called 'kāmaṃgamo', with the 'm' (niggahīta) being an augment.
129:
In this context, in the word 'dāsabya', the suffix '-bya' is shown to have the sense of state (bhāva) by the word 'dāsabhāva' (the state of a slave). Because he does not depend on others and can be employed in his own affairs like his own arm, he is called 'bhujissa'; the definition is 'one who is self-controlled'. In the Mūlapaṇṇāsaka-ṭīkā, it is said: 'Bhujā means managing according to one's own pleasure; since this management is desired (issitabba) in this person, he is called bhujissa, meaning one who has no master.' Intending to show just the meaning, it says 'one's own property'; it means that one is one's own property, not another's. Because of the lack of water, one crosses over drinking water with difficulty in this place, hence it is called 'kantāra' (wilderness); and since the word 'addhāna' has the meaning of 'long', it is called 'a long journey without water'.

'Sesāni' refers to ill-will (byāpāda) and the others. 'Tatra' refers to the illustration [of the similes]. 'Ayaṃ' refers to the similarity that is about to be stated, by which similarity debt etc. become the similes (upamā) and sensual desire etc. become the subjects of comparison (upameyya); that relationship between the simile and the subject of comparison should be understood as similarity (sadisatā). 'Tehi' refers to others who are the creditors. 'To prevent anything' means that because of the inability to repay the debt, one is unable to prevent even a single thing such as harsh speech. Why? It is said 'the cause for forbearance' and so on, meaning that the debt is the cause for having to practice forbearance.

'Whoever is infatuated by sensual desire for a certain object' means that a certain person is infatuated by sensual desire for another person who is the object of that sensual desire. 'He takes hold of that object with a mind accompanied by craving' means that with sensual desire which is craving, he grasps that person who is the object of sensual desire, thinking 'This is mine.' Here, the word 'sahagata' (accompanied by) means merely the state of that [craving], as in the passages: 'This craving which leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust (nandīrāgasahagatā)', and so on. 'By that person' means by the person who is the object of sensual desire. Why? It says 'the cause for forbearance' and so on, meaning that sensual desire is the cause for having to practice forbearance.

In this context, the arising of an unwholesome mind dominated by lust, which is similar to forbearance, is called 'forbearance' (titikkhā); it is not the arising of a mind dominated by non-hatred which is a form of ascetic practice, as in the passages: 'Forbearance is the highest austerity (khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā)', and so on. 'By the house-lords' refers to the mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband who are the masters of the house. The connection is: just as for women, sensual desire is the cause for forbearance.

By the words 'Yathā pana' and so on, the similarity of the remaining hindrances to disease etc. is stated. Therein, there is one who is afflicted with a bile-disease due to the provocation of the bile-humor. For him, because of the provocation of bile...
130:
For a person suffering from a bile-related illness, because of the bile disorder, everything such as honey and sugar becomes unsweet; this is the intended meaning of the statement, "He vomits, saying 'How bitter, how bitter!'"

In the old sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), there is the excerpted text "Tumhe upaddavetha." It carries the meaning "Do create trouble" by way of a denominative verb. However, at present, the reading "Tumhehi upaddutā" is seen. "Vibbhamati" means wandering here and there, or returning to the lower life (disrobing). The connection should be made as: just as one cannot enjoy, experience, know, or obtain the taste of honey and sugar, etc. "Sāsanarasaṃ" refers to the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa) of the Sasana, or the Sasana itself as the taste.

A constellation festival is called "Nakkhatta." Therefore, it is said, "Oh, what a fine dance! Oh, what a fine song!" "Mutto" refers to a person who is released from bonds. (This is the meaning) of the Dhamma that is to be heard.

A task that must be performed quickly is called "Accāyika." Indeed, the word "ati" has the meaning of speed, as in terms like "pāṇātipāta" (taking life), etc. One who is unskilled in the sequence of Vinaya is called "Vinaye apakataññū." One who knows the completed decision is called "pakataññū"; it means one who is not such a knower. Such a person does not know what is allowable and what is not allowable as it truly is. Therefore, it is said, "even in a certain thing," and so on. This refers to the perception (saññā) of thinking that allowable meat such as pork is unallowable meat such as bear meat.

By the word "daṇḍaka," the sound of branches and the sound of sticks are also meant. "Ussaṅkitaparisaṅkita" means being startled and apprehensive, as well as being fearful from all sides; it means being extremely terrified. In showing that manner, it is said, "he even goes," and so on. That person indeed goes a little. While going, because of that state of being startled and terrified, he also stops here and there. While traveling in such a difficult journey, he also turns back, thinking, "Who can know? What will happen?" Therefore, the places he has not yet reached are more numerous than the places he has already traveled. For that very reason, that person may or may not reach the safe ground with difficulty and hardship. "Kicchena kasirena" are synonymous terms. Fatigue through physical suffering is called "kiccha," while being oppressed by mental suffering is called "kasira." "Khemanthabhūmiṃ" refers to a land that is free from danger. The word "anta" signifies that state, or it is called "khemanthabhūmi" because it is a land where the end of fear is delimited. It means a fearless region.

Regarding the "eight places," it refers to the eight places taught in the Vibhaṅga: "What is that doubt (vicikicchā)? One doubts and is perplexed about the Teacher. About the Dhamma. About the Saṅgha. About the Training. About the past. About the future. About both the past and the future. One doubts and is perplexed about the phenomena of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda)."
131:
In the eight places taught in the Vibhaṅga (doubt may arise). "Adhimuccitvā" means having decided or having believed. "Saddhāya gaṇhituṃ" means being unable to grasp or believe in a believable object by way of faith, thinking "This is exactly so." "Iti" should be connected as: because of the inability in the manner stated, it creates an obstacle. The doubt that occurs only at the beginning for one who has entered a forest is called "sappana," thinking "Is there [danger] or is there not?" The doubt that occurs beyond that, all around or repeatedly, is called "parisappana." By both terms, it shows the wandering around in that very forest by way of doubt. Therefore, it is said "apariyogāhana," which means not thoroughly plunging in and grasping, thinking "This is so." "Chambhitattaṃ" refers to the trembling of the heart-flesh, the state of being paralyzed with fear that arises due to the perception of the forest; it means terror. In the side of the thing to be compared (the hindrances), this meaning should also be understood accordingly.

Regarding the similarity here: the similarity should be understood according to the manner stated in the side of what has not yet been abandoned. To the extent that sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so on are like a debt, etc., to that same extent, the abandoning of them is like being free from debt, etc. This is merely the meaning of the obscure terms—"Samiddhataṃ" means being wealthy. It is called "savaḍḍhikaṃ" because it exists together with the interest that was previously recorded. "Paṇṇaṃ" refers to a written contract as a mark when taking a loan. Again, "paṇṇaṃ" refers to a message written to request the debt. "Nillepatāya" means the state of not being smeared because of the absence of connection with wealth; likewise, it is because of the state of being unattached. These two are synonymous terms. Or, "nillepatāya" means the state of being unattached, characterized by the manner of not being smeared as stated. The "six things" are: the grasping of the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta), devotion to the meditation on foulness, being one with guarded doors in the senses, moderation in eating, having good friends, and suitable talk. "Bhāveတွာ" means having developed or having produced within oneself. Because it appears specifically in the Pali of the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta by way of explaining the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states and the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states, etc., it is said, "We shall explain in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta." And "in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta" refers to the one recited in this Dīgha Nikāya, not the one in the Majjhima Nikāya, because they belong to different Nikāyas. They say that teachers usually state the meaning coming from another Nikāya elsewhere as well. This method should also be understood in the part concerning the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda), etc. "Paravatthumhi" means in the object of another which is the sense-object. There is no attachment because of the absence of the sense of "mine." There is no bond because of the absence of possession. The word "api" is used in the sense of commendation: if defilements do not arise even for one seeing divine forms, how much less so for human ones.
132:
*Anatthakaro* means one who brings about harm to oneself and to others. The six things are: learning the sign of loving-kindness (*metta-nimitta*), devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness (*metta-bhavana*), reflection on the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakata*), frequency of wise reflection (*patisankhana-bahulata*), good friendship (*kalyanamittata*), and suitable talk (*sappaya-katha*). "Right there" means in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* itself. The training rule prescribed with reference only to positive conduct (*caritta-sila*) is called "regulation of conduct" (*acara-pannatti*). By the word "beginning" (*adi*), the training rule of negative conduct (*varitta-pannatti*) is included.

*Pavesito* means caused to enter (imprisoned). Indeed, a man who does not get to enjoy the festival because he was put in prison is called "a man put in prison on the day of the festival." Or it can be said that a man who was treated thus specifically to prevent him from enjoying the festival on that day is so called. "On another day" means after that day or on another festival day. *Okasa* means the cause for punishment (*kammakarana*) or the moment of punishment. *Mahanatthakara* means causing great harm through the loss of benefits in the present life and so forth. The six things (for sloth and torpor) are: noting the cause of overeating, changing postures, attention to the perception of light, living in the open air, good friendship, and suitable talk. *Dhamma-nakkhattassa* means of the festival consisting of the Dhamma to be heard as mentioned. Indeed, because it generates delight for the virtuous, the Dhamma is also called a "festival" (*nakkhatta*) in the sense of being similar to a celebration.

In restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*), "causing great harm" means causing great harm in the manner mentioned by bringing about dependence on others. The six things are: great learning (*bahussutata*), inquiry (*paripucchakata*), proficiency in the Vinaya, associating with elders, good friendship, and suitable talk. Doing what one desires by strength or by force is called coercion (*balakkara*); by that coercion. The practice for renunciation (*nekkhamma-patipada*) means only access concentration (*upacara-bhavana*), which is the practice for emerging from the hindrances, not the first jhāna. For this is the domain of access concentration.

*Balava* (strong) means being endowed with the strength capable of crushing enemies. This is because the suffix *-vantu* indicates the sense of possession characterized by excellence. *Hatthasara* means the essence of wealth in hand. *Sajjavudho* means one with prepared weapons like bows, etc.; it means one equipped with the five types of weapons. Accompanied by a retinue by virtue of brave and heroic servants. "That person" refers to the man mentioned above. Because of his strength, ready weapons, and retinue, thieves would flee just by seeing him from afar. "Causing harm" means causing harm in the manner mentioned by creating obstacles to right practice. The six things are: great learning...
133:
...being an inquirer (*paripucchakata*), being one who knows the nature of the Vinaya (*vinaye pakatannuta*), abundance of determination (*adhimokkha-bahulata*), good friendship, and suitable talk. Just as great learning and so forth lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, so they also lead to the abandoning of doubt (*vicikiccha*). Therefore, here too, the three things starting with great learning are taken. Good friendship and suitable talk lead to the abandoning of all five hindrances. Therefore, in those matters, one should understand the appropriate association for each respective hindrance.

"Like grass" means as if not counting it as anything due to fearlessness. "Having crossed the wilderness of misconduct" means having crossed the wilderness known as misconduct by way of crossing doubt, which is the means for practicing misconduct. For doubt, by way of being the cause for not undertaking right practice, fosters only wrong practice. Therefore, not abandoning doubt is the means for practicing misconduct, and abandoning it is the means for shaking off misconduct.

By the phrase "aspect of gladness" (*tuttha-kara*), he shows the tender joy (*taruna-piti*) called gladness (*pamojja*). Because it is tender, it is just a moment of being glad in some way, merely an aspect of gladness. *Tutthassa* is a word explaining the meaning of *pamuditassa*. The meaning of *tutthassa* is stated in the Sub-commentary (*Tika*) as "of one who is glad by way of joy that has reached the stage of descending (*okkanti-bhava*)." If this is so, by the word *pamojja*, only descending joy (*okkantika-piti*) should be taken. The meaning of the phrase "joy arises, agitating the whole body" is stated as "joy characterized by pervading (*pharana-lakkhana*) arises, agitating the whole body because of its own expansiveness and because of the arising of refined matter produced by itself." If this is so, by the word *piti*, only pervading joy (*pharana-piti*) should be taken. However, the reason for this should be investigated.

In this *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* and elsewhere, because the meaning of the two words is explained by the commonality of being tender or strong, any tender joy is called *pamojja*, and strong joy is called *piti*. Or, since tenderness and strength can occur sequentially among the five kinds of joy, teachers say that the preceding ones are *pamojja* and the succeeding ones are *piti*. This is the appropriate meaning here. *Tutthassa* means of one who has become glad by way of the tender joy called *pamojja*. The suffix *-ta* (in *tuttha*) has a past sense. This is because if it were taken in the present sense, there would be no cause-and-effect relationship, and the cause-and-effect relationship has been stated. By the phrase "agitating the whole body," he shows that *piti* here means strong joy. For it arises agitating the whole body because of its own expansiveness and because of the arising of refined matter produced by itself. Here, "agitating" (*sankhobhana*) means producing the impulse of joy and the expansion of joy throughout the whole body.
134:
In the term 'pītisahitaṃ', the latter part 'sahita' is elided, leaving 'pīti'. What is that which is accompanied by joy? It is the mind (citta). Because there is a mind accompanied by joy, the compound 'pītimano' is formed. It can also be said to be 'a person who has a mind associated with joy.' To show just the meaning, it is stated as 'to the person who has a mind associated with joy.'

In this context, 'kāya' refers to the entire collection of mental phenomena (nāmakāya). It does not mean only the three aggregates starting with feeling (vedanā), as in the case of 'kāyalahutā' (lightness of body), nor does it refer to the physical body (rūpakāya), as in the case of 'kāyāyatana' (body-base); this is indicated by the word 'nāmakāya'. Here, 'tranquillity' (passambhana) refers to the tranquillity achieved through the power of both 'kāyapassaddhi' (tranquillity of the mental body) and 'cittapassaddhi' (tranquillity of consciousness). Since tranquillity is the absence of the fever of defilements (kilesadaratha), it is said 'he becomes one whose fever has subsided,' meaning one whose fever of defilements such as restlessness (uddhacca) has been abandoned.

It is said that 'he experiences both physical and mental happiness' because, while experiencing mental happiness (cetasika sukha) by way of the aforementioned preliminary meditation (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā), he also experiences physical happiness (kāyika sukha) due to his body being suffused with refined matter produced by that mental happiness. When it is said 'he experiences happiness,' it refers to the happiness of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha). This happiness consists of both access happiness (upacāra-sukha) and absorption happiness (appanā-sukha), as appropriate, because it has emerged from the side of the defiling hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and because it is a factor of the first jhana. Here, 'concentration' (samādhāna) is also by way of both access and absorption; thus it is said 'by way of access and by way of absorption.'

The meaning here is: from the abandonment of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) until the experience of happiness by one whose body is tranquil, as stated before, here too only preliminary meditation (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) is intended, not yet absorption (appanā). Therefore, regarding the abandonment of sensual desire, the Elder Dhammapāla stated: 'In this context, "by way of suppression" (vikkhambhana) means non-arising and non-occurrence; it is not the absolute abandonment of opposing states. It is called "abandoned" only because it resembles being abandoned, as jhana has not yet been attained.' Regarding the experience of happiness by one whose body is tranquil, while experiencing mental happiness by way of the aforementioned preliminary meditation, he also experiences physical happiness because his body is suffused with refined matter produced by that happiness.

Let alone the words of others, even in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated in various places as 'having developed the six qualities,' referring only to preliminary meditation. Because happiness is a cause for absorption as it is for access meditation in the concentration of a happy person, and because it is connected by way of cause and effect with the absorption to be described later as 'He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...', both preliminary concentration and absorption concentration are mentioned. Alternatively, just as preliminary happiness is a cause, absorption happiness is also a cause for absorption concentration; thus Elder Dhammapāla considered that absorption happiness as a cause for absorption concentration. Some teachers, not carefully noting this meaning and not correctly grasping the meaning of the term 'nekkhamma', cause confusion in both the Pali and the Commentary.

## The Explanation of the Abandonment of the Hindrances is finished.
135:
Some teachers, not noting this meaning grasped by the Elder Dhammapāla—that [absorption happiness] is a cause for absorption concentration—and not correctly grasping the meaning of the term 'nekkhamma', cause confusion and disorder in both the Pali and the Commentary.

## Explanation of the First Jhana

If the concentration of the mind by way of both access and absorption were already stated by the words 'the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated,' then for what purpose is the teaching 'He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures...'? In response to this objection (codanā), it is said: 'It should be understood that it is stated as "He, secluded... etc."' In that context, the two words 'well-concentrated' (sumāhita) should be connected with the words 'stated for the purpose of seeing' (dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ); the meaning should be understood as 'stated for the purpose of seeing in that way because of being well-concentrated.'

'For the purpose of seeing the higher distinction' means for the purpose of seeing the distinction of the first jhana, second jhana, etc., which are to be attained above access concentration and above the concentration of the first jhana, etc. Indeed, only by attaining access concentration can the distinction of the first jhana, etc., be attained; it cannot be attained without it. In attaining the second jhana, etc., a succession of causes such as the arising of joy (pāmojja), etc., is required, just as the purification of knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) is required in attaining the second path (magga), etc.

'By absorption concentration' means by the absorption concentration of the first jhana, etc. 'Of that concentration' refers to that concentration characterized by absorption, which was stated in a general sense as 'the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated,' for the purpose of showing its varieties. 'For the purpose of showing the varieties' means for the purpose of showing the classification of the second jhana, etc., as well as the classification of the first direct knowledge (abhiññā), etc.

'Karajakāya' (Body born of action) refers to the body composed of the four great elements, which is a collection of the four types of physical continuity (catusantati-rūpa). It is called 'karaja' because it is produced in the mother's womb, or because it is born from the 'kara,' which refers to the parents' reproductive essence (semen and blood). 'Kara' is the name for the 'flower' (menses) known as the mother's blood and the 'source' (sambhava) known as the father's semen. The body born from that, by way of egg-born (aṇḍaja) or womb-born (jalābuja), is the body of a womb-dwelling being. Although the attainment of the aforementioned concentration is certainly possible for spontaneously born (opapātika) beings who possess the necessary causes, this [physical] body is mentioned here because it is the most common and the most evident. Some teachers also say 'kara' means that which produces sons and daughters, referring to the semen and blood, and 'karaja' means born from that 'kara.'

Is it not the case that the mental body (nāmakāya) would also be similarly aided by the joy and happiness born of seclusion? If so, why is only the aforementioned physical body (rūpakāya) taken here? It is because it is understood through its connection with other words. Because of the connection with other words such as 'suffuses' (abhisandeti)...
136: Because of the connection with other words such as abhisandeti, it should be understood that in this context, the Blessed One spoke only of the physical body (rūpakāya). This is because only the physical body is suitable for actions such as drenching (abhisandana). Abhisandeti means 'to perform drenching'. In the scriptural sentence, 'With joy and bliss born of seclusion, he [the monk] [drenches] this very body,' a causal-active verb (hetukattukiriya) is obtained, established merely by conceptualization through distinction or through the whole and its parts. This drenching (abhisandana) is the act of making the physical body (karajakāya) moist with the joy and bliss born of jhāna. It also removes the roughness present throughout the body. Therefore, in the phrase 'he moistens, he pervades with oil,' it means he makes it wet and saturated. In terms of meaning, drenching (abhisandana) should be seen as the pervading of the body with refined matter (rūpa) produced by the aforementioned joy and bliss. Thus it is said, 'He produces joy and bliss throughout the whole body.' It is through the pervasion of matter produced by that joy and bliss that joy and bliss occur throughout the whole body. The same method applies to verbs like parissandeti. Bhastā refers to a leather bag. The word parippharati is a simple active verb. Thus it is said, 'He touches from all around.' It means that the monk, with joy and bliss born of seclusion, is touched all over in this very body. Here, the action of touching is appropriate, not the action of pervading, because the monk is the simple agent (suddhakattā). Just as with the word guṇavā, one is called sabbavā because of having all parts. To show the state of the body as having all parts, and to show the whole through its parts such as skin and flesh, it is said, 'of the body having all parts'. The meaning of the word kiñci is 'a small place where there is matter born of kamma (kammajarūpa) following the skin, flesh, and blood, in the place where the continuity of what is grasped (upādinnakasantati) occurs'. The connection is that there is no place where the continuity of kammajarūpa occurs that is not pervaded. Chavimaṃsalohitānugataṃ means following the kammajarūpa such as skin, flesh, and blood. Wherever there is kammajarūpa, there is also the pervasion of mind-produced matter (cittajarūpa). Referring to the state of the body being pervaded by that mind-produced matter, it is said, 'there is no part not pervaded'. Cheko means skillful (kusala). That skillfulness is known through its proximity to words like 'having scattered bath powder in a bronze dish' and through the context of being capable of preparing, combining, and kneading the bath powder; this is shown by words like paṭibhalo. The word kaṃsa appears in the sense of gold (or a golden dish) in places like 'with a large golden dish'. In places like 'as a bronze dish is struck', it appears in the sense of a bronze dish. In places like 'Prince Upakaṃsa is the son of King Mahākaṃsa', it appears merely as a name. In this context, it refers to any metal without specific distinction. Therefore, it is said, 'in a dish made of any kind of metal'. This is merely a simile, is it not? Nevertheless, the question of why the Blessed One specifically took a bronze dish is explained by the words starting with 'clay vessel'.
137: In passages like 'kaṃsapātiyā', the word kaṃsa refers to gold (a golden dish). In passages like 'kaṃso upahato yathā', it refers to manufactured bronze metal (a bronze dish). In passages like 'Upakaṃsa by name was the king, the son of Mahākaṃsa', it refers merely to a name. In this context, however, it refers to any metal without specific distinction; thus it means 'in a dish made of any kind of metal'. This is merely a simile, is it not? Nevertheless, the question of why the Blessed One specifically took a bronze dish is answered by the words starting with 'mattikābhājanaṃ'. 'Sandentassa' means that while one is kneading and making it into a ball from all sides, it tends to break; it cannot withstand the kneading. This is a genitive case used in the sense of anādara-lakkhaṇa. The occurrence of one action while another is occurring is called anādara-lakkhaṇa. The phrase 'paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ' is shown to be an abstract neuter (bhāvanapuṃsaka) by the words 'siñcitvā siñcitvā'. Here, the root phusa is used in the sense of sprinkling all around. It is like when it rains with wind, and it is said, 'the sky sprinkles a little at a time'. Therefore, it means sprinkling and sprinkling with water to make it permeate above the various bath powders. A word without a prefix can also express the meaning understood from the context, just like a word with a prefix. The phrase 'sprinkling and sprinkling' is used to clarify that 'paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ' is a modifier for the verb 'sandeyya'. This should be understood in such cases. In the word 'sandeyya', the root sand is used in the sense of forming a ball; thus it means 'he should form a ball'. 'Anugatā' means reached by way of entering. 'Pariggahitā' means pervaded because it is taken from all sides or touched from all sides. Because it occurs with both the internal and external parts, the ball of bath powder is called 'santarabāhirā'. There is also a reading 'samantarabāhirā'; the letter 'm' is an augment due to word-junction (sandhi). Due to the aforementioned reason of being pervaded from all sides, the ball of bath powder, including its inside and outside, is saturated with the moisture of water. Thus it is said, 'it is pervaded by the moisture of water in every part'. 'Sabbatthakaṃ' means occurring in every part and is an abstract neuter. It means being in every part and thus pervaded. By the words 'santarabāhirā phuṭā', the moistening of all parts of the ball of bath powder with water is stated. By the words 'na ca paggharaṇī', however, the solid and firm state of that bath powder is stated, even though it is moist. Therefore, it is said, 'there is no trickling drop by drop.' It means that the water does not leak out drop by drop.
138:
It means that there is no oozing at every point of contact or at every drop. In some versions, there is the reading 'binduṃ udakaṃ', which should be understood as a drop of water. Indeed, the word 'bindu' refers to a part of a stream of water, as in words like 'vyālambambudharabindū'. Because it does not ooze in this way, it is possible to take it with the hand, or with two or three fingers, or to make it into a ball (avaṭṭikā). If that mass of bathing powder were to ooze, it would become hard due to the exhaustion of moisture and drying up, and thus it would not be possible to take it or make it so. 'Avaṭṭikā' means that the mass can be made round all over or made into a ball like a treacle ball.

## Explanation of the Second Jhāna

It is called 'ubbhida' because it pushes upwards and emerges through various water veins. A lake having such water is called 'ubbhidodaka'. When the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta', it becomes 'ubbhitodaka'. To show this meaning, it is said 'ubbhinnudaka'. It means a lake with seeping water, like a well dug on a riverbank. In some places, seeping water pushes up from below, rises as a stream, and flows outside. No one can make that water stay only inside because it rises as a stream. In this example, however, like a hand-dug well on a sandy beach, it seeps only inside the lake and remains right there. It should be understood that it does not rise as a stream and flow outside. This is because only still, calm water is intended. With this meaning in mind, it is said 'na heṭṭhā' and so on.

'Heṭṭhā' means there is a great water vein beneath the lake. A place in the earth where a flow of water follows, like a blood vessel where blood follows, is called 'udakasirā' (water vein). 'Uggacchanaka-udaka' means having water that rises as a stream. 'Antoyeva' means only on the level ground inside the lake. 'Ubbhijjanaka-udaka' means having water that seeps and remains right there. 'Āgamanamagga' is the path through which water enters from the outside towards the lake. The term 'kālena kālaṃ' is a conventional term (ruḷhī), as in 'eko ekāya' and so on. Therefore, it is said 'kāle kāle' (at all times). In the term 'anvaddhamāsaṃ', the word 'anu' has the sense of pervading (byāpana). It means every half-month of the rainy season. In the term 'anudasāhaṃ', it should be understood in the same way. 'Vuṭṭhi' means raining. 'Anuppavaceyya' means it should not be interrupted. The fact that the term 'anuppavaceyya' is accomplished by the word 'vassa' is shown by the words 'na vasseyya' (it should not rain).
139:
The explanation of the feminine term 'sītā vāridhārā' as the neuter 'sītaṃ dhāraṃ' is to show that the word 'dhāra' has two genders. 'Sītaṃ' means cool because there is no disturbance, or it means pure (setaṃ) because it is not mixed with old leaves, old grass, old wood, and so on. 'Setaṃ' and 'sītaṃ' are synonyms. The question of why only a lake with seeping water is taken here and not other lakes is answered and dismissed by 'heṭṭhā uggacchana-udakañhi' and so on. 'Ugghantvā ugghantvā bhijjanatṃ' means emerging or breaking up by way of rising and spreading as a stream. 'Khobheti' means to disturb or agitate. 'Vuṭṭhi' means raining. 'Dhārānipātapubbuḷakehi' means by the falling of water streams and by the layers of foam known as water bubbles arising therefrom. After stating how the three types of lakes should not be taken in order, it is stated that only the lake with seeping water should be taken by 'sannisinnameva' and so on. There, 'sannisinnameva' means staying well or evenly, being still because of no agitation, and being very clear. 'Iddhinimmitamiva' means as if created by a person of psychic power through psychic power. 'Tattha' refers to that statement of simile and the thing compared. The remaining words are 'abhisandeti' and so on.

## Explanation of the Third Jhāna

'Uppalinī' and so on are names for the plant as well as for the forest. Here, however, because of the connection with the words 'yāva aggā yāva ca mūlā' (up to the tips, up to the roots) and because only lotus plants are to be taken by the words 'appekaccāni' (some) and so on, only a lotus forest is intended. Therefore, 'uppalāni' means lotus plants. 'Ettha' should be understood as meaning in the lotus forest. The whole (forest) is described by its part (plant). Although a single lotus plant is called 'uppala', even if there are only four or five, it is called 'uppalavana' (lotus forest). In the Sāratthadīpanī, however, a body of water is also called by names such as 'uppalinī'. 'Ettha ca' means in these three terms or in the three meanings known as 'uppala', 'paduma', and 'puṇḍarīka'. By the words 'setarattanīlesu', only the lotus is meant; it means among white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses. Any lotus whatsoever is called 'uppala' because it applies to all of them by the general name of the word 'uppala'. In the term 'satapatta', the word 'sata' is a synonym with many meanings, as in 'satagghī', 'sataransi sūriyo', and so on, because of its state of having many numbers. By doing so, the inclusion of a lotus with many petals as a 'paduma' is established. 'Patta' is intended as a petal. According to the rule of color, a white lotus is called 'paduma'.
140:
Calling the red lotus 'puṇḍarīka' is a usage (vohāra) within the Dispensation (Sāsana). In the world, however, they say, "The red lotus is a paduma, and the white lotus is a puṇḍarīka." It is stated (in lexicons): "The white lotus is called puṇḍarīka; the red lotus is called kokanada or kokāsaka." Indeed, because of its red color, it causes dogs named 'koka' to bark or cry out, and because it is eaten by them, the paduma lotus is called 'kokanada' and 'kokāsaka.' As the Blessed One said: "Just as one beholds the fragrant paduma lotus called kokanada."

The word-definition (vacanattha) in these terms is as follows: It is called 'uppala' because it protects water or floats in water. It is called 'paduma' because it grows in the mud or because it grows in a special way. It is called 'puṇḍarīka' because it has a white color or because, due to its large size, it is to be divided or broken. (In this term, the word is formed by substituting the letter 'ma' with 'pa', etc.) Grammarians desire the word 'muḍi' or 'muḍari' to have the meaning of 'dividing'; the formation of the word 'puṇḍarīka' should be understood according to the methods of grammar. In the Pāḷi text, the phrase 'udakānuggatāni' (not risen above the water) is spoken to show the state of being thoroughly saturated with water from the tip to the root. Therefore, the meaning should be understood only as 'not having risen out of the water.' Since it does not mean 'not occurring suitably in water,' He said, 'udakā... gatāni.' In this simile, the physical body (karajakāya) should be understood as the uppala lotus and others, and the happiness of the third jhāna should be understood as the water.

## Description of the Fourth Jhāna (Catutthajjhānakathāvaṇṇanā)

Only the fourth jhāna mind is referred to as 'cetasā' (with the mind). Because that mind is free from the stain of defilements (upakkilesa) such as lust, it is without defilement and stainless. Therefore, the very absence of defilements is called 'purified' (parisuddha); thus He said, 'parisuddhaṃ in the sense of being without defilement.' And because the special occurrence of only the purified mind due to special causes (such as faith) is 'pariyodāta' (bright/cleansed), like the brilliance of pure gold when rubbed, He said, 'pariyodātaṃ in the sense of being luminous.' 'Pabhassara' (luminous) means radiating here and there with light like lightning, as in the word 'Ābhassara.' In the phrase 'odātena vatthena' (with a white cloth), referring to the qualitative term (adjective) 'odātena,' the statement 'odātena... idaṃ' was made.

'Utupharaṇatthaṃ' means for the purpose of showing the pervasion of the (comfortable) temperature. Why is this said? He said, 'kiliṭṭhavatthena' (with a soiled cloth), etc. 'Utupharaṇaṃ na hoti' means that the pervasion of temperature does not occur in a special way as it does with a white cloth; the meaning is that only a slight pervasion occurs. Therefore, He said, 'taṅkhaṇa... balavaṃ hoti.' By the phrase 'taṅkhaṇadhota-parisuddhena' (purified by being freshly washed), it is shown that the word 'odāta' here means 'purified' (parisuddha), just as in the phrase 'gihī odātavatthavasano' (a layman wearing white/pure clothes)...
141:
...as in that case, it does not mean the color white, because it shows that the pervasion of temperature is possible only with a cloth that is purified by being freshly washed at that moment.

In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta Pāḷi, is it not said, "There would be no part of his entire body not pervaded by the white cloth," thus speaking only of the pervasion of the body by the white cloth, and not the pervasion of the cloth by temperature? Then why is the pervasion of temperature mentioned here? To address this inquiry, He said, 'imissāya hi,' etc. Since the physical body (karajakāya) is like the cloth, and the happiness of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion of temperature, it should be understood that this is the meaning. By this, it is shown that since the pervasion of the entire body by a white cloth is impossible, and because it would be unsuitable for the thing being compared (upameyya), by taking 'body' (kāya), the cloth dependent on that body should be taken; and by taking 'cloth' (vatthu), the pervasion of temperature caused by it should be taken. Indeed, this simile is spoken in terms of the meaning to be inferred (neyyattha). The Blessed Buddhas possess diverse and varied teachings (vicitra-desanā).

The yogi's physical body should be understood as the cloth because it is pervaded by the happiness of the fourth jhāna, which is like the pervasion of temperature. The happiness of the fourth jhāna should be understood as the pervasion of temperature because it pervades the physical body just as temperature pervades the cloth. The fourth jhāna should be understood as the man's body because it is the support for the happiness that occupies the place of the pervasion of temperature. Therefore, He said, 'tasmā,' etc. This statement is indeed a demonstration of the quality of the aforementioned words. In this simile, it should be understood that the Blessed One spoke of the happiness of the fourth jhāna by taking 'mind' (ceto) in the Pāḷi phrase 'parisuddhena cetasā' (with a purified mind); thus He said, 'fourth jhāna happiness' and 'by the fourth jhāna happiness.'

Is it not true that the happiness of the fourth jhāna does not have the characteristic of being felt as pleasant (sāta)? True, but because it has a peaceful nature, only equanimity (upekkhā) is intended here as 'happiness' (sukha). Therefore, it is said in the Sammohavinodanī Commentary: "Equanimity, because it is peaceful, is spoken of as happiness."

'By this much' (ettāvatā) means by that much sequence of words, from the explanation of the attainment of the first jhāna to the explanation of the attainment of the fourth jhāna. Obtaining is 'lābha'; one who has that obtaining is a 'lābhī.' One who has the obtaining of the fine-material jhānas is a 'rūpajjhāna-lābhī.' For example, as in the phrase, "One who obtains (lābhī) robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites." Or, one who has the habit of obtaining is a 'lābhī.' What does he have the habit of obtaining? 'Fine-material jhānas' is also a suitable answer. The same applies to the others. It should be connected that one should not understand that he is not an attainer of immaterial jhānas (arūpajjhāna-lābhī). Why should it not be so understood? He said, 'na hi,' etc., because in the attainment of direct knowledge (abhiññā) above all eight attainments...
142:
It means being inseparable (from the eight attainments). "By the fourteen modes" refers to the fourteen modes mentioned in the Visuddhimagga: in forward order of kasiṇa, in reverse order of kasiṇa, in forward and reverse order of kasiṇa, in forward order of jhāna, in reverse order of jhāna, in forward and reverse order of jhāna, by skipping jhānas, by skipping kasiṇas, by skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas, by shifting the jhāna factors, by shifting the objects, by shifting both jhāna factors and objects, by defining the jhāna factors, and by defining the objects. Although there are five kinds of mastery (vasi-bhāva) such as reflection (āvajjana) and so on in the jhānas, it is said "mastery practiced by the fourteen modes" to show that only these fourteen modes of mastery are definitely required for the production of direct knowledge (abhiññā). By saying this, it should be understood that it shows the inseparability of the formless jhānas in attaining those direct knowledges, as the attainment cannot be perfected through mastery practiced only in the fine-material attainments without the mastery practiced in the formless attainments.

To the objection, "Should not the decision be stated exactly as it is in the text (Pāli)?" he clarifies starting with "In the Pāli, however," and so on. It means that this decision is stated by extracting it from the fact that the Pāli text is incomplete (has an omission). If that is so, the formless jhānas should also be included in the Pāli; why then did the Blessed One make the Pāli text incomplete without including those formless jhānas? It is because all direct knowledges specifically have the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as their basis. For even though they are inseparable from the formless jhānas, they specifically have the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as their basis; therefore, the teaching was given by stopping at that fine-material jhāna to make known that they have it as their basis, but not because the formless sphere jhānas are of no use here. Therefore, it is said, "The formless jhānas should be brought forth and stated."

## Explanation of the Talk on Insight Knowledge

To answer the objection, "Why did the Blessed One state the word 'He (So)' again, even after saying 'Furthermore, O King, a monk...'?" he said, "He... shows." The intention is that it was stated this way to show the monk who is distinguished by the mastery practiced in the eight attainments, which were taught by way of the direct Pāli meaning and by way of the inferred meaning. "The rest (sesaṃ)" refers to the nature of the meaning along with the intended purpose to be stated in the words such as "When the mind is thus concentrated," which remain after the meaning of the word "He." Because it knows what should be known, it is called knowledge (ñāṇa). Because it sees that very knowledge by making it manifest (realizing it), it is called vision (dassana). Because only knowledge is vision, and not the eye etc., it is called knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana). It is also the fivefold knowledge; and this term "knowledge and vision"...
143:
In the Dispensation, the term "knowledge and vision" is a conventional term (ruḷhī) applied to certain specific knowledges. To show all of them by way of extracting the meaning, he said, "Knowledge and vision also refers to Path knowledge," and so on. "For the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision" means for the purpose of the purification of knowledge and vision (Path knowledge). "Dwelling in comfort (phāsu-vihāra)" is the pleasant dwelling which is the dwelling of the Noble Ones (ariya-vihāra). "Even to the Blessed One (bhagavato pi)" means that it was not merely the announcement by the deities, but rather that at the time of the deities' announcement, the knowledge and vision (omniscience) also arose in the Blessed One.

One who has been dead for seven days is called "one who died seven days ago (sattāha-kālaṅkata)." "Kālāma" is stated by way of his lineage (gotta). "Liberation of mind (cetovimutti)" is the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. Because insight knowledge knows the conditioned phenomena of the three planes, called the "knowable," by way of impermanence and so on, and sees them clearly starting from the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), it is therefore shown starting with "But here," and so on, that "knowledge and vision" has arisen in the sense already mentioned.

"He directs (abhinīharati)" literally means he leads the mind that is facing insight by extracting it from other duties; this is the literal meaning. But to show it according to the intention, he said, "of insight knowledge," and so on. For the mind's state of facing that (insight) is its inclining towards it, etc. But that should be understood as the sending (directing) of the mind towards insight when that mind, endowed with the eight factors, has arisen through the sequence of insight in the manner described. "Inclined towards that (tanninnaṃ)" means inclined towards that insight. The other two terms (poṇa, pabbhāra) are just synonyms for that word "ninna." It means sloping and slanting towards that insight. This meaning has already been stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta.

It is said "by boiled rice," and so on, referring to the meaning that it is nourished or increased by boiled rice and porridge, or that it grows through nourishment. In the phrase "subject to impermanence, anointing, massaging, breaking, and disintegration," the word "nature (dhamma)" should be applied to each term, such as "nature of impermanence," and so on. Therein, "nature of impermanence" means the state of being non-permanent due to fragility. "For the sake of removing bad odors" means for the disappearance of bad odors in the body. "Nature of anointing (ucchādana-dhamma)" means having the nature of being anointed; it means that because this foul body has a bad odor, it is of the nature to be rubbed and smeared with scented water and so on. For by anointing, the heaviness and bad odors caused by sweat, wind, bile, phlegm, etc., in the foul body disappear. "Great massage (mahā-sambahana)" is only for the purpose of increasing the strength of the arms for wrestlers and such; but for the purpose of dispelling the ailments of the limbs and body, only "minor massage (khuddaka-sambahana)" is appropriate; intending this, he said "by minor massage," which means by gentle massage. "Nature of massaging (parimaddana-dhamma)" means having the nature of being massaged all around.
144:
Having thus explained the meaning by way of indefinite time, he now says "daharakāle" etc., wishing to explain the meaning by way of definite time. Here, the word "vā" (or) is not used because another variation of meaning is understood simply by showing the sense, or it is indicated by omission. "Daharakāle" means in the time shortly after birth. It should be connected as "having the nature of being massaged from all sides by way of stretching and pressing while being laid down." "Mitaṃ" is a neuter designation of state (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa); by that term, he shows stretching, pressing, etc., according to measure or moderately. Here, stretching is called "añchana." Pressing is called "pīḷana." By the word "ādi" (etc.), he includes bending, extending, and so on. "Even though thus cared for" means even though made to grow comfortably by anointing and so forth. "It breaks" means it perishes by way of the nature of impermanence and so on. "It is scattered" means that even though it breaks in this way, it is simply scattered without achieving any purpose. Thus, with these nine terms, he shows the contemplation of the nature of arising and passing away in the body as appropriate; wishing to clarify this meaning, he said "tattha" etc. There, "by six terms" refers to these six terms: "rūpī, cātumahābhūtiko, mātāpettikasambhavo, odanakummāsūpacayo, ucchādanadhammo, parimaddanadhammo." Let it be granted that the statement of the body's arising by the three middle terms is appropriate because they clarify that meaning. However, one might ask: "How can the statement by the three terms 'rūpī, ucchādanadhammo, parimaddanadhammo' be appropriate, since they do not clarify that meaning?" It is indeed appropriate because they also clarify that meaning. The term "rūpī" clarifies the meaning of "possessing form" by way of form characterized by temperature (utu) and nutriment (āhāra), which are its conditions. This suffix "ī" is used in the sense of "that is in this" (tadassatthi), distinguished by the combination of conditions. The two terms "ucchādanadhammo" and "parimaddanadhammo" clarify the meaning of the perfection of the physical form by producing such form. "By two terms" refers to the two terms: "bhedanadhammo, viddhaṃsanadhammo." The insight-consciousness is "dependent" because it is dependent on the heart-base (hadayavatthu) included within the body. The insight-consciousness occurring at that time is spoken of by way of immediate perception as "And this is my consciousness." It is "bound" because it does not occur without the body, and because it takes as its object the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) designated as the body.

Because it shines well, it is called "subha," meaning a gem endowed with radiance. To show only the meaning that the excellence of the gem is due to that very attainment of radiance, it is said: "subha means sundara (beautiful)." Since being produced in a pure manner from all sides is the very nature of a gem's pure origin, he said: "jātimā means produced in a pure manner." The meaning is: produced from a very pure mine of jewels. Having its root in the purity of the source from all sides...
145:
Indeed, it should be known that the special origin of a gem, such as the kuruvinda origin, has its root in the purity of the source from all sides. In this simile, the pure source (mine) of the veḷuriya gem (or cat's eye gem) is near Mount Vijjha and the village of Viḷūra. Indeed, that gem is mostly produced from that Mount Viḷūra and Viḷūra village. This statement is true; this gem became famous as 'veḷuriya' because it was produced near the mountain and village named Viḷūra. The gem occurring in the celestial realm also has the same name, veḷuriya, because it has a color and luster similar to the gem produced in that Viḷūra mountain and village. Just as the names of deities in the celestial realm (such as Magha, etc.) are given by way of the names obtained in the human world.

That veḷuriya gem is either the color of a peacock's neck, the color of a crow's wing, or the color of a smooth bamboo leaf; thus it was said by the Teacher Dhammapāla Thera in the Paramatthadīpanī. In the Vinaya commentaries, however, they say "the color of wet bamboo." For that reason, the name "vaṃsavaṇṇa" (gem with the color of bamboo) also arose for that gem. It is also said to have "the color of a cat's eye circle"; for that reason, that gem is well-known in this region of Jambudīpa as "mañjāramaṇi" (cat's eye). Since it is a most excellent gem worthy of use by a Universal Monarch, the words spoken in the Mahāsudassana Sutta Pali itself should be understood. The Buddha said: "Ananda, furthermore, for the King Mahāsudassana, the jewel-treasure named veḷuriya appeared, radiant, beautiful, of pure origin, and eight-faceted," and so on. By the words "from which stones and grit have been removed," he shows the meaning that "the preparation of the work is completed only by removing defects such as stones and grit."

Transparency exists only because of the smoothness of the surface (skin), not because of polishing; wishing to say this, he said: "accha means having a thin (or natural) surface color." For that reason, to show that it is especially clear, it is said: "extremely clear." The perfection of the features of a jewel-treasure that is used is called "perfection in all aspects." Therefore, he said: "by washing, piercing, etc." The state of being washed on a touchstone and so on is called washing (dhovana). The state of being pierced both to remove black spots and so on and to thread with a string is called piercing (vedhana). By the word "ādi" (etc.), roasting by fire, smoothing, and so on are included. "Vaṇṇasampatti" refers to the perfection of the color of the threaded string. Why is this said? It means: "Because only a gem threaded with such a string is clearly visible."

The physical body (karajakāya) is like the gem because it is to be contemplated. Consciousness is like the threaded string because it exists having entered and stayed within. The monk who has attained insight is like the man with vision.
146:
Because the monk clearly sees that physical body (karaja-kāya), he is seen like a man with eyesight. Just as the time when the gem is manifest to that man, the time when the physical body is manifest to that monk is to be seen. This is because the body, which is the support of that consciousness, is manifest. Just as the time when the thread is manifest, the time when those conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra-dhamma) are manifest is to be seen. This is because the consciousness dependent on that physical body is manifest. What has been said here is the clarification of the reason for completing this simile.

Although some palm-leaf manuscripts read 'insight knowledge like a strung thread,' the reading 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) is much better because the Buddha taught, 'And this consciousness.' Alternatively, it should be 'insight consciousness' (vipassanā-viññāṇa). 'Directing the mind towards insight knowledge' means directing the mind towards insight knowledge.

'Therein' means in the veḷuriya gem. 'Having those as objects' means those phenomena having the material phenomena known as the body as their object. This term 'tadārammaṇānaṃ' is a qualifier (visesana) for the group of three terms beginning with 'phassapañcamakānaṃ.' This is because, by the power of the meaning, there is a transformation of gender, case, and number, and thus it is also a qualifier for the subsequent term. It should be understood that the phenomena grasped by the term 'phassapañcamaka' and by the grasping of all consciousness and mental factors are included only within the arising of insight consciousness (vipassanā-cittuppāda). When they are thus included in the arising of insight consciousness, because those phenomena have the nature of insight consciousness, the statement made below, 'insight consciousness like a strung thread,' is not contradictory.

Why is only insight consciousness taken? It is taken because the Buddha taught only that insight consciousness with the words, 'This consciousness of mine is supported here, is bound here.' Having seen with insight knowledge such as 'This is my body,' one adverts to it by way of support and object, etc., as 'This very consciousness associated with insight knowledge is supported here, is bound here.' Therefore, it should be understood that only that insight consciousness is appropriate to be taken in this context, and not any other consciousness. Therefore, he said, 'Or rather, the time when only insight consciousness is manifest.'

In this context, the 'phassapañcamaka' phenomena are taken because they are manifest according to the method taught in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and other texts. All consciousness and mental factors are taken by way of grasping without remainder. It should be understood that insight consciousness is taken because it is primary, as taught directly in the Pali.

Do these phenomena become manifest to the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) or to the person? They become manifest only to the knowledge of reviewing. However, because that knowledge of reviewing is manifest, they are also said to be manifest to the person. Therefore, it is said, 'the time when it is manifest to the monk.'

Furthermore, this insight knowledge occurs immediately after the path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Therefore, it should be mentioned after the mundane supernormal knowledges and before the sixth supernormal knowledge. Having shown a hint of an objection as to why it is mentioned only before all the supernormal knowledges...
147:
The commentator, wishing to resolve and dispel the objection, said 'And this insight knowledge,' etc. With these words, 'And this is immediate to the path knowledge,' he shows the hint of the objection mentioned above. In that statement, 'immediate to the path knowledge' is said with reference to the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), which is insight that has reached its peak. For that change-of-lineage knowledge alone occurs immediately after the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga) or after all paths and fruits. However, primarily, by that statement 'immediate to the path knowledge,' it should be understood that all insight knowledge is taken, because insight knowledge is mentioned here in a general sense without distinction. By the word 'path' (magga), only the path of Arahatship is taken, because only that is included in the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), and because an objection can arise in connection with the supernormal knowledges.

Insight knowledge mentioned before the mundane supernormal knowledges cannot be of benefit because it does not occur immediately after those mundane supernormal knowledges. Only insight knowledge mentioned before the supramundane supernormal knowledge known as the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) can be of benefit because it occurs immediately before that supramundane supernormal knowledge. Therefore, this insight knowledge should be mentioned after the mundane supernormal knowledges and before the sixth supernormal knowledge. However, an objection may arise: 'Why did the Blessed One not speak thus in the place where it is beneficial, but spoke only in the place where it is not beneficial?' The phrase 'Even so' (evaṃ santepi), etc., shows the answer. In that context, 'Even so' means 'Even though it is beneficial because it occurs immediately after the path knowledge according to the sequence of knowledges, even if this is the case.'

'In the section on supernormal knowledges' (abhiññā-vāre) means in the teaching section spoken by way of the six supernormal knowledges. 'There is no section in between' means that when the five mundane supernormal knowledges are taught, as in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and others, the sixth supernormal knowledge must also be taught without fail because it possesses the characteristic of a supernormal knowledge and is included therein. Insight knowledge, however, is not a mundane supernormal knowledge, and because it does not possess the characteristic of a supernormal knowledge and is not included therein, it should not be taught by inserting it between the mundane supernormal knowledges and the sixth supernormal knowledge. Thus, there is no section for this insight knowledge between those supernormal knowledges. Because there is no opportunity there, the intention is that insight knowledge is taught right here, immediately after the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-catuttha-jhāna).

With the words 'And because' (yasmā ca), etc., he states another meaning. In that phrase, the word 'and' (ca) has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya). By that word 'and,' the Teacher [Dhammapāla] stated that not only is that the reason for showing insight knowledge here, but this reason also exists, thus conjoining this meaning. However, scholars of grammar say that in such a place, the word 'and' (ca) has the sense of the word 'or' (vā), and expresses the sense of alternative (vikappa). That statement is also appropriate because it is used in showing another meaning. Indeed, prefixes (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) only illuminate an existing meaning associated with them, like broken branches placed to point out a path, or like lamps used to illuminate what is not clear. In this regard, there is the following: 'If the word ca is found in showing another meaning, the wise should take it in the sense of conjunction or alternative.'
148:
"If the word *ca* is clearly present when showing another meaning, the wise should take that *ca* in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or in the sense of alternative (*vikappa*)."

The term '*akatasammasanassa*' is a term containing a causal meaning. Likewise, the term '*katasammasanassa*' is also a term containing a causal meaning. In the statement, 'seeing a terrifying form with the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*)', the teacher (Venerable Dhammapāla) stated that it should also be said of one who, having created a terrifying form through the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), views it with the fleshly eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*). In this way, even for one who has attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), if they have an object that is not fully comprehended, fear and terror can arise, just as it did for the Elder Mahānāga who resided in the Uccavālika region. Just as it is said here, in the case of 'hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear-element (*dibba-sotadhātu*)', it should also be said of one who, having created a terrifying sound through the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power, hears it with the fleshly ear (*maṃsa-sota*). In this way, even for one who has attained the higher knowledges, if they have an object that is not fully comprehended, fear and terror can arise, just as it did for the Elder Mahānāga, resident of Uccavālika.

It is stated in the Commentaries that the Elder Mahānāga, having created a great white elephant that trumpeted like a crane, felt fear and terror upon seeing and hearing it. It should be connected thus: for one who has performed contemplation (*sammasana*) by way of impermanence and so on, fear and terror do not arise due to the divine eye and so forth. The cause for dispelling fear is the performance of contemplation through insight knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*); the meaning is that it is for the purpose of accomplishing that [contemplation] for the one who has attained higher knowledge, or by means of that [insight].

'*Idheva*' (right here) means immediately after the fourth jhāna. With the words starting with '*api ca*', [the teacher] shows the most appropriate method in accordance with the text. The happiness that arises in succession—joy, rapture, and tranquility—born of insight is called the 'happiness of insight' (*vipassanā-sukha*). '*Pāṭiyekkaṃ*' (separately) refers to the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) that is distinct and unmixed with jhāna, higher knowledges, and so on, which is to be realized in this very life. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the Dhammapada:

'Whenever one contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
one gains rapture and joy;
for those who know, that is the Deathless (or the path to the Deathless).'

Since it is also said here, 'Great King, this too is a fruit of recluseship visible in this very life... and more excellent,' the teachers say that this method alone is most appropriate when compared with the Pāḷi text. '*Āditova*' (from the beginning) means the higher knowledge is mentioned at the very beginning.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Mind-made Power

236-7. In this context of '*manomaya*', the word '*maya*' occurs in many senses such as another designation, transformation, a word-filler, or arising. Here, to show that it is in the sense of arising, the teacher said, 'produced by the mind' (*manena nibbattitaṃ*). The meaning is 'produced by the mind of higher knowledge (*abhiññā-mana*)'. In the Visuddhimagga, however, it is said to be called 'manomaya' because it arises from the mind of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-mana*).
149:
In the word '*manomaya*', the word '*maya*' is said to be in the sense of arising to show that it is 'produced by the mind'. The meaning is 'produced by the mind of higher knowledge (*abhiññā-mana*)', as stated by the teacher (Venerable Dhammapāla). In the Visuddhimagga, however, it appears as 'called mind-made (*manomaya*) because it is created by the mind of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-mana*)'. Since it is produced in both ways—by the mind of higher knowledge and by the mind of resolution—both [explanations] are indeed appropriate. The collection of hands, feet, and so on is called '*aṅga*' (major limbs). The parts included in those respective collections, such as elbows and knees, are called '*paccaṅga*' (minor limbs). In the phrase '*ahīnindriya*' (undiminished faculties), 'undiminished' means only completeness, not excellence; and the completeness of the eye, ear, and so on is only by way of their shape. To show that in a created form (*nimmita-rūpa*) there is no such thing as sensitive matter (*pasāda-rūpa*), it is said, 'having faculties that are not defective by way of shape.' By this statement, it should be understood that the absence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so on in that created form is also stated. 'By way of shape' means only by way of a shape similar to a lotus petal and so on, not by way of faculties such as the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhu-pasāda*) which clarifies the great elements and is capable of being struck by visible forms. Seeking to substantiate the meaning already stated as 'complete in all limbs, major and minor, with undiminished faculties,' the commentator said, 'a person with supernormal power,' and so on. 'With unpierced ears' refers to a person whose ears are not pierced for the purpose of wearing ear-ornaments according to family custom; this is merely an illustration. Therefore, it is said, 'in all aspects,' meaning in all aspects such as color, shape, and specific parts. '*Tena*' means by the person with supernormal power.

The teacher says that this very meaning is also clarified in the Pāḷi text: 'The three similes such as [pulling out] a reed from the muñja grass... etc., are stated.' In some versions, the text appears as: 'The similes such as [pulling out] a reed from the muñja grass are merely illustrations. They are stated only to show the state of similarity.' In that text, the phrase 'merely illustrations' excludes the showing of another distinct meaning, while the words '*yampi hi*' and so on substantiate its status as a simile of the reed. The word '*yaṃ*', which does not depend on a fixed [relative] word, refers back to the statement 'a reed from the muñja grass,' and so on. 'Only to show the state of similarity' means only for the purpose of showing similarity in shape, color, and specific parts. To the question 'How is there similarity?', it is said, 'For they are just like the muñja grass,' and so on. *Muñja* is a specific type of grass used for making mats and so forth. By the word 'one might pull out,' it is shown that only the reed situated inside is intended, as indicated by the words 'the reed is inside.' '*Īsikā*' means the reed or sprout. In the Visuddhimagga-ṭီကာ, however, it is called 'the shaft of an arrow.' '*Vaṭṭāya kosiyā*' means from a scabbard that is rounded all around. '*Patthaṭāya*' means [the sword] is in the scabbard. It is called '*karaṇḍa*' because it is to be divided; it refers to a casket (basket). It is called '*karaṇḍa*' because it is to be loathed; it refers to a snake's slough.
150:
In this context as well, it is meant to refer only to the snake's slough (nimmoka), as stated in the passage beginning with "Kāraṇḍāti idampī." A basket made of bamboo strips is called a viliwakāraṇḍa (peḷā). The question of why the name "kāraṇḍa" refers only to the snake's slough and not to the bamboo basket is explained by the passage beginning with "Ahikañjuko hī." That slough greatly resembles the snake itself; therefore, it is meant that the name belongs only to that slough. However, in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, it is stated: "Teachers say that 'kāraṇḍā' refers to both the basket and the slough." Regarding that Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā, the interpretation as a basket (peḷā) should be scrutinized because it does not resemble a snake.

If it were interpreted as a basket, the meaning would contradict the simile of a man pulling a snake out of a basket, as in: "Great King, just as if a man were to pull a snake out of a basket." This is because it is impossible for that man to pull a snake out of its slough with his hand; thus, it is analyzed in the passage beginning with "Tattha." Even in the indefinite expression "should pull out (uddhareyya)," since pulling out with the hand is the most obvious meaning, it appears as if showing the act of pulling out with the hand. Therefore, it is said, "He shows it as if pulling it out with the hand." The passage beginning with "Ayañhī" shows the reason for pulling it out by the mind. It is stated in "Sajātiyaṃ ṭhito" that snakes cannot transcend their own species' nature in these five instances: at the time of conception, at the time of death, during sleep, during sexual intercourse, and when shedding the old skin. The meaning is that it sheds the old skin while remaining only in the form of the serpent (uraga) species, and does not shed it by changing into another form through nāga potency. This statement is made with reference to highly powerful nāgas. "As if devouring its own body" means it is as if its own skin is devouring its own body. "Being disgusted with the old skin" means being disgusted with the old skin that is worn out and decaying, detached in some places and hanging down in others. "By four reasons" refers to the four reasons already mentioned: "remaining in its own species, depending [on something], strength, and disgust." "Tato" means from the slough (kañjuka). "Anyena" means by another person (the man) other than itself. "Cittena" means only by the man's mind, not by his hand. For example, a man seeing a snake might think, "Oh, how good it would be if I could pull this snake out of its slough," and thus pull the snake out of the slough with his mind; it would occur to that man: "This is the snake, this is the slough; the snake is one thing, the slough is another; the snake has been pulled out from the slough." In the same way ... etc. ... that monk creates another body from this body ... etc. ... creates a body with unimpaired faculties (ahinindriyaṃ); this is the intended meaning here.
151:
## Explanation of the Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power (Iddhividha-ñāṇa) and others.

Iddhividha-ñāṇa should be understood as the basis for the act of creating various transformations, just as well-prepared fine clay is the basis for the act of making various types of vessels. Unlike the previous section on abandoning the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), here the concept of a wilderness (kantāra) is not used; instead, only the concept of a long journey (addhānamagga) is used to show the safe path.
