Why is only the safe path shown and not the wilderness path? Is this not merely for the sake of showing a simile? To resolve this objection, the passage beginning with "Yasmā" is stated. The passage beginning with "Appaṭibhayañhi" shows the reason for taking only the safe path. Placing a cloth on the head to ward off wind, sun, etc. Describing the simile and the thing compared (upameyya) in such various ways serves the purpose of completing the upameyya through the completeness of the simile; it also serves the purpose of making the intended meaning of the upameyya easily understood; and it should be known that it serves the purpose of pleasing the minds of wise people through speech endowed with reasons, examples, and distinctions. This should be understood in the same way everywhere. "Sukhaṃ vavatthepeti" means noting and defining without difficulty or hardship.

A small infant lying on its back is also called "dahara" (young). Thinking that the word "yuva" (youthful) is used to distinguish from such an infant, the word "taruṇa" (tender/young) is used to show the meaning of the word dahara as qualified by the word yuva. Similarly, even if one is a youth, some may not desire adornment, and because of that lack of desire, they do not have the nature of adorning themselves. Thinking that the word "maṇḍanajātika" (having a nature to adorn) is used to distinguish from such persons, the phrase "endowed with [youthful] age" is used to show the meaning of the word yuva as qualified by the word maṇḍanajātika. In the Pali text, the explanation is made in this way because the three terms are spoken in order as the qualified and the qualifier; otherwise, an explanation with its attendants that could convey the intended meaning even with a single term would have been made. To expand upon the explanation already given as "maṇḍanapakatika," the passage beginning with "Divasassa" is stated. The word "kaṇika" is a synonym for a blemish (dosa); that a blemish refers to black moles, pimples, etc., is shown by the passage beginning with "Kāḷatilakā." Spots the size of black sesame seeds are called kāḷatilaka; or they are black variegated spots, which are also called "sāsapabījika" (the size of mustard seeds). Spots the size of sesame seeds are called tilaka. "Vaṅga" refers to vyaṅga (a deformed or discolored limb). Pimples caused by age, etc., are called facial-disfiguring pimples (mukhadūsipīḷakā), which are also called "khara-pīḷakā" (rough pimples) in the world. "Mukhanimitta" refers to the facial reflection. A blemish occurring on the face is a facial blemish (mukha-dosa). This is merely a statement of a characteristic, because the clear state of one without facial blemishes is also intended; or, just as there are blemishes on the face, so too for one without blemishes on the face...
152:
The term 'Mukhadoso' is stated by the method of vowel elision (saralopa) and also by the method of general designation (sāmaññaniddesa). This is because it should be understood as having multiple meanings. Alternatively, this meaning should be understood by the method of eliding the word 'pi'. Indeed, even if the meaning is not explicitly stated [by the Buddha], it is understood as if it were stated by way of combining the meanings. In this context, the meaning should be regarded by the method of ekasesa (one remains), where 'Mukhadoso' represents both the person with a facial defect and the person without a facial defect. Only when the meaning is taken by this ekasesa method will the meaning be complete, and the statement 'the sixteen types of minds of others become manifest' will be fully established. Therefore, it is said:

Taking the remaining meaning of what has been stated,
Through the methods of nidassana, elision of the word 'api', or ekasesa.
In three ways for dissimilar words, and in four ways for similar words,
Including the method of general designation, should be understood by the wise.

These are the sixteen types of minds stated in the Pāḷi text beginning with 'Sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ' (the mind with lust).

245. 'Pubbenivāsañāṇūpamāya' means either by the simile of the knowledge of past lives, or by the simile shown in the knowledge of past lives. To resolve the question of why only three villages were taken as a simile in the Pāḷi text, the words beginning with 'Taṃ divasaṃ' (that day) are stated. An action performed on that day is generally manifest even to ordinary beings. Therefore, the Blessed One took only the three villages that could be reached within that same day, and not those beyond them; this is the intention. Although the words 'Taṃ divasaṃ' do not appear in the Pāḷi text, it should be understood that the Commentary included the words 'Taṃ divasaṃ' considering that by taking three villages, the action performed on that very day was intended. By taking the three villages visited on that day, it should be understood that it is shown that for others who have attained the knowledge of past lives through great effort, the actions performed in the three existences are generally manifest. For this purpose also, the three villages were taken. 'Actions performed in the three existences' refers to actions in future existences, as well as actions performed in the present existence, both now and in the past.

27. In the Pāḷi text, 'rathikāya vīthiṃ sañcarante' means wandering from one carriage road to another street. To show the wandering back and forth by that statement, it is said 'aparāparaṃ sañcarante'. It means wandering here and there according to various tasks. This very meaning should be understood because the words 'rathi' and 'vīthi' have the same meaning. 'Siṅghāṭakamhi' means at the four-way junction. The physical body (karajakāya) of the monk should be regarded as a palace.
153:
Just as a person standing in that palace sees the objects to be seen, the monk standing in that physical body (karajakāya) should be understood through the accomplishment of seeing the objects to be seen. Indeed, for one endowed with the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu), the attainment of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) occurs. As it is said: 'The arising of the fleshly eye is the path for the divine eye.' Like a man with sight, this monk who has attained the divine eye should be understood through the seeing of the objects to be seen. He should be understood like a person entering a house and exiting from it, or like a person entering the mother's womb by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and exiting from it by way of birth. This is because the mother's womb is similar to a house. Thus it is said: 'You call the mother a hut, you call the wife a nest.' This is a method not directly included in the Commentary: he should be understood like a person entering a house by way of descending into an individual existence (attabhāva), and like a person exiting a house by way of departing from the individual existence through passing away (cavana). This is because the individual existence is similar to a house. For has it not been said: 'O house-builder, you are seen; you shall not build the house again'?

'Beings wandering back and forth' refers to beings revolving repeatedly in Saṃsāra. 'In an open space' means in a place that is an open area. 'In the middle' means at the junction in the middle of the city. 'In various places' means in a particular part of various existences. 'Beings who have arisen' means beings who are currently arising. By this term, it refers to beings who are born and have grown up in various existences. However, by the term 'beings wandering back and forth', it refers to ordinary beings whose time is not thus fixed. In this way, the simile of people walking and sitting in order is appropriate for those beings. In this context of 'the manifest time of beings arisen in the three realms', it should be understood that all beings of the described types are to be taken without restriction.

Is this not a discussion about the divine eye? If so, why is the four-constituent existence (catuvokārabhava) also included by saying 'in the three realms'? Is it not true that the divine eye cannot have mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) as its object? To resolve this inquiry, the words beginning with 'And this statement' are said. In that context, 'this statement refers to the words: of beings arisen in the three realms'; this is the teacher's view. If this is so, it should be understood that the teachers of the Commentary have already resolved the aforementioned inquiry within the Commentary itself. Our preferred view in this matter is: Is this not a discussion about the divine eye? If so, why are those who have reached the four-constituent existence also included without distinction by saying 'with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn' etc.? Indeed, that divine eye does not have mental phenomena as its object...
154:
Indeed, to dispel the objection that the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) cannot have formless phenomena as its object, the phrase "this also" and so forth was stated. In that context, "this" refers to the statement: "He sees beings passing away and being reborn." If this is so, it should be understood that the Teachers of the Commentaries have already resolved the aforementioned objection within the Pali text itself. To the extent that the objection is resolved in the Pali, it is also resolved in the Commentary, as the latter is the explanation of the meaning of that Pali. The phrase "only for the ease of the teaching" is stated generally for the sake of the teaching's clarity, not because the divine eye can clearly manifest to beings in the four-constituent realm (catuvokāra-bhava). A teaching that specifies "excluding the formless existence," or "in the two existences," or "sees beings passing away from the sense-sphere and fine-material existences," or "sees beings being reborn in the sense-sphere and fine-material existences," would not be easily understood through the distinction of qualifiers and the qualified. Only when stated generally in this way is it easily understood. The benefit of ease in teaching and understanding is what is meant by "for the ease of the teaching." Why? Because it is stated: "In the formless realm... there is none." This means that since material phenomena, which are the range of the divine eye, do not exist in the formless realm, there is no object for the divine eye's range.

## Commentary on the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints

In this context, the fourth jhāna consciousness which is the basis for insight (vipassanā-pādaka) should be understood; it does not mean the fourth jhāna which is the basis for supernormal powers (abhiññā-pādaka) as in the case of mundane supernormal powers. "Basis for insight" means being the proximate cause of insight. That insight is of three kinds according to the distinction of the persons practicing insight: the insight of Great Bodhisattas, the insight of Paccekabodhisattas, and the insight of Disciples (sāvaka). Among them, the insight of Great Bodhisattas and Paccekabodhisattas is self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) associated with knowledge consisting in reflection (cintāmaya-ñāṇa). The insight of Disciples, however, arises from the teaching of others and is associated with knowledge consisting in hearing (sutamaya-ñāṇa). That insight is explained in various ways in the Visuddhimagga, such as "having emerged from one of the fine-material or formless jhānas, excluding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," and through various methods of grasping the elements, starting with the four-element definition by way of the formless. For Great Bodhisattas, however, because it reaches distinction through 2.4 trillion modes, it is the preliminary stage of knowledge (pubba-bhāga-ñāṇa) which is the foundation for the Path of the Ariyas (ariya-magga-ñāṇa), the support for Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and it is the womb of various methods...
155:
...reaching maturity, extremely deep, extremely subtle, and not shared with Paccekabuddhas and Disciples. This insight is called "Great Diamond Knowledge" (Maha-vajira-ñāṇa) in the Commentaries. Furthermore, the 2.4 trillion attainments (samāpatti) entered into as the basis for the insight knowledge, which has 2.4 trillion modes according to its occurrence in the Teacher (the Buddha), are called the "attainments for daily use" (vaḷañjana-samāpatti) of the Buddha. This practice of insight of the Buddhas was briefly shown by the Teacher (Ācariya Dhammapāla) in the Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā named Paramattha-mañjūsā. Therefore, those who desire that practice of insight should take it from that sub-commentary. In this context, however, only the insight of Disciples is intended.

"For the knowledge of the destruction of taints" (āsavānaṃ khaya-ñāṇāya) uses the dative case (sampadāna) in the sense of the purpose of the action. Therefore, even though the word "attha" (purpose) which expresses benefit is not present, the meaning should be understood by the power of the purpose; thus it is said: "for the purpose of producing the knowledge of destruction" (khaya-ñāṇa-nibbattanatthāya). The same applies to other such terms. In this context, Nibbāna and the Path of Arahatship are called "destruction" (khaya) by way of superior designation (ukkaṭṭha-niddesa). Knowledge regarding that destruction is "knowledge of destruction" (khaya-ñāṇa). The benefit known as the production of that knowledge of destruction is the purpose (payojana). It means "for that purpose." The Path is called "destruction" because it exhausts or utterly cuts off evil states. That destruction of evil (pāpa-khaya) is not possible without the destruction of taints (āsava-khaya). Therefore, in the phrase "knowledge in destruction" (khaye ñāṇaṃ), the word "destruction" refers only to the destruction of taints, as shown by the phrase "destruction of taints" (āsavānaṃ khayo).

"Knowledge in non-arising" (anuppāde ñāṇaṃ) is knowledge in the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala) where taints do not arise. The Fruit is called "destruction" because taints are destroyed therein. One is a "recluse" (samaṇa) because of the stilling of evil; and since the stilling of evil truly occurs only through the Fruit of Arahatship, it is said: "In the phrase 'one becomes a recluse through the destruction of taints,' it refers to the Fruit." "Through destruction" (khayā) means because of being destroyed. Nibbāna is called "destruction" because taints are exhausted therein. Since "destruction of taints" (āsavakkhayā) is stated as a compound, the term "āsavakkhaya" is taken when extracting the meaning of the phrase "destruction of taints" (āsavānaṃ khayo).

The verse beginning with "Paravajjānupassissa" is taught in the Dhammapada. In that verse, "ujjhāna-saññino" means those who have the perception of blaming. "Arā" means far. As in the passages "Arā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ" and so forth, this particle (nipāta) has the meaning of "far." There is also a reading "ārā." It should be understood that like the word "arā," the word "ārā" is also a particle meaning "far." That very word is cited in grammatical texts. Although the Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā states, "He is one who has gone far from what is called the Path of Arahatship," nevertheless, due to the increase of taints in the formations (saṅkhāra)...
156:
One who increases the taints (āsavas) is very far from the unconditioned (visankhāra). Therefore, in the phrase "he is far from the destruction of taints," the term āsavakkhaya (destruction of taints) can also be a synonym for visankhāra (the unconditioned); thus, it is said to be "Nibbāna." Khaya means destruction, referring to the momentary cessation of the taints. The remaining terms are merely synonyms of this word khaya. The connection of the sentence should be understood as: "Destruction is the cessation of the taints." Here, however, both Nibbāna and the Path (magga) are referred to as āsavakkhaya because they are inseparable. This is because the destruction of taints by the Path is impossible without taking Nibbāna as an object.

"Tanninna" means inclining towards that knowledge of the destruction of taints. The remaining terms are merely synonyms (vevacana) of that term. In the Pali, the phrase "This is suffering" is stated to show that the monk at that time has personally grasped the Noble Truth of Suffering, defining it and leaving nothing out; thus, terms like "this much" are used. In that context, "this much suffering" shows the state of having grasped the Truth of Suffering by defining its limits. "Nothing further than this" shows the state of having grasped it without remainder. Therefore, it was said, "the entire Truth of Suffering," and so on. Knowing by way of penetrating the individual essence (sarasalakkhaṇa) is what is called "knowing as it really is" (yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti); this is shown by the phrase "sarasalakkhaṇappaṭivedhena." Rasa refers to the nature that should be experienced or known; thus, one's own known nature is sarasa, and that itself is the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). The meaning is: by penetrating that individual characteristic without delusion. Penetrating without delusion means the very occurrence of that knowledge such that, when it arises, no delusion occurs later in defining the specific forms and details of the Truth of Suffering. Therefore, it is said, "he knows as it really is."

By the word "nibbattika," the definition (nibbacana) is shown: "Suffering arises from this cause of craving; therefore, it is the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaya)." "Tadubhaya" refers to both suffering and the origin of suffering. "Having reached which state (ṭhāna)" means having relied on that Nibbāna which is the cause in the sense of being the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for the Path. Indeed, a cause is called "ṭhāna" because the fruit stands there, being dependent on it. The phrase "having reached those two" is spoken as if the person who possesses both suffering and its origin reaches Nibbāna, representing the reaching of those two truths. In reality, it is only the person who reaches Nibbāna by way of making it an object, not the two truths themselves. Alternatively, "having reached" means because of reaching, meaning the person attains it by way of making it an object. The use of the suffix "tvā" to indicate cause (hetu) is well-known in grammatical treatises, occurring in sentences with the same agent as well as those with different agents. "Appavatti" (non-occurrence) refers to the cause of non-occurrence, meaning "those two do not occur because of this Nibbāna," or it refers to the place of non-occurrence, meaning "those two do not occur in this Nibbāna." By this, the definition is shown: "Suffering ceases in this Nibbāna, or because of this Nibbāna; therefore, it is the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodha)." The inclusion of the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaya) should be understood as intended to show that because the suffering produced by that origin ceases, that origin also ceases.
157:
In the term "Nibbāna," the pronoun "ta" (that) recedes, so the pronoun "ayaṃ" (this) is stated again. This is because a pronominal word takes the gender of either what has been mentioned or what is about to be mentioned. "Tassa" (of that) means "towards the cessation of suffering (Nibbāna)." "Sampāpakaṃ" has the meaning of reaching well by way of realization (sacchikiriyā). By this, the definition is shown: "Because it leads to the cessation of suffering, or because one reaches the cessation of suffering through that practice, it is called dukkhanirodhagāminī; that very dukkhanirodhagāminī, being a practice, is called dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā (the practice leading to the cessation of suffering)."

"Kilesavasena" means by way of the defilements known as taints (āsavas). The intention is that there is no fault of tautology (punaruttidosa) here because it is stated again to show those very defilements through the synonym "āsava." As mentioned below, teaching by way of synonyms (pariyāyadesanā) is a unique quality of the Buddha's Dhamma. One might ask: "Do the taints not have only the synonym of the Truth of Suffering? Since they do not have synonyms for the remaining three truths, why are the truths that have already been shown in their specific forms shown again by way of synonyms through the power of defilements?" It is true, but it should be understood that because they are connected to the Truth of Suffering, the synonyms of the remaining truths, such as origin (samudaya), etc., can also be obtained. It should also be connected thus: because they are connected to the taints which are synonyms of the Truth of Suffering, the truths are shown as the origin of taints, and so on. Because the effort was started "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of taints," only the taints are taken here, and the remaining defilements are not taken because no such effort was started for them. Thus, by the phrase "the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire," etc., liberation from all defilements is stated, headed by liberation from the taints.

By the phrase "he knows as it really is: 'This is suffering'," etc., only the mixed path (missakamagga) is taught here, because the supramundane path is mixed with mundane insight (lokiya vipassanā). Thus it is said, "He taught the path that has reached its peak along with insight." By the phrase "for one who knows and sees," the three types of penetration—full understanding (pariññā), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā)—are stated, because the four functions are accomplished only by knowing the four truths. Abandoning (pahāna-abhisamaya), however, is stated by the word "is liberated" (vimuccati) as a remainder; thus it is said, "it shows the path-moment (maggakkhaṇa)." In fact, the four functions are accomplished only by knowing the four truths. As He said: "Bhikkhus, the eye (of wisdom) arose in me regarding things unheard before, that 'this Noble Truth of Suffering has been fully understood'," and so on. This is a method not explicitly mentioned in the commentary (aṭṭhakathāmuttaka). "Jānato passato" (for one who knows and sees) is a causal indication (hetuniddesa), connected as: "Because of the cause of knowing, because of the cause of seeing, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire," and so on. In this context, although the actions of knowing and seeing and the action of being liberated occur simultaneously...
158:
Even so, teachers say that the state of being cause and result through the aspect of conditions such as conascence (sahajāta) among ultimate realities (paramattha) existing at the same time is established as a method distinct from the commentary, and that the phrase 'knowing and seeing' (jānato passato) merely shows the state of being a specific qualifier included within the cause.

In this context, by taking the taint of existence (bhavāsava), the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava) should also be understood as included, because the view of existence is well-encompassed just like the craving for existence. Although some Pali versions now contain the reading 'the mind is also liberated from the taint of views,' it should be known that this is not an ancient reading but a later scribal error. This is because it is explained in that same way in many texts such as the commentary on the Bhayabherava Sutta.

In this matter, although the penetration of the truths is stated in the Pali according to an unspecified person and an unspecified time, the present tense 'one who knows thus, one who sees thus' is used based on the present nature of that truth at the time of realization. That present time, in truth, for any person, is indeed past from the moment of the path (magga) until today. However, because it should be known through the moment of fruition (phala) that it is past prior to all those present moments, the teacher said, 'By this word "in the liberated" (vimuttasmiṃ), the moment of fruition is shown.'

'Reviewing knowledge' (paccavekkhana-ñāṇa) refers to the knowledge that reviews fruition. This is because it is taught only in the manner of reviewing that fruition. By taking that reviewing knowledge of fruition, all remaining reviewing knowledges should be included as they are inseparable from it. Alternatively, partial reviewing knowledges may be taken, because incomplete reviewing can also occur.

The ground (bhūmi) of that reviewing knowledge is shown by the words beginning with 'Birth is exhausted' (khīṇā jāti) and ending with 'There is no more of this state' (nāparaṃ itthattāya). Is it not that only the fruition taught as 'in the liberated, there is liberation' (vimuttasmiṃ vimuttaṃ) is the ground called the object of that reviewing knowledge? To resolve the objection as to why its ground is shown by 'Birth is exhausted' and so on, the words beginning with 'Therefore' (tena hi) were spoken.

Because one knows 'Birth is exhausted' due to the fact that kamma, which still exists, cannot provide rebirth in the future through the reviewing of abandoned defilements (kilesa), and because one knows 'The holy life has been lived' and so on through the reviewing of the path and so forth, it is meant that the object-ground of that reviewing knowledge is shown by 'Birth is exhausted' and so on. 'By that knowledge' (tena ñāṇena) means by the fivefold reviewing knowledge taken either directly from the Pali or by way of inseparability.

In this passage 'Birth is exhausted,' for the sake of making it easy for the listeners to understand, an objection is raised as if in their absence, starting with 'Which one, however' (katamā pana). Having revealed the intention with which the objection was made, the teacher said 'Not yet of him' (na tāvassa) and so on, wishing to state the answer. This objection was raised with the future meaning in mind. In that context, 'Not yet of him' means...
159:
The past birth of that bhikkhu is not yet exhausted by the development of the path. Regarding that non-exhaustion, the reason is stated: 'Because it has already been exhausted' (pubbeva khīṇattā). The meaning is that it was exhausted by way of cessation even before the development of the path. It should be construed that the future birth of that bhikkhu is not yet exhausted by the development of the path. Regarding that non-exhaustion, the reason is stated: 'Because of the absence of effort in the future' (anāgate vāyāmābhāvato). This statement is made to clarify the intention of the objection by taking only the general nature of the future, and it does not refer to the specific future; the meaning is that there is no application of effort to exhaust it by developing the path in the future. For effort is possible only when something is manifest, not when it is not manifest.

However, the specific future is intended here, and effort is indeed obtained in exhausting that future birth. Therefore, he said 'That which, however, of the path' (yā pana maggassa) and so on. 'Specific future' (anāgata-visesa) refers to the various subsequent births that would have been fit to arise if the path had not been developed. It should be construed that the present birth of that bhikkhu is not yet exhausted by the development of the path. Regarding that non-exhaustion, the reason is stated: 'Because it is manifest' (vijjamānattā). The meaning is that it is manifest by being included within a single existence. In truth, birth has the characteristic of first arising in various existences. By the words 'That which, however' (yā panā) and so on, it should be understood that only the exhaustion of future birth is shown by way of destroying the cause, which is defilement (kilesa), through the development of the path.

'In existences with one, four, or five aggregates' (ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu)—the three types of existence are mentioned to show the exhaustion of birth without remainder according to the method already stated. In the first two terms here, the latter part 'bhava' is elided. In the phrase 'distinctions of one, four, or five aggregates' (ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā), the same method applies. The words beginning with 'That, he' (taṃ so) and so on are the words resolving the objection 'And how does he know it?' (kathañca naṃ pajānāti). There, 'that' (taṃ) refers to the aforementioned birth. 'He' (so) refers to the bhikkhu who is an Arahant. 'Having reviewed' (paccavekkhitvā) shows the reviewing of abandoned defilements prior to the specific understanding. By doing so, it should be understood that such specific understanding is accomplished through the sequence of reviewing. To clarify another reviewing, the two present-tense verbs 'knowing, he understands' (jānanto pajānāti) are used; the meaning is that being one who knows, or because of the cause of knowing, he is said to 'understand specifically.'

'The living of the holy life' (brahmacariyavāsa), by way of an excellent description, is the very arising of the holy life of the path; thus he said 'fully lived' (parivutthaṃ). The meaning is that it has been lived and practiced all around without remainder. Because there might be an inquiry as to why he understands this practice of the path by way of past time, he said 'Indeed, together with a noble worldling' (puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ) and so on. Indeed, even a noble worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana) who has the characteristics mentioned above, for the sake of realizing the fruit of stream-entry...
160:
Because it is taught thus in the Dakkhiṇavibhaṅga Sutta and other texts, one is called a practitioner (paṭipanna). The term 'vasanti' refers only to those who are currently residing, not to those who have already completed their residence. Therefore, because one has completed the residence, one is called 'vutthavāsa' (one who has lived the life).

In the Pali text, it is stated, 'He understands as it really is: This is suffering,' and so on, mentioning only Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) and not Right Thought (sammāsaṅkappa) etc. Why then is it said that 'the sixteen-fold task has been completed through the four paths by way of full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development regarding the Four Truths,' referring to the entire Eightfold Path in general? It is because Right Thought and the others also function in accomplishing the four tasks. While Right View occurs by way of accomplishing tasks such as full understanding regarding the Four Truths, the remaining factors like Right Thought also occur in a manner consistent with the full understanding and penetration of the Truth of Suffering; and their occurrence by way of abandoning and realization regarding the other Truths is also quite evident.

Since full understanding, realization, and development regarding the Truths of Suffering, Cessation, and the Path respectively are only for the purpose of abandoning the Origin (samudaya), they are included within that sense of abandoning the Origin. To clarify the meaning of the phrase 'Done is what was to be done' (kataṃ karaṇီyaṃ), the words 'tena' etc. are stated. By the phrase 'The root of suffering is cut off,' this same meaning is clarified in another way.

As to why the past tense is used here in 'Done is what was to be done,' the text says 'puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo' etc. These various modes are such; the state of these modes is 'itthattā.' This is shown by the word 'itthabhāvāya.' The word 'āya' is in the dative sense, meaning 'for that purpose.' These modes are intended here as the functions of the Noble Path, such as full understanding (pariññā), etc., as stated: 'thus for the sake of the sixteen-fold task.' These sixteen tasks appear clearly to one who reviews the Path through the power of the Path. This is because when the Path is reviewed, the reviewing of its tasks is also easily accomplished. Thus, after showing the sixteen-fold task by way of the four tasks for each of the four paths in general, the text says 'or for the sake of the destruction of defilements' to specifically show that among those tasks, abandoning (pahāna) is primary, as the others like full understanding are for the sake of that abandoning.

Furthermore, having shown the method of reviewing according to the previous sequence of reviewing, it should be understood that this is said now to show only the method of reviewing the abandoned defilements because it is primary. In the second alternative, this mode is 'itthaṃ,' and the state of that mode is 'itthatta.' Here, the word 'āya' is shown by the word 'itthabhāvato' to be in the ablative (nissakka) sense, which is the effect of the dative case. Even if one says 'from this mode,' the mode (pakāra) is not distinct from the subject of the mode (pakāravanta). If that mode were distinct, it could not be the mode of that subject. Therefore, the word 'itthaṃ' denotes the subject of the mode. Although there is no difference in essence, there can be a slight difference in meaning through the consideration of the part and the whole, etc. Therefore, the word 'itthatta' denotes the meaning of 'mode.' This is the method found in this sub-commentary (ṭīkā), as well as in the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā and the Vinaya Ṭīkā. Wise teachers desire this following method regarding the cause of the word's occurrence (pavattinimitta): This mode of this meaning exists, therefore that meaning is called 'itthaṃ'; the subject of the mode is obtained. The occurrence of words is very diverse. The state of that subject of the mode is also called 'itthatta,' which means 'mode' (pakāra).
161:
A mode (pakāra) has no distinct difference from the entity that possesses that mode. If there were such a distinction, that mode would not be the mode of that entity. Therefore, the word 'itthaṃ' denotes the entity possessing the mode. Although there is no difference in terms of essence, a slight distinction in meaning may exist due to the conceptualization of parts and the whole, etc. Thus, the word 'itthattā' is shown to denote the mode itself. This is the method found in this sub-commentary (ṭīkā), as well as in the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā, the Vinaya Ṭīkā, and others.

Grammarians, however, following the occasion for the word's occurrence (pavatti-nimitta), desire it thus: 'This mode belongs to this [entity],' hence it is 'itthaṃ,' the entity possessing the mode. Indeed, the applications of secondary derivatives (taddhita-vutti) are diverse. The state of that entity possessing the mode is 'itthattā,' which means the mode itself. To show this meaning, it is said, 'from this entity having such a mode.' In the first alternative as well, this method should be applied accordingly. Now, 'vattamānakhandhasantāna' (the continuity of the present aggregates) is a description of the actual nature [of the aggregates]. 'Aparaṃ' refers to the future.

The text, 'These five aggregates, being fully understood, remain,' exists at present. However, the reading, 'These five aggregates, known as the final state of existence (carimakattabhāva), being fully understood, remain,' is cited in the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā, the Vinaya Ṭīkā, etc., and is the reading indicated in this sub-commentary. Therein, 'known as the final state of existence' refers to the state of existence in the last life included within a single continuity. 'Fully understood' (pariññātā) means known by being delimited through the Path. 'Remain' (tiṭṭhanti) means they remain without a footing (appatiṭṭhā) and without a place of occurrence (anokāsā).

By this, it shows that those aggregates are without a footing because they lack the root of non-comprehension (apariññā). Indeed, a footing has non-comprehension as its root; due to the absence of that [root], there is the state of being without a footing. As it was said: 'Bhikkhus, if there is lust for edible food, if there is delight (nandī), if there is craving, then consciousness is established there and grows,' and so on. He clarifies this with the simile: 'Like trees with severed roots.' Just as trees with severed roots remain without a footing and without a place because they lack roots, so too do these aggregates [remain] because they lack the root of non-comprehension. This is the comparison of the simile and the thing illustrated here.

'By the cessation of the final consciousness' means by the cessation of the consciousness of final passing away (parinibbāna-citta). 'Anupādāno' means without fuel (like a fire). 'To the state of being beyond designation' means that while those aggregates exist, there is a designation (paññatti) established through conceptualization in various ways; because those aggregates no longer exist, that designation of a living being also no longer exists, and thus they will reach the state of being beyond designation. The words 'paṇṇatti' and 'paññatti' are identical in meaning. For example, just as 'paññāsa' is used as 'paṇṇāsa.' Grammarians say that 'paṇṇā' is a substitution for 'paññāsa.'
162:
Because it is generally narrow and contracted, a mountain peak is called 'saṅkhepa.' That mountain peak is greatly narrowed and contracted gradually from the foot of the mountain. Therefore, it is said 'pabbata-matthake,' meaning on the mountain crest or peak. This is a method outside the commentaries: it is called 'saṅkhepa' because it is counted as the state of a mountain; it refers to a place included in the mountain, meaning in a place belonging to that mountain. 'Anāvilo' means without turbidity. That state of being untroubled occurs because of the absence of mud; thus, he said 'nikkaddamo' (mudless).

Because it moves even though it has no feet, it is called 'sippi' (a mussel/bivalve). A small mussel is called 'sippiya' by changing the letter 'ka' to 'ya'; it is also called 'muttika' (pearl oyster). Because it is produced or arises, it is called 'sambuka' (a snail/shellfish), which people also refer to as 'jalasutti' or 'saṅkhalika' (chank/shell). In a collective noun (samāhāra), the neuter gender is mostly used, hence it is said 'sippiyasambukaṃ.' It is the same in such cases. 'Sakkharā' refers to stones about the size of a fist. 'Kathalāni' refers to potsherds. Since the word 'ghaṭā,' which denotes a group, is also seen in the feminine gender, he shows the meaning of the word 'gumba' (thicket/cluster) with the word 'ghaṭā.'

In the passage, 'sippiyasambukampi sakkharakathalampi macchagumbampi tiṭṭhantampi carantampi,' the pebbles and potsherds only remain stationary (tiṭṭhanti), while the mussels, snails, and clusters of fish both move (caranti) and stay still (tiṭṭhanti). Nevertheless, by the method of association (sahasacaraṇa-naya), all are spoken of as if they were moving; to show this meaning, he said 'tiṭṭhantampi carantampīti ettha,' and so on. Therein, with 'sakkharakathalaṃ tiṭṭhatiyeva,' etc., he shows the meaning as it is possible; with 'yathā pana,' etc., he shows the method of association. The word 'pana' is used to indicate a lack of preference [for the literal sense], meaning 'even so.' 'Antarantarā' means even though there are cows standing in between many [moving] cows, those other cows that are standing or lying down are also said to be 'moving' by the method of association.

In the words 'tiṭṭhantameva,' etc., this is the intention: since the mussels, snails, and clusters of fish are also connected with the action of moving, their action of standing is not absolute. Therefore, in reference to the pebbles and potsherds which only stand and never move, the mussels, snails, and clusters of fish are also said to be 'standing,' but not in reference to their own action of standing. However, in reference to their action of moving, it is said 'carantampi'; here, the word 'pi' should be understood as being elided. 'Itarampi dvayaṃ' refers to the mussels, snails, and clusters of fish being spoken of in this way by the power of the words. In the phrase 'carantaṃ' as well, the word 'pi' is elided in 'tiṭṭhantampi' in reference to their action of standing. Thus, the teachers of the commentaries show the method of association here, while the teacher Dhammapāla Thera also shows the method of 'as it occurs' (yathālābha-naya).
163:
Indeed, it has been said: 'What is the use of this concomitance (sahacariyā)? Rather, in this context, it should be understood according to the method of taking what is available (yathālābha). By virtue of the gravel and potsherds, it is said "they stand"; but by virtue of the shells, snails, and schools of fish, the construction should be "they both stand and move"' (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.249). Both ways are appropriate: the 'concomitance method' (sahacaraṇa-naya), which relies on the mere teaching by way of association even for a meaning that is not obtained; and the 'as-available method' (yathālābha-naya), which relies on selection by way of possibility even for a meaning taught in a general sense.

In this regard, teachers say: In the Commentary, by the words 'the gravel and potsherds only stand, while the others, such as shells, both move and stand,' the yathālābha method is shown because the meaning is selected according to possibility. By the words 'just as,' etc., the sahacaraṇa method is shown because the mere teaching is clarified by way of association even for a meaning that is not obtained. This statement of the teachers should also be understood as faultless because the meaning is logical and such a presentation is possible in the Commentary. 'Therein,' etc., is the comparison of the simile and the thing illustrated. 'On the bank' means on the bank of the water-pool. A 'water-pool' (udakarahada) is sometimes called an 'ocean' in some Pali texts, as in 'The deep pool there is the ocean, with its flowing waters' (Dī. Ni. 3.278). In some Pali texts, it refers to a reservoir, as in 'The pool there is called Dharaṇī, from which clouds rain and from which old rainwaters flow' (Dī. Ni. 3.281). In this Sāmaññaphala Sutta as well, it refers only to a reservoir. For that reservoir, by virtue of the water, gives seclusion to the eyes (cakkhu-raha), etc.; thus it is called udakarahada, changing the 'o' to 'a'. However, those skilled in grammar say that according to the etymological method (nirutti-naya), it is called udakarahada because it 'carries water' (udakaṃ harati).

By the words 'By this much,' etc., there is a summary of the meanings already stated, starting from the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) shown immediately after the fourth jhāna. In that context, 'by this much' means by this much of the sequence of words, or by a sequence of words of this extent, such as 'Again, Great King, when the mind is thus concentrated... he directs the mind toward knowledge and vision.' Insight knowledge refers to the insight knowledge shown by the name 'knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana). It should be understood that by showing this insight knowledge separately, it also indicates that among the three methods mentioned below for the reasons to be stated immediately after the fourth jhāna, the third method is the most appropriate. Although it is stated in the Visuddhimagga that the mind-made [body] knowledge (manomaya-ñāṇa) is included within the variety of supernormal powers (iddhividha), it is taken separately here because it is taught separately in this Pali text. Such a teaching is for the purpose of [showing] the individual, visible fruit of recluseship (sandiṭṭhika-sāmaññaphala).
164:
Since the two knowledges—the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa)—do not appear directly in the Pali text, it is said that they are accomplished by the power of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). This means that because they are accomplished by the power of the divine eye, by taking the divine eye, these two knowledges are also taken. In fact, both the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma are attendants of the divine eye. The 'divine eye knowledge' (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) is the divine eye knowledge shown by the name 'knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings' (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa).

However, since the classification of the objects of all ten knowledges is not present in the Visuddhimagga, the words 'of them' (tesaṃ), etc., are stated to show the classification of the objects of those knowledges not included there. 'Of them' refers to the ten knowledges. 'Therein' means in that classification of objects, or among those ten knowledges. Insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) has seven types of objects: limited (paritta) and exalted (mahaggata) by way of plane; past, future, and present by way of time; and internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddhā) by way of continuity. Indeed, the classification of the objects of that insight knowledge is stated only by way of the three triads such as the 'limited object triad' (parittārammaṇa-tika), and not by the 'path object triad' (maggārammaṇa-tika).

'Only the created visible-form base' (nimmitarūpāyatana-mattam-eva) means only the object of visible form created by oneself; or it is also appropriate to say it means only the visible-form base existing in the mind-made body created by oneself. This is said because that knowledge arises by taking only the visible-form base in the mind-made body being created as its object, and not because of the absence of the odor base (gandhāyatana), etc., therein. Indeed, there is no materiality-group (rūpa-kalāpa) devoid of the odor base, etc.; therefore, the created form is a fully produced form (parinipphanna-rūpa) in every respect. Thus it is said: '[It has] a limited, present, external object.' This means it has three types of objects according to the divisions of plane, time, and continuity respectively.

Although the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa) takes only a single phenomenon as its object by way of Nibbāna, the words 'an immeasurable, external, undeclarable object' (appamāṇa-bahiddhā-navattabba-ārammaṇa) are stated to show that it has three types of objects by way of the triads such as the 'limited triad.' In fact, that knowledge of the destruction of taints has an immeasurable object by way of the 'limited triad,' an external object by way of the 'internal triad,' and an undeclarable object (an object that cannot be said to be past, future, or present) by way of the 'past triad.'

By the word 'most excellent' (seṭṭhatara), it is shown that the words uttaritara and paṇītatara are synonyms. Like the jeweled pinnacle of a gabled house, Arahantship is called the 'pinnacle' because it is the supreme limb. Since the Blessed One's teaching culminates in Arahantship, it is said 'with the pinnacle of Arahantship' (arahatta-nikūṭena).

'He concluded the teaching' means that he concluded the Sāmaññaphala Sutta—which clarifies the refutation of the doctrines of sectarians, destroys wrong livelihoods such as various types of deception and flattery, illustrates the practice of supreme effacement adorned with the three types of virtue, is beautified by superhuman states such as jhānas and direct knowledges, is decorated with the fourteen types of noble fruits of recluseship, and is not shared with others—with the pinnacle of Arahantship, just as one completes a jeweled house with a jeweled pinnacle. Because Arahantship is taught by the word 'of one who is liberated' (vimuttassa), it has this meaning. The explanation of the discourse on the knowledge of the destruction of taints is finished.
165:
Just as a jeweled house is completed with a jeweled crest, so too [the Buddha] concluded [the discourse] with the crest of Arahatship. By the words "vimuttasmiṃ" (in the liberated state), the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) is taught; this is the meaning.

## Commentary on the Explanation of King Ajātasattu’s Declaration of Being a Lay Follower

Having thus provided the explanation of the meaning of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta taught by the Blessed One, the commentator now wishes to explain the meaning of the text beginning with "evaṃ vutte" (when this was said), which was recited by the Elders who were the Dhamma-collectors (dhammasaṅgāhakas). To show the initial connection, he said "rājā" (the king) and so forth. In that text, "tattha" means in that particular fruit of recluseship, or in that particular section of the Sutta. The act of doing is called "kāra." The act of saying "sādhu" (excellent) is the same. It means uttering that exclamation of approval such as "Excellent, Blessed One! Excellent, Sugata!"

"Ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ" refers to the beginning, the middle, and the end of the teaching. Having heard with respect and reverence, the word "sutvā" (having heard) is a preceding action (pubbakālakiriyā) to the word "cintetvā" (having reflected).

[The King reflected:] "I have spent a long time asking these questions to many recluses and brahmins. Even though I asked in this way, I did not obtain any essence of the Dhamma, just as a person pounding husks does not obtain the essence of grain." This is how the connection should be understood. Similarly, "That Blessed One... answered; oh, how wonderful is the perfection of the qualities of that Blessed One! Not knowing the power of the qualities of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), I have been deceived for a very long time." "Vañcito" (deceived) means being misled and turned around by ignorance (aññāṇa), and covered by delusion (moha). Therefore, he said, "Not knowing the power of the qualities of the Dasabala." Indeed, a general indication (sāmañña) stands for a specific instance (visesa). "Cintetvā āvikaronto" (reflecting and making clear) is the connection.

Intending to show that even when uplifting joy (ubbegapīti) capable of making one leap into the air arises, such leaping might not occur, he said, "one whose body is touched by the fivefold joy." "Phuṭasarīro" means one whose body is touched; it does not mean one whose body is entirely suffused, because it is not suffused by all types of joy. "Taṃ" refers to making clear his own devotion and declaring his status as a lay follower (upāsaka). This was undertaken by the Dhamma-collectors.

"Abhikkantā" means surpassed or gone. Since the state of being gone is indeed exhaustion/end, he said, "it is seen in the sense of exhaustion." For that reason, it is said, "The first watch [of the night] has passed (abhikkanto)." "Abhikkantataro" means extremely delightful or pleasing to the heart. Since such a person is called good or auspicious, he said "sundare" (in the sense of beautiful/good).

The verse beginning with "ko me" appears in the Vimānavatthu Pali. In that verse, "ko" means who among the devas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so forth. "Me" means of me (the Buddha). "Pādāni" means the feet; this is a word with a change of gender (liṅgavipariyāya). "Iddhiyā" means by such divine power of a deva. "Yasasā" means with such a retinue.
166:
And by the attendants (parijana) [one shines]. "Jalanti" means shining or resplendent (vijjotamāno). "Abhikkantena" means very delightful, desirable, or one of exceeding beauty. "Vaṇṇena" means by the complexion of the skin or the radiance of the body. "Sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā" means illuminating all ten directions. Making a single radiance and a single light like the moon and the sun, the connection is "Who is it that pays homage?"

"Abhirūpe" refers to one with an extraordinary form or a form endowed with noble radiance. "Abbhānumodane" means in the state of great rejoicing or being greatly delighted. To answer the question "What is the purpose of the word 'abbhānumodane'?", the teacher said "tasmā" and so forth. While the word "abbhānumodane" is appropriate in the sense of great rejoicing, why is it said twice? In response to this objection, he clarifies the scope of reduplication (āmeḍita) by saying "bhaye kodhe" (in fear, in anger) and so forth. It means that by this linguistic principle as the cause, it is said twice in this or that context.

Showing the meaning through the power of reduplication as in "Excellent, excellent, Bhante," some teachers also state the connection saying he spoke thus to define the scope of that reduplication. Among those reduplications, a wise person should use reduplication in fear (bhaya) as in "Thief! Thief!" or "Snake! Snake!"; in anger (kodha) as in "Pierce! Pierce!" or "Strike! Strike!"; in praise (pasaṃsā) as in "Excellent! Excellent!"; in haste (turita) as in "Go! Go!" or "Reap! Reap!"; in excitement/curiosity (kotūhala) as in "Come! Come!"; in wonder (acchara) as in one thinking "Buddha! Buddha!"; in joy (hāsa) as in "Proceed, venerable ones! Proceed!"; in grief (soka) as in "Where is my only son? Where is my only son?"; and a wise person should use reduplication in confidence or clarity (pasāda) as in "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!"

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned; by this, censure (garahā), disrespect (asammāna), and so forth should be understood as included. Indeed, reduplication is used in censure as in "Evil! Evil!" and in disrespect as in "Ugly one! Ugly one!" Thus, in these nine contexts and in others, a wise person should use or apply reduplicated speech. "Āmeḍana" means repeating again and again. Alternatively, it is called "āmeḍita" because it is repeated again and again; it refers to saying the same meaning twice or thrice. Indeed, the word "meḍi" is used in the sense of madness/confusion, but with the prefix "ā," it signifies uttering twice or thrice, as in: "Sakka repeats this very sentence."
167:
Having thus shown that the word was spoken twice by way of repetition (āmēḍita), he now says "Atha vā" (Or else), etc., wishing to show that this was not spoken twice only by way of repetition, but also by way of two distinct meanings. Some teachers also say that after showing the meaning by way of repetition, he speaks thus wishing to show it by way of distributive pervasiveness (vicchā). That is improper, because the object to be pervaded is not mentioned twice. 

Indeed, vicchā is the desire to pervade an object to be pervaded with a pervading quality, action, or substance, expressed by repeating a word two or three times. For example, "Every village, every village is delightful." In that context, "Abhikkantaṃ" means that which is to be greatly enjoyed; and because it is an extremely desirable object, it is said to be "ati-iṭṭhaṃ" (extremely desirable), etc. All three of these terms are synonyms. 

"Ettha" means among the two words "Abhikkantaṃ." The word "Abhikkantaṃ" is used in the neuter gender with reference to the word itself. Since that word of the Blessed One is indeed the Dhamma teaching, he said, "Yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadēsanā" (which is the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One). The meaning is: "This word of the Blessed One, known as the Dhamma teaching, which I have heard, is excellent." Such a restatement is appropriate because there is no difference in meaning, just as in the passage, "Yattha ca dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ āhū" (Where it is said that what is given bears great fruit), etc. 

Alternatively, this is merely showing the meaning of the spoken word "Abhikkantaṃ." Therefore, the change of gender and case should be understood according to the sense. Here, the change of case is due to the change in the effect to be produced. The word "vacanaṃ" (speech) is understood to be remaining here. The meaning is: "The speech of the Blessed One is excellent. This Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One which I have heard is excellent, excellent." In the second instance as well, this method should be applied as appropriate, such as "Abhikkantaṃ is used in the neuter gender with reference to the word pasādanaṃ (clarity/devotion)." 

He shows the nature of the two meanings with the words "Bhagavato vacanaṃ," etc. Among those two meanings, "dōsanāsanatō" (by way of destroying faults) means by way of destroying the faults of defilements such as lust. "Guṇādhigamanatō" (by way of attaining virtues) means by way of causing the attainment of virtues such as morality through their fulfillment. Since the teaching causes the attainment of certain virtues, and those virtues are mentioned as "guṇādhigamanatō," the primary virtues among them should be shown. To show those primary virtues first, he said, "saddhājananatō paññājananatō" (by way of generating faith and generating wisdom). Indeed, mundane virtues have faith as their chief, and supramundane virtues have wisdom as their chief. This mention of the primary ones is also because they can be associated with the groups of Dhamma such as morality and concentration which are to be attained through the teaching. He shows another pair of meanings with "sātthatō," etc.
168:
Because it is endowed with benefits such as morality, it is "with meaning" (sātthatō). Because it is endowed with natural linguistic perfection, it is "with phrasing" (sabyañjanatō). Because it uses easily understandable terminology, it has "clear words" (uttānapadatō). Because it has a subtle nature and thus a meaning difficult to understand, it has "profound meaning" (gambhīratthatō). Because it uses smooth, soft, and sweet terminology, it is "pleasant to the ear" (kaṇṇasukhatō). Because it has an extensive, pure, and lovely meaning, it "goes to the heart" (hadayangamatō). By removing conceit and excessive pride, there is "no self-exaltation" (anattukkaṃsanatō). By subduing stubbornness and hostility, there is "no disparaging of others" (aparavambhanatō). Because it arises with the intention for welfare and extinguishes the heat of others' lust, etc., it is "cool with compassion" (karuṇāsītalatō). By dispelling the darkness of defilements, "wisdom is pure" (paññāvadātatō). The terms "avadāta" and "ōdāta" are the same in meaning. Because it has a voice as sweet as the song of the Karavīka bird, it is "delightful upon hearing" (āpātharamanīyatō). Because it is extremely pure and without internal contradictions, it "withstands scrutiny" (vimaddakkhamatō). Because it is delightful upon hearing, it is "blissful to listen to" (sūyamānasukhatō). Because it withstands scrutiny and arises from a desire for welfare, it is "beneficial when investigated" (vīmaṃsiyamānahitatō). Thus should the meaning be understood here. 

By the word "ādi" (etc.), one should understand the inclusion of such points as: stopping the wheel of Saṃsāra, turning the wheel of the True Dhamma, destroying wrong views, establishing right views, uprooting the roots of the unwholesome, planting the roots of the wholesome, closing the doors to the woeful states, opening the doors to heaven and the paths and fruits, calming the outbursts of defilements, and uprooting the underlying tendencies. 

In the phrase "not only with the two words, but also with the four similes thereafter," the word "pi" (also) has the sense of conjunction. The statement "those with eyes will see forms" is merely showing the manner of the fourth simile, "as if one were to hold up a lamp," and not showing another simile; therefore the teacher said, "with four similes." "Placed face down" (adhōmukhaṭṭhapitaṃ) means placed face down by someone. "Born face down" (heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ) means naturally born face down. "Would open" (ugghāṭeyya) means would make it open. The phrase "taking by the hand" is spoken for the purpose of showing clear guidance. It means that instead of merely saying "Go east" or "Go north," etc., one would take him by the hand and show him without doubt, saying, "This is the path, go this way." The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight is called "kāḷapakkhasātuddasī." A dense forest that is a solid mass due to trees without gaps is called "ghanavanaṣaṇḍa." A layer of clouds is "mēghapaṭala," meaning being covered by clouds. "Setting upright what was overturned" (nikkuñjitaṃ ukkujjeyya) means to set upright a vessel that was not a container for anything, making it a container by placing its opening upwards. These two points—being hidden because of being face down, and falling into false Dhamma (asaddhamma) because of being placed face down—are the meaning of the word "nikkuñjita."
169:
It should be applied appropriately according to the two meanings shown, not in successive order. Indeed, this king, by his own nature, was one who turned away from the True Dhamma; however, because he was urged by the evil friend Devadatta toward parricide and other crimes, he fell into unrighteousness. The connection is: "The Blessed One who causes [him] to rise up."

By saying "of the Blessed One Kassapa" and so forth, it shows only the implication of the meaning, even though the king did not say so at that time. While it is true that sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and others are also covering factors because they are hindrances (nīvaraṇa), wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is especially covering because of its power to make beings adhere wrongly. Therefore, it is said: "covered by the thicket of wrong view." For this reason, the Blessed One said: "Monks, I say that wrong view is the greatest fault." The meaning is: covered by the brushwood known as wrong view. The commentator, by saying "opening the Dispensation (Sāsana) covered by the thicket of wrong view," considers that the sequence of all Buddhas is one and the Dispensation is one; thus, the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa is made one with this Dispensation. This is also stated in the Aṅguttara Commentary and others. By doing so, the statement about opening the Dispensation covered by the thicket of wrong view becomes appropriate.

The path leading to the states of deprivation (apāya), which is all unwholesome states, is called "kummagga" (vile path) because it is a loathsome path. The eight factors of wrongness (micchatta), such as wrong view, are called "micchāmagga" (false path) because they are directly opposite to right view and others, and are a path that deviates from the path to liberation. Therefore, intending the opposite of both, it is said: "revealing the path to heaven and liberation." All wholesome states are the path to heaven. The eight factors of rightness (sammatta), such as right view, are the path to liberation. Because a lamp depending on ghee and such is not as bright as a lamp depending on oil, the term "oil lamp" (telapajjota) is used. "Dhāreyya" means one should carry, one should bring forth, or one should light up. "Buddhadiratana-rūpāni" refers to the visible forms of the Three Jewels, starting with the Buddha. Just as the light of the teaching (desanā) destroys the darkness of delusion (moha) that covers the forms of the Three Jewels, so it is. Combining both by way of apposition, in the sense of one who carries or lights that lamp of teaching, it is said: "one who carries the lamp of teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion covering those jewels." "By these means" refers to the fourfold methods of comparison and the things compared: overturning what was set upright, revealing what was hidden, showing the way, and holding an oil lamp...
170:
Or, [the Dhamma was shown] by the methods of explaining the removal of various forms of wrong livelihood such as scheming (kuhana) and talk (lapana). Therefore, it was said: "The Dhamma has been explained in many ways."

With the word "Evaṃ" and so forth, the connection to the passage "Esāhaṃ" is shown. With a confident mind, he makes a gesture of devotion. To make known the meaning that the confident mind arose only after hearing this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, it is said: "because of this teaching." This teaching is the cause [of the confidence].

The gesture of devotion refers to the respect (sakkāra) that should be performed by virtuous people who are confident. "Refuge" (saraṇa) means a resort (paṭisaraṇa). Therefore, it is called "parāyaṇa" (final resort). The state of being a final resort is through the prevention of harm and the accomplishment of welfare; thus it is said: "Protector from evil, provider of welfare."

The word "aghassa" is in the genitive case with an ablative sense, meaning "from evil/sin." Some teachers also say "from suffering." He is called "tātā" (protector) because he protects or provides a support. The word "hitassa" is in the genitive case with an accusative sense. He is called "vidhātā" (provider) because he arranges or provides welfare.

The teacher, by saying "with this intention," indicates that the word "iti" is elided here, and that "iti" has the sense of "manner" (ākāra). "Saraṇa" means "going" (gamana). It is the act of resorting to (bhajana) or knowing (jānana) with the intention of welfare. For this reason, in the Vinaya Commentary and others, the meaning is stated only with the word "iti" as "saraṇanti gacchāmi" (I go for refuge).

In fact, the verb "gami" (to go) is not a bitransitive verb (dvikammika) like the verb "nī" (to lead). Therefore, while one can say "He leads the goat to the village" (ajaṃ gါမံ နေတိ), one cannot say "I go to the Blessed One the refuge" (bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi) [in the sense of two direct objects]. Rather, one should say "I go [to him], [taking him] as a refuge" (saraṇanti gacchāmi). Thus, it should be understood that the word "iti" is elided here.

Consequently, the objection raised in the Khuddakanikāya Commentary—"He who goes to the Buddha as a refuge might go either to the Buddha or to the refuge"—is out of place. For grammarians do not classify the verb "gami" under the Duhādi or Nyādi groups [of bitransitive verbs].

Even if the verb "gami" were monotransitive, would it not be proper for the two words "bhagavantaṃ" and "saraṇaṃ" to be in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa), as in the passages "He goes to the eastern direction, he goes to the western direction"? No, because the apposition of those two words is untenable. If their apposition were intended, then even someone with a hostile mind approaching the Blessed One would be called "one who has gone to the Buddha for refuge." For he has gone to that refuge which is specified as "Buddha." But here, an untenable meaning is not intended. Therefore, the word "bhagavantaṃ" clarifies the object to be approached, while the word "saraṇaṃ" clarifies the manner of approaching.
171:
In the manner already stated, the meaning should be understood through the elision of the word *iti*. The same method applies to the phrase "*dhammañca saṅghañca*". In this regard, there are these verses:

"Because the root *gam* has only one object, it should be known that *iti* is elided. Because there is the possibility of a mind of aversion (towards the Buddha), the two terms (*buddhaṃ* and *saraṇaṃ*) cannot have the same meaning. Therefore, in the three refuges, the preceding word indicates the object to be resorted to, while the following word indicates the manner of resorting; thus it is said in the refuge-formula."

One who says, "With such an intention, I go to the Blessed One," regards the act of resorting to or knowing with this very intention as the taking of refuge (*saraṇagamana*). Among those words beginning with "*gacchāmi*", each subsequent word is an explanation of the meaning of each preceding word. Alternatively, to show the unique meaning of the word "*gacchāmi*" that is not shared with other words, the three words beginning with "*bhajami*" are used as separate explanatory terms. Resorting (*bhajana*) means approaching with the intention of seeking refuge. Associating (*sevana*) means frequenting or staying in the presence of. Attending (*payirupāsana*) means serving by performing major and minor duties. In this way, in every respect, it shows only the unique meaning not shared with other words.

Having thus shown the meaning of "going" for the word "*gacchāmi*", the phrase beginning with "*evaṃ vā*" is said to show the meaning of "knowing" as well. In that context, "*evaṃ*" refers to the intention such as "The Blessed One is my refuge." The objection as to why the meaning "*bujjhāmi*" (I know) is obtained from the word "*gacchāmi*" is resolved by the passage beginning with "*yeseñhi*". By this, it is shown that even without following the method of etymology (*nirutti*), the root *gam* by its very nature possesses the meaning of knowing. "Roots" (*dhātūnaṃ*) refers to those known as original sounds such as *i*, *yā*, *kamu*, and *gamu*.

By the two terms "*adhigatamagge*" (having attained the path) and "*sacchikatanirodhe*" (having realized cessation), only those established in the Fruit (*phalaṭṭha*) are shown, not those established in the Path (*maggaṭṭha*). To show those established in the Path, it is said, "*yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca*" (and those practicing as instructed). Is it not said that a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) also "practices as instructed"? Although it is so said, in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), only those established in the Path should be so described. Others (worldlings) should not be so described because they have not yet transcended the state of uncertain destiny. For that very reason, only those established in the Path are said to be "held so as not to fall into woeful states." This is because the possibility of liberation from the woeful states arises only through the attainment of the certainty of rightness (*sammatta-niyāma*). Thus it has been stated by many teachers of the Vinaya and Suttanta sub-commentaries (*Ṭīkās*). That statement was made with reference to those established in the Path who are liberated from woeful states in the primary sense by virtue of entering the certainty of rightness. However, it should be understood that by the term "*yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne*", the noble worldling who is liberated from woeful states in a figurative sense (*pariyāyena*) due to practicing in accordance with those on the Path is also shown.
172:
Similarly, such a person is described in the *Dakkhiṇavibhaṅga Sutta* and other texts as one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. The youth Chatta in the *Chattavimāna* is an illustration here. The construction with the remaining text is: "He holds those who have attained the path, those who have realized cessation, and those practicing as instructed, preventing them from falling into woeful states." By the first two terms in the past tense (*adhigatamagga*, *sacchikatanirodha*), only those established in the Fruit are taken. By the last term in the present tense (*paṭipajjamāna*), those established in the Path along with the noble worldling are taken. In showing the manner of holding by the term "*apatamāne*", it may mean holding by preventing them from falling, or it may show the nature of the holding itself. Holding means the very act of preventing falling; and preventing falling is the escape from the round of suffering (*vaṭṭa*) by destroying the defilements that cause rebirth in woeful states and so on. Although "in woeful states" (*apāyesu*) is said primarily because they are places of abundant suffering, the meaning should be understood as holding them so they do not fall into any of the sufferings of the round of rebirth.

Accordingly, it is stated in the Abhidhamma Commentary: "In this Dispensation, the Path of Stream-entry rises above the existence in woeful states; the Path of Once-returning rises above a portion of the fortunate sense-sphere realm; the Path of Non-returning rises above the sense-sphere existence; the Path of Arahatship rises above the fine-material and immaterial existences; indeed, they say it rises above all existences." By doing so, because the Noble Path leads out of suffering (*niyyānika*), and because Nibbāna is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose, both are shown in their true nature as being "Dhamma" in the primary sense; thus it is said, "That (Dhamma) in essence is both the Noble Path and Nibbāna." Only by taking Nibbāna as an object can the accomplishment of that purpose of the Noble Path occur. Since this meaning is established by the Pali text itself, it is said, "*vuttañcetaṃ*" and so on. "*Yāvatā*" means as many as. "*Tesaṃ*" means of those many dhammas. Where it should be said "*aggo akkhāyati*", the 'o' is changed to 'a' and the letter 'm' is added as an augment, thus it is said "*aggamakkhāyati*". Here, the word *iti* in "*akkhāyati*" has the meaning of "beginning with" or "variety"; by that, it includes the sutta passage: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are dhammas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is said to be the foremost of them," and so on. Or, by the word "*vitthāro*", the rest of the Pali texts are included.

As for the Noble Fruits, according to the words "because that faith is not yet stilled," etc., they possess the quality of being conducive to liberation and being the consummation of liberation, because they have the function of abandoning defilements through the stilling of those already cut off by the Path. *Pariyatti* (scriptural study) is also conducive to liberation because it is the cause for obtaining the Dhamma that leads out of the round of rebirth. By the method thus stated, it attains the status of Dhamma through this figurative sense (*pariyāya*). Therefore, wishing to include both of these (*phala* and *pariyatti*), it is said, "*na kevalaṃ*" and so on. That this meaning is also clear in the Pali is shown by "*vuttañcetaṃ*" and so on. In that Pali, Chatta Māṇavaka was a brahmin youth living in the city of Setabyā. That youth Chatta, having completed his studies under the brahmin Pokkharasāti in the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, was traveling towards Ukkaṭṭhā to give the teacher's fee. At that time, the Blessed One, seeing that the youth faced the danger of robbers on the way and that he was destined to be reborn in heaven, taught him the procedure for taking the refuges by means of composing verses.
173:
The state of Dhamma is attained in this manner because it is the cause for achieving the Dhamma of Nibbāna, Path, and Fruit, which leads to liberation from the suffering of the round of rebirths, and because it possesses qualities conducive to liberation. Therefore, desiring to encompass both [the Noble Fruit and the Scriptural Dhamma], he said "Na kevalañca" and so forth. He shows that this meaning is indeed evident in the Pali Canon by saying "Vuttañhetaṃ" and so forth.

In that text, the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna is as follows: A young Brahmin named Chatta, a resident of the city of Setabyā, having studied the arts under the Brahmin Pokkharasāti in the city of Ukkhaṭṭhā, set out for Ukkhaṭṭhā with the intention, "I shall give the teacher's fee (garudakkhiṇa)." At that time, the Blessed One, seeing that the young man faced danger from robbers on the road and that he was destined to be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, taught him the method of taking refuge by means of verses. The thirty-yojana mansion of that young man who reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is called the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna. Even in the celestial realm, he is known by his name from his human life, just as "Maṇḍūka Devaputta" and "Kuvera Devarāja." Here, however, based on the origin of the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna and by eliding the subsequent term, the teaching beginning with "Na tathā tapati nabhe sūriyo, cando ca na bhāsati na phusso, yathā" is called the "Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna." Since this verse is included in that Pali text, the meaning should be understood as being within the teaching of the Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna story.

"Rāga-virāga" (detachment from lust) refers to the Path (Magga), because by this Path, all forms of lust—such as lust for sensual pleasures (kāma-rāga) and lust for existence (bhava-rāga)—which have been manifest since beginningless time, are faded away and abandoned. "Anejaṃ" (unshakable) and "Asokaṃ" (sorrowless) refer to the Fruit (Phala), because in that Fruit, craving (taṇhā) known as agitation (ejā) and sorrow (soka) characterized by internal burning are entirely exhausted upon its arising. In the commentary on that Vimānavatthu, however, it is stated: "It is called Asoka because it stills the defilements that are the causes of sorrow remaining from craving." "Asaṅkhata Dhamma" (Unconditioned Dhamma) refers to Nibbāna, which is the ultimate reality (paramattha dhamma) that maintains its own nature, called unconditioned because it is not compounded or produced by causes. In that same commentary, it is said: "Dhamma means the nature-dhamma (sabhāva-dhamma). These are the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna, which are to be taken as realities by their nature, and not as conceptual dhammas like the Scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti Dhamma)." Thus, the word Dhamma can be applied in all three places. By the word "Appaṭikūla" (not repulsive), Nibbāna itself is taken, meaning "there is nothing repulsive in it." Appaṭikūla means the absence of any opposition, being desirable, or being sublime, as it illustrates non-opposition.
174:
It is called "Paguna" because it is practiced in a well-mastered manner, or because it clearly manifests noble qualities. As the Blessed One said: "O Brahma, I do not speak a sublime Dhamma that is well-mastered (or carries noble qualities) with an intention to harm among men."

The connection is: "Eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma (Dhammakkhandha) were taught." Thus, in this verse, only the Scriptural Dhamma (Pariyatti Dhamma) is taken by the four terms. However, in that commentary, it is stated: "It is called 'Madhura' (sweet/pleasant) because it is desirable at all times—during the time of hearing, the time of reflection, and the time of practice. It is called 'Paguna' because it is well-proceeding and subtle, having been produced with the accomplishment of analytical insight (paṭibhāna-sampadā) based on Omniscient Wisdom. It is called 'Suvibhatta' (well-classified) because the meaning to be analyzed is well-divided by way of aggregates (khandha), wholesome states (kusala), and summaries (uddesa), etc." Thus, it is said that by these three terms, only the Scriptural Dhamma is spoken of.

To show the immediate presence to both [the speaker and the listener], just as when an object appears to the senses or when it is being reflected upon, and for the listener as much as for the speaker, the word of immediate presence "Imaṃ" (this) is used in this very verse. Furthermore, the word "Dhammaṃ" is a general term relating to the four types of Dhamma already mentioned. For the Scriptural Dhamma also protects one from falling into the lower realms (apāya) through the correct practice of merely being established in the refuges and the precepts. The Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna Pali text itself should be seen as evidence for this meaning. Desiring to demonstrate the aforementioned Dhamma as a present reality in a general sense, he said "Imaṃ" once more. Since this verse is a Dodhaka verse adorned with three 'Bha' groups (gaṇa), the letter 'ma' in the word 'Madhura' in the third line, though extra, should be regarded as faultless because it is joined with a word of many syllables, similar to terms like 'Ariyacariyā'.

"Diṭṭhi-sīla-saṅghātena" means: by the combination of the view and virtue described as, "That view which is noble and liberating, and leads the one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering; he dwells possessing such a view in common [with the Saṅgha]," and the virtue described as, "Those virtues which are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unmisapprehended, and leading to concentration; he dwells possessing such virtues in common [with the Saṅgha]." This means the equality of view and virtue. "Saṃhata" means combined or harmoniously attained.
175:
Noble persons (ariyapuggala), wherever they may be, even if staying far away, are united by the harmony of their virtues such as morality. He confirms this with the direct scriptural passage beginning with "Vuttañcetaṃ."

"Yattha" means in which Saṅgha. "Dinnaṃ" refers to the gift to be given, such as alms-food, which has been relinquished; it should be noted that in this word, the nasal sound (anunāsika) is dropped due to the metrical structure of the verse.
