This verse is in the Dodhaka meter. "Mahapphalāmāhu" means the Buddhas and other noble ones have said it is of great fruit. In the word "catūsu," the letter "ca" is extra, but according to the method already mentioned, it is not a fault. It means among those who are pure (sucīsu), being extremely purified from defilements. "Catūsu purisayugesu" refers to the four pairs of men as taught in the passage: "The stream-enterer practices for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry," and so on. They are called dhammadassā (seers of the Dhamma) because they see the four Noble Truths and the Dhamma of Nibbāna directly, or because they are direct seers of the Noble Dhamma. If these persons are counted individually, not as pairs of those standing in the Path and those standing in the Fruit, they are eight. The meaning should be understood along with the connection: "Approach, resort to, or serve this Saṅgha as a refuge, as a protection from the suffering of the states of deprivation and the suffering of the round of rebirths; or know it thus." Alternatively, the connection is: "The gift given to those four pairs of pure noble men is said to be of great fruit; those persons who see the Dhamma are eight; approach this Saṅgha as a refuge." This alternative explanation is also appropriate because it is not different in meaning. In the verses, for the sake of metrical ease, the word "purisa" is expressed with a long "ī" and the word "puggalā" with a short vowel.

Going to the Three Jewels as a refuge by this sequence of words beginning with "Eso’haṃ," or going to the refuge three times, is called saraṇagamana (taking refuge). "Paṭivedesi" means he declared with words what was in his heart.

## Commentary on the Discussion of Taking Refuge

Just as the clarification of the objects, fruits, defilements, and breaches of taking refuge leads to proficiency in that taking of refuge, so too does the clarification of the agent (the doer). Therefore, to show the procedure of taking refuge along with the agent, it was said: "Now, for the sake of proficiency in those takings of refuge... should be understood." By the words "He who goes for refuge," the agent is clarified, because without that agent, the taking of refuge itself is impossible. By the word "saraṇagamana," the taking of refuge itself is shown, and by the words "saraṇa" and so on, the objects (visaya) and so forth are shown in order. Why is purification (vodāna) not taken separately here? Is not the clarification of purification also for the sake of proficiency? That is true, but since purification is already clarified by the inclusion of defilement (saṅkilesa) in terms of meaning, it is not taken separately. For those who have taken refuge, there are causes such as delusion (moha) that produce defilement. Purification occurs by not letting those delusions and so on arise if they have not yet arisen, and by abandoning them if they have arisen. Therefore, purification is not taken separately. "By way of meaning" refers to the meaning of the word "saraṇa." There is also a variant reading "saraṇatthato." This meaning is established by the word "sara" which has the meaning of the root "sṛ" (to crush/destroy). Desiring to show this meaning by the power of the root meaning, after saying "saratīti saraṇaṃ" (it is a refuge because it destroys), he answers the questions "Whose [suffering] does it destroy?", "By what means does it destroy?", and "What does it destroy?" with the words "saraṇagatānaṃ." "Sarati" means it cleanses. To whom...
176:
Because it has been clarified by way of meaning, purification (vodāna) is not taken separately. This is because for those who have gone for refuge, there exist ignorance (aññāṇa) and other states which are the causes of defilement. Purification (vodāna) occurs by not allowing those unarisen states of ignorance and so forth to arise, and by abandoning those that have already arisen. Therefore, purification is not taken separately.

'By way of meaning' (atthato) means by way of the meaning of the word 'saraṇa'. Although there is a variant reading 'saraṇatthato', the meaning is the same. To show that this word 'saraṇa' is derived from the verbal root 'sar', which has the meaning of 'to destroy', it is said: 'It is called saraṇa because it destroys.' Then, to clarify the questions of whom it destroys for, how it destroys, and what it destroys, the text explains starting with 'saraṇagatānaṃ' (for those who have gone for refuge). For whom? For those who have approached it as a refuge. How? By that very wholesome state of going for refuge. What? It is an explanation in sequence that it destroys fear and so forth. In that context, 'saraṇagatānaṃ' means of those who have gone [to it] as a 'refuge'. 'Saraṇagamaneṇa' means by the wholesome state of going [to it] as a 'refuge'. 'Bhayaṃ' refers to the fear of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭabhaya). 'Santāsaṃ' refers to terror of the mind; by this term, mental suffering (cetasika dukkha) is also included. By the term 'dukkhaṃ', physical suffering (kāyika dukkha) is to be understood. 'Duggatiparikilesaṃ' refers to all suffering included within the woeful states; it means 'the burning, the severe oppression, or the intense affliction in the woeful states'. All of this will be made clear later in the Section on Fruits (Phalakathā). Here, 'hiṃsana' (destroying) means only destruction (vināsana), and not like the harming of living beings; this is shown by the words 'hanati vināseti' (it strikes, it destroys). 'Etaṃ' refers to the word 'saraṇa'. 'Adhivacanaṃ' means a name, or a well-known expression, or a term that proceeds based on actual qualities. Therefore, it is said, 'of the Triple Gem itself'.

Having thus shown the meaning of the word 'saraṇa' generally by way of the meaning of destruction, the text now says 'atha vā' (or else) and so forth to show it specifically by way of that same meaning. The specific distinction of this method over the previous one is the showing of the individual causes of destruction by each of the Three Jewels. In that context, 'by promoting welfare' (hite pavattanena) means by urging beings toward their benefit through such sayings as, 'Monks, dwell possessed of accomplished virtue' and so forth. 'By turning away from harm' (ahitā ca nivattanena) means by restraining beings from what is not beneficial through methods such as showing the danger, as in 'The result of taking life is evil, it has an evil result in the future life' and so forth. 'It destroys fear' (bhayaṃ hiṃsati) means it destroys by preventing the ruin that has as its cause the non-occurrence of benefit and the occurrence of harm. The Dhamma known as the Path (magga) destroys the fear of beings by leading them out of the wilderness of existence; the Dhamma known as Fruition and Nibbāna (phala-nibbāna) destroys the fear of beings by giving them relief; this is how the connection should be made. 'Kārānaṃ' refers to the offerings and honors brought through giving and worship. Even a word without a prefix (upasagga) can express a special meaning like a word with a prefix, as in such places as 'Even a small honor (kāraṃ) performed becomes a merit of great fruit'.
177:
It should be understood that [the Buddha] destroys the fear of beings by causing them to obtain abundant fruits because he is the unsurpassed recipient of offerings. 'By this method also' (imināpi pariyāyena) means by this reason also, which is stated by analyzing the individual reasons for the destructive nature of the Triple Gem. However, because this word 'saraṇa', like the word 'nātha', is a pure noun, it incorporates the meaning of the verbal root within it and also expresses a conventional meaning; therefore, it should be understood that below, 'saraṇa' is said to have the meaning of 'resort' (parāyaṇa).

Having thus shown the meaning of 'saraṇa', the text now says 'tappasādā' and so forth, wishing to show the meaning of 'saraṇagamana' (going for refuge). In that passage, 'tappasāda' (confidence in that) is the confidence in those Three Jewels through such ways as 'The Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, the Saṅgha is well-practiced'. The act of holding those Three Jewels in high esteem is 'taggaru', and the state of one who holds them in such esteem is 'taggarutā'. [Going for refuge occurs] by that confidence (tappasāda) and that esteem (taggarutā). Because one has dispelled evil states such as doubt (vicikiccha), delusion (sammoha), and lack of faith (asaddhiya), one is purified of defilements; and because those Three Jewels alone are one's resort, protection, and shelter, they are 'tapparāyaṇa'. That state is 'tapparāyaṇatā', and that very mode is the 'mode of having them as one's resort'; thus, the arising in that mode is 'tapparāyaṇatākārappavatta'.

In this context, by the mention of 'pasāda' (confidence), the mundane (lokiya) going for refuge is meant. That mundane refuge is led by faith (saddhā), not primarily by wisdom (ñāṇa). By the mention of 'garutā' (esteem), the supramundane (lokuttara) refuge is meant. For the Noble Ones (ariyas), because they specially realize the qualities of the Triple Gem, they see it with esteem like a stone umbrella. Therefore, it should be understood that through 'tappasāda', one dispels defilements by way of abandonment of factors (tadaṅgapahāna), and through 'taggarutā', one dispels the causes of disrespect by way of abandonment by cutting off (samucchedapahāna). 

Here, 'tapparāyaṇatā' means the state of having those Three Jewels as one's destination. By that state, the fourfold going for refuge to be mentioned later is included. Or, by mentioning 'pasāda' and 'garutā' without distinction: by the word 'pasāda', both the mundane refuge characterized by 'unshakeable confidence' (anaveccappasāda - used here in a general sense) and the supramundane refuge characterized by 'verified confidence' (aveccappasāda) are taken. Similarly, by the word 'garutā', both mundane esteem and supramundane esteem are taken. Therefore, by both terms, both mundane and supramundane going for refuge should be understood as connected.

Because consciousness arises by means of these associated states, it is called 'uppāda'; this is a group of associated states. It is consciousness (citta) and it is also that arising (uppāda), thus it is 'cittuppāda' (arising of consciousness). Even in a collective compound (samāhāradvanda), some masters of grammar desire the masculine gender in certain places. Consciousness together with associated states such as faith and wisdom, proceeding in that mode, is called 'going for refuge' (saraṇagamana), meaning 'one goes to (knows) the refuge by means of this [consciousness]'. The phrase 'taṃsamanggī' (one endowed with that) and so forth is a clarification of the agent (kattā). One who is endowed with the aforementioned arising of consciousness is 'taṃsamanggī'. Therefore, it is said, 'by the arising of consciousness of the kind described'.
178:
"Cittuppādena" means [it occurs] by being endowed with the arising of consciousness. "Upeti" means one approaches, resorts to, serves and attends upon, or it means one knows or understands. To whom does the supramundane refuge occur? It is said, "diṭṭhasaccānaṃ," which means the refuge of the eight Noble Persons (ariya-puggala). When is that refuge accomplished? It is said, "maggakkhaṇe" (at the moment of the Path). The word "ijjhati" (is accomplished) should be connected here. Indeed, only by the realization of the Four Truths accomplished at the moment of the Path is the state of having gone for refuge also fulfilled for those established in the Fruition (phalaṭṭhāna). This is because the supramundane refuge is indestructible, and because those [Noble Persons] share the same continuum (ekasantāna).

How is it accomplished? It is said, "saraṇagamanūpakkilesasamucchedena," and so on. It means it is accomplished in the Triple Gem in its entirety by the total eradication of the defilements of going for refuge, by way of the object (ārammaṇato), and by way of function (kiccato). Here, the phrase "saraṇagamanūpakkilesasamucchedena" is said with reference to the realization by abandoning (pahānābhisamaya), and the phrase "ārammaṇato" is said with reference to the realization by witnessing (sacchikiriyābhisamaya). It should be construed as: "It is accomplished by way of object by having Nibbāna as the object." The word "tvā" in "hutvā" expresses the sense of cause (hetu), as in the example "Sakka hutvā nibbattī" (he was reborn because of being Sakka). Alternatively, the meaning already stated as "ārammaṇato" is specifically defined by the phrase "having Nibbāna as the object." The phrase "kiccato" is said with reference to the remaining realization by development (bhāvanābhisamaya) and realization by full understanding (pariññābhisamaya). Or else, by the phrase "ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā," the single object corresponding to the Path-moment is shown, and by the phrase "kiccato," the three functions other than the function of abandoning (i.e., full understanding, witnessing, and development) are shown. Since it is said, "at the moment of the Path, having Nibbāna as the object," it should be understood that in terms of meaning, the realization of the Four Truths known as Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) is itself the supramundane refuge. Indeed, in that realization of the Four Truths, there is the total eradication of the defilements of going for refuge by way of the realization by abandoning. The Dhamma of Nibbāna fulfills the meaning of going for refuge only when it is penetrated by way of the realization by witnessing; and the Dhamma of the Path [fulfills it] by way of the realization by development. The qualities of the Buddha, which are the domain of the Noble Disciples, fulfill the meaning of going for refuge when they are penetrated by way of the realization by full understanding. Likewise, the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha fulfill the meaning of going for refuge. Therefore, it is said, "It is accomplished in the Triple Gem in its entirety."

In this supramundane refuge, Fruition (phala) and Learning (pariyatti) should also be understood as being included by way of their occurrence in conformity with the Path, according to the method already stated. The qualities of the Buddha and the Saṅgha, which are not to be fully understood [by disciples], should be understood in this way because they share the same nature as those qualities. Only in this way is the statement regarding the distinction of the entire state appropriate. Furthermore, the accomplishment occurs simultaneously; it is not accomplished sequentially like the mundane refuge. This is because it is realized through non-delusive penetration (asammoha-paṭivedha). It is like a lamp that completes four functions in a single moment.
179:
Just as a lamp [performs its functions], the Path accomplishes the four functions in a single moment. However, as for those teachers who say, "Taking refuge does not occur by making Nibbāna the object; rather, because the Path has been attained, that refuge is simply already attained, just as mundane sciences are attained by some who possess the three [supramundane] knowledges (tevijjā)," according to their words, the taking of refuge would be merely mundane (lokiya) and not supramundane. That is improper, as both [mundane and supramundane] are desired. By the abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna), the defilements of taking refuge are suppressed. In the phrase "by way of the object, having made the virtues of the Buddha etc. the object," the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. It means that by the suppression of the defilements of taking refuge and by way of the object, it is accomplished in regard to the entire Triple Gem.

"Taṃ" refers to the mundane refuge. The acquisition of faith (saddhā) occurs through such thoughts as "The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One," and so on. "Saddhāmūlikā" means having the aforementioned faith as the precursor. Indeed, having faith as the precursor by way of coexistence (sahajāta) is what is meant by being rooted in that [faith], because right vision (sammādassana) regarding the Buddha and so on is impossible for one devoid of faith. Right View (Sammādiṭṭhi) means seeing the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's excellence, and the Saṅgha's good practice through the power of mundane understanding in the correct manner. By the phrase "acquisition of faith," it is shown that even faith devoid of right view constitutes mundane refuge. By the phrase "Right view rooted in faith," the aforementioned wisdom based on faith is shown.

Indeed, mundane refuge is also of two kinds: associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) and dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta). Among these, by the first phrase [acquisition of faith], the refuge dissociated from knowledge—such as that of children encouraged by their mothers and so on—is included. By the second phrase, the refuge associated with knowledge is included. To show both of these as a specific type of base of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu), it is said: "Among the ten bases of meritorious action, it is called the straightening of views (diṭṭhijukamma)." Right view is the straightening of views in the sense that the view itself is made straight by its own causes. Faith is also [called] the straightening of views in the sense that the view is made straight by this [faith].

By the inclusion of faith and right view here, the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) in which they are predominant is also included. This is also included by the term "straightening of views" through the aforementioned sense of instrumental achievement (karaṇa-sādhana). By doing so, the statement made below, "The arising of consciousness occurring in the mode of having those [Three Jewels] as one's mainstay," is substantiated. The separate mention of faith and right view should be understood as being due to their predominance in the arising of consciousness associated with them.

"Tayidaṃ" (this very thing) refers only to the mundane refuge, because there is no such division in the supramundane. Indeed, because that [supramundane refuge] is accomplished at the moment of the path in the manner already stated, such a formal undertaking (samādāna) does not exist, and thus this division is not possible.
180:
(That distinction) is not possible. Dedicating oneself or relinquishing oneself is called attasanniyyātana; it is indeed the aforementioned diṭṭhijukamma (straightening of views) known as taking refuge. That the Triple Gem is the destination and refuge of this person or this thought-arising is called tapparāyaṇatā; it should be known that this is also that same diṭṭhijukamma. Approaching the state of a disciple or a resident pupil by performing major and minor duties with the intention of taking refuge is called sissabhāvūpagamana. Veneration performed solely with the intention of taking refuge is called paṇipāta. In this context, veneration (paṇipatana) refers to salutation, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and proper respect. In all these meanings, it should be understood as only the aforementioned diṭṭhijukamma.

Relinquishing one's own self-identity (attabhāva) to escape the suffering of the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) is called attapariccajana. The same method applies to tapparāyaṇatā and so forth. By way of figurative speech indicating benefit, the Dhamma's role as a teacher is also expressed as in the following verse: "The mango tree with fruit and the one without fruit, both are my teachers." Therefore, it is said, "a resident pupil of the Dhamma." The words beginning with "abhivādanā" show the meaning of paṇipāta. The restriction "only to the Buddha and so forth" should be understood as applying to attasanniyyātana etc., by way of the sīhagatikana (lion's gaze) method. By doing so, any refuge other than that is excluded. The words beginning with "imesañci" support the occurrence in four ways, or show the reason.

Having shown attasanniyyātana etc. in one way, the author now begins with "api ca" to show them in other ways. By this statement, the four types of refuge such as attasanniyyātana and tapparāyaṇatā are also performed through other synonyms, because the meaning is not different. For example, "renouncing the training" and "falsely claiming superhuman states" are not different in meaning. The word "jīvitapariyantika" is a neuter abstract noun and means "I go for refuge as long as life lasts."

Venerable Mahākassapa, having taken the guise of a monk himself, departed from the Mahātittha Brahmin village. While traveling, the Buddha came to meet him after a journey of three gāvutas. He saw the Blessed One sitting alone at the foot of the Bahuputtaka Banyan tree between Rājagaha and Nālandā. Even without knowing for certain, "This Blessed One is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One," he took refuge, thinking, "If I were to see a teacher, I should see only the Blessed One," and so forth. Therefore, the teacher said, "like the refuge of Mahākassapa." The details should be seen in the Commentary on the Kassapa Saṃyutta. In that commentary, it means: "If I were to see a teacher, I would see only this Blessed One, because there can be no other teacher for me besides this Blessed One." Regarding "If I were to see a Sugata, I would see only this Blessed One," it means: because of His good conduct, if I were to see a Blessed One named Sugata, I would see only this Blessed One, for there can be no other Sugata for me besides this Sugata. Regarding "If I were to see a Fully Enlightened One, I would see only the Blessed One," it means: if I... truly...
181:
(Mahākassapa) performed the taking of refuge with the words beginning with, "If I were to see the Blessed One..." (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidānavagga, 154). Because of this, the Teacher said, "Like the taking of refuge by Mahākassapa." The details should be taken from the Kassapa Saṃyutta Aṭṭhakathā. In that commentary, it is explained: "If I were to see a teacher, may I see only this Blessed One; for me, there can be no other teacher besides this Blessed One." It is also stated: "If I were to see a Sugata (Well-gone One), who has gone well through right practice, may I see only this Blessed One; for me, there can be no other Sugata besides this Blessed One." And: "If I were to see a Sammāsambuddha (Perfectly Enlightened One), who has rightly and by himself realized the Four Noble Truths, may I see only this Blessed One; for me, there can be no other Sammāsambuddha besides this Blessed One." This is the commentary's explanation here. In every instance, the words 'ca' and 'vata' are merely for completing the verse (padapūraṇa). Alternatively, it should be the word 'ce' (if), as the commentary says 'sace'. It is also appropriate to say that the word 'vata' expresses a sense of certainty due to the desire to see.

The words beginning with "That I..." are found in the Āḷavaka Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta. In that Āḷavaka Sutta, although the yakkha Āḷavaka's taking of refuge occurred through the Path (magga), the commentary states that he spoke these words to show his status as a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) and to demonstrate his devotion. "From village to village" means from one celestial village to another celestial village, or it refers to the small and large villages of the deities. The same method applies to the phrase "from city to city." "The goodness of the Dhamma" means, after praising the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma's excellence, and the Saṅgha's good practice, and using the word 'ca' in the sense of conjunction along with the remaining text, it means: "I will wander about, worshipping the Blessed One and being a proclaimer of the Dhamma."

In the phrase "Āḷavaka and others," the word 'ādi' (and others) includes Sātāgiri, Hemavata, and so on. Is it not true that these beings, such as Āḷavaka, having attained the Path, took refuge through the Path itself? Why then is their refuge called 'tapparāyaṇatā' (devotion/total reliance)? It is because, even though they reached refuge through the Path, they manifested the quality of total reliance (tapparāyaṇatā). For they declared their devotion thus: "That I will wander... the goodness of the Dhamma" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.246, Sutta Nipāta 194), and "We will wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain... the goodness of the Dhamma" (Sutta Nipāta 182). Therefore, it should be understood that the commentator said this intending to show only the manner of their declaration, without regarding the specific type of refuge. "Thereafter" refers to the time at the conclusion of the explanation of the eight questions asked, beginning with "How does one become a brahmin?", by answering with "He who knows his former births..." This is stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa. "Paricumbati" means he touches; "parisambāhati" means he massages or rubs. The phrase "In this way, the refuge through prostration (paṇipāta-saraṇagamana) should be understood" means it should be understood as taking refuge through an act of extreme humility. This refuge through prostration can be by power of relatives, by power of fear, by power of a teacher...
182:
Paricumbati means touching. Parisambāhati means massaging (rubbing). "In this way, the refuge through prostration (paṇipāta-saraṇagamana) should be understood" means that by performing such an act of extreme humility, the refuge through prostration is to be understood.

This refuge through prostration should be understood as being connected respectively with: by power of relatives, by power of fear, by power of a teacher, and by power of one worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya). This is because the word 'vasena' (by power of) is heard after the dvanda compound 'ñāti' etc. Therein, 'ñātivasena' means by power of the state of being a relative. This is a designation emphasizing the state (bhāva-ppadhāna) or a designation where the word 'bhāva' is elided, because only that state of being a relative is intended. Similarly, in the remaining terms, they should be connected with the word 'paṇipāta', because prostration is fourfold by power of being a relative and so on. Therefore, it is said, "dakkhiṇeyya-paṇipātena," which means only by prostration caused by the fact of being one worthy of offerings. "By others" means by prostrations caused by being a relative and so on. The words beginning with "only by power of the best" support this very meaning. Now, to show in detail the three meanings already mentioned with "not by others" etc., in their respective order, the words beginning with "therefore" are spoken. "A Sakyan or" shows the lineage of relatives from the father's side, while "a Koliyan or" shows the lineage of relatives from the mother's side. The word 'vandati' (he worships) is a term used to mark the act of prostration. 'Rājapūjito' means honored by kings or of the kings, similar to the term 'gāmapūjito' (honored by villagers). When used with a word expressing honor, grammarians desire the genitive case (sāmivacana) in the sense of the agent (kattā). 'Bhagavato' means of the Blessed One who is a Bodhisatta or who has become a Buddha. 'Uggahitaṃ' means the art or knowledge that has been learned.

Phrases beginning with "fourfold" (catudhā) are taught in the Siṅgālovāda Sutta. 'Gharamāvasaṃ' means one who lives in a house. Here, because of the connection with a kammappavacanīya, the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of the locative (bummattha). 'Kammaṃ payojeyya' means one should engage in work such as farming or trade. For families, things do not remain the same at all times; sometimes dangers arise due to kings and so on. Therefore, intending that "it will be useful when dangers arise," one should store or bury wealth; thus it is said, "āpadāsu bhavissati" (it will be for emergencies). Among these four portions, from the portion mentioned as "with one portion he should enjoy his wealth," one should give gifts to monks as well as to the poor and travelers. Wages should also be given to weavers, barbers, and so on. This is the instruction on the management of wealth; it means having learned such instruction. This statement is made with reference only to the benefits in the present life. However, it should be understood that one who desires instruction for the benefit of the future life or for liberation also performs only the dakkhiṇeyya-paṇipāta refuge. The words beginning with "But he who..." are a detailed explanation of the meaning already stated as "only by power of the best... he takes."
183:
The word beginning with "Evaṃ" shows the contrast (vyatireka) to the statement "it breaks by way of superiority." It should be applied to a female lay follower (upāsikā) who has taken refuge, considering the change in gender and inflection (liṅga-vibhatti-vipariṇāma) according to the meaning. In such words, it should be understood in this way. In the word "pabbajitampi," the particle "pi" has the sense of commendation (sambhāvanattha), meaning "not to mention a layperson, but even a monk." The refuge does not break because one does not bow by way of superiority. The particle "tathā" is used in the sense of pulling forward (anukaḍḍhana) and pulls the phrase "the refuge does not break." "Raṭṭhapūjitattā" means because of being honored in the country or by the inhabitants of the country. This statement only confirms the fact of bowing out of fear; it is not a demonstration of the cause for the non-breaking of refuge. The cause for the non-breaking of refuge should be understood as not bowing by way of superiority. For it was said, "it breaks by way of superiority." "By way of superiority" means by way of being the supreme object of offerings (agga-dakkhiṇeyya) in the world. Therefore, it is said, "one bows (thinking) this person is the supreme object of offerings in the world." If the refuge does not break even for one who bows to a sectarian (titthiya), there is no need to mention one who bows to someone other than a sectarian. "Saraṇagamanappabheda" refers to the analysis of the going for refuge. Since the non-breaking of refuge can also be easily shown in connection with that analysis, the demonstration of non-breaking is made here.

Since it is said that only the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is the supramundane refuge, the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) are spoken of as resultant fruits (vipākaphala). "Sabbadukkhakkhaya" refers to Nibbāna, which is the non-arising and cessation of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha). Here, the fruit that is similar to the action (kamma) should be understood as the resultant fruit (vipākaphala), and the fruit that is the opposite (different from the action) should be understood as the beneficial fruit (ānisaṃsaphala). Just as the fruits of hill paddy seeds and so on are called "ripened" (vipakka) because they are similar to those seeds and receive the designation "vipāka," but the roots, sprouts, leaves, stems, and stalks do not receive the designation "vipāka" because they are dissimilar; likewise, the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions receive the designation "vipāka" because they are similar in being mental phenomena (arūpadhamma) and having objects (sārammaṇa). Other fruits produced by kamma that are dissimilar to the kamma do not receive the designation "vipāka"; they only receive the name "ānisaṃsa" (benefit/blessing) and the designation "ānisaṃsa." With the words "vuttañhetaṃ" etc., the text cites the Aggidatta Brāhmaṇa story from the Dhammapada.

In the phrase "yo ca," the particle "ca" is in the sense of contrast (vyatireka), meaning "yo pana" (but whoever). The intention in that verse is as follows: In demonstrating the contrast, if it is asked, "If the refuge described by the words 'Many go for refuge to mountains and forests' (Dhp. 188) is not a secure refuge, not the supreme refuge, and by following this refuge one is not released from all suffering, then what object is a secure refuge, what is the supreme refuge, and by following what object as a refuge is one released from all suffering?"
184:
"But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha... this is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge; by following this refuge, one is released from all suffering" (Dhp. 190-192).

In such cases, because the mundane refuge is liable to be broken or shaken by bowing to other sectarians and so on, the Buddha spoke the words "sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom" to manifest only the supramundane refuge, which is unshakable and firm. Here, the shortening of the word "sammā" to "samma" is for the sake of euphony (vācāsiliṭṭhattha). The words beginning with "dukkha" are a demonstration of the nature of the truths spoken of as the "Four Noble Truths." "Dukkhassa atikkamaṃ" refers to the cessation of suffering (nirodha-sacca). "Dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ" refers to the path leading to the subsiding of suffering (magga-sacca). The word "etaṃ" refers to the seeing of the Noble Truths, known as the supramundane refuge, which was spoken of as "sees the Four Noble Truths." The particle "kho" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa) and should be applied to all three terms.

"Niccato anupagamanādivasena" means by way of not taking things as "permanent" and so on. Grammarians desire the suffix "-to" after words indicated by "iti." With the words "vuttañhetaṃ" etc., the Buddha cites the Pali from the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts as evidence. "Aṭṭhānaṃ" (impossible) is the rejection of a generative cause (janaka-hetu). "Anavakāso" (no possibility) is the rejection of a supporting cause (paccaya-hetu). By both terms, the Buddha rejects the cause. "Yaṃ" means by which cause. A Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) who is endowed with the right view of the Path cannot take even a single conditioned formation (saṅkhāra) among the conditioned things of the four planes as "permanent." "Sukhato upagaccheyya" means taking it as "pleasant" through the view of self, such as "the self is exclusively happy and healthy after death." However, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, a Noble Disciple might approach a certain formation as pleasant for the sake of allaying distress, just as the Brahmin Cokkha, terrified by a rogue elephant, might jump into a place of excrement (or a cesspit). In the section on self (attavāra), the word "dhamma" is used instead of "saṅkhāra" to include concepts (paññatti) such as kasinas. 

As it is said in the Parivāra:
"All formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent; conditioned things are suffering and non-self.
Nibbāna and concepts (paññatti) are determined to be non-self."

In all these three sections (vāra), the discernment of the Noble Disciple should be understood by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes. For whatever a worldling (puthujjana)...
185:
A worldling holds to such views as 'it is permanent, it is pleasant, it is self.' A noble disciple, holding the view that 'it is impermanent, it is suffering, it is not under one's control (non-self),' unravels and clears away that clinging view.

In the words beginning with 'mātaraṃ' (mother), 'mātā' refers to one's own biological mother, 'pitā' to one's own biological father, and 'arahā' to an Arahant who is a true human being and has destroyed the taints (āsavas). Would a noble disciple deprive any other living being of life besides these (mother, father, Arahant)? Depriving a living being of life is also an impossibility for them. The reason is that a noble disciple would not deprive a living being of life even for the sake of attaining universal kingship or for their own life. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was said to show the great fault of being a worldling and to manifest the power of being a noble one. 'Paduṭṭhacitto' means one with a mind corrupted by the intent to kill, or a mind destroyed by anger. 'Lohitaṃ uppādeyya' means causing blood to flow (bruising) from the body of a living Buddha, even as much as a small fly might drink. 'Saṅghaṃ bhindeyya' means causing a schism among the Saṅgha who share the same communion and stay within the same boundary (sīmā), through five means. As it is said (in the Parivāra): 'Upāli, the Saṅgha is split by five means: by a legal act, by the recitation of the Pātimokkha, by speaking (words that cause a split), by proclamation, and by the taking of voting tickets.' 'Aññaṃ satthāraṃ' means taking another sectarian teacher outside of this Dispensation, thinking 'This is my teacher.' The meaning is that such a thing is impossible. 'Bhavasampadā' is success in a happy destination; this is the resultant fruit (vipāka-phala). 'Bhogasampadā' is success in human and divine wealth; this is the blessing fruit (ānisaṃsa-phala). With the words 'vuttañhetaṃ' etc., the Pali texts such as the Devatā Saṃyutta are shown as evidence.

In the phrase 'gatā se', 'se' is merely a particle. 'Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ' means those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge will not go to the states of deprivation (apāya) because of that refuge. The word 'mānusaṃ' is a description without conjunction (visaññoga-niddesa) due to the nature of the verse; it means 'born among humans.' 'Devakāyaṃ' means either the host of devas or the celestial realm, meaning 'the group or collection of devas is here.'

With the words 'aparampi' etc., another benefit found in the Moggallāna Saṃyutta of the Saḷāyatana Vagga is stated. It means another benefit of going for refuge was taught by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. 'Aññe deve' refers to other devas who have not gone for refuge to the Triple Gem. 'Dasahi ဌာနေဟိ' means by ten reasons. The words beginning with 'dibbeṇa' show the nature of those benefits. 'Adhigaṇhanti' means they surpass and stand superior. By the words 'esa nayo', the scriptural passage 'O Sakka, Lord of Devas, taking refuge in the Dhamma is truly good' is indicated.

## Velāma Sutta
The Velāma Sutta is a discourse connected with the talk on giving by the Brahmin Velāma, the teacher of eighty-four thousand kings and a Bodhisatta, who was endowed with noble qualities that surpassed the limits of birth, lineage, appearance, wealth, faith, and wisdom, as found in the Navaka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. In that Velāma Sutta, 'karīsaṃ' refers to those having the measure of a quarter...
186:
In the Navaka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, there is the Velāma Sutta (A. ix, 20) connected with the talk on giving by the Brahmin Velāma, who was a Bodhisatta and the teacher of eighty-four thousand kings, endowed with noble qualities that surpassed the limits of birth, lineage, appearance, wealth, faith, and wisdom.

In that Velāma Sutta, it is shown that more fruitful than the great Velāma sacrifice—which was carried out continuously for seven years and seven months by giving away eighty-four thousand gold bowls, silver bowls, and bronze bowls, each having the measure of a quarter of a karīsa, filled respectively with silver, gold, and the seven kinds of jewels; eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand milch cows, eighty-four thousand maidens, eighty-four thousand couches, and eighty-four thousand crores of garments, all adorned with every ornament; and immeasurable food such as hard and soft food—is the gift given to a single stream-enterer (sotāpanna). More fruitful than a gift given to a hundred stream-enterers is a gift given to a single once-returner (sakadāgāmī). From there, to a single non-returner (anāgāmī); then to a single Arahant; then to a single Private Buddha (paccekabuddha); then to the Fully Enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha); then to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. More fruitful than that is the building and offering of a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters. More fruitful than that is the undertaking of the refuges. This meaning is manifested.

And thus it was said: 'Householder, the Brahmin Velāma gave that gift, that great gift; but if one were to feed one person of right view (a stream-enterer), this would be more fruitful than that. If one were to feed a hundred persons of right view... and if one were to feed one once-returner, this would be more fruitful than that,' and so on (A. ix, 20).

By this, it should be understood that the fruit of the supramundane refuge is specifically shown. Thus, it is said in the Velāma Sutta Commentary: 'In the phrase "saraṇaṃ gaccheyya," the irreversible refuge attained through the Path is intended. Others, however, say: "Because it is undertaken by dedicating oneself, taking refuge is more fruitful than that."' In the Kūṭadanta Sutta Commentary, it will be said: 'Since taking refuge is a meritorious deed consisting of the sacrifice of one's life to the Triple Gem and gives the success of the heavenly realms, it should be understood as being more fruitful and of greater advantage.' By this statement...
187:
In this way, it should be understood that the fruit of mundane refuge (lokiya-saraṇagamana) is also shown here. It is understood that the teacher Dhammapāla Thera also intended this meaning, because it is stated without distinction (generally) in this sub-commentary as well as in other sub-commentaries such as the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā. The teacher Sāriputta Thera would also favor this meaning, as it is stated in the Sāratthadīpanī and the Aṅguttara Ṭīkā with words common to both mundane and supramundane types.

Other teachers, however, say: "In the Kūṭadanta Sutta Aṭṭhakathā, only the fruit of supramundane refuge is mentioned." That statement is improper because it is not stated in that way. Indeed, because of the reason common to both—"Because... he gives"—the fruit of both types is mentioned in that commentary. In the phrase "Velāma Sutta, etc.," the word "ādi" (etc.) includes the Aggappasāda Sutta, Chattamāṇavaka Vimāna, and so forth.

Ignorance (aññāṇa) means not knowing the virtues of the Triple Gem, being deluded regarding them. Doubt (saṃsaya) means skepticism (vicikicchā) such as "Is he truly the Buddha or not?" and so on. Wrong knowledge (micchā-ñāṇa) means a perverted grasp by imagining the virtues of the Triple Gem as non-virtues. By the word "ādi" (etc.), disrespect, lack of reverence, and so forth are included. "Saṃkiliဿti" means to be defiled or soiled. Phrases such as "na mahājutikaṃ" (not of great brilliance) are also synonyms for defilement. Therein, "na mahājutikaṃ" means not having great radiance, being impure, and lacking luster. "Na mahāvipphāraṃ" means not having great power, not being noble, and not being grand. "Sāvajjo" means being blameworthy through the power of craving (taṇhā), wrong view (diṭṭhi), and so forth. To clarify that very blameworthiness by way of its result, it is called "aniṭṭhaphala" (having undesirable fruit); it means that because it is blameworthy, it has a fruit that is not desired.

Mundane refuge, like the undertaking of training rules (sikkhāpada), is only for the duration of life without a fixed time limit. Therefore, it is broken by the dissolution of the aggregates (death). Such a breaking is blameless (anavajja) because it is free from craving, wrong view, and so forth. Thus it is said: "It is a breaking that is blameless through the act of dying." "So" (that) refers to that blameless breaking of refuge. Even though it is blameless, it is not a state that yields a [karmic] result, so it cannot give a desired fruit; it goes without saying that it does not give an undesired fruit. This is because such a breaking is not unwholesome (akusala), but merely a cessation. "Bhavantarepi" means in another life as well.

Because the word "dhara" takes two objects, the term "upāsakaṃ" is also an object. To show that it stands in the place of a mode (ākāra), it is said: "Please remember this person as an upāsaka." "Dhāretu" means "please remember" or "please know." In this context, knowing itself is called remembering (upadhāraṇa). That meaning is shown by the word "jānātu." "Upāsakasikkhākousallatthaṃ" means for the sake of proficiency in the practices of an upāsaka. The question "Ko upāsako?" (Who is an upāsaka?) is an inquiry into the essence (sarūpa). It means: "What are the identifying characteristics of an upāsaka?" The question "Kena nāma?" (By what reason is he so called?) is an inquiry into the cause. It means: "By what cause of occurrence (pavattinimitta) is the name 'upāsaka' applied to that person?" Therefore, it is asked: "Why is he called an upāsaka?"

Indeed, in expressing the meaning of a word, the cause of occurrence (pavattinimitta) is the only reason for that word's meaning. The question "Kimassa sīlaṃ?" (What is his virtue?) is an inquiry into the undertaking of practice. It means: "What is the nature of that upāsaka's virtue? By undertaking how much practice is this upāsaka said to be endowed with virtue?" The question "Ko ājīvo?" (What is his livelihood?) is an inquiry into the undertaking of his activities.
188:
"Dhāretu" is said. "Dhāretu" means "please bear in mind" or "please know." In this context, bearing in mind (upadhāraṇa) is shown to be just knowing by the word "jānātu" (please know). "Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ" means for the sake of proficiency in the regulations of a lay follower. The question "Ko upāsako?" (Who is a lay follower?) is an inquiry into the nature (sarūpa). It means what are the characteristics of one called a lay follower. The question "Kasmā?" (Why?) is an inquiry into the cause. It means by what reason for its occurrence (pavattinimitta) is the term "upāsaka" established for that person. Therefore, the teacher said, "Why is he called a lay follower?" Indeed, in expressing the meaning of a word, the reason for the word's occurrence is the cause of its meaning. The question "Kimassa sīlaṃ?" (What is his virtue?) is an inquiry into the undertaking of vows. It means what is the nature of this lay follower's virtue, and by how much undertaking of vows is he called one accomplished in virtue. The question "Ko ājīvo?" (What is his livelihood?) is an inquiry into the undertaking of work. It asks what is his right livelihood, and by what undertaking of work does his livelihood come about. Since that right livelihood occurs by avoiding wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva), wrong livelihood is also analyzed. The question "Kā vipatti?" (What is failure?) is an inquiry into the deviation from both [virtue and livelihood]. It means what is the failure of this lay follower's virtue and livelihood. When a general statement is made, the regulation or prohibition of the most immediate thing is taken; thus, the immediate thing is taken. The question "Kā sampatti?" (What is accomplishment?) is an inquiry into the right practice of both. It means what is the accomplishment of this lay follower's virtue and livelihood, understood in the same manner as previously stated. It is called "pakiṇṇaka" (miscellaneous) because it decides through various ways such as showing the nature and the word-meaning (vacanattha). That same "pakiṇṇaka" is called "pakiṇṇakaṃ." It means the determination of meaning occurring in many aspects.

"Yo koci" (anyone) refers to anyone among the Khattiyas, Brahmins, etc. By this word, it is shown that distinctions such as birth (jāti) are not the cause here. By the word "saraṇagato" (one who has gone for refuge), it is shown that only going for refuge is the standard here. By the word "gahaṭṭho" (householder), it is shown that the name "upāsaka" is established only among those living in houses, and not among those who have gone forth [as monks]. To prove this meaning by the Mahānāma Sutta of the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta, he said "Vuttañhetaṃ," etc. In that statement, "yato" means because of going for refuge to the Triple Gem, starting with the Buddha. "Mahānāma" is the Buddha's address to the Sakyan King named Mahānāma, who was the son of His paternal uncle, Sukkodana. "Ettāvatā" (by this much) means that by this much going for refuge to the Buddha, etc., one is called a lay follower; it does not mean one is called so because of birth, etc. Although the state of being a "two-word" (dvevācika) lay follower exists, as in the case of Tapussa and Bhallika, that occurs only occasionally because the three objects [of refuge] were not yet complete at that time.
189:
To show the state of being a "three-word" (tevācika) lay follower, "saraṇagato" is said. For even they [Tapussa and Bhallika] later became those who went to the three refuges. It should be understood that this is said to make it known that one who rejects one or two of these three refuges and goes to only one or two cannot be called a lay follower.

"Upāsanato" means by that very going for refuge, and because of attending (payirupāsana) with respect, esteem, and devotion through performing it carefully. By this, the agent-meaning (kattuttha) of the word "upāsaka" is shown. Therefore, he said "So hi," etc.

"Veramaṇiyo" in this term, "vera" refers to the loss of virtue such as killing living beings. Because it destroys, kills, or ruins that "vera," it is called "veramaṇiya." Since abstinence (virati) is the chief part of that virtue, there are five abstinences. Thus, in the cited Mahānāma Sutta, it is said: "He is one who abstains from killing living beings," etc. By "Yathāha," etc., he shows the evidence and the nature. It is like the gardener's single effort (payoga) in establishing water which completes both the watering of the mango tree and the bathing of the teacher. As said in the Ambavimāna:

"The mango tree is watered, and the ascetic is bathed;
And by me, no small merit has been accumulated.
Thus, with joy, he pervades his entire body."

(In the original Tika: "The mango tree was watered, and the ascetic was bathed; much merit was accumulated. Oh, how fruitful is my life!") In such matters, it should be understood thus. "Ettāvatā" means by just this much, the five abstinences from vice.

"Micchāvaṇijjā" means improper trade, not right trade; it refers to unsuitable trading activities. "Pahāya" means abandoning by simply not doing. "Dhammena" means righteously (not departing from the Dhamma). By that word "dhammena," other unrighteous livelihoods besides trading in wrong goods are also rejected. "Samena" means evenly, not unevenly. By this, he shows livelihood through good conduct, avoiding misconduct such as bodily unevenness. By "Vuttañhetaṃ," etc., he brings the Pañcaṅguttara Pali as evidence and shows the nature. The property of merchants is called "vaṇijjā"; it is the selling to anyone. This is a feminine noun. "Satthavaṇijjā" means selling weapons that have been obtained, whether by making them oneself or having them made by others. "Sattavaṇijjā" means the selling of human beings. "Maṃsavaṇijjā" means breeding animals such as deer and pigs like a butcher...
190:
Or it refers to the sale of weapons after obtaining them in a finished state. 'Sattavaṇijjā' means the sale of human beings. 'Maṃsavaṇijjā' means the sale of meat by breeding animals such as deer and pigs to produce meat, similar to the practice of butchers. 'Majjavaṇijjā' means the sale of any kind of intoxicant after preparing it. 'Visavaṇijjā' means the sale of poison after preparing or collecting it. Among these five types of trade, it is stated that the trade in weapons should not be practiced because it is a cause for the oppression of others. The trade in human beings should not be practiced because it leads to enslavement; the trade in meat because it is a cause for the killing of living beings; the trade in intoxicants because it is a cause for negligence; and the trade in poison because it is a cause for the destruction of others.

'Tasseva' refers back to the virtue (sīla) characterized by the observance of the five precepts mentioned earlier, and to the livelihood (ājīva) characterized by the abandonment of the five types of wrong trade. 'Vipatti' means failure or corruption. Having shown the failure of a lay follower (upāsaka) through the failure of virtue and livelihood, the text says 'api ca' etc., to show it also through the lack of faith and so on. 'Yāya' refers to the wrong practice such as lack of faith. 'Caṇḍālo' means an outcast lay follower (upāsaka-caṇḍāla) in the sense of having low qualities. 'Malaṃ' means a stain of a lay follower (upāsaka-mala) in the sense of being defiled. 'Patikiṭṭho' means a lowly lay follower (upāsaka-nihīna) in the sense of being despicable. That wrong practice, such as lack of faith, should also be understood as the failure (vipatti) of that lay follower.

Asking what that failure is, the text says 'te ca' etc. The Upāsakacaṇḍāla Sutta and the Upāsakaratana Sutta are found in the Book of the Fives of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. In those suttas, 'assaddhiya' (faithlessness) is the perversion of faith and wrong reflection regarding the Triple Gem (the Buddha, etc.) and the law of kamma and its results. One endowed with that faithlessness is called 'assaddha' (faithless). One is called 'dussīla' (immoral) due to the aforementioned failure of virtue and failure of livelihood. One who is endowed with the belief in omens regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed—which is a commotion conceived by foolish people thinking, 'By seeing this, such and such a blessing will occur'—is called 'koṭūhalamangalika' (one who follows superstitions).

'Maṅgalaṃ pacceti' means believing only in omens such as the omen of what is seen, and not believing in the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), which is the belief that only kamma is one's own property. 'Ito ca bahiddhā' refers to those who hold views outside of this Dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha. Since the word 'ca' is applied to terms where it is not usually placed, it should be understood as connected to all terms like 'assaddha' and so on. 'Dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati' means seeking out a person of bad conduct, regarding them as one worthy of offerings. 'Tattha' refers to those with views outside the Dispensation. 'Pubbakāraṃ karoti' means performing meritorious deeds such as giving and honoring first. It means performing meritorious deeds first for those outside the Dispensation and only afterwards in the Dispensation.
191:
Regarding the word 'hoti', teachers also say that 'tattha' refers to those outsiders, the sectarians (titthiyas). In this context, seeking a person worthy of offerings and performing the initial service are treated as one, making five qualities to be known.

'Assa' means 'of the lay follower'. 'Sīlasampadā' means the perfection of virtue characterized by the avoidance of the five aforementioned enmities. 'Ājīvasampadā' means the perfection of livelihood characterized by the abandonment of the five types of wrong trade and so on. Thus, having shown the success (sampatti) of a lay follower through the perfection of virtue and livelihood, the text says 'ye cassa' etc., to show it also through faith and so on. The construction is: those five qualities are also the success (sampatti) of that lay follower. 'Dhammehi' means 'by qualities'.

A lay follower is called 'upāsakaratana' (a jewel of a lay follower) because they bring delight to the four assemblies. A lay follower is called 'upāsakapaduma' (a lotus of a lay follower) because of their beauty of qualities, fame, and the fragrance of their good reputation. Similarly, they are called 'upāsakapuṇဍarīka' (a white lotus of a lay follower). The rest should be understood as the opposite of what was said regarding failure (vipatti).

'Nigaṇṭhīnaṃ' means 'to the Jain nuns'. 'Ādimhi' is used in the sense of 'at the beginning' or 'firstly'. 'Ucchaggaṃ' means the tip or the end of a sugarcane. The same applies to the word 'veḷaggaṃ' (tip of a bamboo). 'Koṭiyaṃ' means at the extreme end, in the sense of the limit. 'Ambilaggaṃ' means a portion of sour taste. The same applies to the word 'tittakaggaṃ' (portion of bitter taste).

'Vihāraggena' means by the portion of the dwelling cells, in the sense of 'to the monks living in this cell, such and such a benefit accrues,' and so on, referring to the portions of various living places. The same method applies to the word 'pariveṇaggena'. In the word 'agge', the accusative case ending is replaced by the letter 'e', or it is a case substitution (vacanavipallāsa); and since the word 'katvā' is omitted, the teacher said 'ādiṃ katvā' (starting from). By the word 'ajjabhāvaṃ', it is shown that the suffix '-tā' is used in the sense of 'state' (bhāva). The 'state of today' (ajjabhāva) means reaching the state of being present at the time of hearing the Dhamma.

This is because, at that time, based on being present, and taking that as the cause, the word 'ajja' (today) applies to the interval from the dawn associated with that day of hearing the Dhamma until the next dawn. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'starting from the state of today,' which is defined as being present at that time. Alternatively, 'ajjataṃ' simply means 'ajja' (today), because the suffix '-tā' is used in its own sense (sakattha), as in the word 'devatā'. This is the opinion of the teachers.

Thus, having shown the meaning in accordance with the text appearing with the first letter (ca), the text says 'ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho' etc., to show the meaning in accordance with the text appearing with the third letter (ja). The letter 'da' is merely an augment (āgama) used for euphonic combination (sandhi). In fact, the word 'ajja' is an indeclinable (nipāta). Therefore, it is stated that the meaning is 'ajja aggaṃ'.

The word 'pāṇa' (life) in the ultimate sense refers only to the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). To show that the word 'pāṇupetaṃ' is a compound (samāsa) in the instrumental sense (karaṇa), it is said: 'for as long as my life lasts, I go for refuge'.
192:
After explaining the meaning according to the reading prominent with the first dental letter, the teacher now says "Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho" etc., to explain the meaning according to the reading prominent with the third dental letter. The letter 'da' is an augment (āgama) used for euphonic combination. Indeed, the word 'ajja' is an indeclinable (nipāta). Therefore, the teacher says, "starting from today." The word 'pāṇā' refers to the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) in the ultimate sense. To show that the word 'pāṇupetaṃ' is a Tatiya-tappurisa compound in the instrumental sense, the teacher says, "approached as long as life lasts." Indeed, one who approaches is called 'upeta.' The teachers intend the meaning: 'pāṇupeta' means approached by means of life (the life-faculty) as the instrument. By this, he clarifies the meaning that the word 'pāṇupeta' shows that the limit of that going for refuge is the end of life. By the word 'pāṇupeta,' it is shown that "I approach the refuge as long as my life-faculty lasts"; this approaching is not merely by speech, nor by a single moment of thought, but rather an approaching for the rest of one's life by way of sacrificing one's life-faculty. "Tīhi... pe... gataṃ" is the explanation of the meaning of "saraṇaṃ gataṃ." The word "ananyasatthukaṃ" shows the meaning of excluding other teachers by way of internal limitation and the rejection of others. In the view of some teachers, the meaning of the word 'kappiyakāraka' (one who makes things allowable) is also the meaning to be expressed by the word 'upāsaka'; therefore it is said, "a lay follower, a kappiyakāraka." Or it should be understood that this is said with reference to the going for refuge by way of self-dedication (attasanniyyātana). Thus, after showing the limit of that going for refuge as the end of life through the direct meaning (nītattha) of the word 'pāṇupeta,' the King, speaking thus, clarifies his intention: "I shall protect the refuge while honoring the Triple Gem along with my life." To clarify the King's intention through the inferred meaning (neyyattha), he says "Ahañhi" etc. There, the word 'hi' is used in the sense of strengthening or in the sense of cause; by this reasoning or for this reason, the meaning "May the Blessed One recognize me as a lay follower" is expressed. 

'Accaya' (transgression) means proceeding by overstepping and trampling upon the boundaries of the virtuous. It is a fault known as bodily misconduct, etc. Therefore, he says "offense" (aparādha). Alternatively, it is called 'accaya' because it proceeds by overcoming [virtue] through this [defilement]. It is simply the fault known as unwholesome states that cause the occurrence of bodily transgression, etc. And it is called 'aparādha' because one offends by it. Indeed, it proceeds by overcoming the person who is offending. Therefore, he says, "it proceeds by overstepping and overcoming." 'Dhamma' refers to the ten royal virtues (dasa-rājadhamma). Its details should be understood from the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka and others. 'Carati' means he practices or performs. 'Dhammenev' means only by Dhamma, not departing from it; the meaning is only by unswerving wholesome states. Therefore, he says, "not by unrighteousness such as parricide." The meaning of the word 'paṭiggaṇhātu' is, literally, "please acknowledge the acceptance"; according to the intention...
193:
...according to the intention, however, "please forgive" (khamatu) is said to show another meaning. In this context, not doing it again is itself restraint; this is shown by "in the future, such..." etc. The words "aparādhassa" etc. are synonyms of each other. 

By the phrase "just as the Dhamma stands, even so," he states the appropriate meaning of the word 'yathā.' The meaning is: in accordance with the wholesome Dhamma practiced by the virtuous. By the word "karoti" (he does), he shows the lack of specific meaning of the prefix 'paṭi.' They also say "he performs a remedy" (paṭikamma). Since remedying according to the Dhamma means making one's committed offense forgiven, he says, "it means 'he has asked for forgiveness'." The meaning of "we accept" is "we forgive," showing the acknowledgement of forgiveness. 

In "vuddhi hesa," the letter 'ha' is an augment (āgama) for the sake of euphony, or the word 'hi' is a mere indeclinable. "This (esā)" refers to the act of remedying according to the Dhamma and attaining restraint in the future. Therefore, he says, "Whoever [sees] the offense... attains restraint." Because he is to be approached and reached as a "refuge" by the world including the devas, the Tathāgata is called "Ariya" (Noble One); this is expressed by the words "of the Buddha, the Blessed One." Because he disciplines beings through this, the Teaching (Sāsana) is called "Vinaya." Because one grows in the attainment of heaven and liberation through this remedy, it is called "vuddhi" (growth). 

To remove the objection as to what this "growth" (vuddhi) pointed out as "this (esā)" is, he shows the connection by saying "katamā" etc., stating "Whoever [sees] the offense..." etc. The meaning is: this attainment of restraint is what is called "growth" pointed out as "this (esā)." The phrase "he remedies according to the Dhamma" is said to make it known that this is the preliminary action for attaining restraint in the future; thus it is said, "having remedied according to the Dhamma, he attains restraint in the future." 

It is the nature of the teachers (commentators) to make known a specific intention in some way or another. However, by this word, the further explanation of that [restraint] is also possible, because of the appearance of the further explanation "he remedies according to the Dhamma." Some teachers, however, say: "The phrase 'he remedies according to the Dhamma' shows only the preliminary action, not the further explanation. The phrase 'and he attains restraint in the future' is said to make it known that this alone is the further explanation." That is not proper, because asking for forgiveness is also stated in the context of "offending the Noble Ones" (ariyūpavāda) as a cause for growth. Otherwise, if there were no asking for forgiveness, the departure from the offense against Noble Ones would occur merely by attaining restraint in the future, but that is not stated. Therefore, the meaning should be understood only by the method already mentioned. 

Why is the description of the Dhamma (dhammaniddesa) shown by "yāyaṃ" etc.? Is it not the case that in the Pali text, the description of the person (puggalaniddesa) is made by "yo accayaṃ" etc.? To clear this objection, he begins with "Desanaṃ panā" etc. Desiring to give a discourse based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna)...
194:
Wishing to deliver a Dhamma teaching based on a person (it is said thus). Person-based teaching (Puggalādhiṭṭhāna-desanā) is of two kinds: person-based Dhamma teaching and person-based person teaching. The meaning here is: although a teaching based on the Dhamma (Dhammādhiṭṭhāna-desanā) was commenced with "Vuddhi hesā" etc., yet, wishing to base it on a person again, the person-based teaching was commenced with "Yo accayaṃ" etc., by virtue of the elegance of the teaching and the disposition of those to be guided. By virtue of both these factors, the teaching is of four kinds, categorized as Dhammādhiṭṭhāna and so forth.

"Vacasāyatte" means in connection with the words expressing the desire to go. Some teachers say it means the state of being connected with speech; that statement seems to contradict the words "So hi" etc. If it is said as "Vacasāyatthe", it is appropriate in the sense of the conclusion of speech. Because the word "sāya" is formed by the power of the word "sā" which has the meaning of making an end, it is like the word "dāyo". In this way, the concluding speech mentioned in the Commentary is also complete. Since it is spoken by making an end of the speech made for the purpose of going, it should be understood that the word "handa" occurs only in the sense of the conclusion of speech. The word "handa" is desired in the sense of urging (exhortation) and in the sense of relinquishing speech (conclusion of speech). In such Pali passages as "Handa dāni bhikkhave āmantayāmi", it is desired in the sense of urging. In such Pali passages as "Handa dāni apāyāmi", it is desired in the sense of relinquishing speech. Relinquishing speech means the releasing of speech, and it should be noted that this is indeed the conclusion of speech.

Due to the state of having many duties by virtue of tasks that are difficult to perform, it is said "balavakiccā" (having strong duties). A task that must be done without fail is called "kicca", and the remaining tasks are called "karaṇīya". Or, the task to be done first is called "kicca", and the task to be done later is called "karaṇīya". Or, a small task is called "kicca", and a large task is called "karaṇīya", as stated in the Udāna Commentary and elsewhere. Because the words "yaṃ" and "taṃ" are always connected, because of knowing the time of departure, and because of not being engaged in other tasks, it is said, "You alone know the time for that departure". The meaning is: "Knowing for yourself the time of departure known by you, you may depart". Alternatively, just as in urging someone regarding a task to be done, one says, "Know this, give this, bring this", so here too, to show the urging towards departure by saying "Knowing for yourself the time known by you, act by way of departing", the remaining text "tvameva jānāsi" (you yourself know) is spoken.

"Having circumambulated three times" etc., are spoken to indicate the performance according to the practiced custom. Therein, "padakkhiṇa" means circumambulation performed in a specific manner. Therefore, it is said "three times". "Dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ" means shining with the meeting together of the ten fingernails on both hands (the gesture of respect). By this word, the placing of both palms together equally (añjali) is shown.
195:
The act of joining the palms (samatṭhapana) is shown. 'Añjali' means the cavity formed by the palms. It is called 'añjali' because it clearly manifests (añjati) one's devotion. Masters of grammar desire that the word 'añju' is in the sense of manifestation and that the suffix 'ali' is applied. 'Abhimukhova' means only in the presence, meaning not showing the back to the Blessed One. The method of the five-point prostration (pañcappatiṭṭhitavandanā) should be understood as already mentioned.

He is called 'khato' (destroyed) because of the uprooting of his own roots of merit performed in the past which would have matured in this very existence. He is called 'upahato' (injured/smitten) because of the destruction of those same roots of merit. By both these words, only the fault of King Ajātasattu's heinous crime (ānantariya-kamma) is shown, because these two words are synonymous. To show the state of being destroyed due to the breaking of the foundation (patiṭṭhā) known as the root of merit, it is said 'he has become one whose foundation is broken' (bhinnapatiṭṭho jāto). Foundation (patiṭṭhā) and root (mūla) are the same in meaning. The entering into the path of certainty (sammatta-niyāma) occurs by means of this merit, thus it is called 'patiṭṭhā'. That king's achievement of the sufficing condition (upanissaya) of merit was broken and destroyed by the fault of the act of parricide; therefore, he is called 'one whose foundation is broken' (bhinnapatiṭṭho). Desiring to elaborate on that very point, the words 'tathā' and so on were spoken. Just as his own foundation known as the root of merit did not arise, so too, it should be understood that this king has destroyed himself by himself. Here, the word 'khato' is established by way of the object (kamma-vasa), but in the Pali, it should be regarded by way of the agent (kattu-vasa). Because the two words are synonymous, the word 'upahato' is not repeated here.

According to the words 'Lust is a stain (raja), but dust is not called a stain' and so on, only lust, hatred, and delusion are called 'stains' here; therefore, it is said 'free from the stains of lust and so on'. The word 'vīta' is shown to have the meaning of 'gone away' (vigata) by the word 'vigatattā'. 'The eye in the Dhammas' (dhammesu cakkhu) is called 'eye' in the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths that have arisen. Or, 'dhammesu' means in the three lower path-factors, and 'cakkhu' means the single eye known as the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). This compound is an ādhārattha-samāsa based on a part of a whole, but not a niddhāraṇattha-samāsa (partitive compound). For that partitive compound is forbidden everywhere in the Sasana texts and Sanskrit texts. 'Dhammamaya' means produced by the Dhamma of tranquility and insight; thus the meaning is given as 'the eye produced by Dhamma is the Dhamma-eye'. Furthermore, 'dhammamaya' refers to the three groups of Dhamma such as virtue and so on, because the word 'maya' occurs in its own sense (sakattha); by this, the meaning 'Dhamma itself is the eye, the Dhamma-eye' is obtained. In other places in the Suttas, the three-fold meaning is shown according to the text. However, here it is a designation only for the Path of Stream-entry, because if even that Path of Stream-entry is not yet attained, there is no possibility of speaking about the others (higher paths); this is the intention.
196:
Now, to show the easily understandable meaning of the Pali passage beginning with "Khātāyaṃ bhikkhave rājā," he said the words beginning with "Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti." In that context, "na abhavissatha" means "if it had not happened," or "if it were not so." Indeed, this usage of the kālātipatti (conditional) should be understood as referring only to the past, not the future. In this instance, "sotāpattimaggaṃ patto abhavissa" (he would have attained the path of stream-entry) should also be understood in this same way. One might ask: "Is not the statement about attaining the path a future-oriented matter, and thus refers to the future?" While that is true in cases where the time is indefinite (aniyamita), in this case, because the time is specifically defined by the phrase "while sitting right here," it should be known to refer only to the past. This is because the Blessed One spoke these words shortly after King Ajātasattu had risen from his seat and departed. "Pāpamittasaṃsaggena" means due to association with Devadatta and the evil friends known as Devadatta’s followers. "Assa" refers to (the fruit of) the path of stream-entry. With the words beginning with "evaṃ santepi," he shows the remaining meaning not directly included in the Pali text. "Tasmā" is connected to the meaning that he will be released because he has gone for refuge. The reading "mama ca sāsanama-hantatāya" is very appropriate. Although the word "ca" is not found in some versions, it should be understood that "ca" is elided there. The intended meaning, combined by the word "ca," is that he will be released not merely by going for refuge, but also because this king has faith in the Dispensation, shows signs of devotion, and because of the excellence of that threefold Dispensation.

The passage beginning with "yathā nāma" is an illustration by way of an easy release from the results of a difficult deed. "Koci" refers to a certain man. "Kassaci" means "of a certain man." In the word "vadhaṃ," the genitive case is used in the sense of the object because of its connection with the state (bhāva). "Pupphamuṭṭhimattena daṇḍena" means by a fine consisting of merely a handful of flowers. "Mucceyya" means he would be released from the punishment of execution. Alternatively, the word "daṇḍena" uses the instrumental case in the sense of the ablative, as in passages like "sumuttā mayaṃ tena mahāsamaṇena" (we are well released from that Great Ascetic); thus it means he would be released from the punishment of execution by a fine of merely a handful of flowers. "Lohakumbhiyaṃ" means in the Iron Cauldron Hell. Because a large iron cauldron is produced by the power of the kamma of the beings suffering there, that hell is called "Lohakumbhī." Falling from the upper surface to the bottom takes thirty thousand years, and rising from the bottom to the upper surface takes thirty thousand years; in both ways, it amounts to sixty thousand years. It is said:

"Sixty thousand years have passed in their entirety;
For us cooking in hell, when will there be an end?"
197:
The commentator, saying "having reached the bottom and then reaching the upper surface, he will be released," explains this meaning: unlike other sons of wealthy merchants and so on who fall down and go up, cooking in that hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, this king will not suffer so. In fact, for the reasons mentioned, this King Ajātasattu will fall down once and go up once, being released after cooking for only sixty thousand years.

To answer the question of where this meaning is obtained from, he said: "This too, it is said, was spoken by the Blessed One." Here, the word "kira" (it is said) has the sense of hearsay. By this, he shows that the fact of it being spoken by the Blessed One is heard through the lineage of teachers, and that this meaning has been brought down by the lineage of teachers. Then, he removes the objection, "If it was spoken by the Buddha, why was it not included in the Pali text?" with the words "But it was not included in the Pali." The meaning is that because it is a miscellaneous teaching (pakiṇṇakadesanā), it was not included in the Pali text and thus was not chanted (in the councils) as a formal text. It is stated in the commentaries that miscellaneous teachings are not included in the Pali text.

If he is to be cooked in hell in the immediately following existence, one might wonder what benefit the king obtained from hearing this discourse. To remove that doubt by raising and answering the objection, he said the words beginning with "idaṃ pana" (but this...). With the words "ayañhi" (for this...), he specifically defines and shows the various great benefits in the present life and the future life, such as obtaining sleep. Here, by the words "this king... obtains sleep," he shows the attainment of sleep. At that time, the state of being free from physical and mental suffering is also shown by way of obtaining sleep. By the words "to the Triple Gem... he performed," he shows the performance of great honor to the Triple Gem. By the words "of the worldlings... there was not," he shows the acquisition of an extraordinary worldling's faith. Such benefits are those of the present life. By the words "in the future... he will attain Parinibbāna," he shows the supreme benefit of the future life. In an exhaustive sense, the future benefits in successive lives should be understood as immeasurable.

In that context, "madhurāya" means having a sweet taste. "Ojavantiyā" means endowed with the essence (ojā) which is the core of the sweet taste. It is called "pothujjanikā" because it occurs in a worldling (puthujjana). He is called "vijitāvī" because he has specially conquered the five Maras; here, the special quality is knowing by oneself without the instruction of others. He is called "paccekabuddho" because he is enlightened individually; the meaning is that he becomes enlightened to the Path of Arahatship by himself without a teacher. This is true: "Paccekabuddhas realize the truth by themselves; they do not make others realize it."
198:
Paccekabuddhas penetrate only the essence of meaning (attharasa), but not the essence of the Dhamma (dhammarasa). Indeed, they are unable to teach by formulating the supramundane Dhamma into designations (paññatti). Their penetration of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) is like a mute person who is unable to describe the dream they saw, or like a forest dweller who is unable to describe the taste of a dish eaten in the city. However, they attain all the varieties of psychic powers, meditative attainments, and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This is stated in the commentaries.

Here, an objector says: "If the Eye of Dhamma (dhammacakkhu) would have arisen for King Ajātasattu in that very seat had there been no obstruction of kamma (kammantarāya), then how can he attain final nibbāna as a Paccekabuddha in the future? If he is to attain final nibbāna as a Paccekabuddha in the future, how could the Eye of Dhamma have arisen in that very seat? Are not the powerful supports (upanissaya) for Disciple Enlightenment (sāvakabodhi) and Private Enlightenment (paccekabodhi) different, since these two types of enlightenment are mutually exclusive? For these two are distinct respectively based on the fulfillment of five factors and two factors, the success of the resolution (abhinīhāra), the duration of accumulating perfections (pāramī), and the manner of awakening to the Truths (abhisambujjhana)."

This is not a contradiction. It is because the requisites (sambhāra) for his Private Enlightenment are to be fulfilled only after this present life. Even beings who would awaken through Disciple Enlightenment, if the conditions for that Disciple Enlightenment are not met, will awaken through Private Enlightenment at another time. This is because such a resolution is possible in that manner.

Other teachers, however, say: "This King is one who had made a resolution for Private Enlightenment only. Although he had made a resolution for Private Enlightenment, because he had not yet reached the state of certainty (niyata) and his knowledge had not yet matured, he could have attained Disciple Enlightenment in the presence of the Teacher. With this intention, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, if this King...' and so on. Only for Great Bodhisattas (those destined for full Buddhahood) is there exemption from the results of heinous crimes (ānantariyakamma); there is no such exemption for other Bodhisattas.
