Therefore, even though Devadatta was certain of Private Enlightenment, due to the grudge he held against the Protector of the World over a long period, he committed grave heinous crimes. Therefore, it should be understood that although the King cannot attain the penetration of the Truths now due to the obstruction of kamma, by virtue of his certainty of Private Enlightenment, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī in the future and attain final nibbāna." In this matter, one should investigate and accept what is appropriate.

Showing the aforementioned Pāḷi text itself by way of the conclusion of the commentary, he said "Idamavoca" and so on. The meaning of those words has been stated below (in the Brahmajāla Sutta). Furthermore, it should be understood that he makes the conclusion with "Idamavoca" etc., to encompass the meaning even if it is not explicitly included in the Pāḷi text.
199:
Thus, the sub-commentary (Līnatthappakāsanī) on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta Commentary, titled Sādhuvilāsinī—which clarifies the extremely subtle, deep, and difficult-to-understand meanings in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumangalavilāsinī, which generates the rapid arising of pure and extensive wisdom; which was composed by the Great Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati, who is endowed with virtues such as uprightness, gentleness, grace, faith, mindfulness, stability, wisdom, patience, and energy; who wanders with courageous knowledge without attachment in the three Pitakas along with their commentaries; who possesses the intellectual power to plunge into the thicket of various own-doctrines and other-doctrines; who has many groups of disciples; who is an expert in great grammar; and who is the teacher of the Great King of Kings—is finished.

## The Explanation of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta is finished.
200:
## 3. Ambaṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā
## Addhānagamanavaṇṇanā
Having thus commented on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the commentator, now wishing to comment on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, speaks the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ... pe... Kosalesu" in order to clarify that the opportunity to comment in sequence has arrived, and to show that the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is the sutta recited immediately after the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. In suttas of this nature, the word "Evaṃ" should be understood in this way. In this phrase "Kosalesu", the word "iti" has the sense of "beginning" (ādi). The word "iti", which indicates a variation in the meaning of the word, is shown to be elided; or it is the elision of the word "ādi"; or it is an indication by way of implication (upalakkhaṇa).

The analysis of the meaning of a word that is not prominent (or is new) because it has not been taken up below is called "Apubbapadavaṇṇanā". In the Nidānakathā, the commentator stated, "Leaving aside the meanings that appear repeatedly, I shall explain other meanings." Although some versions have the reading "Anupubbapadavaṇṇanā", that reading is inappropriate because it is not extracted in the Ṭīkā and is not explained in sequence.

The teacher Dhammapāla stated, "The princes are called Kosala by virtue of their lineage (gotta)." However, teachers who are grammarians (akkharacintaka) say, "They are called Kosala because they take up treasure (kosaṃ lanti), or because they ask about welfare (kusalaṃ pucchanti)." "Janapadino" refers to those who possess a country or the lords of a country. Although it would be sufficient to say "the princes named Kosala," the inclusion of "Janapadino" is to show that even though other famous princes lived in that country, because they were inhabitants, this country is known as "Kosala" based on the residence of those specific princes. By the phrase "the residence of those princes," he shows the derivative of residence (nivāsa-taddhita): "The country which is the residence of the Kosala princes is called Kosala." By the phrase "even though it is a single country," he clarifies that although it is plural in terms of grammar, in terms of meaning, this country is only one.

In this context, the word "api" is used in the sense of concession (anuggaha). By that word "api," he speaks supportively, saying that even if this country is indeed only one, the use of the plural is appropriate for this reason. If it is asked why the plural is used if the country is only one, he states "ruḷhī-saddena" etc. It means that the use of the plural is appropriate because the word Kosala is a conventional term (ruḷhī). In this context, "ruḷhī" refers to the attribution of the plural, which is associated with the dependent meanings, to the word that is the basis. Therefore, the teacher Dhammapāla stated here and in other places such as the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā: "Grammarians desire such genders and numbers in such places as if they were appropriate; this is the convention (ruḷhī) here, just as it is said elsewhere, 'He dwells among the Kurūs (Kurūsu viharati)', 'among the Angas (Angesu)'..."
201:
..."viharati" etc. In this regard, some teachers desire the name "Kosala" to be a metaphor (upacāra). This is inappropriate because it should not be used with the plural suffix. For in metaphorical naming, the singular also occurs, as in "The lion roars (sīho gajjati)". Even in the word "janapada" which is qualified by it, it is only singular because it is a generic noun (jāti-sadda). Therefore, the teacher said, "In that Kosala country (tasmiṃ Kosalesu janapade)", meaning "in that country named Kosala". Indeed, a mere designation that is not literally true is called convention (ruḷhī). The meaning must be determined only according to the truth.

For example:
"The Videhan kings have sons who cause the country to prosper and are long-lived; those sons shall exercise sovereignty in the city of Mithilā and shall be lords of creatures (pajāpati)." In such verses—
Just as the plural "puttā" (sons) is used by virtue of convention for a single meaning referred to as "son," so too in this context, the plural "Kosalesu" is used by virtue of convention for a single meaning referred to as the residence of those princes.

Furthermore, just as in "One should not kill a living being, nor take what is not given" etc., the singular is used for many meanings by virtue of the class (jāti), so too in this context, the singular is used in the word "janapade," which has many meanings by way of its various parts, by virtue of the class. The teacher Dhammapāla also stated in the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā: "Even in the word 'janapada', which is a generic noun qualified by that word 'Anga', it is only singular. Therefore, it is said, 'In that Anga country (tasmiṃ Angesu janapade)'."

Having thus shown the plural as if it were for many by virtue of convention, he now speaks "The ancient teachers, however, say (porāṇā panāhū)" etc., wishing to show the plural when it should indeed be spoken as plural by virtue of having many meanings. In this context, the word "pana" is a particle indicating a distinction. By that word "pana," he indicates the distinction he is about to state: that this word "Kosalesu" is plural only because it has many meanings as its object, not by virtue of convention. For that region has many divisions because its measurement is three hundred yojanas. In this method, the meaning should be understood as "in those Kosala countries."

The word "Mahāpanādaṃ" refers to the prince named Mahāpanāda, the son of the Videhan king named Suruci, who appears in the Mahāpanāda Jātaka and Suruci Jātaka. The word "nānānāṭakāni" refers to six hundred thousand various kinds of dancers/performers led by great performers such as Bhaṇḍuka and Paṇḍuka. In some versions, the word "ādi" is found, but it is not seen in the Jātaka Aṭṭhakathā. If it were present, one should understand it to include dancers, acrobats, and so on. The word "sitamattampi" means even a mere smile. That prince did not enjoy the dancing of human performers because he had previously seen celestial dancers in his immediate past life as a deva.

The phrase "naṅgalāni pahaṭetvā" means abandoning the plows by way of giving up the work of plowing. This statement is merely an example. In truth, not only the farmers but the people living in both the countries of Videha and Kāsi (Mithilā and Bārāṇasī) abandoned their respective duties and gathered at the place where the festival was held. At that time, it is said that the three festivals of Prince Mahāpanāda—the palace-entry festival, the coronation festival, and the marriage festival—were performed simultaneously.
202:
Prince Mahāpanāda found human dancing unpleasant because he had seen celestial dancers in his immediately preceding life as a deva. The phrase "having abandoned the plows" means abandoning the work of plowing; this is merely an illustration. In truth, not only farmers but also people living in both kingdoms (Kāsi and Videha) abandoned their respective duties and gathered at that place of the auspicious ceremony. At that time, three auspicious ceremonies of Prince Mahāpanāda were performed simultaneously: the ceremony of entering the palace, the ceremony of the white parasol, and the marriage ceremony. Those living in the Kāsi and Videha kingdoms gathered there and celebrated the festival for more than seven years. Although the reading "nangalādīni" is found now, it is not an ancient reading because it was not extracted in the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā).

When the great crowd gathered, some thought, "We will make the prince laugh by showing him a humorous performance," while others thought, "We will watch that game," and thus the great multitude assembled. They displayed various games such as climbing the incomparable mango tree and entering a pyre of wood. A celestial dancer sent by Sakka stood in the air in the royal courtyard and displayed only half of his body. He danced, moved, and trembled with only one hand, one foot, one eye, and one tusk, while the rest of his body remained still. Upon seeing that celestial dancer, Prince Mahāpanāda smiled slightly. Intending this meaning, it is said, "He made him laugh by showing that celestial dancer." Those with good hearts are called "suhajja" (friends). By the word "ādi," relatives and attendants are included.

Because of such speech, from the questioning and answering, "Are these people kusala (healthy)? Yes, they are kusala," those people first acquired the name "Kusala." Because they were the lords of those healthy people (Kusala), the princes became known as "Kosala." Because it was the place where they resided, that region is called "Kosala," as previously stated. Therefore, it is said, "That region is called Kosala." This was stated by the teacher in the Majjhima Nikāya Ṭīkā. The meaning there would be: since the name "Kosala" and those who possess the name are spoken of in the singular and plural respectively, here too, as in the previous method, it is plural by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī). The only distinction here is the reason for the princes obtaining their name. Here, however, when the teacher says "that region," it is either spoken in a general sense of the region or by way of grammatical substitution (vacanavippallāsa, changing plural to singular), meaning "those regions." It is called Kosala.
203:
## Explanation of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta

In the statement "Considering that the Kusalas are indeed the Kosalas" (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.254), the meaning could be this—since that region is spoken of either by the power of the generic term (jātisadda) or by grammatical substitution (vacanavippallāsa, changing plural to singular), it becomes plural due to having many referents. Here, there is a special reason for the region obtaining its name. Based on the word "Kusala," it is called "Kosala" by the power of conventional usage (rūḷhī). For example, as in "The Yevāpanaka teaching is not your section (vaggō)." Alternatively, it is called "Kosala" because people in this region say "Kusala" (Are you free from illness?) during mutual conversation. The derivation of the Taddhita suffix is indeed multifaceted. The word "Kusala" means "freedom from illness" (ārogya), as in "Is the venerable one kusala? Is the venerable one free from ailment?" etc. Thus, it means "Are you free from illness?" Or it means "skillfulness" (cheka), as in "The women are kusala (skilled) in dance and song, and well-trained in the four arts," etc. Thus, it means "Is there skillfulness in those dancers?"

Caraṇaṃ is called cārikā (wandering). Or caraṇaṃ is called cāra, and that cāra itself is cārikā. Here, only traveling on a road (maggagamana) is intended; to show that merely walking slowly (cuṇṇikagamana) is not intended, it is called "addhānagamana" (long-distance travel). This is an adverbial neuter (bhāvanapuṃsaka). It means one who is wandering by way of the wandering known as long-distance travel. Or, although there is no distinction, it is spoken of as if there were a distinction, as in "He sat for the day-abiding (divāvihāraṃ nisīdi)"; it means one who is wandering the cārikā known as long-distance travel, one who is performing the act of going. For the meaning of the roots 'kar' and 'bhū' encompasses the meaning of all roots. In some versions, the reading "addhānamaggaṃ" is found, but that reading is not good. This is because the word cārikā is not a word that denotes a road (magga).

Now, to analyze that cārikā and define the intended meaning here, he says "Cārikā ca nāmesa," etc. Since cārikā can also occur among disciples by way of conventional usage, to distinguish it from them, he says "Bhagavato" (of the Blessed One). Therefore, it is said in the Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā: "In this phrase 'wandering the wandering' (cārikāṃ caramāno), although this cārikā for the purpose of helping the great multitude is obtained only by the Buddhas, by taking the Buddha as the basis, it is also spoken of for the disciples by way of conventional usage. For example, a fan made of bamboo mats and the like is also called a palmyra-leaf fan (tālavaṇṭa)." In the word "dūrepi," by the word "pi" (or "api"), the meaning "not very far" is also included because cārikā can occur there as well. "Bodheneyya-puggala" means a person who is capable of being enlightened by way of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. "Sahasā gamanaṃ" means going quickly. To show in detail what was stated briefly as "going out to meet Mahākassapa and others," he says "Bhagavā hi," etc. "Paccuggacchanto" means going forward to welcome someone. By the word "tathā," the word "thirty yojanas" (tiṃsayojana) should be drawn in. The King of Gandhāra named Pukkusāti...
204:
In the city of Kukkuṭavatī, there was a king named Mahākappina. There was also a cowherd named Dhaniya, who was the son of the merchant Koraṇḍa.

Thus, having first praised the act of paying great respect to the Dhamma and partially showing the welcoming of the Elder Mahākassapa and so forth, the text beginning with "Ekadivasaṃ" is now commenced to elaborate on the story of the novice Vanavāsī Tissa and to show the journey on wandering. Who is this novice named Tissa? He was born in Sāvatthī into a family that supported the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta. He was a novice of great merit who, in his previous lay life, was known as "Piṇḍapātadāyaka Tissa" and "Kambaladāyaka Tissa," and later became famous as the Arahant novice "Vanavāsī Tissa." The detailed account should be sought in the Dhammapada Commentary (Vanavāsī Tissa Sāmaṇera Vatthu). The Blessed One, wishing to travel through the air only with those monks who were accustomed to traveling through the air, said, "Inform the monks who possess the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā)." The word "tassa" refers to the novice Tissa. "Taṃ" refers to the Blessed One who was donning his robes together with the community of monks. The phrase should be connected as "no thero no oramattako vata," meaning he was not an elder of inferior measure in terms of the quality of virtue.

"Attano pattāsane" means at the end of the monks' seats. After preaching the auspicious Dhamma related to alms-giving to those village lay-devotees, the phrase "Bhagavā kira" and so forth was said to resolve the question: "Why did the Blessed One, being the guide of the world including the devas, speak in this way?" A guide (maggadesaka) is one who points out the path to Nibbāna or the path to a happy rebirth (sugati).

"Tāya" means by that perception of the forest. Although the higher ordination (upasampadā) is accomplished by the power of the formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), teachers say it was said, "I will give you the inheritance of the Buddha," because it is accomplished by the power of the Buddha's command. Other teachers, however, say that the Teacher, wishing to allow the higher ordination for that novice who was not yet twenty years old, said, "I will give you the inheritance of the Buddha." Because the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, acted as the preceptor (upajjhāya) and ordained him, it is stated in the Commentaries that this novice is a co-resident (saddhivihārika) of the General of the Dhamma. In the Dhammapada Commentary, however, it is stated according to the view of the reciters of the Khuddaka Nikāya (Khuddaka-bhāṇakas) that the elders such as the General of the Dhamma, each with a retinue of forty thousand monks, departed separately with their own retinues, while the Blessed One departed alone. In this commentary and in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, it should be understood that the departure is described differently according to the view of the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya. "Ayaṃ" refers to the wandering for the benefit of the elders such as Mahākassapa. The journey of the Blessed One, who wished to show favor, is connected as "aturitacārikā" (unhurried wandering).
205:
This term "cārikaṃ" refers to unhurried wandering (aturitacārikā). "Mahāmaṇḍala" (Great Circuit) is a very large circle because it is defined by the outer measurement within the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). "Majjhimamaṇḍala" (Middle Circuit) is the circle that exists in the middle of the other two, the Mahāmaṇḍala and the Antomaṇḍala. "Antomaṇḍala" (Inner Circuit) is a circle smaller than the others, or it means the final, innermost circle because it is contained within the others. To answer the question "What is the measurement of these circuits?", the teacher said "kattha" and so forth.

In that context, the fact that it is nine hundred yojanas should be taken only as being comprised within the Middle Country, because the Buddha does not travel by unhurried wandering (aturitacārikā) beyond those nine hundred yojanas. Indeed, beyond that, the Tathāgata travels only by hurried wandering (turitacārikā), not by unhurried wandering. It is the custom of the Buddhas to set out on wandering only after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony; thus it was said, "Having performed the Pavāraṇā with the Great Pavāraṇā," and so forth. "Pāṭipada-divase" refers to the first day of the waning moon, immediately following the full moon of the first Kattika (Thadingyut). "Samantā" means from all four sides around the places he visited. Because the great multitude of people gathered, those who arrived first received the opportunity to invite him. To show such gathering, the phrase "itaresu" and so forth was said.

In the phrase "tranquillity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) are tender," the tenderness of tranquillity should be understood by way of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). The tenderness of insight, however, should be understood by way of the four knowledges: the knowledge of defining formations (saṅkhāra-pariccheda-ñāṇa), the knowledge of discerning causes (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-ñāṇa), the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of path and non-path (maggāmagga-ñāṇa). Indeed, "tender insight" (taruṇa-vipassanā) is a designation for those four knowledges. "Pavāraṇā-saṅgahaṃ datvā" means giving by way of granting permission for the monks' wishes. "Kattika-puṇṇamāyaṃ" refers to the full moon of the late Kattika (Tazaungmon). The phrase "on the first pāṭipada day of Migasīra" was said with reference to the first day of the waning moon of the month of Migasīra (Natdaw) according to the usage of the Middle Country. However, according to current usage, it should be understood as the first day of the waning moon of the late Kattika month (Tazaungmon).

"By another reason also" means by a reason other than the tenderness of the monks' tranquillity and insight, such as the ripening of the knowledge of the veneyya beings (those to be tamed) in the Middle Circuit. "For four months" means for the four months from the day after the full moon of Āsaḷhī until the full moon of the late Kattika. It is in the same manner as stated by "one hundred yojanas all around" and so forth. Dwelling is called "vassa"; it is the act of dwelling (vasana-kiriyā). Because the Blessed One has a vassa (rains retreat) that has been dwelt in, he is called "vutthavasso" (one who has completed the rains). "Of that one who has completed the rains" (vutthavassassa). Because they are to be disciplined by the Tathāgata, the possessive designation "Bhagavato veneyyasattā" (the Blessed One's veneyya beings) is used; or this may be an agent designation. "Veneyyasattā" means beings who are to be disciplined according to their temperaments. "Indriya-paripākaṃ āgamayamāno" means waiting for the ripening of the faculties such as faith (saddhā) into the state of ripening for liberation from defilements.
206:
It should be understood that because the departure for wandering occurs on the first day of one of the months of Phussa, Māgha, Phagguṇa, or Citta, a fixed determination of the month is not made here. Therefore, it is said: "Having stayed there for one month, or two, three, or four months." "There" means only in the place where the rains-retreat was observed.

The words "or for seven months" and so on should be applied in order with the words "or for one month" and so on. If he stays there for another full month, he completes the wandering in seven months. If he stays for two months, then in six; if for three months, then in five; if he stays there for four months, he completes the wandering in four months. To dispel the doubt as to why he sets out on wandering, the words "Thus" and so on are spoken. One who is very old and weak is called "bāḷhajinna". When will such people be able to see [the Buddha]? They simply will not be able to see him. "Out of compassion for the world" means solely out of compassion for the world. Therefore, it is said: "Not for the sake of robes and so forth."

"By way of jaṅghavihāra" means by way of wandering on foot, or by way of wandering on foot and staying for a few days in various places. For the word "vihāra" (dwelling/abiding) is common to all postures. "For the sake of bodily comfort" means for the sake of the comfort of the body, which has an excess of elements due to constant residence in a single place, by means of wandering. "For the sake of expecting the occasion of an occurrence" means for the sake of the occasion of an occurrence desired for preaching the Dhamma, like the discourses of the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta, Maghadeva Jātaka, and so forth; or for the sake of desiring the occasion of an occurrence; or it means for the sake of preaching the Dhamma at the time of an occurrence. "For the sake of prescribing training rules" means for the sake of prescribing training rules, as in the case of prescribing the Surāpāna training rule and others. "For the sake of enlightening" means for the sake of making beings who are capable of enlightenment, such as Aṅgulimāla and others, realize the Four Noble Truths.

"Mahatā" means with a large (assembly). Wandering intended for some or a few individuals is called "nibaddhacārikā" (fixed wandering). Other than that, wandering through a succession of villages, market towns, and cities intended for many people is called "anibaddhacārikā" (unfixed wandering). Therefore, the words "There" and so on are spoken. "As he wanders" refers to the action.

To show in detail what has already been said, "This (anibaddhacārikā) is intended here," the words "At that time, it is said" and so on are spoken. "In the ten thousand world systems" is said with reference to the ten thousand universes which constitute the field of birth (jātikhetta). Why? Because only in those ten thousand universes do beings capable of enlightenment arise. For it is said that the Blessed One, standing with his Buddha-knowledge directed toward seeing beings in those ten thousand universes who are capable and whose faculties are mature, spreads the net of knowledge. And this word...
207:
...is spoken with reference to the devas and Brahmās. As for humans, they are capable of enlightenment only in this universe and in this Jambudīpa together with its surrounding islands. "Bodhaneyyabandhave" means the kinsmen of the Blessed One, known as beings capable of enlightenment. For just as there are relations by lineage and so forth, those veneyya beings who are related by the penetration of the Four Noble Truths are called the kinsmen of the Blessed One. With reference to their coming into the range of his knowledge, it is said: "They have entered within the net of omniscience." It is said that the Blessed One, having attained the attainment of Great Compassion and having emerged from it, resolves and adverts his mind, thinking: "May those beings who are capable and whose knowledge is mature appear in my knowledge." Upon that adverting, one, two, or many veneyya beings who are ready to be disciplined come into the range of his knowledge; this is the Buddha-power in this matter. He then surveys the supporting conditions (upanissaya), past conduct, past causes, and the present practice of those who have thus come into range. For when adverting is made to grasp veneyya beings, first their state as veneyya beings appears. Then, investigating some achievement by way of taking refuge and so forth, thinking "What will it be?", he surveys their past supporting conditions and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Atha Bhagavā" and so forth.

"So" refers to the youth Ambaṭṭha. "Vādapaṭivādaṃ katvā" means having given a reply such as "O Gautama, those shavelings, those petty recluses" and so forth to the words spoken by me such as "Ambaṭṭha, do you think so?" and so forth. "Asabbhivākyaṃ" means the speech of the ignoble, words that are unfit to be spoken by a virtuous person in various ways, having fallen into the way of speaking three times with the derogatory term "ibbha" (menial/householder) and thus uttering speech that should not be spoken. "Nibbisēvanaṃ" means free from verbal piercing, meaning free from the agitation caused by the pride of conceit.

"Avasaritabbaṃ" means should be approached. The name of that village is just this much; what is the use of searching for a meaning here? With this intention, it is said: "There is also a reading as Ijjhānaṅgala." In accordance with the instrumental designation "yena disābhāgena", the accusative case (upayoga) is shown in the sense of the instrumental as "tena avasarī". However, in accordance with the locative designation "yasmiṃ padese", it is said "taṃ vā avasarī". Both of those meanings are explained by "tena disābhāgena" and so forth. "Gato" means approached, meaning he went. "Puna gato" means arrived, meaning he reached. "Icchānaṅgale" is an indication of the village where the Blessed One went for alms at that time, and this is the locative case in the sense of proximity (samīpa). "Icchānaṅgalavanasaṇḍe" is an indication of the place of residence, and this is the locative case in the sense of the actual location (adhikaraṇa). Desiring to explain both terms by showing their specific meanings, he said "Icchānaṅgalaṃ" and so forth.
208:
The teacher says "Upanissāya" and so forth. The phrase "Sīlakkhandhāvāraṃ" etc., shows the Blessed One's dwelling through the power of considering the welfare of those to be guided, in the manner already stated. In that context, the practice of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, is entirely devoted to the suppression of unrighteousness (adhamma); and that practice is through the power of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, the teacher takes only the group of three starting with virtue. "Sīlakkhandhāvāraṃ" means that he dwells having established a camp-fence called virtue, similar to a wooden camp made of wood, bricks, etc., by a wheel-turning monarch. In this word "khandhāvāra", they surround (varenti) from all sides with logs (dāru-khandha) etc.; thus, by lengthening the "a", it is called "khandhāvāra", meaning a temporary residence of kings. In that phrase, virtue is also called "khandhāvāra" because it is connected to the Blessed One's temporary dwelling, and because it wards off danger, thus being similar to a king's camp. "Samādhikontaṃ" refers to the auspicious spear called right concentration. "Sabbaññutañāṇapadaṃ" refers to the mantra-word of victory called the knowledge of omniscience. "Parivattayamāno" means reciting or chanting. There is also a reading "Sabbaññutañāṇasaraṃ", meaning repeatedly revolving the arrow tipped with the diamond of the knowledge of omniscience. The phrase "Yathābhirucitena vihārena" shows the connection with all types of dwellings; it means he dwells in whichever dwelling he himself delights in among the divine dwellings (dibba-vihāra) and so forth.

## Explanation of the Story of Pokkharasāti
"Mante" refers to the Vedic texts such as the Iruveda. Indeed, the Iruveda and others are called "manta" because they are to be recited protectively. The word "aṇa" is used in the sense of sound; therefore, he says "he recites" (sajjhāyati). Worldly teachers, however, say: "A Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa) is the offspring of Brahma; there is the arrival of 'na', the state of 'ṇa', lengthening, etc." Why is only this etymological definition (Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇā) stated? He says "Only this meaning" and so forth. He removes the objection regarding whose definition the other one is by saying "But the Noble Ones" and so forth. Or rather, this is said to reject the etymology stated by worldly teachers such as "He is called a Brahmin because he is born from Brahma". By the word "eva" (only) in "Only this meaning", he rejects that worldly etymology. To show the etymology of the "Brahmins of purity" (visuddhi-brāhmaṇa) among the two types of Brahmins—Brahmins by birth and Brahmins of purity—shown by the other word "jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ", he says "But the Noble Ones" and so forth. Indeed, the Noble Ones are called "Brahmins" by way of etymology because they exclude (bahanti) or put outside evil deeds. "The body of that Brahmin is like a white lotus (padumma)"—this statement alone shows the reason for obtaining his name; the remaining words merely show the specific qualities that exist in connection with him. Therefore, he says "Thus they recognize him as Pokkharasāti because he is like a lotus (pokkhara)". He whose body is like a lotus is Pokkharasāti.
209:
By way of etymology, the word "sāta" has the meaning of "similar" (sadisa). Because his body is like a lotus (pokkhara), he is called "Pokkharasāti". "Setapokkharasadiso" means having the color of a white lotus (setapaduma). "Devanagare" means in the city of gods such as Ālakamandā. "Ussāpitarajatatoraṇaṃ" means the beauty like a silver city-pillar (indakhīla) that is deeply planted and very high. "Kāḷamegharājī" means appearing like a streak of dark clouds seen occasionally. "Rajatapaṇāḷikā" means being well-rounded like a silver tube. "Suvaṭṭitā" means being perfectly rounded in places where rounding is appropriate. Because there are no blemishes such as dark moles, it is extremely pure. By the words "Arajake" and so forth, he also illustrates the state of reaching the pinnacle of beauty.

Now, to show another reason for his obtaining the name, he says "Ayaṃ pana" and so forth. Therein, the statement "He was born inside a lotus bud in a great lake in the Himalayan region" is the only reason for obtaining the name. The remaining words merely show the manner of his existence in connection with that. Therefore, he says "Thus they recognize him as Pokkharasāti because he slept (lay) in a lotus". Because he sleeps in a lotus (kamala), he is "Pokkharasāti". Or, the word "sāta" is said to mean a uniform shape; thus, one who has a uniform shape born in a lotus is called "Pokkharasāti".

The commentator asks, "What kind of former merit did this Brahmin have, and for what reason did the Blessed One go to that place to favor him?", referring to the phrase "Ayaṃ pana" etc. as a partial explanation. According to the words "From there to the human world..." etc., it should be understood that successive births in the deva world are meant. Referring to the birth due to such kamma, he says "Being disgusted with dwelling in a mother's womb" and so forth. By the phrase "born in a lotus bud", he shows that he was born by way of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) rebirth. "Na pupphati" means it does not bloom. That ascetic took it from the stalk (nāḷa). "Suvaṇṇacuṇṇapiñjaro" means being like a silver image that has a golden hue because it is covered with gold dust. The word "piñjara" is a synonym for golden hue, as stated in the Sāratthadīpanī. This same method should be understood in the phrase "padumareṇupiñjaraṃ". "Rajatabimbakaṃ" means like a figure made of silver. "Paṭijaggāmi" means "I will feed and care for him". "Pāraṃ" means reaching the end, or completion like the shore of a river or ocean. He is wise (paṇḍita) by way of natural wisdom called rebirth-linking wisdom. Or, he is skilled through the wisdom called proficient wisdom in the Vedas or in things to be done.
210:
## 
'Veyyattiyena byatto' means being skilled or proficient through clear or quick wisdom. 'Aggabrāhmaṇo' refers to a world-renowned (disāpāmokkha) brahmin. 'Sippaṃ' refers to the Vedic arts, because he has mastered those Vedic texts. 'Brahmadeyyaṃ adāsī' means he gave it as a noble gift (brahmadeyya) according to the method to be described.

In the word 'ajjhāvasati,' the prefixes 'adhi-' and 'ā-' are merely prefixes (upasagga). Therefore, the word 'Ukkaṭṭhaṃ' takes the accusative case (upayogavacana) in the sense of the locative (bhummatttha) because it is used with the root √vas preceded by 'ā-'. Alternatively, 'adhi-' has the sense of lordship and 'ā-' has the sense of a limit (mariyāda). Thus, the word 'Ukkaṭṭhaṃ' is in the accusative case in the sense of the locative because of its connection with the 'kammappavacanīya,' as shown by 'Ukkaṭṭhanāmake,' etc. To explain that very meaning, 'tassa,' etc., is stated. 'Being the lord of that city' is an explanation of the meaning 'having overcome/subdued.' Therefore, it shows that lordship is indeed overcoming. 'Yāya mariyādāya,' etc., is an explanation of the meaning of the prefix 'ā-'. Thus, it shows that 'ā-' has the sense of a limit, and a limit means the state of independence by which one must reside there. 'Yāya mariyādāya' means by the condition of not being shared with others, which is called independence. 'Upasaggavasena,' etc., is an explanation of the word 'Ukkaṭṭhanāmake.' By this, it shows that although the locative case (sattamī) would be appropriate, the accusative case is prescribed here because it is joined with two kinds of prefixes that follow or distinguish the meaning of the root. 'Tassa kira,' etc., is a demonstration of the name (samñā) following the meaning. 'Vatthu' refers to a piece of land suitable for founding a city, as in 'ārāmavatthu' (site for a park) or 'vihāravatthu' (site for a monastery).

'Ukkā' means torches. 'Aggahesuṃ' means they took/marked the site for the city while the torches were blazing, guarding the light of the night, thinking, 'Today is an auspicious day, therefore the constellation is good; let this auspicious moment not pass.' Therefore, it is called 'Ukkaṭṭha' because it was established where the torches were (ukkāsu ṭhitā). Whether by inclusion in the 'ākati' group such as 'mūlavibhuja,' etc., or by the method of etymology (nirutti), it is called 'Ukkaṭṭha' because it was established while the torches were shining. Furthermore, it is called 'Ukkaṭṭha' because it was established while the torches were present. In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, it is said: 'That city is called Ukkaṭṭha because it was founded while torches were present even at night so that the auspicious day, the good moment, and the good constellation would not pass; it means it was founded while torches were lit and held.' This also agrees with the words of this Ṭīkā on the Sīlakkhandhavagga.
211:
## 
It should be understood that the acquisition of the city site is also consistent (with the aforementioned meaning) because it is included in the founding and creation of the city. Other teachers, however, say: 'That city receives the name "Ukkaṭṭhā" because it is endowed with noble qualities (ukkaṭṭhaguna), being perfect in terms of the ground, resources, and population.' Secular teachers say: 'It is called "Ukkaṭṭhā" because torches (ukkā) were held (dhāriyanti) at the time of its founding; this is a phonetic variation (vaṇṇavikāra).'

This name is designated in the feminine gender (itthilinga). Therefore, in this Pali text, the usage is seen as: 'The Venerable Gotama approaches other families of lay followers in Ukkaṭṭhā,' and in the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, etc.: 'At one time the Blessed One was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā, in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a royal Sāla tree.' Thus, in this word 'Ukkaṭṭhaṃ,' let there be the accusative case (upayogavacana) by the power of the prefix 'adhi-'; but how could that accusative case occur in the remaining words? To investigate this, it is said: 'Tassa anupayogattā sesapadesu.'

In that sentence, 'tassa' refers to the word 'Ukkaṭṭhaṃ' which is joined with the accusative case by the power of the prefix. 'Anupayogattā' means because it is not joined as an adjective (visesana). 'Sesapadesu' refers to the seven words beginning with 'sattussadaṃ.'

The objection as to whether this grammatical usage follows the rules of grammar (saddalakkhaṇa) is dismissed by the statement: 'Tattha... pariyesitabbaṃ.' In that statement, 'tattha' refers to the two types of prescriptions mentioned as the accusative case by the power of the prefix and by the power of connection with the substantive word. 'Lakkhaṇaṃ' refers to the grammatical rule or sutta that is the means of understanding. 'Pariyesitabbaṃ' means it should be sought and grasped by wisdom because it exists in the grammatical treatises.

Thus, it is shown that this grammatical usage indeed follows the rules of grammar. Grammatical experts also desire that: 'When the root √vas is preceded by prefixes such as upa, anu, adhi, and ā, the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used in the sense of the locative (sattamī); and just as the accusative case applies to the substantive word (visesya), it also applies to the adjectives (visesana) that are in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa).' In that regard, when the words 'adhi' and 'ā' are merely prefixes, the accusative case is used with the root √vas preceded by 'adhi' and 'ā' according to the rule 'tatiyāsattamīnañca.'

For that very reason, teachers say: 'The accusative case occurs in the sense of the locative regarding time and direction; when used with the root √vas preceded by upa, anu, adhi, and ā; in the usage of the roots √si (to lie down), √ṭhā (to stand), and √vas (to dwell) preceded by adhi; and in the senses of drinking water or wandering therein.' In the sense of time: 'Having dressed in the morning,' 'At one time the Blessed One,' 'At some time it assists by way of the pre-nascence condition,' 'On this night the four Great Kings.' In the sense of direction: 'King Dhataraṭṭha in the eastern direction.' In connection with the root √vas preceded by prefixes like upa, etc.: 'He dwells near the village (gāmaṃ upavasati),' 'He dwells entering the village (gāmaṃ anuvasati),' 'He dwells facing the village (gāmaṃ āvasati),' 'He dwells presiding over the house (agāraṃ ajjhāvasati).' In the usage of roots √si, √ṭhā, and √vas preceded by adhi: 'He will sleep pressing upon the ground,' 'He stands dominating (as a leader) in the village,' 'He dwells presiding over the village.' In the senses of drinking water or wandering: 'In the river...'
212:
When associated with the roots si (to lie), ṭhā (to stand), and vas (to dwell) preceded by the prefix adhi-, there are expressions such as "he will lie on the ground (pathaviṃ adhiseeti)", "he stands over the village (gāmaṃ adhitiṭṭhati)", and "he dwells in the village (gāmaṃ ajjhāvasati)". In the sense of drinking water or wandering, there are "he drinks in the river (nadiṃ pivati)" and "he wanders in the village (gāmaṃ carati)", etc.

When the word adhi has the sense of lordship (issariya) and the word ā has the sense of limitation (mariyāda), then by the rule "kamma-ppavacanīya-yutte", the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) occurs due to the association with a governing particle (kamma-ppavacanīya). Thus it is said: "Prefixes such as anu and particles such as dhi are called kamma-ppavacanīya. Those which express an action (kiriya) as an object (kamma) are called kamma-ppavacanīya." By which rule does the accusative case occur when the remaining words are connected as adjectives according to grammatical usage? It occurs by the aforementioned rule itself. If it is so, since those words are also a locus (ādhāra), would there not be various loci? No, because many words become a single meaning by virtue of the city. This is because their own meanings (sakatta) merely cause the distinction.

Other grammarians desire this: Adjectives having the same grammatical relation (samānādhikaraṇa) are associated with the verb individually and thus have the same case as the word being qualified (visesitabba). For example, in the phrase "kaṭaṃ karoti, vipulaṃ, dassanīyaṃ", it is considered that the accusative case occurs in the sense of an object because they are individually connected to the verb as "he makes a mat, he makes a large (mat), he makes a beautiful (mat)". This statement should be examined. This is because adjectives having the same grammatical relation do not have a direct connection with the verb. If they were connected with the verb, they would no longer be adjectives.

In this context, ussadatā means abundance; therefore, it is said "populous (bahujanaṃ)". That abundance is shown by "crowded with people (ākiṇṇamanussaṃ)", etc. Because there are animals such as elephants that are caught in the forest and nourished, it is called "posāvanīyā". By this word, the state of those animals being tamed is shown. "Āvijjhitvā" means surrounding. A rectangular pond made by digging is called a "pokkharaṇī", and a reservoir made by constructing an embankment is called a "taḷāka". Aquatic flowers bloom only in places where water is constant; therefore, it is said "always filled with water (udakassa niccabharitāneva)". The word "udakassa" is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental (karaṇa) when associated with the action of filling (pūraṇa). It is like in the passage "having caused large hemp sacks to be made and having caused them to be filled with gold and bullion (hiraññasuvaṇṇassa pūrāpetvā)", etc. Because of the sense "together with grain (saha dhaññena)", it becomes "sadhaññaṃ". It is spoken in the neuter gender in consideration of the word nagara (city). Or, it is spoken in the accusative case in accordance with the sentence. It is the same in all words. In the phrase "pubbaṇṇa-aparaṇṇa-ādi-bhedaṃ bahudhañña-sannicayaṃ", the word ādi includes food items such as gourds and pumpkins which are distinct from those two types of crops. Therefore, this meaning should be understood: here the word dhañña does not only denote specific grains like Sāli rice, but denotes all crops and food items without exception, merely by being good for nourishment.
213:
Or it means it is associated by way of virūpeka-sesa (one remains from different forms). "Ettāvatā" means by the combination of the three aforementioned words. "Rājalīlāya" means by the grace (vilāsa) of kings. "Samiddhi-sampatti" is the prosperity complete with the fullness of internal and external enjoyments.

When "rājabhogga" is said, there is inevitably a question "By which king was it given?"; therefore, it is shown by the words starting with "kena". Another method from the Commentaries is that it is called "rājabhogga" because it is to be enjoyed like a king. Because it was received from the king as a family possession down through the generations of sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, it is called "the king's heritage (rañño dāyabhūtaṃ)". As in the teachings "Monks, be my heirs in Dhamma (dhammadāyādā me bhikkhave bhavatha)", etc., the word dāya is a synonym for dāyajja (inheritance); thus it is said "the meaning is inheritance (dāyajjanti attho)". The objection "How is it called brahmadeyya (noble gift) because of being given?" is resolved by the words "having raised the white parasol (chattaṃ ussāpetvā)", etc. Indeed, there is no enjoyment of gains superior to that which is enjoyed in the manner of a king, which is called brahmadeyya; and this was given in such a manner, therefore it is called brahmadeyya.

"Chejja-bhejja" refers to punishment consisting of physical punishment, fines of wealth, and so on. "Nadī-tittha-pabbata-ādīsu" means at river crossings, at the foot of mountains, at village gates, at the entrance of forests, and so on. By the mention of the white parasol, the remaining royal regalia are also included, as the white parasol is the chief among them.

If it were only said "to be enjoyed by the king", the intended meaning in this context would not be clear; therefore, the word "hutvā" (having become) is included. The intended meaning here is that although the Brahmin Pokkharasāti was not born of the royal line, he gets to enjoy it by becoming like a king. It is called dāya because it is given. While the fact of it being given by the king is already established by the word "rāja-dāya", what is the purpose of saying again "given by King Pasenadi of Kosala"? It is said "for the purpose of indicating the donor king (dāyaka-rāja-dīpanatthaṃ)", etc. The intention is that this is said because the donor king had not yet been indicated as "given by such-and-such a king". In this regard, in the first method, this is said because a question might arise regarding the word "rājabhogga"; in the second method, however, this is said because a question might arise regarding the word "rāja-dāya". This distinction should also be noted.

In the word "Pasenadi", because the food items are so abundant that there is no space to place them in front, rice, curries, and side dishes are also given at the sides (passena); thus he is called Pasenadi by way of an alutta-samāsa (a compound where the case ending is not dropped). Indeed, that king eats even a doṇa of rice with curries and side dishes suitable for it. Thus, having come to the presence of the Teacher after eating his breakfast, he would roll here and there, overcome by drowsiness, and being unable to sit upright, the Blessed One—
214:
“When a foolish person is drowsy and a glutton, sleeping and rolling around like a great hog fed on grain, that dullard enters the womb again and again.” (Dhp. 325). He gave advice with this verse. The King also had a young man, his nephew named Sudassana, learn this verse from the Blessed One: “For a man who is always mindful, knowing the measure in the food he has received, his pains become thin; he ages slowly, guarding his life.” (SN 1.24). He had him recite this verse every day at the time of his final morsel of food while he was eating. Later, the King, reflecting on the meaning of that verse, gradually reduced his final morsels until he was satisfied with just one nāḷika of rice; thus he became slim, strong, and attained happiness. In the Udāna Commentary, however, it is said: “He is called Pasenadi because he conquers (jināti) the opposing army (parasena).” Scholars of grammar also cite this name ‘Pasenadi’ as an example of the letter ‘j’ being transformed into ‘d’. This is because he conquered his nephew King Ajātasattu and the five hundred thieves who were imprisoned. He is called ‘Kosala’ because he is the lord of the Kosala kingdom. Therefore, it should be understood as a gift given by the King named Pasenadi, the ruler of Kosala. It is called ‘Brahmadayya’ here because it was given in the manner of being relinquished and surrendered, not to be taken back again. It was not given merely for royal enjoyment as in the previous method; this is why it says “Yathā,” etc. ‘Nissaṭṭhapariiccattatā’ means giving freely in the sense of relinquishment.

‘Hearing’ (savanaṃ) is shown as ‘attained’ (upalabbho) by the word ‘upalabhī’. That this attainment is knowing by way of hearing is stated as: “He knew according to the sound of the words that reached the ear-door.” In this context, ‘hearing’ means knowing by way of the cognitive process (vīthi) following the ear-door. This is because only through such knowing can the meaning of the words “Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama...” be understood. It does not mean mere hearing by way of the ear-door process alone, because the meaning cannot be grasped by that alone.
215:
It is not just mere hearing through the ear-door process, because the meaning is not grasped by that ear-door process alone. Since the use of words has the benefit of delimitation (avadhāraṇa), all sentences are inclusive of the meaning of delimitation (the word eva). Therefore, even without the word that expresses that meaning, it is understood as ‘he certainly heard’ by way of excluding other meanings. Because it is understood that there was no obstacle to hearing for the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa, the teacher said, “It is a particle (nipāta) merely for filling the verse (padapūraṇa).” In all sentences where delimitation is inherent, the use of the word ‘kho’ is for the purpose of delimitation according to the direct meaning (nītattha). The first alternative was stated because the power of the word ‘eva’ makes this meaning exceedingly clear. As for what benefit there is in delimitation according to the direct meaning, it is said “Tattha,” etc., that it makes the delimitation certain.

Furthermore, the objection “What is the use of the word ‘kho’ if it is merely for filling the verse?” is dismissed with the words “Padapūraṇena,” etc. The meaning is that it serves only the purpose of making the words (groups of letters) and sentences (groups of words) smooth and elegant. When the word ‘kho’ is included, this word ‘assosi’ (he heard) becomes as if it were blossomed, adorned, and beautified, and thus it is called ‘filled’. Because of that word, the preceding and succeeding words become smooth and easy to pronounce. Without it, they would not be smooth. Therefore, even if it is merely for filling the verse, it serves the purpose of making the words and syllables smooth. Here, the word ‘matta’ (merely) has the sense of excluding any special additional meaning. By this, it shows that the word ‘kho’ has no other distinct meaning. However, with the word ‘eva’, the certainty of the smoothness of words and syllables is shown.

The words “Indeed, the ascetic...” etc., are shown to be an illustration of the meaning as heard, starting with “Idāni,” etc. In the term ‘samitapāpattā’ (because of having stilled evil), the meaning should be taken as having stilled evil perpetually and without remainder, along with the latent tendencies (savāsana). Only in this way is the Blessed One’s stilling of evil appropriately distinguished from the stilling of evil by outsiders, those who are not yet free from lust, and those in training (sekha) or beyond training (asekha). Therefore, the teacher said, “The Blessed One has stilled evil through the unsurpassed Noble Path.” To prove that meaning with the text of the Niddesa, he said “Vuttañhetaṃ,” etc. ‘Assa’ means for this monk or for this Blessed One. ‘Samitā’ means ended or brought to a state of tranquility. It means that for this monk or Blessed One, who is the recipient (sampadāna), the evils are stilled. That this designation is in accordance with the meaning in the Blessed One is stated with “Bhagavā ca,” etc. ‘Tena’ means because of thus having stilled evil. It is a name attained through the quality that exists in reality (yathābhūta). This word ‘khalu’ is merely a particle (nipāta), as in the term ‘khalupacchābhattika’; it is not a noun. Since particles have many meanings, here the meaning of ‘report’ (anussavana) is intended; thus the teacher said, “It is a particle in the sense of report.”
216:
In this context, hearing successively from others is called *anussavana* (oral tradition). *Brāhmaṇajātisamudāgata* means one who has come by way of Brahmin birth, or is accomplished by birth. *Ālapanamatta* is just a term of affectionate address, and does not indicate a meaning beyond that address. Indeed, they are accustomed to addressing affectionately as "Bho," "Āvuso," or "Devānaṃ Piya." To clarify the nature of addressing those of Brahmin birth, the teacher said "Vuttampi cetaṃ," etc., citing the *Brāhmaṇavatthu* text of the *Dhammapada* and the *Vāseṭṭha Sutta* verse of the *Sutta Nipāta*.

The meaning in that Pali text is as follows: If one has impediments (*kiñcana*) such as lust (*rāga*), etc., because he wanders about saying "Bho, Bho" in addresses, he is merely a *Bhovādī* (one who says "Bho"), not a true Brahmin who has discarded defilements. The remaining verse "Akiñcanaṃ anādānaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ" should also be understood. In that term *sakiñcana*, defilements like lust are called *kiñcana* (impediments/crushing) because they crush and oppress beings. It is said that when people make oxen tread the threshing floor, they say "Tread, Kapila! Tread, Kālaka!" Therefore, the word *kiñcana* should be understood in the sense of crushing (*maddana*). As stated in the *Mahāniddesa*: "*Akiñcana* means the absence of the impediments of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, defilements, and misconduct. For whom these impediments are abandoned by the Path, calmed by the Fruit, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, such that they are not liable to arise again, he is called *akiñcana*."

"Gotama" is praise by way of lineage (*gotta*). This lineage is also called *Ādiccagotta* (Solar lineage) in the world. "Sakyaputta" is praise by way of birth (*jāti*), and "*Sākiya*" is a synonym for that term "Sakyaputta." In the *Pabbajjā Sutta*, the Blessed One said: "By lineage I am an Ādicca, by birth a Sākiya. Having gone forth from that family, I do not desire sensual pleasures." Therefore, the teacher said, "He praises the Blessed One by way of lineage as Gotama," etc. In this context, it is called *gotta* (lineage) because it protects "*ga*" (speech and knowledge). It means that the meaning of lineage protects the name "Gotama" and the knowledge by being a certain object. Just as knowledge does not exist without an object, so a name does not exist without a named meaning. Therefore, that meaning called *gotta* is said to protect that knowledge and name. Here, the word "*go*" refers to both the name and knowledge.

Wise men say this regarding that fact:
217:
"The word *go* occurs in the senses of cow, sense organ, earth, speech, knowledge, sun, ray, and water. Among these meanings, in the sense of cow, it can be both feminine and masculine; in the other meanings, it is only masculine."

Among those meanings, in phrases such as "*gosu duyhamānāsu gato*" and "*gopañcamo*," the word *go* is used in the sense of a cow. In "*gocaro*," etc., it is in the sense of a sense organ. In "*gorakkha*," etc., it is in the sense of earth. As stated in the *Sutta Nipāta* Commentary on the *Vāseṭṭha Sutta*: "*Gorakkha* means guarding the field, referring to the work of farming. For the earth is called *go*, and a specific part of that earth is called a field." In "*Gottaṃ nāma dve gottāni hīnañca gottaṃ ukkaṭṭhañca gottaṃ*," etc., it is in the sense of speech and knowledge. In the composition of ancient poets, "*Gogottaṃ Gotamaṃ name*," it is in the sense of the sun. It means "I bow to the Buddha Gotama, the kinsman of the sun." In "*uṇhagu*," etc., it is in the sense of a ray. "*Uṇhagu*" means the sun because it has hot rays. In "*gosītacandana*," etc., it is in the sense of water. It means sandalwood that is as cool as the water called *go*. This is because if that sandalwood is placed in boiling oil just taken off the stove, the oil becomes cool instantly. Among these meanings, the word *go* in the sense of a cow can be feminine or masculine as appropriate, but in the other meanings, it is only masculine.

What is this lineage (*gotta*)? It is called *gotta* because it protects knowledge and speech. It should be understood as a general characteristic (*sāmañña-rūpa*) that is not shared with other family lineages, descends from the first person of that family, and is common to all who belong to that family. Because it is common to those belonging to that family, it is a general characteristic. Therefore, even King Suddhodana and others born in that family are called "Gotama." Thus, the Blessed One said to his father, King Suddhodana: "O Gotama, the Tathāgatas are indeed an excellent goal." King Vessavaṇa also addressed the Blessed One: "We bow to the Buddha Gotama, endowed with knowledge and conduct." Venerable Vangīsa said to Venerable Ānanda: "O Gotama, out of compassion, tell me the way to extinguish defilements." In this context, it refers only to the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said, "He praises the Blessed One by way of lineage." The word "*tasmā*" is a review of the three meanings mentioned. Here, with the word "*samaṇo*"...
218:
By this term 'Samaṇa', common people show great affection for the Blessed One. This is because they praise him as one whose unwholesome states are calmed, which is their domain. By this term 'Gotama', famous and prominent people show their affection for the Blessed One. This is because they praise him as one born of a noble lineage, which is their domain.

He is called 'Sakyaputta' because he is the son of the Great King Suddhodana of the Sakyan clan. By this term, his noble birth is shown by praising him as one born into an extremely prosperous and famous royal lineage. From the Great King Mahāsammata, the first of all kings, the Sakyan royal lineage has remained unmixed and most noble. Regarding this, the teachers said in the Mahāvaṃsa:

"The Great Sage is a descendant of King Mahāsammata.
Indeed, at the beginning of the aeon, there was a king named Mahāsammata."

As for why he is shown to have gone forth out of faith—it is said starting with 'kenaci'. 'Pārijuñña' means decline or loss. The meaning is that he went forth without being oppressed or overwhelmed by any kind of loss, such as loss of relatives or loss of wealth. To clarify this same point in another way, it is said, "having left that clan which had not yet declined." 'Not declined' means there was no depletion due to any loss such as loss of relatives or wealth. He went forth solely out of faith. Only in this way is the statement of negation starting with 'kenaci' well-established.

One might object: "Does not the phrase 'Sakyakulā pabbajito' (gone forth from the Sakyan clan) only indicate going forth from a noble family? It cannot indicate going forth out of faith because that meaning is not perceived." It should not be viewed that way. Since he went forth after abandoning a large circle of relatives and a great mass of wealth, the meaning of going forth out of faith is established by implication. In fact, at the time of the Lord of the World's conception, there was no decline in that royal family; rather, there was only growth. Therefore, the extreme prosperity of that clan is well-known in the world. Thus, it should be understood that by merely saying "gone forth from the Sakyan clan," the meaning of going forth out of faith by abandoning such a prosperous family is already established, as explained by "kenaci pārijuññena" and so on.

Furthermore, in the words "while wandering on tour in the Kosala country," the word 'Sādhu' expresses a good meaning, as in the following verses. Therefore, the teacher said "Sundaraṃ kho pana."

"A king who delights in the Dhamma is good.
A man who possesses wisdom is good.
Not betraying friends is good.
Not doing evil brings happiness."

The word 'Kho' is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa). The word 'Pana' is a particle used in the sense of another aspect (pakkhantara). These words are included in the commentary to make their meaningfulness known. Or, 'Sundaraṃ' simply means 'bhaddakaṃ' (good/auspicious).
219:
In this context, the word "Sādhu" has the meaning of "good" (sundara), so it is said "Sundaraṃ kho pana" (Indeed, it is truly good). The word "Kho" is a particle with the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), and the word "Pana" is a particle with the sense of another aspect (pakkhantara). These words are included and explained in the commentary to make this meaning known.

"Sundara" means "auspicious" (bhaddaka). It is called good because it brings welfare and happiness to those who behold it; thus it is said, "bringing benefit, bringing happiness." Here, "Attha" (benefit/welfare) refers to the three types of welfare: welfare in the present life, welfare in future lives, and the ultimate welfare. "Sukha" (happiness) likewise refers to the three types of happiness.

"Tathārūpānaṃ" means "of such a nature" (tādisānaṃ). This is the literal meaning, but to show the general sense, it is said "evarūpānaṃ" (of this nature). The Blessed One is endowed with such qualities; because those qualities are true to reality, he is one who should always be truly revered with faith by the world of beings who are of four measures (pamāṇa). Intending to show that he is endowed with such qualities, it is said "Tathārūpānaṃ arahatāṃ," and to demonstrate this, the passage beginning with "Yathārūpo" is stated.

"Laddhasaddhānaṃ" means those who have gained faith, or those who have gained the faith of others. Alternatively, "Laddhasaddānaṃ" means those who have gained a reputation (fame). By this term, the meaning of "arahantānaṃ" for the word "arahatāṃ" is shown, as well as the fact of being well-known by the name "Arahant."

Furthermore, after showing the meaning of the word "Tathārūpānaṃ" in a general way with the phrase "Yathārūpo so bhavaṃ Gotamo," it is said "those who have gained the reputation of Arahant in the world by attaining true qualities" to show it specifically. This statement also explains the meaning of the word "Tathārūpānaṃ." This is the method intended by the teachers. This is because it is stated in the same way in this sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) and in the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā.

The use of the singular "Yathārūpo so bhavaṃ Gotamo" instead of the plural "Yathārūpā te bhavanto arahanto" is to make known that "Tathārūpānaṃ arahatāṃ" was stated in the plural out of great respect for the Blessed One. This is because experts in grammar (saddavidū) desire the use of the plural when referring to oneself or to persons worthy of respect.

By the words "Yathābhujja... arahatāṃ," it is directly shown that the Blessed One brings inspiration to beings who are measured by the Dhamma (dhammapamāṇa) and those who are measured by austerity (lūkhapamāṇa). This is because the state of being an Arahant is the appropriate object for them. By showing this, it should be understood that it is also shown that he brings inspiration to the remaining beings who are measured by form (rūpapamāṇa) and those measured by sound (ghosapamāṇa), as that inspiration is inseparable from the others.

"Pasādasommāni" means those that are clear and cool, or cool due to clarity. This term shows the state of having a clear mind. Although "dassana" (seeing/beholding) is mentioned, because there is much more to be done beyond that beholding...
220:
Because there is a possibility of something to be done, here [the word api] obtains the sense of commendation (sambhāvanattha). Therefore, it is said: "Even the mere sight is good." Otherwise, it would lead to the undesired meaning: "Only the sight is good, there is nothing more to be done." Here, the word pi has the sense of commendation, or the word api is indicated as being elided. In the phrase "He proclaims the holy life" (brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti), the word iti is connected with the word "renowned" (abbhuggato). Therefore, the word iti in "It is good" (sādhu hoti) here should be connected with the statement "The Brahmin Pokkharasāti addressed the youth Ambaṭṭha." The phrase "having made the intention" (ajjhāsayaṃ katvā) is also an ellipsis (pāṭhasesa), because its meaning can be understood. When the meaning of a text is understood but the word is not explicitly used, it is called an ellipsis (pāṭhasesa). To clarify this meaning, it is said: "Having thus intended that even the mere sight is good." The story of the Kosiya bird, which appears in the commentary to the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, should also be told here.

## Explanation of the Story of the Youth Ambaṭṭha

The word "reciter" (ajjhāyaka) was originally a term of reproach, but later it came to be used as a term of praise. To demonstrate this example, the phrase from the Aggañña Sutta beginning with "a person, a man" (puriso naro) is cited. In that Sutta, those designated by the name "meditators" (jhāyaka) no longer meditated; they did not produce jhāna in their leaf huts, but descended to the vicinity of villages and market towns and remained there composing Vedic texts. Based on their first and second names, known as "Brahmin meditators" (brāhmaṇa-jhāyaka), only the third name "reciter" (ajjhāyaka) arose. Therefore, it is said: "The third name (syllable), namely ajjhāyaka, arose." "Syllable" (akkhara) is a linguistic designation. It is called akkhara because it remains fixed in that specific meaning and does not shift elsewhere. "He recites the mantras" (mante parivatteti) means he chants or learns the Vedas. In this word ajjhāyaka, the euphonic combination (padasandhi) occurs through the power of the root i preceded by adhi-ā. In the other word jhāyaka, it occurs through the power of the root jhe. "He remembers the mantras" (mante dhāreti) means keeping the learned mantras well in mind without confusion.

The Athabbana Veda is a text that should not be used by the virtuous because it involves harming others. Therefore, it is only said: "the Iru Veda, Yaju Veda, and Sāma Veda." Among them, because the deities are praised by it, it is called Iru, by changing the letter ca from the root ic to the letter ra.
221: By the power of the root ic, changing the letter ca to ra, it is called Iru. This word Iru is feminine. Because the deities are worshipped with this Veda, it is called Yaju in the masculine and neuter genders. Because one makes an end with this Veda, or because one thins out evil with it, it is called Sāma, by changing the vowel o to ā in the root so. Because one knows the Dhamma or duty through these texts, they are called Vedas. These same Vedas are called Mantas because they are the means of knowing good destinations and are heard. One is called an "expert" (pāragū) because one has reached the end by moving the lips and mastering the texts. It does not mean reaching the end by clearly perceiving the meaning. The word pāragū is a compound ending in a primary derivative (kitanta-samāsa) which always requires a complement. In the sentence beginning with "together with the Nighaṇṭu" (saha nighaṇṭunā), the definition is shown by way of case endings. Nighaṇṭu is the name of a specific tree. Because it shows meanings such as the Nighaṇṭu tree, it is called Nighaṇṭu. In this text, starting with the synonyms of the Nighaṇṭu tree and placing those synonyms first, the remaining synonyms are shown; therefore, the text is called Nighaṇṭu, similar to the Pārājika-kaṇḍa or Kusala-ttika. This is because the meaning is understood directly through this word. Some teachers, however, say: "Because it divides, analyzes, and shows the meaning to be expressed and the word that expresses it, it is called nikhaṇḍu, and by changing kha to gha, it becomes nighaṇṭu." This should be understood as a method other than the commentarial method. Otherwise, it might contradict the commentary, so it should be considered carefully. Grammarians, however, desire this: "Because the names occurring in various texts are collected here without remainder, it is called nighaṇṭu with the addition of a nasal (niggahīta)." Vevacana-ppakāsaka means a text that explains synonyms. It means clarifying many synonyms for a single meaning. This is just an example; it also shows the expression of many meanings by a single word. Nowadays, these are texts such as the Nāmaliṅgānusāsana, Ratanamālā, and Abhidhānappadīpikā. Because the action characterized by vocal expression is devised by it, it is called kiriyā-kappa. Similarly, because various things are devised by it, it is called vikappa. Combining these two, it is called kiriyā-kappa-vikappa. Because it has many varieties by way of analyzing syllables, words, and word-meanings, it is called kiriyā-kappa-vikappa. It is a text that is beneficial to poets. It is a text that brings about benefits such as the perfection of being a poet and the perfection of wealth for the four types of poets. What is that text? It refers to works on poetics such as the Kavyālaṅkāra and Subodhālaṅkāra. This kiriyā-kappa refers to the original Kiriyā-kappa text. That text is extensive, containing about one hundred thousand verses. Teachers also call it the Nayacariya text. Because it makes known the analysis of actions according to its etymology, it is called Ketubha. Or, because it completely encompasses and perfects the analysis of actions, it is called Ketubha. Or, because poets attain skill in poetic composition through this text, it is called Ketubha. In this etymology, as in the previous method, it is shown in the masculine and neuter genders. Because it distinguishes syllables by way of the places of articulation, the instruments of articulation, and analytical definitions, that text is called Akkharappabheda.
222:
## Meaning
What is this treatise? It refers to works such as the Kavyālaṅkāra and Subodhālaṅkāra, which establish the methods of poetic composition. This statement is made with reference to the Mūlakiriyākappa treatise. Indeed, that work has a vast scope, consisting of one hundred thousand verses; it is also called the 'Nayacariyādi-pakaraṇa'.

In terms of etymology, it is called 'Keṭubha' because it makes known (kiṭayati) the distinctions of actions (kiriya) and so forth. It is formed from the root 'kiṭ' with the suffix 'abha', and the vowel 'a' is changed to 'u'. Alternatively, it is called 'Keṭubha' because it illuminates or completes (obheti/pūreti) by grasping without remainder the distinctions of actions and so forth. This is derived by the power of the root 'ubha' preceded by the word 'kiṭ'. Furthermore, it is called 'Keṭubha' because through it, wise poets attain (gacchanti/kiṭanti) skill in compositions. The formation of the word here is the same as in the previous method.

It is called 'Akkharappabheda' (Classification of Letters) because letters are classified through the analysis of the places of articulation (ṭhāna) and instruments (karaṇa), and through the analysis of etymological definitions (nibbacana). Intending that this Akkharappabheda consists only of the two treatises included among the six limbs of the Veda (Vedāṅga), it is said: "Sikkhā and Nirutti."

Among those two, it is called 'Sikkhā' because the conventions of letters are learned (sikkhanti) through this treatise. It is the science that explains the places of articulation (ṭhāna), instruments (karaṇa), and efforts (payatana) of the letters beginning with 'a'. 'Nirutti' means speaking with certainty or without remainder. It is characterized by the addition of letters, the metathesis of letters, and so forth.

And it is said:
"Addition of letters, metathesis of letters,
And the other two: transformation and elision of letters,
Connection with the excellence of the root's meaning—
These are said to be the fivefold Nirutti."

In this context, however, 'Nirutti' is intended as the treatise that illustrates etymological definitions in many ways through the power of those factors like 'vaṇṇāgama', by dropping the latter word (uttarapada-lopa). This is intended because teachers have stated that the classification of letters also exists through the analysis of etymological definitions, and because, apart from that classification of letters, the analysis of etymological definitions is included within the limb of grammar (byākaraṇa). Indeed, grammar and Nirutti are each separate limbs of the Veda. As teachers have said:

"Kappa, Byākaraṇa, Jotisa, Sikkhā, Nirutti,
And Chandoviciti—these are said to be the six limbs of the Veda."

Therefore, in this context, etymological definition is intended according to the method of Nirutti, which is unmixed with the limb of grammar. It should be understood that the etymological definition common to both, as in the case of the six types of syllables (vyañjanapada), is not intended here because this is the domain of the limbs of the Veda. This is the decision on the method of Nirutti as found in the Mahāniddesa Commentary.

I shall further elaborate on that decision. Among those five methods of Nirutti, the arrival of a letter that was not previously present—such as the arrival of the letter 'r' in the word "nakkhattarājāriva"—is called 'vaṇṇāgama' (addition of letters). The reversal of existing letters, such as when "hiṃsa" (one who harms) is changed to "sīha" (lion), is called 'vaṇṇavipariyāya' (metathesis of letters). The transformation of one letter into another—such as the letter 'a' becoming 'e' in the passage "navakammantike dāni dissanti"—is called 'vaṇṇavikāra' (transformation of letters). The disappearance or destruction of existing letters—such as the elision of the letters 'va' and 'na' in the word "jīmūta" instead of "jīvanamūta"—is called 'vaṇṇanāsa' (elision of letters).
223:
This is the decision on the method of Nirutti as it has come down. In elaborating thus: the arrival of a new letter that was not previously present—such as the arrival of the letter 'r' in the phrase "nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ"—is called 'vaṇṇāgama'. The reversal of existing letters, such as when "hiṃsa" (because of the meaning 'to harm') is reversed to "sīha", is called 'vaṇṇavipariyāya'. The transformation of one letter into another—such as the letter 'a' changing to 'e' in the phrase "navachannakedāni diyyati"—is called 'vaṇṇavikāra'. The disappearance of existing letters—such as the elision of the letters 'va' and 'na' in "jīmūta" instead of "jīvanamūta"—is called 'vaṇṇanāsa'. In the verse, "Pharusāhi vācāhi pakubbamāno, āsajja maṃ tvaṃ vadase kumāra," the word "pakubbamāno" is explained as "abhibhavamāno" (overpowering/oppressing); such presentation of a special meaning as appropriate in various instances is called 'yoga' (connection with the excellence of the root's meaning).

Among the three Vedas of the aforementioned classifications, this Itihāsa treatise should be the fourth. If so, one might ask with which treatise it becomes the fifth; thus it was said, "making the Athabbaṇaveda the fourth." The Athabbaṇaveda refers to the mantras composed by those proficient in the Atharvaveda which cause harm or death to others. That Athabbaṇaveda is included here merely for the sake of counting, to clarify that the Itihāsa treatise is the fifth, and not by way of its actual substance. Therefore, the meaning of the word "etesaṃ" (of these) should be taken as referring only to those three Vedas. This is because that word is an adjective for "tiṇṇāṃ vedānaṃ" (of the three Vedas). "Iti ha asa" means "Thus indeed it was in this world." In some versions, the reading is "āsa," but the meaning is the same. In this context, it can also mean "desire this action" or "desire this object" in this manner. The use of the repetitive (vicchā) word here is to indicate the vast scope of that treatise. It is shown that the treatise connected with this phrase "itihāsa" is called 'Itihāsa' by the power of the taddhita (derivative) suffix. Teachers also say that the treatise connected with such words as "iti ha āsa, iti ha āsa" is called 'Itihāsa' according to the method of Nirutti. Grammarians (akkhara-cintaka), however, prefer this: the word "itiha" is a single indeclinable (nipāta) meaning traditional instruction. That which exists is called "asa." Because traditional instruction exists in this treatise, it is called 'Itihāsa' by the power of compound (samāsa). In their view, the phrase "iti ha asa" means that such traditional instruction was clearly present. By the phrase "known as ancient stories," the special nature of that Itihāsa treatise is meant. These include the story of the battle between the two brother kings named Bharata, the story of the abduction of Queen Sītā from King Rāma, the story of the appearance of King Narasīha, and so forth.
224:
The texts known as ancient lore, such as the Bhārata-purāṇa, Rāma-purāṇa, Narasiha-purāṇa, etc., are meant by the term "Itihāsa" (History/Epics). By the phrase "of the Vedas, with Itihāsa as the fifth", it shows the status of an adjective here for "of the three Vedas" in accordance with the sentence.

It is called a "pada" (word) because it is the means of knowing the meaning. It is a word ending in an inflection (vibhatti) which has many divisions such as noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), prefix (upasagga), and particle (nipāta). Since that word also appears in the science of grammar, it is said "tadavasesaṃ" (the remainder of that). It means the sense of linguistic characteristics such as roots (dhātu) and suffixes (paccaya) which remain from the word. It is called "Vyākaraṇa" (Grammar) because it explains various words and their meanings through this text. Alternatively, it is called Vyākaraṇa because roots, suffixes, etc., are specifically produced in this text (or by this text). It refers to the grammatical treatises that are still extant today, such as the Mugdhabodha-vyākaraṇa, Sārassata-vyākaraṇa, Pāṇini-vyākaraṇa, Candra-vyākaraṇa, etc., which correctly explain proper words. "Adhīyati" means studying (ajjhāyati). "Vedeti" means teaching others (vāceti). The word "ca" has the sense of connecting two meanings, or it has an alternative (vkappa) sense because another meaning is specifically considered. The Taddhita-vutti (derivative formation) is diverse.

"Padaka" is said with reference to proficiency in words as they appear in grammatical treatises. "Veyyākaraṇa" refers to proficiency in the linguistic rules of the remaining roots, suffixes, and so forth. To make this meaning known, the two words are defined together. It is the nature of teachers to make another meaning known by some means. This is another method from the Commentary: he is called "Padaka" because he recites those very Vedas word by word. Therein, "word by word" means by way of prose (gajjabandha) and verse (pajjabandha) words. "Recites" is spoken like the word "Jātaka". By this word, the ability to compose Vedic texts is shown. By showing this, the distinction of this "Padaka" from terms like "Ajjhāyaka" becomes clear.

It is called "Lokāyata" because the world, known as the foolish, does not strive for future welfare through this text. Depending on that text, beings do not even give rise to the thought of performing merit. Or, it is called Lokāyata because the foolish strive in this text due to the relish of its doctrines.
