It is called "Vitaṇḍā" because it spreads views that are mutually contradictory or contradictory to heaven and liberation, by virtue of the suffix "-ḍa" and by changing the letter "n" to "ṇ". Or, it is called Vitaṇḍā because it strikes opponents with the stick of contradictory doctrine, by virtue of the root "taḍi" and by the addition of the niggahīta (nasalization). Even though it is not a proper basis, the doctrine of disputants arises depending on a certain text; that text is figuratively called their basis. For example—
225:
'In the world, the eye is of a lovable nature, of a pleasant nature. Here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; when ceasing, it ceases.' Alternatively, it is called 'Vitaṇḍa' because it specifically shakes or agitates the minds of the wise through this text. Because they speak that Vitaṇḍa text, they are called 'Vitaṇḍavādīs'. Or, because they hold that doctrine, they are called 'Vitaṇḍavādīs'. Their text is also like that.

A treatise that illustrates marks (lakkhaṇa) is shown as 'Lakkhaṇa' (Marks) by the elision of the latter word or by the power of a derivative suffix (taddhita), as in 'Lakkhaṇadīpaka' (Illustrator of Marks). It is called 'Lakkhaṇa' because the state of a Buddha, etc., is marked by it. Examples include having a body as round as the circumference of a banyan tree, etc. Therefore, it is said, 'by the power of which marks,' and so on.

In the phrase 'having the extent of twelve thousand ganthas,' just as in the measurements of bhāṇavāras, etc., a 'gantha' consisting of thirty-two syllables is intended. Indeed, it is said:
'Eight syllables make one foot (pāda). Four feet make one verse (gāthā). One verse is known as one gantha. One gantha consists of thirty-two syllables.'
The meaning is the extent of one thousand thirty-two-syllable ganthas multiplied by twelve (12,000).

'Yattha' means in which treatise on marks. As in the phrase 'a branch on a tree,' this locative case (sattamī vibhatti) is in the sense of a locus (ādhāra). Adding 16 and 1,000 makes 16,000. It means it has the extent of 16,000 verses. Only by taking the meaning in this way will the usage of locus (ādhāra) and the located (ādheyya) be properly fulfilled. Because they primarily illustrate the marks of Buddhas, they are called 'Buddhamanta' (Buddha-mantras). Indeed, the marks of Paccekabuddhas, etc., are also illustrated in that text. Therefore, it is said, 'by the power of which marks,' and so on.

'One who performs completely without deficiency' is just a demonstration of the meaning. To show the meaning obtained through the word itself, it is said 'avayo na hoti' (he is not an 'avaya'). The question 'What is this avaya?' is dismissed by the phrase 'avayo nāma,' etc. The intention here is: he who is able to maintain those texts is called 'vaya'. He who is unable is called 'avaya'. One who is not an 'avaya' is 'vaya' itself, according to the logic that 'two negatives result in the original meaning' (dve paṭisedhā pakatiyatthagamakā). He is called 'vaya' because he maintains (vayati). The meaning is that he carries and uses those texts in his continuity (santāna) without becoming weary or hesitating at any point—beginning, middle, or end.

This is the method of the Vinaya Commentary: 'Anavayo' is 'anu' + 'avayo'. By the power of euphonic combination (sandhi), the letter 'u' is elided. Because he is repeatedly not deficient, he is 'anūna' (not less), meaning one who has complete skill. 'Vaya' means decline (hāni), as in 'āyavaya' (income and expenditure/decline). Since there is no decline (ūnatā) in the aforementioned texts for him, he is called 'avaya'. Because he is repeatedly not deficient, he is called 'anavaya'.
226:
The words beginning with "Ācariyena" are spoken to show the meaning of the word "Anuññāto" in the sense of the passive object (kamma-sādhana) and the word "Paṭiññāto" in the sense of the active agent (kattu-sādhana). "Assa" refers to the youth Ambaṭṭha. In the Pāḷi, the statement "What I know, you know" shows the manner of permission (anuññānana), while the statement "What you know, I know" shows the manner of acknowledgment (paṭijānana); this is shown by the words beginning with "Yaṃ ahaṃ". "Āma ācariya" (Yes, teacher) is the word of acknowledgment as it appears in the Pāḷi, spoken according to its meaning. "Yaṃ" refers to the scripture (pāvacana) endowed with the three Vedas (tevijjaka). "Tassa" refers to the teacher. The mere acknowledgment of the teacher's words is called a promise (paṭiññā); the meaning is that by such acknowledgment, he himself has promised. The words beginning with "Sake" show the basis for permission and acknowledgment. Although it is not a physical location, the words beginning with "Katarasmiṃ" are spoken merely by way of conceptualizing it as a location. One's own property is called "sakaṃ". That which has come down through a lineage of teachers is called "ācariyakaṃ". The collection of the three Vedas is called "tevijjakaṃ". The principal words, or the well-known words of sages such as Aṭṭhaka, are called "pāvacanaṃ".

Now, to clarify the intention with which the Brahmin Pokkharasāti addressed the youth Ambaṭṭha and spoke the words beginning with "Ayaṃ tāta", the words beginning with "Esa kira" are spoken. In that context, "Uggatassa" refers to the ancient people who were already famous in the past. "Bahu janā" (many people) is spoken with reference to Pūraṇa Kassapa and others. "Ekaccaṃ" refers to a person of noble birth such as a Khattiya, or someone esteemed by the world. "Garū" means a heavy matter. It is meant that it is difficult enough just to free oneself and depart from that heavy state; what need is there to say anything about doing more than that? "Anattho" refers to the blame, harassment, oppression, etc., that arise from such departure.

In the word "Abbhuggato", because of its connection with the prefix "abhi", the accusative case is used in "Gotamaṃ" in the sense of describing a particular state (itthambhūtākhyāna). In the words "Taṃ bhavantaṃ, tathā santamyeva", the accusative case is also used because of the influence of that prefix "abhi", as shown by the words beginning with "Tassa bhoto". Therefore, the words beginning with "Idhāpi" are spoken. "Tathā satoyeva" means that just as the report of his fame has spread by way of his qualities such as being an Arahat, the report of that Venerable Gotama has spread because he truly exists in that manner. Furthermore, the connection of the same meaning twice as "Taṃ bhavantaṃ Gotamaṃ tathā santamyeva" is for the purpose of making known a specific meaning by conceptualizing general and specific attributes. Therefore, after separating it as a general connection (sāmañña-sambandha) as "Tassa bhoto Gotamassa", then "Tathā... (text is cut off).
227:
The word "Satoyeva" should be construed as a specific connection (visesa-sambandha). Here, the word "yadi" has the sense of doubt (saṃsaya) because both meanings are to be doubted. The word "vā" also has the sense of an alternative (vikappa) because one of the two is to be chosen as an alternative. However, grammarians say that in instances such as "Whether this person's word is true or false," both "yadi" and "vā" are used only in the sense of an alternative. This is because the word "yadi" is seen in the sense of "vā" in passages such as "Whatever assembly he approaches, whether an assembly of Khattiyas or an assembly of Brahmins." As in the passage "Life is short, a hundred years; it exists now and at this time," here too, words of similar meaning are used together. In the Pāḷi, the words "Yadi vā no tathā" should also be connected with the words "Santamyeva saddo abbhuggato" and construed in the same manner as mentioned above.

If there is an objection that the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) should only apply to the word "Gotamaṃ" and not here, the words beginning with "Idhāpi" are spoken. It means that either because the prefix "abhi" is not directly connected, or because it should be construed as a specific connection after being separated, the accusative case here is also by virtue of the sense of "itthambhūtākhyāna". "Itthambhūtākhyāna" refers to the prefix "abhi" having the meaning of expressing the attainment of a certain specific quality; or, it simply means that "itthambhūtākhyāna" is the meaning. For if there is a connection with the word in one respect, there is also a connection with the meaning in that same respect.

"Bho" is an address to one's own teacher. The words beginning with "Yathā sakkā" are spoken to make the word "yathā" meaningful and to connect it with the rest of the text. "So" refers to the Blessed One. In the previous method, because of the connection with the word "yathā" which clarifies the manner (ākāra), it was merely a question as "kathaṃ" (how?); but here, because it is not so connected, it is called an "inquiry into the state" (ākāra-pucchā). Since it is customary in non-Buddhist traditions to address a teacher as "upajjhāya", it is said "Atha naṃ upajjhāyo"; the meaning is the Brahmin teacher who is designated as a preceptor.

Although there are actually three types of Vedas—Manta, Brahma, and Kappa—the principal root text spoken by sages such as Aṭṭhaka is the "Manta". The text for the purpose of explaining the meaning of that Manta is the "Brahma", and the text showing the procedure for performing sacrifices according to the methods stated therein is the "Kappa". Since the Manta is the principal one and the others arise only in dependence on it, the inclusion of the Manta also establishes the inclusion of the Brahma and Kappa; this is shown by the words "Tīsu vedesū". For "Manta" is the name only of the original Veda spoken by sages like Aṭṭhaka, while "Veda" is the name for the whole. Therefore, by saying "Vedesū", the inclusion of everything is completed.
228:
When it is said "in the Vedas," it should be understood that the inclusion of all Vedic texts is also accomplished. "Marks" (lakkhaṇāni) refers to the Vedic passages that indicate the marks of a Great Man. By means of inserting them into verse and prose arrangements. "Only in the guise of a brahmin" means only in the guise of a brahmin who teaches the Vedas. "In the Vedas" refers to the Vedas that show the marks of a Great Man. Thinking, "Wise beings of great merit will know," they teach and pass them down; this is the connection. Because of such teaching and passing down, "formerly" means from the time it was said "The Buddha will arise" until the time the Buddha was alive. They come down and become manifest as subjects to be recited and taught. They gradually disappear by way of one verse, two verses, and so on. It is not only the Vedic texts on the marks that disappear; indeed, other Vedas also gradually disappear due to the ignorance of the brahmins—so says the Teacher.

Aspiration for Buddhahood is called paṇidhi. The accumulation of the perfections is called samādāna. Wisdom such as that of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā) is called ñāṇa. The Teacher said, "The word 'great' (mahanta) should be applied to each, as in 'great by way of aspiration,' 'great by way of undertaking,' and so on." This being so, faith, virtue, and so on, starting with compassion, are called "compassion etc." (karuṇādi). These qualities themselves are the virtues. Because he is great through aspiration, undertaking, wisdom, and the virtues of compassion etc., the definition should be made as "great in the virtues of aspiration, undertaking, wisdom, compassion, etc." (paṇidhi-samādāna-ñāṇa-karuṇādi-guṇa-mahanta). Thus, the word "great" placed after the compound (dvanda) is applied to each member. Alternatively, the meaning is well-established by the definition "great through the virtues of aspiration, undertaking, wisdom, compassion, and so on." The greatness of that Great Man's aspiration and so forth should be understood by way of the Buddhavaṃsa, Cariyāpiṭaka, etc. In the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary, however, it is said: "'Of the Great Man' (mahāpurisassa) means of the man who is great by way of birth, lineage, family, region, and so on." Among those, "Kshatriya, Brahmin," etc., is called birth (jāti). "Koṇḍañña, Gotama," etc., is called lineage (gotta). "Poṇika, Cikkhallika, Sakyan, Koliyan," etc., is called family (kula). All of these should be understood as included here by the word "and so on" (ādi). This being so, the statement common to both—"There are only two destinies"—is substantiated.

"Perfection" (niṭṭhā) means completions or successes. If it is asked, "Since this word gati has many meanings, why is it mentioned only in the sense of perfection?" the Teacher says, "Granted that this..." and so on.
229:
"Distinction of existence" refers to specific existences such as hell. That specific existence is called gati (destiny) because it is reached by beings through the power of rebirth according to their good and bad deeds. It is called gati because it occurs or spreads in this place; it means a dwelling place (nivāsaṭṭhāna). It is called gati because one knows according to the true nature; it means wisdom (paññā). Pervasion (byāpana) is called gati; it is the state of being spread out. That pervasion is simply the state of remaining spread out from here to there. Completion (nipphattana) is called gati; it means the end or perfection (niṭṭhā). The meanings of intention (ajjhāsaya) and refuge (paṭisaraṇa) are also taken by way of illustration.

This is indeed true: in the passage, "I do not know the coming (āgati) or the going (gati) of these virtuous monks of good character," it occurs in the sense of intention (ajjhāsaya). In the passage, "Nirvana is the gati of the Arahant," it occurs in the sense of refuge (paṭisaraṇa), final resort (parāyaṇa), and support (apassaya). It is called gati because it occurs according to one's wish; it is intention (ajjhāsaya). It is called gati because it occurs or moves in this Nirvana; it is refuge (paṭisaraṇa). For the Arahant who is disconnected from all conditioned things, Nirvana alone is the refuge. Here, however, it should be understood that it occurs in the sense of perfection (niṭṭhā), because it is not the domain of others.

Are not the marks that are the causes of the two completions (Buddhahood and Universal Monarch) dissimilar? Nevertheless, why is their similarity mentioned in such phrases as "to one endowed with these marks"? To show a slight objection and then clear it up, he said, "Even though it is so," and so on. To show that even though marks like the roundness of a banyan tree (nigrodhabimbatā) are similar, there is indeed some distinction in those marks, it is said, "He does not become a Buddha by those marks alone." The Elder Dhammapāla explained this distinction: "Just as the marks of the Buddhas are very clear, very distinct, and complete, it is not so for Universal Monarchs." Although meanings differ, the non-different cognition and word arise because of this nature; thus it is called jāti (genus/class); it is merely the state of being a mark. It is said:

"In different things such as a brindled cow, that nature by which non-different cognition and words occur is called jāti. This jāti follows through (all instances) like a thread in a garland."

Therefore, because they are similar merely by being marks, even though they are dissimilar, those very marks which are the causes for the completion of a Universal Monarch are treated as if they were similar, and this statement is made calling them the marks which are the causes for the completion of a Buddha. When the root vas is combined with the prefixes adhi and ā, the accusative case is used in the sense of location (bummattha); thus it says, "he dwells in the house" (agāre vasati). "By the four marvelous things" refers to these four marvelous powers (iddhi): being very handsome, being long-lived, being free from illness, and being beloved and pleasing to brahmins and householders. As the Blessed One said:
230:
“Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with four powers. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was handsome, pleasant to look at, and inspiring confidence,” and so forth, as stated in (DN 2.252).

Taking the method found in the Cetiya Jātaka (JA. Aṭṭha. 3.8.44), they also say: “The scent of sandalwood wafts from his body; this is the first power. The scent of the blue lotus wafts from his mouth; this is the second power. Four young deities, holding swords, provide protection in the four directions at all times; this is the third power. He travels through the sky; this is the fourth power.”

In the Anāgatavaṃsa Commentary, however, it is said: “Being handsome is the first power; being endowed with a balanced digestive heat (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) is the second power; being such that the entire world of beings never tires of looking at him for as long as he lives is the third power; and the ability to travel through the sky is the fourth power.”

In that context, “being endowed with a balanced digestive heat” means the perfection of the fire element born of kamma that digests food evenly. Indeed, for one whose food is digested immediately after eating, or for one whose food remains just as it was, like a bag of rice, both are not endowed with balanced digestion. Only for one whose desire to eat arises again at the next mealtime is said to be endowed with balanced digestion; this is the meaning of having such a nature.

“By the bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu)” refers to these means of integration: giving (dāna), kindly speech (piyavacana), useful conduct (atthacariyā), and impartiality (samānattatā). As the Blessed One said:

“Giving, kindly speech, 
Useful conduct here in this world,
And impartiality in various matters as is appropriate;
These bases of sympathy in the world
Are like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
If these bases of sympathy did not exist,
A mother would not receive honor or worship 
Because of her son, nor would a father because of his son.
Because the wise observe these bases of sympathy 
With equanimity, they attain greatness 
And become worthy of praise.” (DN 3.273).

“Because of pleasing” means pleasing by way of joy and satisfaction (pīti-somanassa), not by way of lust (rāga); it means generating joy and satisfaction. The name “Rājā” (King) is the common designation for all kings because of the sense of pleasing others through the four bases of sympathy, even for those who do not actually do so.
231:
Just as the term ‘tālavaᅁᅡa’ (palm-leaf fan) is used for bamboo fans and others by way of convention (ruᄷhġ), it should be understood that the specific definition ‘endowed with wonderful qualities’ is stated here as an extraordinary derivation not shared by other kings. To show the various meanings of the word ‘Cakkavatti’ (Wheel-turning Monarch) through the power of the term, the primary meaning is shown first by saying ‘cakkaratana’ (wheel-treasure) and so forth. This is indeed the primary meaning because one cannot attain the status of a Cakkavatti without the occurrence of the wheel-treasure. Thus, it is said in the commentaries: ‘By what measure does one become a Cakkavatti? When the wheel-treasure rises into the air even by one or two finger-breadths and revolves.’ (DA 2.243, MA 3.256). Since the Cakkavatti king, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, lifting a golden pitcher shaped like an elephant's trunk with his left hand, and sprinkling the wheel-treasure with water with his right hand, says, ‘Roll forth, O Wheel-treasure! Conquer, O Wheel-treasure!’ (DN 2.244), and causes the wheel-treasure to rise into the sky and revolve, it is said ‘he turns the wheel-treasure’ (cakkaratanaᅃ vatteti) with reference to such a turning. As it is said: ‘Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana, rising from his seat... sprinkled the wheel-treasure, saying ‘Roll forth, O Wheel-treasure!’ and so forth (DN 2.244).

Furthermore, the word ‘cakka’ (wheel) does not only apply to the wheel-treasure, but also to the wheels of fortune (sampatti-cakka) and others. Therefore, the meaning is also shown through the power of the word ‘cakka’ as expressing those various meanings by saying ‘sampatti-cakkehi’ and so forth. In that sentence, ‘by the wheels of fortune’ refers to the four wheels of fortune taught in the Aᅃguttara Nikāya (AN 4.31):

‘Living in a suitable locality, associating with noble friends,
Being endowed with right self-aspiration, and having performed merit in the past;
Grain, wealth, fame, glory, and happiness follow this person.’

‘Vattati’ means it occurs, it is accomplished, or one attains higher and higher wholesome states. ‘Tehi’ means by those wheels of fortune. ‘Paraᅃ’ refers to the multitude of beings. Just as the word ‘sayaᅃ’ (self) indicates the sense of a pure agent, the word ‘paraᅃ’ should be understood to indicate the sense of a causative agent. ‘Vatteti’ means he causes to occur, he causes to be accomplished, or he causes others to attain higher and higher wholesome states. As it is said for evidence: ‘King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: ‘Living beings should not be killed, what is not given should not be taken, sexual misconduct should not be practiced, false speech should not be spoken, intoxicants should not be drunk, and eat as you have eaten (continue your livelihoods as before).’’

‘Iriyāpatha-cakkānaᅃ’ refers to the wheels that are the postures. In places such as ‘four wheels, nine doors,’ the postures are also called wheels. In the Abhidhānappadġpikā, the Elder Moggallāna stated: ‘The word ‘cakka’ occurs in the sense of a chariot wheel, a mark on the feet, the wheel of Dhamma, a weapon-wheel, a posture, a wheel of fortune, the wheel-treasure, and a circle.’
232:
Ananda, in the eastern direction, whatever rival kings there are, those kings have become followers of King Mahāsudassana. (That king admonishes: 'One should not kill living beings, one should not take what is not given, one should not practice misconduct in sensual pleasures, one should not speak false speech, one should not drink intoxicants; consume only the taxes as they are normally collected'), and so forth, as taught (in the Mahāvagga Pāḷi of the Dīgha Nikāya).

'Iriyāpathacakkānaṃ' means the wheels which are the postures. This is because in sentences such as 'four wheels, nine doors,' the posture is also called a 'wheel.' How is this so?
'The word "cakka" (wheel) occurs in the sense of a chariot part (wheel), a mark (on the feet), the Dhamma-wheel, a circular blade (razor) at the chest, a posture, success (sampatti-cakka), the wheel-treasure, a circle, an army, a potter's wheel, the wheel of authority, a weapon-wheel, and a collection of gifts,' as stated (in the dictionary).

'Vatto' means occurrence (pavattana, uppajjana). By this word 'vatto,' the definition 'one who causes the wheel of postures to occur (uppādeti) for the benefit of others' is also shown, as they are identical in meaning. Thus it is also taught: 'Ananda, then the wheel-treasure rolled towards the eastern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed the wheel-treasure together with his fourfold army. Ananda, in whatever place the wheel-treasure stopped, there King Mahāsudassana took up residence with his fourfold army,' and so forth, as taught (in the Mahāvagga Pāḷi of the Dīgha Nikāya).

This is another method from the Commentary: He is called 'Cakkavattī' (Wheel-turning Monarch) because he sets in motion the wheel known as unobstructed authority. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch endowed with five qualities sets the wheel in motion by righteousness alone; that wheel cannot be turned back by any human enemy. What are the five? Here, bhikkhus, a wheel-turning monarch is a knower of the meaning (atthaññū), a knower of the Dhamma (dhammaññū), a knower of moderation (mattaññū), a knower of the right time (kālaññū), and a knower of the assembly (parisaññū). Endowed with these five... cannot be turned back by living beings,' and so forth, as taught (in the Aṅguttara Nikāya).

He is also called 'Cakkavattī' because he brings the wheel known as the assembly of kings (khattiyamaṇḍala) under his own control. For it is said: 'Ananda, those rival kings in the eastern direction became followers of King Mahāsudassana,' and so forth, as taught (in the Mahāsudassana Sutta). The wheel-mark (cakkalakkhaṇa) occurs for him, therefore he is called 'Cakkavattī.' Thus it is said: 'Your Majesty, on the soles of the feet of this prince...'
233:
...on the soles of the feet, wheels have appeared with a thousand spokes, with rims, and with hubs, complete in every respect,' and so forth, as taught (in the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Mahāvagga, Dīgha Nikāya). Great physical strength like a wheel occurs for him, therefore he is called 'Cakkavattī.' For it is said: 'Your Majesty, this prince has flesh that is full in seven places... Your Majesty, this prince has a torso like the front half of a lion,' and so forth. By that mark, the state of great strength of this child is known. Alternatively, he is called 'Cakkavattī' because he practices the duty (vatta) known as the wheel, which has ten or twelve aspects. Thus it is said: 'Dear son, the divine wheel-treasure is not a paternal inheritance of yours. Come, dear son, practice the noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch (ariya-cakkavatti-vatta),' and so forth, as taught (in the Cakkavatti Sutta). He is also called 'Cakkavattī' because he sets in motion the great wheel of giving. Thus it is also taught:

'Ananda, King Mahāsudassana established such a gift on the banks of those lotus ponds: food for those desiring food, drink for those desiring drink, clothing for those desiring clothing, vehicles for those desiring vehicles, beds for those desiring beds, women for those desiring women, silver for those desiring silver, and gold for those desiring gold,' and so forth, as taught (in the Mahāsudassana Sutta).

The name 'Rājā' (King) is a general name because it is shared with other kings. The name 'Cakkavattī' is a specific name because it is not shared with other kings. The word 'Dhamma' occurs in the sense of the proper way (ñāya), and only suitability is called 'ñāya'; therefore, it is said 'with the proper and suitable way.' 'Vattati' means it occurs, or it is practiced. Although it is not specifically said 'he practices such and such a practice,' because it is shown generally without being fixed in a specific sense, and because a teacher desiring a specific sense must apply a specific sense, it is applied as 'for one's own benefit and the benefit of others.' If a part is not taken, the state of having no remainder of the meaning to be taken is known, for example, as in saying 'the shaven-headed one does not give.' Because a wheel-turning monarch attains kingship only by righteousness, and not by unrighteousness such as harming others, it is said 'having obtained kingship by righteousness,' and so forth. 'By righteousness' (dhammena) means by the proper way or by wholesome Dhamma. The state of being a king is 'rajjaṃ,' which is indeed sovereignty (issariya).

He is called 'Dhammika' because he performs or practices the Dhamma which is the means for the benefit of others. He is called 'Dhammarāja' because he is a king who performs or practices the Dhamma which is the means for his own benefit; this specific meaning is shown by 'or by performing the Dhamma for the benefit of others,' and so forth. This is the method of the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary: He is called 'Dhammika' because he is devoted to the ten types of wholesome Dhamma, or to the kingly duties (rāja-dhamma) free from bias. By that same Dhamma...
234:
He is called the King of Dhamma (Dhammarājā) because he makes the world rejoice. These two terms (Dhammika and Dhammarājā) are essentially the same in a figurative sense. However, the Teacher (the sub-commentator) stated: "He is called 'Dhammika' because he practices the Dhamma known as the duties of a Universal Monarch, or because that Dhamma exists in him. He is 'Dhamma' because he does not deviate from the Dhamma, and he is 'Rājā' (King) in the sense of pleasing (the people); therefore, he is called the King of Dhamma (Dhammarājā)" (Dīgha Nikāya Ṭīkā 1, 258).

According to the words "He becomes a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti)," the term "Cāturanta" clarifies the state of being the sovereign of the four great islands; thus, it was said "Cāturantāya," and so on. The earth is called "Cāturantā" because it has the four oceans as its boundaries. This is said because the earth, in all four directions, ends at the four oceans, such as the eastern ocean. Therefore, it is said, "having the four oceans as its boundaries." This earth is shown to be the very earth adorned with the four types of islands as its parts, which is included within a single world system (lokadhātu), by the phrase "the earth adorned with the four types of islands." As it is said:

"As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters,
All beings dwelling on the earth are but servants of King Mandhātu."
(Mandhātu Jātaka).

In this context, the word "vidha" (type/kind) is included in the phrase "adorned with four types of islands" instead of just saying "adorned with four islands" in order to include the five hundred small islands associated with each great island. This should be understood either because the extra meaning is understood through the extra word, or because the word "vidha," which denotes a portion, includes similar parts. In the term "kopādipaccatthike," the word "ādi" (and so on) includes lust (kāma), delusion (moha), conceit (māna), and pride (mada). The word "vijeti" (conquers), although used in the present tense in consideration of that time, means "has conquered." Grammarians desire the suffix "tāvī" for the past tense. In saying "he conquers all kings," although a Universal Monarch has no need to fight any enemy, he is described as "one who has won the battle" (vijitasaṅgāmo) because he has achieved the kind of victory that is normally accomplished through battle.

The state of being firm and stable is called "thāvariya." To show how stability is attained in the realm, it was said "no one is able," and so on. By this, the Tappurisa compound is shown as "one who has attained stability in the realm" in the sense that no one can shake him. Alternatively, it shows the Aññapadattha compound as "the realm in which stability has been attained exists in that king" because of his firm faith. "Tamhi" means in that king. To reveal how the realm attains stability in that king, it was said "anuyutto," and so on. There, "anuyutto" means constantly engaged. "Devoted to his own duties" means always engaged in the royal duties of a Universal Monarch...
235:
The two terms "acalo" (unshakable) and "asampavedhī" (unwavering) are synonyms (pariyāyavacana). Alternatively, he is "acala" because he is not moved by mere robbery by thieves, and "asampavedhī" because he is not violently shaken by plunder. Or, he is "acala" because of thieves and "asampavedhī" because of rival kings. Or, he is "acala" because he is not excessively soft, and "asampavedhī" because he is not excessively harsh.

Indeed, when an excessively harsh king oppresses the world with taxes, punishments, and so on, people abandon the central districts and live in the borderlands, relying on mountains, seashores, and the like. Under an excessively soft king, people who are oppressed by the plunder of thieves and violent men abandon the borderlands and come to live in the central districts. Thus, when there is such a king, the realm cannot reach a state of stability. However, when a king who is free from both extremes and has reached a state of balance like a golden scale governs the kingdom, the realm becomes unshakable and unwavering, reaching a state of stability as if placed on a stone slab and surrounded by iron plates.

"Seyyathidaṃ" is a single indeclinable (nipāta). It is used according to the appropriate gender, case, and number, such as "so katamo," "taṃ katamaṃ," "sā katamā," and so on. In this context, it is used in the sense of "what are those?" and therefore it was said "tassa cetāni," and so on. It is called a wheel (cakka) because it revolves all around to travel through the air and other paths according to the Universal Monarch's wish. The Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) revolves by the power of the internal air element (vāyodhātu) immediately upon the command of the Universal Monarch; it does not revolve by the power of the external air element like the mansions of the moon and sun, as stated in the Vimānavatthu Commentary. It is called a jewel (ratana) in the sense of producing delight (rati). Because of its wonderful nature, great joy and pleasure (pīti-somanassa) arise in those who see or hear of that jewel. According to the etymology (vacanattha), it is called "ratana" because it causes delight (rameti). Or, it is called "ratana" because it brings delight (rataṃ neti). Or, according to grammarians, it is called "ratana" because it produces delight (rataṃ janeti), with the letter 'ja' being elided. This meaning applies in all cases, such as the elephant-jewel and others.

The status of the wheel as a jewel should also be understood through its being highly esteemed (cittīkata), and so on. However, that meaning is not taken separately because it is included within the sense of producing delight. Why is it included? Because being highly esteemed is also a cause for delight. Alternatively, it should be understood that meanings such as "cittīkata" were not included because of a desire to avoid verbosity in the text. In other commentaries, it is stated as follows—
236:
It is called a jewel (ratana) because it generates delight (rati). Alternatively, it is called a jewel because it is highly esteemed, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and used by noble beings.

From the moment the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) appears, there is no other place of worship (shrine); all people offer scents, flowers, etc., and perform acts of homage and salutation to it alone; thus, it is a jewel in the sense of being highly esteemed. The Wheel-treasure cannot be valued at a specific amount of wealth; thus, it is a jewel in the sense of being of great value. The Wheel-treasure is unlike other jewels existing in the world; thus, it is a jewel in the sense of being incomparable. Since Universal Monarchs (cakkavatti) arise only in those aeons where Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only once in a long while, it is a jewel in the sense of being rare to behold. This [treasure] arises only for a noble being of great merit through birth, appearance, family, and power, and not for anyone else; thus, it is a jewel in the sense of being used by noble beings. As with the Wheel-treasure, so it is with the others.

In this regard, the clarification of meaning according to the method stated in the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) and elsewhere is as follows: This statement beginning with 'highly esteemed' (cittīkata) is not made by way of grammatical derivation, but rather how? It is spoken in terms of the state of being worthy of great respect, as is recognized in the world for an object called a 'jewel'. In terms of its nature, it should be understood as gold, silver, etc., recognized by worldly people; the Wheel-treasure, etc., that arises for a Universal Monarch; grateful and appreciative persons; and the Triple Gem—the Buddha, etc.—which is the most supreme. It is called 'cittīkata' because it should be placed in the heart (citta) with the thought, 'Oh, how captivating!' This placing in the heart is due to its worthiness of worship; thus, they say it means 'worthy of worship'. Some teachers say it is 'cittīkata' in the sense of being 'variegatedly made' (vicitrakata), but that should not be accepted here because the word 'citta' refers to the heart, as in the explicitly stated Pali passage: 'Listen to me, having placed [this] in your heart (cittīkatvā)'. Thus, grammarians have said: 'The vowel i is appropriately added to the roots bhū and kar'. However, in places such as 'Behold the form made variegated (cittīkata) with gems and earrings', the meaning should be taken as 'cittīkata' because what was previously not variegated is now made variegated. In that context, the word 'citta' means variegated. It is called 'mahaggha' because it is worth a great, vast, and immeasurable price. It is called 'atula' because there is no comparison or analogy for it. Because it arises only once in a while...
237:
...it is called 'dullabhadassana' (rare to behold) because it is seen only with difficulty. It is called 'anomasattaparibhoga' because it is to be used only by beings of noble and grand qualities.

Now, having shown the specific presence of these meanings like 'highly esteemed' in the Wheel-treasure, the passage beginning with 'As with the Wheel-treasure' is started to extend those meanings to the other [treasures]. In that context, there is no other place of worship (shrine) because it is the cause for the King to obtain the fortune of sovereignty, etc., which is not shared with others, and because it is the cause for other beings to obtain their desired benefits. There is no [fixed] price because it is an exceedingly grand and radiant jewel, and because of its marvelous and wonderful nature. To the extent that it is of great value, to that same extent it is incomparable. A time that is suitable for the arising of a Buddha is one where beings, through their loathing of evil, are free from stains and, being devoted to merit, are like the cream [of society]; in such a time alone is the appearance of Universal Monarchs possible. Therefore, it is said: 'Since, however...' and so on. 'Kadāci karahaci' is a synonymous expression. Alternatively, 'kadāci' is said in reference to the aforementioned time, and 'karahaci' refers to the place known as the island of Jambudīpa. Thus it is said:

'Having observed these five—
the time, the island, the country,
the family, and the mother—
the Great Renowned One is born.'

This is spoken by way of an analogy. The simile and the thing compared are not entirely identical. Therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: just as Buddhas arise only once in a long while, Universal Monarchs do not [arise exactly like that]; rather, Universal Monarchs can arise many times even in an aeon where a Buddha arises. Even so, because fulfilling the duties of a Universal Monarch is difficult, their arising is indeed rare. Thus, by this commonality of being rare to arise, it should be understood that they are said to be rare to behold. Granted, the quality achieved through the power of the Wheel-treasure is shared with the retinue of the Universal Monarch; nevertheless, the Universal Monarch alone deserves to be called its user due to his mastery and intimacy, as it arises for his benefit alone. To show this, the passage beginning with 'This [treasure]...' is said. Because the aforementioned five or six meanings are also found in the remaining jewels, it is said: 'So it is with the others'.

For what purpose does the Universal Monarch enjoy these jewels? Could there not be a Universal Monarch without any of them? To address such an objection, the passage beginning with 'Among these, however...' is started to clarify the state of being inseparable from any [of the treasures] by showing how he enjoys the benefits of those jewels as appropriate. In the eastern direction, etc., which is not yet conquered...
238:
The Universal Monarch conquers all unconquered kings because of the results of kamma that lead to great majesty. By mounting the elephant treasure and the horse treasure, through their power, he can travel around the entire earth bounded by the ocean within the time of a morning meal and return to the royal capital; thus, he can travel comfortably as he wishes. Through the counselor treasure (pariṇāyaka-ratana), he protects the conquered territory. This protection is possible because the counselor manages and carries out the necessary duties in various matters. With the remaining gem treasure, woman treasure, and householder treasure, he enjoys the pleasures of the senses as appropriate. This is because those treasures enable the fulfillment of such enjoyment. That Universal Monarch, by means of the gem treasure, dispels darkness in an area of one yojana and enjoys the happiness of seeing light, and so forth. By means of the woman treasure, he enjoys happiness such as seeing a form superior to that of humans. By means of the householder treasure, he enjoys happiness by obtaining wealth such as gems, gold, and silver as he desires.

Now, to clarify the aforementioned meaning through power and the fruit of power, the words beginning with "Paṭhamena" are said. Kings possess three kinds of power because they are able to achieve things through these powers. As the teachers have said:

"There are three powers: Majesty (pabhāva), Effort (ussāha), and Counsel (manta).
Majesty is the splendor arising from punishment; and Patāpa is that arising from the treasury.
Counsel is consultation; that which involves two people is 'four-eared' (catukkaṇṇa).
That which involves three people is 'six-eared' (chakkaṇṇa); a secret is called 'guyha'."

Among those three, the power of energy is called the power of effort (ussāha-satti). For that Universal Monarch, the association with this power of effort is perfected by the first treasure, the wheel treasure. Why? Because through that wheel treasure, the state of having irresistible authority, which is to be exercised through the power of effort, is accomplished. The power of wisdom is called the power of counsel (manta-satti). The association with this power of counsel is perfected by the last treasure, the counselor treasure. Why? Because that counselor treasure is skilled in all royal affairs and has an unerring application of effort, just like being endowed with the power of counsel. The mastery through discipline and wealth is called the power of dominance (pabhū-satti). For that Universal Monarch, the association with the power of dominance is perfected by the elephant, horse, and householder treasures. Why? Because of the great majesty of the elephant and horse treasures, and because the accomplishment of the perfection of majesty is achieved through the wealth of the treasury obtained from the householder treasure. It should be connected that the fruit of being endowed with the three kinds of power is perfected by the woman treasure and the gem treasure. All the fruits that are to be obtained from being endowed with the aforementioned three kinds of power...
239: For that Wheel-turning Monarch, the association with the final Counselor-gem (pariṇāyakaratana) is complete with the power of counsel (mantasatti). Why is it complete? Because that Counselor-gem is skilled in all royal duties, he is complete with the power of counsel, as well as being endowed with unerring effort. The ability to accomplish through discipline and possession of wealth is called the power of sovereignty (pabhūsatti). For that Wheel-turning Monarch, the association with the Elephant-gem, the Horse-gem, and the Householder-gem is complete with the power of sovereignty. Why is it complete? Because of the great majesty of the Elephant and Horse gems, and because of the abundance of treasury and wealth obtained from the Householder-gem, they reach the fulfillment of power. It means that through the Woman-gem and the Jewel-gem, the benefit of being endowed with the three powers—the power of sovereignty, the power of effort (ussāhasatti), and the power of counsel—is fulfilled. Why is it complete? Because only through those powers can the happiness of wealth to be enjoyed be accomplished. To clarify the aforementioned meaning through the two kinds of happiness—the happiness of wealth (bhogasukha) and the happiness of sovereignty (issariyasukha)—he said, "That king, with the Woman-gem and the Jewel-gem..." and so on. The happiness of wealth (bhogasukha) refers to the happiness that arises through the power of enjoyment by keeping [the gems] nearby. "With the remaining gems" means with the five gems starting with the Wheel-gem, which remain after the Woman-gem and the Jewel-gem. The happiness that arises through the power of having no opposing enemies is called the happiness of sovereignty (issariyasukha). Now, to clarify that these seven gems always arise together without being separated from one another through the power of the causes of their fulfillment, he said "Specially" and so on. "By the majesty of kamma born of the wholesome root of non-hatred" means that (the Elephant and Horse gems, etc.) become complete due to the majesty of kamma produced through the power of the conascence condition (sahajātapaccaya), etc., along with the wholesome root called non-hatred (adosa); this is because they are of a type of gem that is exceedingly pleasant. Indeed, the fruit of kamma usually resembles the kamma that produced it. The middle gems—the Jewel-gem, the Woman-gem, and the Householder-gem—become complete through the majesty of kamma born of the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); this is because they have the cause of fulfillment in generosity (dāna), which is the cause of possessing noble wealth and obtaining noble wealth. The final Counselor-gem (pariṇāyakaratana) becomes complete through the majesty of kamma born of the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha); this is because only a Counselor-gem with great wisdom can carry out all the affairs of a Wheel-turning Monarch, and because the possession of great wisdom is the result of kamma born of the wholesome root of non-delusion. "Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta" refers to the Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta, which is the second [collection] in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi. "Of the Ratana Sutta" refers to the second Ratana Sutta recited in the fifth chapter (vagga) of that Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta. "Upadesa" is the method that arises through the power of investigating and analyzing the seven gems in detail. They are called "sūra" (valiant) because they are a refuge and because they conquer and destroy opposing enemies; it means those who have courage and those who bring safety. Therefore, he said, "Those who are by nature fearless." Because he stands having conquered the Asuras, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, is called "Dhīra"; because he is a limb (a member) of Sakka's army, a son of the devas (devaputta) is called "aṅga"; those whose bodies are like the limb (the son of the devas) of the Dhīra (Sakka) are called "dhīraṅgarūpā"; therefore, he said, "Those whose bodies are like the sons of the devas." "Some teachers" refers to the teachers named Sārasamāsa; the commentator, not accepting their words, said, "But in this matter, it is thus," and so on. "Sabhāva" means the meaning that is the nature [of a thing]. "Noble sūras" refers to noble warriors. Here, the word "sūra" denotes the meaning of a warrior. In this way, this method is more distinctive than the previous one; they also say, "The word sūra has a noble meaning," and the text "Noble ones are called sūras" is also found. "Of the vīras" means of those who possess energy (vīriya). "Aṅga" means a cause (kāraṇa); it is said with the consideration that "by this cause, the result is known." That very energy because of which they are called "dhīra" is itself called "dhīraṅga" (the cause of being a dhīra).
240:
The teacher says by the word 'nāma', "it means effort (vīriya)." 'Rūpa' refers to the body. Therefore, it is said, "as if having bodies made of effort." Just like the word 'dānamaya', effort itself is called 'vīriyamaya'. Therefore, it means "as if having bodies known as effort." Since effort is not literally a physical body, the word 'viya' (as if/like) is used. Alternatively, to show the meaning of 'dhīraṅga' (limb of wisdom/courage) which arises through the factor of effort, it is said "as if having bodies made of effort." Even so, the word 'viya' shows that it is not a physical body literally produced from effort. Or else, it should be construed that 'dhīraṅga' is their body and 'vīriya' is its nature; even then, the phrase "as if having bodies made of effort" indicates that what is called effort has no distinct physical form. Here too, the word 'maya' should be seen in its own sense. Therefore, it means they are like effort that has a distinct physical form. This means: if effort were to have a distinct physical form, those sons would be just like that effort. This is the meaning accepted by the teacher (Dhammapāla).

In the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary, however, it is said: "Because the factor of effort (dhīraṅga) is their body, they are called 'dhīraṅgarūpā'; they are of the nature of effort, made of effort, and are untiring; it means they do not get exhausted even if they fight all day." This should be understood as being said with reference to the natural meaning of the word 'rūpa'. In this place and some other places, the reading "dhitiṅgarūpā" is also found. This is because the word 'dhiti' also expresses the meaning of effort (vīriya), as in the Jātaka verses: "Truth, Dhamma, steadfastness (dhiti), and generosity; he who has these overcomes the enemy." In some places, only the reading "vīraṅga" is found. One may take whichever is preferred.

To resolve the objection: "Since there is no opposing army for the Universal Monarch to suppress, why is it said 'crushers of enemy armies' (parasennappamaddanā)?", the teacher says "If," and so on. Whether there is an enemy army or not, this is said merely by way of supposition—"if there were one"—to show that those sons possess such power and majesty. Even though it is said "crushers of enemy armies," it should be understood as "those capable of crushing enemy armies." This is because the specific meaning can be understood from the context. Just as in the word-analysis of the phrase, "Monks, a monk who is training (sikkhamānena) should know, should inquire, should investigate," the word 'training' (sikkhamānena) is taken to mean 'desiring to train' (sikkhitukāmena). To show this meaning, it is said "those capable of crushing that army." Those sons do not remain constantly crushing enemy armies, but they are simply those capable of crushing them.
241:
they are. Likewise, it should be understood accordingly in other instances as well. Some teachers also say that it shows the meaning "parasennappamaddanā" because they are capable of crushing the enemy army.

To show the Dhamma known as 'payogasampatti' (attainment of application), which is the cause for the long-lasting fruition of the meritorious Dhamma accumulated in previous lives and currently ripening, the teacher explains the meaning of the word 'dhammena' as "by the Dhamma of the five precepts, such as 'one should not kill living beings', etc." This meaning is stated with reference to the Universal Monarch’s Dhamma of instruction found in passages such as: "Ānanda, the rival kings in the eastern direction approached King Mahāsudassana and said: 'Come, Great King! Welcome, Great King! This is your kingdom, Great King! Please instruct us, Great King!' King Mahāsudassana said: 'Living beings should not be killed. What is not given should not be taken. One should not practice misconduct in sensual pleasures. Falsehood should not be spoken. Intoxicants should not be drunk. Consume only the taxes as they have been traditionally consumed.' Ānanda, the rival kings in the eastern direction became followers of King Mahāsudassana." If explained this way, the qualifying words 'adaṇḍena asatthena' (without the rod, without weapons) are also well-established. This same meaning is also stated in other commentaries such as the Suttanipāta Commentary.

In the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary, however, it is said: "'Adaṇḍena' means that those kings who seize hundreds or thousands of guilty beings are said to rule by the rod of wealth (fines). Those who instruct by mutilation of limbs, etc., rule by the rod of weapons. But this Universal Monarch, having abandoned both kinds of rods, dwells without a rod. 'Asatthena' means that those kings who harm others with weapons such as single-edged swords are said to rule by weapons. But this Universal Monarch, without causing even as much blood as a small fly might drink to flow by a weapon, conquers the earth in the manner described—his arrival being accepted by rival kings with the words 'Come, Great King'—and dwells having overcome it and becoming its master by Dhamma alone." This statement is made with reference to the meaning of the word 'dhammena' as "by any meritorious Dhamma accumulated in the past and currently ripening." For it is only because of that meritorious Dhamma that his arrival is accepted by rival kings...
242:
It is said, “Having conquered the earth, he dwells ruling over it.” The sub-commentary teacher, Venerable Dhammapāla, also stated (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.258) that “dhammena” means by the merit (puñña-dhamma) that one has performed and accumulated. Indeed, urged by that merit, all the kings living on the earth bounded by the four oceans come forward to welcome him and, saying such things as “Welcome to you, Great King,” they hand over their respective kingdoms to the Cakkavatti King. Therefore, by the statement, “That Cakkavatti King, having conquered this earth bounded by the oceans without punishment and without weapons, dwells ruling over it by righteousness (dhamma),” the aforementioned meaning is also shown. Thus, it should be understood that both meanings are appropriate in this context. Just as it is impossible to rule in this way solely by past merit without the fulfillment of effort (payoga-sampatti) such as fulfilling the duties of a Cakkavatti King, it is also impossible solely by the fulfillment of effort without past merit.

Having thus explained one accomplishment, the following words beginning with “Sace kho pana” are spoken to explain the second accomplishment. Wishing to show the obscure meaning in those words, he said the passage beginning with “In this context of ‘Arahaṃ... pe... Vivaṭṭacchaddo’.” The seven evil qualities (pāpadhammā) such as lust (rāga) arise in the world; and when they arise, they cover and envelop the continuities of beings, preventing the occurrence of wholesome states. Therefore, he shows that these qualities are called by the name “chadda” (veil/cover) in this context with the words beginning with “rāgadosā.” Misconduct (ducarita) refers to the three types of misconduct along with mental misconduct other than wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). Wrong view, however, is taken separately because it especially covers beings and because it is extremely blameworthy. And it is said (Dī. Ni. 1.146): “All those are caught within the net of these sixty-two grounds; even while emerging, they emerge only within this net.” Similarly, non-knowledge (aññāṇa) is spoken of in two ways according to the difference in the mode of occurrence: as delusion (moha) in the sense of being bewildered, and as ignorance (avijjā) in the sense of making things unknown. Indeed, its sense of covering is stated in both ways: “When delusion overwhelms a man, then there is dense darkness” (Mahāni. 5, 156, 195), and “The world is enclosed by ignorance; it does not shine because of stinginess and negligence” (Su. Ni. 1039; Cūḷani. Pārāyanavagga, 2). In this same way, the sense of covering for lust, hatred, etc., should also be stated. In the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.33), however, seven evil qualities are taken by way of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, defilements, and craving. Among those, greed (lobha) itself is spoken of in two ways according to the difference in the mode of occurrence: as lust (rāga) in the sense of being attached, and as craving (taṇhā) in the sense of desiring. Indeed, its sense of covering in both ways is absolute. As the Blessed One said: “When lust overwhelms a man, then there is dense darkness,” and “Blinded by sensual pleasures, covered by the net of craving, obstructed by the veil of craving...”
243:
“...enveloped by the veil of craving” (Udā. 94); and by the inclusion of defilements (kilesa), the remaining factors such as doubt (vicikicchā) are also mentioned.

The phrase “covered by the seven” is a statement containing the cause (hetu). It means that in the world which is darkness by the power of defilements, one is covered by the seven evil qualities. “That veil” refers to the veil known as the seven unwholesome qualities. “Having opened” means having made it open, having removed it. That same meaning is stated in another way as “having become one who has light produced all around.” The absence of the veil of defilements is itself the light (the light of wisdom). By this, it is “vivaṭṭa” because it should be removed, and it is “chadda” because it covers or conceals; thus, the meaning is shown that this Blessed One is “vivaṭṭacchadda” or “vivaṭṭacchadā” because the veil of defilements has been removed by Him.

This word “vivaṭṭacchadda,” like the words “daḷhadhamma” and “paccakkhadhamma,” can be either ākāranta (ending in -ā) or okāranta (ending in -o) by the power of the masculine gender. Because of this, it is said in the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary: “He is ‘vivaṭṭacchaddo’ because the veil and obstruction known as lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, defilements, and craving have been destroyed and opened by Him; there is also the reading ‘vivaṭṭacchadā,’ which has the same meaning” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.33). In the Līnatthappakāsanī sub-commentary to that commentary, it is also said: “‘Vivaṭṭacchadā’ is a designation made by changing the letter ‘o’ to the letter ‘a’.” Grammarians, however, say that by the rule “ādhanvādito,” the suffix “ā” sometimes occurs after words like “dhanu” at the end of a compound, and they cite examples such as “kaṇḍivadhanvā,” “paccakkhadhammā,” and “vivaṭṭacchadā.”

To resolve the inquiry as to why these three terms are spoken, he said the passage beginning with “Tattha” using the method of Hetālaṅkāra (ornament of cause). “Tattha” means among those three terms. By the meaning that He is worthy to receive special offerings, the state of being worthy of offerings is stated as “Arahaṃ.” Because He is the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), He is worthy of offerings; thus, the cause for that worthiness of offerings is stated. Because of the state of having previously abandoned all defilements along with latent tendencies (vāsanā), the state of being one who has removed the veil (vivaṭṭacchadatā), which is the cause for Buddhahood, is stated. The threefold round (vaṭṭa) by way of kamma etc., and the sevenfold veil (chadda) by way of lust etc., are called “vaṭṭacchadā.” He is “vivaṭṭacchaddo” or “vivaṭṭacchadā” because He is free from that round and veil, or because the round and veil have been removed for that Blessed One. The prefix “vi-” preceding the dvanda compound should be applied to both the word “vaṭṭa” and the word “chadda”; to show this meaning, it is said: “vivaṭṭo ca vicchado ca” (both free from the round and free from the veil).

Teachers also say this: “He is vivaṭṭacchaddo because He is both vivaṭṭa (free from the round) and vicchada (free from the veil)...”
244:
The commentator explains the meaning as "the elision of the preceding word in the subsequent word." The statement "He is called Arahaṃ because of the absence of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa)" is said with reference to the meaning of "Arahaṃ" as being far from defilements, having killed the enemies which are defilements, having broken the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, and having no secret place for doing evil. This statement shows the inference of the cause from the effect (phaleṇa hetānumāna). For example, just as fire is known by smoke, or as rain falling above is known by the flow of water. In this sense, the state of being "Araha" (worthy of special offerings) is the cause (hetu), and the absence of the three rounds of rebirth is the effect (phala); this is the view of the teacher (the sub-commentator).

However, it could also be an inference of the effect from the cause (hetunā phalānumāna), such as "because of being worthy of special offerings like the four requisites." For example, just as smoke is known to arise because of fire, or the flow of water is known to arise because of rain falling above. The statement "He is called Sammāsambuddha because of the absence of covering" is an inference of the effect from the cause. This is because the state of being a Sammāsambuddha is fundamentally based on the absence of covering, which is all defilements along with their latent tendencies (vāsanā). Indeed, the absence of covering occurs through the Path of Arahantship, and the state of being a Sammāsambuddha occurs through Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). These two terms, "vivaṭṭa" and "vicchada", are two causes. According to the teacher's view, in the inference of the cause from the effect, being free from the three rounds (vivaṭṭatā) is only the effect. However, because it is the cause for the inference of the cause and for that Omniscience, it should be understood as the cause (hetu) itself.

Having thus shown the benefit of stating the three terms through the method of causal ornament (hetvalaṅkāra), the teacher now speaks the words beginning with "Dutiyena", wishing to show it also by the power of the Four Grounds of Self-Confidence (Catu-vesārajja). In that context, "by the second Vesārajja-ñāṇa" refers to the second one in the order taught by the Blessed One: "Monks, there are these four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets the supreme Wheel of Dhamma in motion," and so on. (It refers to) the ground of self-confidence described as: "Monks, I do not see any ground on which any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me, saying: 'While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not destroyed in you.' Monks, seeing no such ground, I abide attained to security, attained to fearlessness, and attained to self-confidence." "The accomplishment of the meaning of the preceding word" means the accomplishment of the state of being worthy of special offerings, which is the meaning of the preceding word "Arahaṃ." Since the second Vesārajja has that meaning, it is meant that the meaning is accomplished by that Vesārajja. Indeed, the second Vesārajja stated as "While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed..." is exactly the meaning of the word "Arahaṃ" stated as "because of being far from defilements," and so on. Therefore, it is understood that just as the meaning of the preceding word is accomplished by the second Vesārajja...
245:
...the accomplishment of the meaning of the preceding word (Arahaṃ) by the second Vesārajja, likewise, the accomplishment of the second Vesārajja by the preceding meaning should be understood. By doing so, showing the benefit in stating the three terms (Arahaṃ, Sammāsambuddho, Vivaṭṭacchado) by the power of the four grounds of self-confidence according to this method is appropriate. Otherwise, as there would be no purpose, this statement should not be made here. This method should be applied to the remaining terms as well.

"By the first" (Paṭhamena) refers to the first ground of self-confidence according to the method already mentioned: "I do not see anyone who could say to you, who claims to be perfectly enlightened, 'These things are not fully understood by you'... I abide." "The second accomplishment" (Dutiya-siddhi) means the accomplishment of the meaning of the second word "Sammāsambuddho," the accomplishment of Buddhahood. This is because that Vesārajja-ñāṇa is the meaning of that word. "By the third and fourth" (Tatiya-catutthehi) refers to the third and fourth grounds of self-confidence according to the same method: "I do not see anyone who could say, 'Those things called obstructive things, though one indulges in them, they are not capable of being an obstacle'... I abide," and "I do not see anyone who could say, 'The Dhamma taught for that purpose does not lead the practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering'... I abide." "The third accomplishment" (Tatiya-siddhi) means the accomplishment of the meaning of the third word "Vivaṭṭacchadā." This is because the Blessed One's state of being a Vivaṭṭacchada (one who has drawn back the veil) becomes evident through those grounds of self-confidence. The teacher stated, "By the teaching of the true obstructive things and the emancipating things, the Blessed One's state of being a Vivaṭṭacchada became evident in the world." Since the teaching of obstructive and emancipating things is accomplished by the very state of being a Vivaṭṭacchada, it is also appropriate to say, "The third and fourth meanings are accomplished by the third Vesārajja-ñāṇa."

Having thus shown the benefit of stating the three terms by the power of the four grounds of self-confidence, the teacher now speaks the words beginning with "Purimañca," wishing to show it also by the power of the three eyes (cakkhu-ttaya). In that context, the word "ca" has the sense of introduction. The first word "Arahaṃ" accomplishes the Dhamma-eye (Dhamma-cakkhu), which is the knowledge of the three lower paths and fruits of the Blessed One. This is because it shows the state of having killed the enemies which are defilements and having broken the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra. The second word "Sammāsambuddho" accomplishes the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu), which is the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the degrees of maturity of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa). This is because those knowledges can only arise in a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha. These two knowledges do not occur in disciples (sāvaka) or Paccekabuddhas. The third word "Vivaṭṭacchadā" accomplishes the All-seeing eye (Samanta-cakkhu), which is the knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). This is because it shows the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies. Stating "Vivaṭṭacchadā" after stating "Sammāsambuddho" clarifies the abandonment of all defilements with latent tendencies for the sake of the state of being a Sammāsambuddha. The statement "Dear Ambaṭṭha, I am a giver of the Vedas" is secondary; only the statement "You are a receiver of the Vedas" is the primary word of encouragement.
246:
The teacher, with the words "You are a receiver of the mantras," instills in Ambaṭṭha a sense of courage regarding the mantras. This means instilling courage characterized by clear knowledge in explaining the marks (lakkhana).

In the phrase "Evaṃ bho," the word "evaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in acceptance of a statement. Here, acceptance of the statement refers to the proper reception of the words of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, which were: "In that manner, we shall know the Venerable Gotama; you are also a receiver of the mantras." The words beginning with "Tassattho" also show this same meaning. Thus it is said, "Having accepted the words of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti." To show that the young man Ambaṭṭha spoke because he saw the mantras describing the Buddha's marks clearly, without confusion, due to his teacher's encouragement, the text says "Sopi," etc. There, "tāya" means "by that aforementioned encouragement," as stated by the teacher. Currently, in the manuscripts, the reading "tāya ācariyakathāya" (by that teacher's talk) is seen. In meaning, there is no contradiction. For a talk that arouses mindfulness regarding the mantras is called encouragement (samuttejanā).

"Ayānabhūmi" means a place that is not a ground for a vehicle, a place where a vehicle cannot go; it means having gone near the gatehouse.

Because the meaning of a word spoken in general should be specifically understood according to the extent of the Commentary, it says "at the time of midday." Having stated the first method according to the general practice of all monks, the second method is stated according to the specific practice of those who are foremost in meditation. "Divāpadhānika" means those monks who are devoted to meditation during the day; it means they walk in the cloister in this manner to practice the Dhamma of a recluse during the day. Therefore, it says "For such [monks]," etc. To clarify Ambaṭṭha's intention in approaching, thinking, "It takes a long time for one coming from one precinct to another; I will enter only after asking," the text says "So kira," etc.

One born in a well-known family is called "Abhiññātakolañña." Although the Ambaṭṭha family was not well-known in the past, as will be explained later, it was well-known at that time; therefore, it says "At that time," etc. "Rūpajātimantakulapadesehi" means by the four—appearance, birth, mantras, and family—which are the reasons for pointing out, "This person is of such a nature." Which...
247:
Those monks reflected; to make their intention clear, the words beginning with "Yo hi" were spoken. To show that it is a statement spoken with reference to a specific meaning understood particularly, even though spoken generally, it says "with reference to the Gandhakuṭi." In other such instances, it should be understood in this same way.

"Aturito" means going without haste (slowly and steadily). Although there is a variant reading "aturanto," the meaning is the same. To answer how one enters without haste, the words beginning with "Saṇikaṃ" were spoken. In that context, "padappamāṇaṭṭhāne" means in a space the size of a fist-length between the two feet. The Sinduvāra (chaste tree) is a type of flowering tree; it has white flowers and is also called "Nigguṇḍီ." "Pamukhaṃ" means the front (porch) of the Gandhakuṭi chamber. To complete the statement "near the keyhole," the words beginning with "The door, indeed" were spoken.

By the words "those who are giving gifts," it shows the door opening by itself due to the power and influence of the perfections (pāramī).

In the phrase "They exchanged greetings with the Blessed One," the word "saṃ," which has the sense of "together/harmoniously," indicates the meaning to be inferred: the joy that first arose in the Blessed One along with those youths. To show this, the words beginning with "Yathā" were spoken. Indeed, the Blessed One also, by asking "O youths, is it bearable? Is it supportable?" etc., experienced joy that arose from the very first words spoken with those youths. "Samappavattamodā" means they had a blending (rejoicing) that arose harmoniously by following the Blessed One's words. To show that meaning with a simile, the words beginning with "Like cool water" were spoken. In that context, the Blessed One should be understood as being like cool water because his fever of defilements is completely extinguished; the youths should be understood as being like hot water because their fever of defilements is not yet extinguished. "Sammoditaṃ" means blending or harmonizing. Here, the word "muda" is used only in the sense of blending, not in the sense of delight; only by taking the sense of blending will the aforementioned simile be complete. Because that is true, the explanation "ekībhāvaṃ" (becoming one) was spoken. It means the state of being similar or of one nature in the act of blending.

"Khamanīya" (bearable) is an inquiry: "This machine of the body, which has four wheels (postures) and nine openings, is naturally difficult to bear due to the abundance of suffering; can that suffering be borne (are you healthy)?" "Yāpanīya" (supportable) means: "Can you support yourself through the maintenance called long-term endurance, which is dependent on requisites such as food?" "Appābādha" (free from illness) means being free from diseases like headaches. "Appātaṅka" (free from distress) means being free from a miserable livelihood. "Lahuṭṭhāna" (lightness in rising) means having the comfort of being able to rise up in performing various duties. "Bala" (strength) means possessing strength suitable for that rising. "Phāsuvihāra" (dwelling in comfort) means having the benefit of living happily. In every instance, the meaning should be understood by connecting the word "kacci" (is it?).
